# JOUST: the full documentation

> JOUST: write Cardano smart contracts in Java as state plus actions. The same method runs on chain and off; JOUST generates the validator and a typed client on cardano-client-lib. Also .jsc, and JavaScript (experimental).

Source: https://joust.julc.dev/ (generated 2026-11-24)

## Start here

### Why JOUST

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/start/why-joust/

JOUST (State Contract Simplified, pronounced "jowst") lets you write a Cardano smart contract as a **state record plus pure
static methods**, much as you would write an account-based contract. From that one class it generates the on-chain
validator and a typed off-chain client. The same Java method runs in both places: on your machine to build the
transaction, and on chain to check it.

##### The problem: a contract is three programs

Cardano uses the extended UTxO model (eUTxO). There are no accounts with storage. Instead:

- A **UTxO** (unspent transaction output) is a coin sitting at an address. A transaction spends some UTxOs and
  creates new ones.
- A UTxO at a script address can carry a **datum**: a piece of data, which is where a contract keeps its state.
- To spend it, the transaction supplies a **redeemer** (the arguments of the call), and the **validator** script
  decides whether the spending transaction is acceptable.

The validator never computes anything for you. It only says yes or no to a transaction someone else built. So a
working contract is really three programs that must agree:

1. **The validator,** which inspects the whole transaction and approves or rejects it.
2. **The off-chain builder,** which finds the current state UTxO, computes the next state, encodes datum and
   redeemer, picks inputs and outputs, sets the validity interval and signers, and submits.
3. **The glue between them:** the datum and redeemer encodings, which both sides must read and write identically.

Most of the validator's code has nothing to do with your business rule. It defends the state against transactions
that are well formed but malicious:

| A validator must check that... | Or an attacker can... |
|---|---|
| the state UTxO carries a unique token, minted once | forge a second "instance" with any state |
| exactly one output continues the state, at the same address | drop the state, or move it to their own address |
| the new datum is exactly the computed next state | write any state they like |
| the output holds exactly the right value | skim lovelace, or add junk tokens that make it unspendable |
| payouts are tagged per instance | let one output pay for two contracts (double satisfaction) |
| the caller signed, and time claims match the transaction | act for someone else, or lie about the time |
| the datum stays small enough for its min-ADA deposit | grow the state until the UTxO can never be spent |

Get any of these wrong and funds can be stolen or locked forever. And every rule you write on chain you write again
off chain, in another shape, and keep in sync by hand.

##### The JOUST model: state plus actions

In JOUST you describe the state and the transitions, and nothing else. This is the whole counter contract from
[`examples/counter`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/counter/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/counter/Counter.java):

```java title="examples/counter/.../Counter.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 128)
public class Counter {

    public record State(BigInteger count, byte[] owner) {}

    @Init
    public static State init(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, ctx.caller());
    }

    @Action
    public static State increment(State s, BigInteger by) {
        Require.that(by.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "increment must be positive");
        return new State(s.count().add(by), s.owner());
    }

    @Action
    @OnlyOwner
    public static State reset(State s) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, s.owner());
    }

    @Destroy
    @OnlyOwner
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance());
    }

    @View
    public static BigInteger count(State s) {
        return s.count();
    }
}
```

No UTxOs, no datums, no redeemers, no thread tokens. The application code is just as plain:

```java title="examples/counter/.../CounterApp.java"
CounterClient counter = CounterClient.deploy(runtime, alice);   // creates an instance; alice owns it
counter.increment(bob, BigInteger.valueOf(5));                   // anyone can increment
counter.reset(bob);                                              // RequireException: bob is not the owner, nothing submitted
counter.close(alice);                                            // the 2.2 ADA deposit goes back to alice
```

##### One method, run twice

![One method, run twice: off chain on the JVM to build the transaction, on chain in the validator to enforce it](../../../assets/diagrams/same-method.svg)

The idea that makes this work is to compute off chain and re-check on chain with the same code:

```text
on your machine:   next = Counter.increment(current, by)        -> build a transaction whose new datum is `next`
on chain:          Counter.increment(datumIn, redeemer.by) == datumOut   (the validator re-runs the same method)
```

[JuLC](https://julc.dev) compiles a subset of Java to UPLC, Cardano's on-chain language, and its data types
(records, `JulcList`, `JulcMap`) also run as plain Java. So the method you wrote is both the transaction builder's
logic and the validator's logic. There is no second implementation to keep in sync.

Two practical consequences:

- **Rules fail early and cheaply.** The generated client runs your method first. A failing `Require.that` throws a
  `RequireException` with your message before anything is built or submitted, and costs nothing.
- **You test the real thing.** The same method is unit-testable as plain Java, and the testkit evaluates the
  validator as compiled, against the transactions the runtime builds.

##### What is generated and checked for you

For each `@StateContract` class, the JOUST annotation processor generates:

- **`<Name>Validator`:** a JuLC multi-validator (minting and spending in one script), compiled to UPLC.
- **`<Name>Client`:** a typed client on [cardano-client-lib](https://github.com/bloxbean/cardano-client-lib), with
  one method per action, destroy and view.
- **A description** (`META-INF/joust/<package>.<Name>.json`): a CIP-57 schema plus JOUST metadata, from which
  JavaScript clients are generated.

The generated validator enforces the invariants of
[ADR-0001 §4](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-option-a-single-utxo-state-machine.md),
whatever your methods do:

| ID | The validator enforces |
|---|---|
| I1 | One seed UTxO gives one instance: it is consumed, and exactly one thread token is minted, named by its hash |
| I2 | The initial datum equals your `@Init` result, at the contract's address |
| I3 | Exact value: no lovelace skimmed or added, no token dust; a destroy allocates everything |
| I4 | Exactly one continuing output, at the same address, whose inline datum equals your method's result |
| I5, I6 | The `Ctx` caller signed; `received`, `balance` and the validity bounds match the transaction |
| I7 | Every payout is paid, tagged with this instance's input, so one output cannot satisfy two instances |
| I8, I9 | A destroy burns the thread token; the burn redeemer can only burn |
| I10 | UTxOs at the script address without a thread token can never be spent |
| I11 | `@OnlyOwner`, `@SignedBy`, `@ValidAfter`, `@ValidBefore` hold against the current state |
| I12 | State outputs sit at the script's own address, with no reference script attached |
| I13 | The serialised state never exceeds `maxDatumBytes`, so no call can outgrow the deposit |
| I14 | Actions never spend the min-ADA deposit |

Each example runs the **attack suite** (`Attacks` in `julc-state-testkit`), which mutates every accepted
transaction in each way these invariants forbid and checks that the validator rejects every mutation. See
[Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/) and the [Security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/).

The cost is measured, not guessed: the counter's validator is 5,631 bytes, and an `increment` costs 73.4M CPU and
213k memory units on chain (from the budgets table in
[`examples/README.md`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/README.md), measured by the harness
tests).

##### Java first; .jsc and JavaScript too

Java is JOUST's first-class language: you write the contract in Java (or in `.jsc`, a smaller syntax that lowers to
the same Java) and call it from Java through a generated client on cardano-client-lib. JavaScript is supported too,
experimentally: its toolchain and runtime run as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, itself experimental.

**Java:**

Write the contract in Java and build it with Gradle on JDK 25. The processor generates the validator and a Java
client; the [Java runtime](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/java-runtime/) builds, submits and confirms transactions. Start with the
[Java quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

**.jsc:**

```jsc
jsc 1
package app

contract Counter(maxDatumBytes = 128) {
  state { count: Int, owner: Key }

  init() {
    return { count: 0, owner: caller }
  }

  action increment(by: Int) {
    require(by > 0, "increment must be positive")
    return { ...state, count: count + by }
  }
}
```

`.jsc` reads like TypeScript, with immutable values, and is lowered to a Java `@StateContract`, then compiled exactly
like hand-written Java. It is a preview. See [.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/).

**JavaScript:**

**Experimental.** The npm path needs only Node: the toolchain compiles `.java` and `.jsc` contracts in Node (no JDK), and pages and
Node apps call them through generated JavaScript clients, with a CIP-30 browser wallet signing. Start with the
[npm quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/) and [JavaScript clients](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/).

##### Beyond one state UTxO

![Six kinds of state: inline, MerkleMaps, owned objects, batched intents, native assets, keyed objects](../../../assets/diagrams/state-kinds.svg)

A single state UTxO can be updated about once per block, and holds only what fits in one datum. JOUST makes the way
state maps onto UTxOs an explicit choice, so you can pick the one your contract needs:

**MerkleMaps.** 
Unbounded maps (token balances, registries) in a 32-byte root, with proofs checked by a shared verifier.
[MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/)

**Owned objects.** 
One UTxO per user object beside shared state, so users never contend with each other.
[Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/)

**Keyed objects.** 
One UTxO per key, at most one per key: ballots, names, positions, updated in parallel.
[Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/)

**Batched intents.** 
Users lock requests in parallel; a permissionless batcher applies many in one transaction.
[Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/)

**Assets and composition.** 
Native tokens, contract-minted tokens, several contracts in one transaction, reads of other contracts.
[Native assets](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/), [Composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/)

There is more: deploy-time parameters, M-of-N quorums, invariants and events, staking and governance purposes,
upgrades, and deposits between contracts. [How JOUST works](https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/) gives the overview.

##### Who it is for

- **Java developers** who want to write Cardano contracts without learning a new language or the eUTxO plumbing.
- **JavaScript and TypeScript developers** who want a typed client and a page that verifies every transaction before
  the wallet signs it.
- **Cardano developers** who want the safety invariants generated, attack-tested and the same every time, and the
  business logic written once.

JOUST is not the right tool if you need to hand-tune every byte of a script, or if your design depends on a
transaction shape that the state-machine model does not express. Generated checks cost bytes and budget, though
the examples stay far below the limits (see [Fees and script size](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/)).

##### Status

> **Experimental: a research and learning project:** 

JOUST is an experimental project created mainly for research and exploration of state-oriented smart contracts on
Cardano. It is AI-generated, with human-assisted design, testing and verification. **Do not use it in production.**

It is pre-release. Its releases are listed on the [releases page](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/releases): the
Maven modules are in the BloxBean release repository, `https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/releases` (nothing is on Maven
Central yet), and the npm packages (`@julclang/joust`, `@julclang/joust-runtime`, `@julclang/state-client`,
`create-joust`) are on npmjs.org. Both quick starts walk through the setup.

What works today: every example in [`examples/`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/examples/) is generated, tested against the attack
suite, and runs end to end on [Yaci DevKit](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/), a local Cardano network. The optimistic
L2 (`examples/rollup`) is a working spike, not a product. APIs can still change before the first release; the
[Status and roadmap](https://joust.julc.dev/project/status-and-roadmap/) page tracks what is next.

### How JOUST works

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/

This page follows one contract from source to chain: what the build generates, what the generated validator checks,
what the runtime does when you call an action, and how an instance lives as a chain of UTxOs. Read it once before
you write anything larger than a counter; the guides under "Writing contracts" build on it.

##### The pieces

![What JOUST generates from one contract: a validator, a Java client and a description](../../../assets/diagrams/joust-overview.svg)

In detail, inside the build:

```text
            Counter.java  (or Counter.jsc, lowered to Java first)
                 |
                 v
   javac + JOUST processor (julc-state-processor)
       SubsetLint         - rejects code whose JVM and on-chain meanings differ
       ContractReader     - checks the contract's shape, builds the State IR
       ValidatorGenerator -> CounterValidator.java   (a JuLC @MultiValidator)
       ClientGenerator    -> CounterClient.java      (typed client on julc-state-runtime)
       DescriptionWriter  -> META-INF/joust/<package>.Counter.json
                 |
                 v
   JuLC annotation processor (julc-annotation-processor)
       compiles CounterValidator, Counter and the julc-state-api sources to UPLC
                 -> META-INF/plutus/CounterValidator.plutus.json
```

| Module | Role |
|---|---|
| `julc-state-api` | What contracts use: the annotations, `Ctx`, `Payout`/`Payouts`, `Require`, `Clock`, `SortedMaps`, `MerkleMaps`, `Funds`, `Send`. JuLC-compilable and JVM-runnable: its sources are shipped to JuLC as library sources |
| `julc-state-processor` | The annotation processor: `ContractReader` (shape rules), the State IR, the generators, `SubsetLint` |
| `julc-state-runtime` | The off-chain runtime the generated clients drive: locate, run, build, check, submit, confirm, retry |
| `julc-state-testkit` | `StateHarness` (evaluates the compiled validator) and `Attacks` (the attack suite) |
| `julc-state-verifier` | Shared withdraw-zero scripts: the MerkleMap verifier and the output verifier |
| `julc-state-dsl` | The `.jsc` lexer, parser, checker and lowering to Java |
| `julc-state-server` | The prepare service: generated clients over HTTP, for JavaScript pages |

##### Build time: two annotation-processing rounds

1. **Round 1: JOUST.** javac runs `JoustProcessor` on every class annotated `@StateContract`.
   - `SubsetLint` checks the class first (syntactic pass now, typed pass once javac has attributed it). It rejects
     `int`, `long` and other fixed-width numbers, narrowing calls such as `intValue()`, and other constructs that
     would run differently on the JVM and on chain. See [Java](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/java/).
   - `ContractReader` checks the contract's shape (exactly one `@Init`, `public static` methods, `Ctx` last, field
     names that `@OnlyOwner` or `@ValidAfter` point at, reserved names) and reports each problem as a compiler
     error on the offending element.
   - It builds the **State IR** (`org.julclang.state.processor.ir`: `ContractIR`, `TransitionIR`, `ViewIR`,
     `ParamIR`), which records the storage, execution and transaction-level strategy of the contract.
   - The generators write `<Name>Validator.java`, `<Name>Client.java` and the description into the contract's
     package.

2. **Round 2: JuLC.** JuLC's annotation processor finds the generated `@MultiValidator` and compiles it to UPLC,
   together with everything it calls: your contract class (JuLC treats `@StateContract` as an alias of its
   `@OnchainLibrary`, so the class is an on-chain library) and the `julc-state-api` sources it finds on the
   annotation processor path. The compiled script lands in `META-INF/plutus/<Name>Validator.plutus.json`, where
   the runtime and the testkit load it.

Code is generated from string templates, so every construct emitted is one JuLC is known to accept
([ADR-0001](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-option-a-single-utxo-state-machine.md) §2).

##### The generated validator

One script per contract type, many instances. `<Name>Validator` is a JuLC multi-validator with a **MINT** and a
**SPEND** entry point, so its policy id, its script hash and its address credential are the same 28 bytes. Every
instance of the contract lives at that one address.

An instance is identified by its **thread token**: a native token minted under the contract's own policy, exactly
once, whose name is `blake2b_256(seedTxId ++ I2OSP(seedIndex, 2))` for a seed UTxO the deployer spends. That
32-byte name is the **instance id**. Because the seed can only be spent once, the id can only ever be minted once.

The redeemers are generated from your methods. For the counter:

```java title="build/generated/.../CounterValidator.java (excerpt)"
public sealed interface Lifecycle permits CreateInstance, BurnInstance {}
public record CreateInstance(TxOutRef seed, Ctx ctx) implements Lifecycle {}
public record BurnInstance() implements Lifecycle {}
public sealed interface Calls permits Increment, Reset, Close {}
public record Increment(BigInteger by) implements Calls {}
public record Reset() implements Calls {}
public record Close(Ctx ctx) implements Calls {}
```

Each spend arm decodes the current state from the input's inline datum, re-runs your method and checks the result.
This is the generated `reset` arm, unedited:

```java title="build/generated/.../CounterValidator.java (excerpt)"
static boolean onReset(Reset r, Counter.State current, TxInfo tx, TxInInfo own, byte[] policy, byte[] id, BigInteger inLovelace) {
    boolean signed_owner = ContextsLib.signedBy(tx, current.owner());   // @OnlyOwner
    Counter.State next = Counter.reset(current);                        // your method, on chain
    boolean continues = continues(tx, own, policy, id, (PlutusData) (Object) next, inLovelace.add(BigInteger.ZERO));
    return signed_owner && continues;
}
```

`continues(...)` checks the invariants every action shares: exactly one output carries the thread token, at the same
address, with an inline datum equal to `next`, no reference script, a datum within `maxDatumBytes`, and a value of
exactly `{lovelace, policy.id: 1}` with the min-ADA deposit untouched.

What the generated code checks, by kind of call:

| Call | Checks |
|---|---|
| **Create** (MINT `CreateInstance`) | The seed is consumed; exactly one token is minted under the policy, named by the seed; one output carries it, at the script address with no stake credential and no reference script; its datum equals `init(...)`; its value is exactly `minAda + received` plus the token; `Ctx` is valid with `balance == 0` |
| **Action** (SPEND) | The input holds a thread token (otherwise it is junk and unspendable); policy annotations hold against the current state; `Ctx` matches the transaction if the method declares it; the continuing output is exact; each payout is paid and tagged |
| **Destroy** (SPEND + MINT `BurnInstance`) | As an action, plus: the payouts total everything the UTxO holds, deposit included; the thread token is burned (quantity -1); the burn redeemer only burns |

**`Ctx` is checked, not trusted.** The client puts the `Ctx` it used into the redeemer, and the validator checks
that every field equals the transaction's facts before calling your method: `caller` signed, `received` matches the
value added (zero unless `@Payable`), `balance` equals the input's lovelace minus the deposit (everything, in a
destroy), and `validFrom`/`validTo` equal the transaction's finite validity bounds, at most `maxValidityMs` apart.
A method without `Ctx` gets none of these checks, and is cheaper.

**Payouts are tagged.** A payout output must go to the recipient's key and carry, as its inline datum, the
`TxOutRef` of the state input that owes it. Two instances spent in one transaction can therefore never count the
same output (double satisfaction).

The full list, with the attack that each check stops, is in [Security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/) and
ADR-0001 §4.

##### The generated client and the runtime

`<Name>Client` is a thin, typed facade. Each method fills in a `Call` (or a `Deploy`) with lambdas that run your
method and build the redeemer, and hands it to the runtime. The generated `reset`:

```java title="build/generated/.../CounterClient.java (excerpt)"
public CallResult<Counter.State> reset(Account callerAccount) {
    return instance.call(Call.<Counter.State>action("reset", callerAccount)
            .usesCtx(false)
            .signedBy("owner", s -> s.owner())
            .run((s, ctx) -> Transition.of(Counter.reset(s)))
            .redeemer(ctx -> new CounterValidator.Reset())
            .build());
}
```

When you call `counter.reset(alice)`, the runtime (`StateInstance.call`) does this:

1. **Locate** the state UTxO by its asset unit (policy id followed by the instance id) at the contract address,
   and decode the state from its inline datum.
2. **Pre-check** the policy annotations: if the caller's key is not the one in `owner`, throw a
   `RequireException` now.
3. **Pick the time window** if the call reads `Ctx` or has a time annotation: slots first (tip to tip + TTL), then
   the milliseconds derived from them, so the JVM run and the on-chain run see identical numbers.
4. **Run your method on the JVM** with the decoded state and a `Ctx`. A failing `Require.that` throws here, and
   nothing has been built.
5. **Build the transaction** with cardano-client-lib's QuickTx: spend the state UTxO with the redeemer, read the
   script from its reference-script UTxO, add the continuing output (exact value, inline datum), the tagged payouts,
   the validity interval and the required signers.
6. **Evaluate, sign and check:** execution budgets come from the configured evaluator (JuLC's local one in the
   examples). Before submitting, the runtime checks that the balanced transaction still has exactly the expected
   state output and payouts.
7. **Submit and confirm:** wait for this transaction to be included, then until the indexer shows the new state.

**Contention.** One state UTxO can be spent by one transaction. If the node rejects a submission and the state has
moved, the runtime re-reads, re-runs your method on the new state and resubmits, up to `maxRetries` times
(`ContentionException` after that). Once a submission has been accepted it never resubmits: if confirmation times
out you get a `PendingTransactionException` with the hash.

The first `deploy` of a contract on a network also publishes its script as a **reference script** (a UTxO holding
the script, at the contract's own address; CIP-33), so later transactions read the script instead of carrying it.

##### An instance's life, as UTxOs

![An instance's life on chain: create, actions, destroy, tied together by a thread token](../../../assets/diagrams/lifecycle.svg)

With the redeemers and the instance id:

```text
 deploy                       action                        action                       destroy
 (MINT CreateInstance)        (SPEND Increment)             (SPEND Reset)                (SPEND Close + MINT BurnInstance)

 seed UTxO (caller) --+
                      |
                      v
              +----------------+            +----------------+           +----------------+
              | state UTxO #1  |  ------->  | state UTxO #2  |  ------>  | state UTxO #3  |  ------>  payouts, tagged with
              | datum: init()  |            | datum: incr()  |           | datum: reset() |           state UTxO #3's ref;
              | 2.2 ADA        |            | 2.2 ADA        |           | 2.2 ADA        |           thread token burned
              | + thread token |            | + thread token |           | + thread token |
              +----------------+            +----------------+           +----------------+
                  instance id = blake2b_256(seed tx id ++ seed index): the same token travels through every state
```

Each transition spends the current state UTxO and creates the next one. The thread token moves with the state, so
"the counter" is "the UTxO holding token `policy.instanceId`". The deposit (`minAda`, 2.2 ADA for the counter,
derived from `maxDatumBytes`) stays locked for the instance's whole life and is paid out by the `@Destroy`.

##### Storage strategies

![Six kinds of state](../../../assets/diagrams/state-kinds.svg)

The single state UTxO above is **INLINE** storage: the whole state is the datum, and every call spends it. That is
right for most contracts, but it allows about one update per block and holds only what fits in `maxDatumBytes`.
JOUST offers other strategies, chosen by how you declare the state:

| Strategy | You declare | For | Guide |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inline (Option A) | A state record | Contracts with modest state and modest traffic | [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/) |
| MerkleMap (Option B) | A `MerkleMap` component in the state | Unbounded maps (balances, registries): the datum keeps a 32-byte root, each call proves the keys it touches, checked by the shared map verifier | [MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/) |
| Owned objects (Option C) | An `@Owned` record and owned methods | Per-user objects in their own UTxOs, beside shared state read by reference, so users do not contend | [Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/) |
| Keyed objects (ADR-0016) | `@Owned(key = "...")` on an owned record | At most one object per key (ballots, names), each its own UTxO in a sorted on-chain list; uniqueness is proved by the neighbours | [Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/) |
| Batched intents (Option D) | `@Batched` on an action | Hot shared state: users lock requests in parallel, a permissionless batcher applies them in one transaction | [Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/) |

On top of these: native assets and contract-minted tokens, deploy-time parameters, quorums and script callers,
invariants and events, staking and governance purposes, composition of several contracts in one transaction, and
upgrades. Each has a guide under "Writing contracts", and an ADR in
[`docs/adr`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/docs/adr).

##### The npm and Wasm path

![A JOUST page from the browser to the chain (npm path, experimental)](../../../assets/diagrams/browser-path.svg)

JavaScript developers use the same processor, validators and runtime, compiled to WebAssembly by JOUST's own build
(ADR-0015), so they need Node and nothing else.

- **The toolchain engine** (in `@julclang/joust`) runs the build in Node: `.jsc` lowering, javac with the JOUST
  processor, and JuLC's compiler, with no JDK. It writes the compiled validators, the descriptions and typed
  JavaScript clients.
- **The runtime engine** (in `@julclang/joust-runtime`) runs JOUST's runtime in Node or in a page's Web Worker. It
  prepares each transaction from a call request and the chain data it asks for; the JavaScript side does all the I/O.
- **The page verifier** (in `@julclang/state-client`) checks every prepared transaction against the contract's
  description and the chain before a CIP-30 wallet is asked to sign. CIP-30 is the standard browser-wallet API
  (Eternl, Lace and others).
- **The prepare service** (`julc-state-server`) is the JVM alternative: it serves generated Java clients over HTTP,
  prepares unsigned transactions for a wallet address, and holds no keys.

> **Note:** 

The npm packages are on npmjs.org (`npm create joust@latest`). Details of the JavaScript side are in
[Quick start: npm](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/) and [JavaScript clients](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/).

##### Next steps

- [Quick start: Java & Gradle](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)
- [Your first contract](https://joust.julc.dev/start/first-contract/)
- [Security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/)
- [Java off-chain runtime](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/java-runtime/)

### Quick start: Java & Gradle

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/

This page takes you from an empty machine to a contract running on a local Cardano network, with Java 25 and
Gradle. It has two parts: first you run the counter example inside a JOUST checkout (the quickest way to see
everything work), then you set up a project of your own.

If you would rather use Node and no JDK, see [Quick start: npm & JavaScript](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/).

> **Experimental, pre-release: nothing is on Maven Central yet:** 

JOUST is a research and learning project: do not use it in production. Its releases, all pre-releases so far, are in
the BloxBean release repository, `https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/releases`, with the JuLC they need; the
[releases page](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/releases) lists them. Part 2 shows the Gradle setup.

##### Prerequisites

- **JDK 25.** The build uses a Java toolchain of version 25.
- **Git,** to clone JOUST for the example in Part 1.
- **Yaci DevKit,** the local Cardano network, for the last step. Start it with Yaci Store (its Blockfrost-compatible
  API) enabled:

  ```sh
  yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store
  ```

  Yaci Store then answers on `http://localhost:8080`, the DevKit admin API on `http://localhost:10000`, and the Yaci
  Viewer explorer on `http://localhost:5173`. See [Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/).

You do not need Gradle installed: the JOUST checkout has a wrapper (Gradle 9.2), and you can copy it.

##### Part 1: run the counter in a JOUST checkout

1. **Get JOUST.**

   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/bloxbean/joust.git
   cd joust
   ```

   The build resolves JuLC and cardano-client-lib (the versions in `gradle/libs.versions.toml`) from Maven Central and
   the BloxBean repositories; nothing needs to be built first.

2. **Run the counter's tests.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:counter:test
   ```

   This compiles `Counter.java`, generates `CounterValidator` and `CounterClient`, compiles the validator to UPLC,
   and runs three kinds of tests: the contract's methods as plain Java, the compiled validator against
   transactions shaped like the runtime's, and the attack suite on each accepted transaction. The DevKit test
   (`CounterDevnetTest`) runs too if DevKit is up, and skips itself otherwise.

3. **Run it on DevKit.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:counter:run
   ```

   `CounterApp` funds two fresh accounts from the DevKit faucet, deploys a counter as Alice, increments it as Bob and
   Alice, shows Bob's reset being refused before anything is submitted, and closes the counter:

   ```text
     [joust] deploy Counter: submitted 34ba07cb2b9d13c18dba4c629966584fe06047283c2d5b5bb9e847f5cd3328b9
   deployed instance d11c40ff686bcc687c6dffb98efd9b25c597c8377df049f12117ca5747b455a9 at addr_test1wptj8x0692g2q3fv8v5a5j90dwgfqkkge76s8cd0sq7fgtq9nldys
   count = 0
     [joust] Counter.increment: submitted 85ec809e34d3d0e37e2a6c62177e2ddb3d2da3da92841e162ced7f81e92af19a
   bob +5   -> count = 5
     [joust] Counter.increment: submitted c1733515f595a25a569ebeb5a4ce7fa73b190d33fe45173714b4722f305633de
   alice +2 -> count = 7
   bob reset rejected off-chain: Counter.reset: must be called by the key in 'owner'
     [joust] Counter.reset: submitted f1f17a47fcb0f0f77888786bbd960def8bfef0b33a57f7ea41b3fdbe7e3c2648
   alice reset -> count = 0
     [joust] Counter.close: submitted c4419d0bb7e0b1f6fdf025eb90ae699e1d6c54c4a8907cb31e85862d36d4306d
   alice closed the counter in c4419d0bb7e0b1f6fdf025eb90ae699e1d6c54c4a8907cb31e85862d36d4306d, paid back [Payout[to=[B@78d39a69, lovelace=2200000]]
   ```

   Your hashes will differ. The first run on a fresh DevKit also logs `published the Counter reference script in
   ...`: the first deploy of a contract on a network publishes its script once, for every later transaction to read.
   Open the address in Yaci Viewer (`http://localhost:5173`) to see the state UTxOs and their datums.

Every example in `examples/` runs the same way: `./gradlew :examples:vault:run`, `:examples:escrow:run`, and so on.
See [Examples](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/examples/).

##### Part 2: your own project

###### Create it with `joust new`

1. **Install `joust`.**

   ```sh
   brew install bloxbean/tap/joust
   ```

   Or unpack the archive for your platform (macOS arm64, Linux x86_64 or arm64) from the
   [releases](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/releases) and put `joust` on your `PATH`.

2. **Create the project.**

   ```sh
   joust new my-counter              # Counter.java; -l jsc for a .jsc contract (a language preview), -p org.example for your package
   cd my-counter
   ```

3. **Build, test and run.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew build                   # or: joust build
   ./gradlew run                     # the counter on DevKit (or: joust run)
   ```

`joust new` (the native `joust` and the Gradle plugin `org.julclang.joust`, [ADR-0017](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/))
writes the files of the sections below, with the Gradle wrapper, and a `build.gradle` that is only this:

```groovy title="build.gradle"
plugins {
    id 'application'
    id 'org.julclang.joust' version '<version>'    // a JOUST release; upgrading JOUST is this version
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    maven {     // BloxBean: JOUST and JuLC releases
        url = uri('https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/releases')
        mavenContent { releasesOnly() }
    }
}

application {
    mainClass = 'app.CounterMain'
}
```

The plugin does what the hand-written `build.gradle` below spells out:

| It adds | At |
|---|---|
| `julc-state-runtime`, and `cardano-client-backend-blockfrost` for DevKit (`joust { blockfrost = false }` leaves it out) | `implementation` |
| `julc-state-processor`, `julc-annotation-processor`, `julc-state-api:<v>:onchain` | the annotation processor path |
| `julc-state-testkit`, `junit-platform-launcher` | the tests |
| UTF-8 and `-parameters`; native access and in-memory map mirrors for tests; native access for `run` | compile, test and run tasks |
| `generateJsc`, when `src/main/jsc` exists: `.jsc` contracts lowered to Java before compiling; with it `acceptJscAbi`, `checkJscAbi` (the [ABI manifest](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc-reference/#the-abi-manifest)) and `remapJscDiagnostics` (javac's errors on the generated Java, at their `.jsc` positions) | the build |

`joust new` fills in the version of the `joust` that runs it; the newest is the newest release whose tag starts with
`v` on the [releases page](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/releases) (`npm view @julclang/joust version`). Every other version comes from the JOUST release the
plugin belongs to, so the JuLC and cardano-client-lib versions always match. It needs a Java 25 toolchain (the default; a lower one is refused with a message).

The same command writes npm projects: `joust new my-app -t node` gives what `npm create joust` gives. In a project, the
native `joust` and the npm one answer the same commands; see [the native `joust`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/joust-cli/#the-native-joust).

###### Or set it up by hand: choose where JOUST comes from

**BloxBean release repository:**

Releases are published to `https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/releases`. Use as `<version>` below the newest release
whose tag starts with `v` on the [releases page](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/releases) (not the "Development
snapshot" entry), without the `v`. The quickest check is `npm view @julclang/joust version`, since each release
publishes the npm packages at the same version. Nothing is on Maven Central yet.

**Your checkout, via mavenLocal:**

To try what is on `main` before it is released, publish the library modules of your checkout to `~/.m2`:

```sh
cd joust
./gradlew publishToMavenLocal
grep '^version' gradle.properties            # the JOUST version you just published
grep '^julc ' gradle/libs.versions.toml     # and the JuLC version it needs
```

This publishes `julc-state-api` (with its `onchain` jar), `-processor`, `-runtime`, `-testkit`, `-verifier`, `-dsl`
and `-server`. Add `mavenLocal()` to the repositories below.

###### The build files by hand

- my-counter/
  - settings.gradle
  - gradle.properties
  - build.gradle
  - gradlew (copied from the JOUST checkout, with gradle/wrapper/)
  - src/
    - main/java/app/
      - Counter.java
      - Devnet.java
      - CounterMain.java
    - test/java/app/
      - CounterTest.java

```groovy title="settings.gradle"
rootProject.name = 'my-counter'
```

```properties title="gradle.properties"
#### The JOUST release: the newest tag starting with v on https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/releases, without the v
#### (not the "Development snapshot" entry); or run: npm view @julclang/joust version
joustVersion=<version>
#### The JuLC and cardano-client-lib it was built with: the julc and cardano-client-lib entries of
#### gradle/libs.versions.toml at that release's tag (v<version>)
julcVersion=<version>
cclVersion=<version>
```

`julcVersion` is JuLC's processor, the one that compiles your validator, and `cclVersion` is cardano-client-lib's.
Take both from the release you chose: its
[`gradle/libs.versions.toml`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/gradle/libs.versions.toml) (open it at the tag
`v<version>`) names the `julc` and `cardano-client-lib` versions it was built and tested with. The Gradle plugin does
this for you.

```groovy title="build.gradle"
plugins {
    id 'application'
}

java {
    toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(25) }
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    maven {          // BloxBean releases: JOUST, JuLC
        url = uri('https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/releases')
        mavenContent { releasesOnly() }
    }
}

dependencies {
    implementation "org.julclang:julc-state-runtime:$joustVersion"
    implementation "com.bloxbean.cardano:cardano-client-backend-blockfrost:$cclVersion"   // Yaci Store / Blockfrost

    annotationProcessor "org.julclang:julc-state-processor:$joustVersion"
    annotationProcessor "org.julclang:julc-annotation-processor:$julcVersion"
    annotationProcessor "org.julclang:julc-state-api:$joustVersion:onchain"   // on-chain sources for JuLC

    testImplementation "org.julclang:julc-state-testkit:$joustVersion"
    testRuntimeOnly 'org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher'
}

tasks.withType(JavaCompile).configureEach {
    options.encoding = 'UTF-8'
    options.compilerArgs << '-parameters'
}

tasks.withType(Test).configureEach {
    useJUnitPlatform()
    jvmArgs '--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED'
    systemProperty 'joust.mapStore', 'memory'    // MerkleMap mirrors in memory for tests
}

application {
    mainClass = 'app.CounterMain'
}

tasks.named('run', JavaExec) {
    jvmArgs '--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED'
}
```

What each line on the annotation processor path is for:

| Dependency | Why it is there |
|---|---|
| `julc-state-processor` | The JOUST processor: generates `<Name>Validator`, `<Name>Client` and the description |
| `julc-annotation-processor` | JuLC's processor: compiles the generated validator to UPLC in the next round |
| `julc-state-api:<version>:onchain` | The `julc-state-api` **sources**, under `META-INF/plutus-sources/`. JuLC compiles against its own on-chain API plus library sources it finds on the processor path; without these it cannot see `Ctx`, `Require`, `Payouts` and the rest |

> **Inside the JOUST build: a directory, not a jar:** 

Modules inside the JOUST repository use the same bundle as a **directory**:
`annotationProcessor project(path: ':julc-state-api', configuration: 'onchainSources')`, as in
[`examples/counter/build.gradle`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/counter/build.gradle). A jar
that is rebuilt while a Gradle daemon is running can make JuLC's source scan silently find nothing (ADR-0001 F8). A
published jar does not change, so this rarely matters outside the repository; if a build suddenly reports that JuLC
cannot resolve `Ctx` or `Require`, run `./gradlew --stop` and build again.

###### Write the contract

```java title="src/main/java/app/Counter.java"
package app;

import org.julclang.core.types.JulcList;
import org.julclang.state.api.Action;
import org.julclang.state.api.Ctx;
import org.julclang.state.api.Destroy;
import org.julclang.state.api.Init;
import org.julclang.state.api.OnlyOwner;
import org.julclang.state.api.Payout;
import org.julclang.state.api.Payouts;
import org.julclang.state.api.Require;
import org.julclang.state.api.StateContract;
import org.julclang.state.api.View;

import java.math.BigInteger;

@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 128)
public class Counter {

    public record State(BigInteger count, byte[] owner) {}

    @Init
    public static State init(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, ctx.caller());
    }

    @Action
    public static State increment(State s, BigInteger by) {
        Require.that(by.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "increment must be positive");
        return new State(s.count().add(by), s.owner());
    }

    @Action
    @OnlyOwner
    public static State reset(State s) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, s.owner());
    }

    @Destroy
    @OnlyOwner
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance());
    }

    @View
    public static BigInteger count(State s) {
        return s.count();
    }
}
```

This is the [counter example](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/counter/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/counter/Counter.java)
in package `app`. [Your first contract](https://joust.julc.dev/start/first-contract/) explains every line.

###### Build

```sh
./gradlew build
```

The build writes:

| Output | Where | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `CounterValidator.java` | `build/generated/sources/annotationProcessor/java/main/app/` | The on-chain validator source (MINT + SPEND) |
| `CounterClient.java` | same | The typed client: `deploy`, `at`, `increment`, `reset`, `close`, `count`, `state` |
| `CounterValidator.plutus.json` | `build/classes/java/main/META-INF/plutus/` | The compiled UPLC script; the runtime and the testkit load it from the classpath |
| `app.Counter.json` | `build/classes/java/main/META-INF/joust/` | The description (CIP-57 plus `x-joust`) JavaScript clients are generated from |

Read the generated sources: they are ordinary Java, and every check the validator makes is visible in
`CounterValidator.java`. If your contract breaks a rule (an `int` in a method, two `@Init` methods, a `@Payable`
without `Ctx`), the build fails with a compiler error on the offending line; see [Java](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/java/).

###### Test it on the JVM

`julc-state-testkit` gives you `StateHarness`, which evaluates the compiled validator against transactions shaped
like the ones the runtime builds, and `Attacks`, which mutates each accepted transaction in every way the
invariants forbid:

```java title="src/test/java/app/CounterTest.java"
package app;

import org.julclang.state.api.Ctx;
import org.julclang.state.api.RequireException;
import org.julclang.state.testkit.Attacks;
import org.julclang.state.testkit.StateHarness;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.math.BigInteger;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows;

class CounterTest {

    static final byte[] ALICE = StateHarness.fill(28, 0x11);
    static final byte[] BOB = StateHarness.fill(28, 0x22);

    final StateHarness<Counter.State> h = StateHarness.of(CounterClient.SPEC);

    @Test
    void plainJava() {
        var s0 = Counter.init(h.ctx(ALICE, BigInteger.ZERO, BigInteger.ZERO));
        var s1 = Counter.increment(s0, BigInteger.valueOf(5));
        assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(5), Counter.count(s1));
        var e = assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> Counter.increment(s1, BigInteger.ZERO));
        assertEquals("increment must be positive", e.getMessage());
    }

    @Test
    void incrementOnChain() {
        var live = h.live(new Counter.State(BigInteger.valueOf(3), ALICE), BigInteger.ZERO);
        var next = Counter.increment(live.state(), BigInteger.TEN);
        var tx = h.act(live, new CounterValidator.Increment(BigInteger.TEN), next, null, null);
        System.out.println(h.assertAccepted(tx));
        Attacks.assertAllRejected(h, tx);
    }

    @Test
    void resetByStrangerRejectedOnChain() {
        var live = h.live(new Counter.State(BigInteger.valueOf(42), ALICE), BigInteger.ZERO);
        h.assertRejected(h.act(live, new CounterValidator.Reset(), Counter.reset(live.state()), BOB, null), "@OnlyOwner");
    }
}
```

```sh
./gradlew test
```

The examples' [`CounterTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/counter/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/counter/CounterTest.java)
covers every call, including the create and the close; [Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/) explains the harness.

###### Run it on DevKit

The runtime needs a `StateRuntime`: a chain backend, the network's slot clock, and a few options. The examples get
one from a small helper, [`examples/devkit/.../DevKit.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/devkit/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/devkit/DevKit.java).
This is a trimmed copy of it:

```java title="src/main/java/app/Devnet.java"
package app;

import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.account.Account;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.backend.api.BackendService;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.backend.api.DefaultProtocolParamsSupplier;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.backend.api.DefaultScriptSupplier;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.backend.api.DefaultUtxoSupplier;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.backend.blockfrost.service.BFBackendService;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.common.model.Networks;
import org.julclang.clientlib.eval.JulcTransactionEvaluator;
import org.julclang.clientlib.eval.SlotConfig;
import org.julclang.state.runtime.SlotChainTime;
import org.julclang.state.runtime.StateRuntime;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/** Yaci DevKit: Yaci Store on :8080, the admin API on :10000. Adapted from the examples' DevKit helper. */
final class Devnet {
    static final String STORE = "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/";
    static final String ADMIN = "http://localhost:10000";
    static final HttpClient HTTP = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

    static StateRuntime runtime() throws Exception {
        BackendService backend = new BFBackendService(STORE, "dummy-key");
        // The DevKit's slot clock, from its genesis.
        String genesis = get(ADMIN + "/local-cluster/api/admin/devnet");
        long startSec = Long.parseLong(find(genesis, "startTime", "-?\\d+"));
        double slotSec = Double.parseDouble(find(genesis, "slotLength", "[\\d.]+"));
        SlotChainTime time = new SlotChainTime(0, startSec * 1000, Math.round(slotSec * 1000), backend);
        return StateRuntime.builder(backend)
                .network(Networks.testnet())
                .chainTime(time)
                .ttl(Duration.ofSeconds(20))      // DevKit's time horizon is minutes: keep the validity window short
                .evaluator(new JulcTransactionEvaluator(   // script budgets computed locally by JuLC
                        new DefaultUtxoSupplier(backend.getUtxoService()),
                        new DefaultProtocolParamsSupplier(backend.getEpochService()),
                        new DefaultScriptSupplier(backend.getScriptService()),
                        new SlotConfig(time.zeroSlot(), time.zeroTimeMs(), time.slotLengthMs())))
                .log(msg -> System.out.println("  [joust] " + msg))
                .build();
    }

    /** A fresh account with {@code ada} ADA from the DevKit faucet. */
    static Account fundedAccount(long ada) throws Exception {
        var account = new Account(Networks.testnet());
        HTTP.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(ADMIN + "/local-cluster/api/addresses/topup"))
                .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(
                        "{\"address\":\"" + account.baseAddress() + "\",\"adaAmount\":" + ada + "}"))
                .build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        Thread.sleep(2000);   // let Yaci Store index the top-up
        return account;
    }

    private static String get(String url) throws Exception {
        return HTTP.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(url)).GET().build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
    }

    private static String find(String json, String key, String valuePattern) {
        var m = Pattern.compile("\"" + key + "\"\\s*:\\s*(" + valuePattern + ")").matcher(json);
        if (!m.find()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("key not found: " + key);
        return m.group(1);
    }
}
```

```java title="src/main/java/app/CounterMain.java"
package app;

import org.julclang.state.api.RequireException;

import java.math.BigInteger;

public class CounterMain {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var runtime = Devnet.runtime();
        var alice = Devnet.fundedAccount(500);
        var bob = Devnet.fundedAccount(500);

        CounterClient counter = CounterClient.deploy(runtime, alice);
        System.out.println("deployed instance " + counter.instanceId());

        counter.increment(bob, BigInteger.valueOf(5));
        counter.increment(alice, BigInteger.TWO);
        System.out.println("count = " + counter.count());               // 7

        try {
            counter.reset(bob);                                         // not the owner
        } catch (RequireException e) {
            System.out.println("refused before submitting: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        var closed = counter.close(alice);                              // the deposit goes back to alice
        System.out.println("closed in " + closed.txHash());
    }
}
```

```sh
./gradlew run
```

##### Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `Could not find org.julclang:julc-...` | A repository is missing, or `julcVersion` is not the one your JOUST needs. Add the BloxBean release repository (and `https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/snapshots` for a development snapshot) and use the `julc` entry of `gradle/libs.versions.toml` at your JOUST release's tag |
| JuLC errors such as "cannot resolve" `Ctx` or `Require` | The `onchain` bundle is missing from the annotation processor path, or a long-lived daemon holds a stale jar: check the dependency, then `./gradlew --stop` |
| `'int' in a @StateContract ... Use BigInteger` | `SubsetLint`: contract code computes in `BigInteger` only. See [Java](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/java/) |
| `PastHorizon` from the node | The validity window reaches beyond what the network can convert to time. Keep `ttl` short on DevKit (20 s in the examples) |

More in [Troubleshooting](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/troubleshooting/).

### Your first contract

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/start/first-contract/

In this tutorial you build the contract from
[`examples/counter`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/counter): a counter anyone can increment,
that only its owner can reset or close. It is small, but it uses every basic part of a JOUST contract, and by the end
you will have created, changed and closed one on a local Cardano network.

You need a working setup from [Quick start: Java & Gradle](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/) (or a JOUST checkout with JuLC
built), and Yaci DevKit for the last part. Each Cardano term is explained the first time it comes up; the
[Glossary](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/glossary/) has them all.

##### Build the contract

1. **Declare the contract and its state.**

   ```java
   @StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 128)
   public class Counter {

       /** The state, stored as the inline datum of the state UTxO. */
       public record State(BigInteger count, byte[] owner) {}
   }
   ```

   `@StateContract` marks the class for the JOUST processor. The state is a plain Java record.

   On Cardano, coins sit in **UTxOs** (unspent transaction outputs). A UTxO at a script's address can carry a
   **datum**, a piece of structured data: JOUST stores your `State` there, as an *inline* datum (in the UTxO
   itself). One instance of the counter is one such UTxO.

   Two details matter already:
   - **Numbers are `BigInteger`.** On chain, integers are unbounded; a Java `int` or `long` would wrap on the JVM
     and not on chain, so the build rejects them in contract code.
   - **`owner` is a `byte[]`**: the 28-byte hash of a payment key, which is how Cardano names who may sign.

   `maxDatumBytes = 128` caps the serialised state. Every UTxO must hold a minimum amount of ADA that grows with its
   size (the **min-ADA deposit**). JOUST derives the counter's deposit from the cap, 2.2 ADA (2,200,000
   **lovelace**; 1 ADA = 1,000,000 lovelace), and the validator refuses any state that grows past it, so no call can
   make the UTxO unspendable.

2. **Create instances with `@Init`.**

   ```java
   /** The deployer becomes the owner. */
   @Init
   public static State init(Ctx ctx) {
       return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, ctx.caller());
   }
   ```

   Exactly one method carries `@Init`. It returns the first state. Every contract method is `public static` and
   pure: it gets everything as arguments and returns the result, so it can run anywhere.

   `Ctx` is an optional **last** parameter with the facts of the transaction:

   | Field | Meaning |
   |---|---|
   | `caller()` | The key hash of whoever calls. The validator requires that key's signature |
   | `received()` | Lovelace this call adds to the contract (zero unless the method is `@Payable`) |
   | `balance()` | Lovelace the call may allocate: the contract's funds minus the deposit (everything, in a `@Destroy`) |
   | `validFrom()`, `validTo()` | The transaction's validity interval, in POSIX milliseconds |

   The client fills these in; the generated validator checks each one against the real transaction before your
   method runs. Here the deployer becomes the owner.

   When you deploy, the transaction spends a UTxO of yours (the *seed*) and **mints** a token under the contract's
   own **minting policy** (the script that decides when a token may be created). That token, the **thread token**,
   marks the state UTxO; its name, derived from the seed, is the **instance id**. Because the seed can be spent only
   once, no one can ever mint a second token for the same instance.

3. **Add an action anyone can call, with no `Ctx`.**

   ```java
   /** Anyone can increment by a positive amount (no Ctx: no signature needed, cheaper). */
   @Action
   public static State increment(State s, BigInteger by) {
       Require.that(by.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "increment must be positive");
       return new State(s.count().add(by), s.owner());
   }
   ```

   An `@Action` takes the current state first, then its arguments, and returns the next state. Records are
   immutable: you build a new one.

   `Require.that(condition, message)` is how a contract states a rule. On the JVM it throws a `RequireException`
   carrying your message, so the client refuses the call before building anything. On chain it records the message
   and fails the script.

   This method does not declare `Ctx`, so the validator does not require a signature or a validity interval: anyone
   can increment, and the check is cheaper. The arguments travel in the **redeemer**, the data a transaction gives
   the validator when it spends a script UTxO.

4. **Add an action only the owner can call.**

   ```java
   /** Only the owner can reset. */
   @Action
   @OnlyOwner
   public static State reset(State s) {
       return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, s.owner());
   }
   ```

   `@OnlyOwner` means "the transaction must be signed by the key in the state's `owner` field". It is shorthand for
   `@SignedBy("owner")`, and it checks the **current** state, before the call. The method itself needs no `Ctx`:
   the generated validator checks the signature, and the generated client refuses the call early if the caller's
   key is not the owner's.

5. **Add a read-only view.**

   ```java
   /** Read-only view (off-chain, no transaction). */
   @View
   public static BigInteger count(State s) {
       return s.count();
   }
   ```

   A `@View` never goes on chain. It becomes a getter on the client that reads the current state and computes the
   answer locally, without a transaction.

6. **Let the owner close it, and return the deposit.**

   ```java
   /** Only the owner can close the counter; the deposit goes back to them. */
   @Destroy
   @OnlyOwner
   public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       return Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance());
   }
   ```

   A `@Destroy` ends the instance: the thread token is burned and the UTxO is not continued. It returns a list of
   `Payout`s (a key hash and an amount of lovelace), and it must pay out **everything** the UTxO holds: in a
   `@Destroy`, `ctx.balance()` is the whole amount, deposit included. That is why `Ctx` is required here. Without a
   `@Destroy`, the deposit of every instance would stay locked forever (the processor warns about it).

The whole file, with its imports, is
[`Counter.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/counter/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/counter/Counter.java).

##### The same contract in .jsc

If you prefer a syntax closer to TypeScript, `.jsc` (a language preview) says the same thing and lowers to an equivalent Java
class.

**Java:**

```java title="Counter.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 128)
public class Counter {
    public record State(BigInteger count, byte[] owner) {}

    @Init
    public static State init(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, ctx.caller());
    }

    @Action
    public static State increment(State s, BigInteger by) {
        Require.that(by.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "increment must be positive");
        return new State(s.count().add(by), s.owner());
    }

    @Action @OnlyOwner
    public static State reset(State s) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, s.owner());
    }

    @Destroy @OnlyOwner
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance());
    }

    @View
    public static BigInteger count(State s) {
        return s.count();
    }
}
```

**.jsc:**

```jsc title="Counter.jsc"
jsc 1
package app

contract Counter(maxDatumBytes = 128) {
  state { count: Int, owner: Key }

  init() {
    return { count: 0, owner: caller }
  }

  action increment(by: Int) {
    require(by > 0, "increment must be positive")
    return { ...state, count: count + by }
  }

  action reset() only owner {
    return { ...state, count: 0 }
  }

  destroy close() only owner {
    pay(owner, balance)
  }

  view count(): Int = count
}
```

`init` returns the first state and an action the next one: `{ ...state, count: count + by }` keeps every other field.
Values never change, so there is no `count += by`. `caller` and `balance` read `Ctx`, which the lowering adds where they
are used; `only owner` becomes `@SignedBy("owner")`. The build also writes `Counter.abi.json`, the contract's encoding,
which you commit beside the file. See [.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/).

##### Build it

```sh
./gradlew :examples:counter:build      # in a JOUST checkout; ./gradlew build in your own project
```

The processor writes `CounterValidator` and `CounterClient` into
`build/generated/sources/annotationProcessor/java/main`, and JuLC compiles the validator into
`META-INF/plutus/CounterValidator.plutus.json`. Open `CounterValidator.java`: you will find your methods called from
the spend arms, and the checks around them. For example, `reset`:

```java title="CounterValidator.java (generated)"
static boolean onReset(Reset r, Counter.State current, TxInfo tx, TxInInfo own, byte[] policy, byte[] id, BigInteger inLovelace) {
    boolean signed_owner = ContextsLib.signedBy(tx, current.owner());
    Counter.State next = Counter.reset(current);
    boolean continues = continues(tx, own, policy, id, (PlutusData) (Object) next, inLovelace.add(BigInteger.ZERO));
    return signed_owner && continues;
}
```

`continues` checks that exactly one output carries the thread token, at the same address, with a datum equal to
`next` and exactly the same value. [How JOUST works](https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/) walks through the rest.

##### Run it

Start Yaci DevKit (`yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`), then drive the counter from an application.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/counter/.../CounterApp.java"
var runtime = DevKit.runtime();
var alice = DevKit.fundedAccount(500);
var bob = DevKit.fundedAccount(500);

CounterClient counter = CounterClient.deploy(runtime, alice);
System.out.println("deployed instance " + counter.instanceId() + " at "
        + CounterClient.contract(runtime).address());
System.out.println("count = " + counter.count());

counter.increment(bob, BigInteger.valueOf(5));
counter.increment(alice, BigInteger.TWO);

try {
    counter.reset(bob);   // not the owner: rejected on the JVM, nothing is submitted
} catch (RequireException e) {
    System.out.println("bob reset rejected off-chain: " + e.getMessage());
}

counter.reset(alice);
var closed = counter.close(alice);
System.out.println("alice closed the counter in " + closed.txHash() + ", paid back " + closed.payouts());
```

```sh
./gradlew :examples:counter:run
```

```text
deployed instance d11c40ff686bcc687c6dffb98efd9b25c597c8377df049f12117ca5747b455a9 at addr_test1wptj8x0692g2q3fv8v5a5j90dwgfqkkge76s8cd0sq7fgtq9nldys
count = 0
bob +5   -> count = 5
alice +2 -> count = 7
bob reset rejected off-chain: Counter.reset: must be called by the key in 'owner'
alice reset -> count = 0
alice closed the counter in c4419d0b..., paid back [Payout[to=[B@78d39a69, lovelace=2200000]]
```

`DevKit` is the examples' helper for a local network: it builds the `StateRuntime` and funds fresh accounts from
the faucet. In your own project you build the runtime yourself, as in the
[quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/#run-it-on-devkit).

**JavaScript:**

The project that `npm create joust` makes contains the same counter, in `.jsc` (`contracts/app/Counter.jsc`; with
`-- --lang java`, `contracts/app/Counter.java`). After
`npm run build` and `npm run deploy`, its test drives it on DevKit from Node:

```js title="test/counter.test.js (create-joust template)"
const rt = joustRuntime({ chainUrl: deployed.chain, contracts, clock: deployed.clock, networkId: deployed.networkId,
  deployments: deployed.contracts, ttlMs: 20_000 });
// A fresh DevKit wallet with 100 ADA from the faucet.
const wallet = devWallet({ chain: rt.chain, mnemonic: generateMnemonic(wordlist, 256) });
await devkitTopUp(wallet.address, 100, config.networks.devkit.admin, { chain: rt.chain });

const counter = new Counter(rt.options('app.Counter'));
const { instance } = await counter.deploy(wallet, {});
await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 5n });
await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 2n });
assert.equal((await instance.state()).count, 7n);
await assert.rejects(instance.increment(wallet, { by: 0n }), /increment must be positive/);
await instance.close(wallet);
assert.equal(await instance.state(), null);
```

The same `Require` message comes back in JavaScript, because the same method ran (compiled to UPLC, in the
runtime engine) before anything was signed.

What happened on chain, call by call:

| Call | Transaction |
|---|---|
| `deploy` | Spends a seed UTxO of Alice, mints the thread token, creates the state UTxO (datum `State(0, alice)`, 2.2 ADA). The first deploy on a network also publishes the script once as a **reference script**, a UTxO other transactions read the script from instead of carrying it |
| `increment(bob, 5)` | Spends the state UTxO with redeemer `Increment(5)`, creates the next one with datum `State(5, alice)` |
| `reset(bob)` | Never built: the client saw Bob is not the owner |
| `reset(alice)` | Spends the state, signed by Alice, datum `State(0, alice)` |
| `close(alice)` | Spends the state, burns the thread token, pays 2,200,000 lovelace to Alice in an output tagged with the state input |

After `close`, `counter.state()` throws `InstanceNotFoundException`: no UTxO holds the token any more.

##### What you learned

- A contract is a state record plus `public static` methods: `@Init` creates, `@Action` changes, `@View` reads,
  `@Destroy` ends and pays out.
- `Ctx` is optional and verified. Leave it out when a method needs no caller, payment or time, and the call is
  cheaper.
- `@OnlyOwner` (`@SignedBy`) checks a key from the current state, on the client and on chain.
- `Require.that` fails early on the JVM with your message, and fails the script on chain.
- The state lives in one UTxO, marked by a thread token; the deposit stays with it until the `@Destroy` pays it out.
