### Quick start: JavaScript & TypeScript

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

This page takes you from an empty folder to a Cardano contract you can call from Node and from a browser page, with
Node and npm only: no JDK, no Gradle, no GraalVM. The contract is written in JOUST's [.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/) language
(or in Java), and `joust build` compiles it with a toolchain engine that runs as WebAssembly in Node.

You will:

- create a project with `npm create joust`: a `Counter` contract and a short Node script that calls it;
- build the contract into a validator and a typed JavaScript client;
- deploy it on a local network (Yaci DevKit) and call it from the script and from a test;
- then create the browser version, connect a wallet and call the contract from a page.

##### Prerequisites

- **Node 22 or newer.** The engines need Wasm exception references, which the runtime switches on itself on Node 22.
- **Yaci DevKit**, a local Cardano network, started with its indexer, Yaci Store:

  ```sh
  yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store
  ```

  This gives a Blockfrost-compatible chain API on `http://localhost:8080/api/v1`, DevKit's admin API (slot clock,
  faucet) on `:10000`, and the Yaci Viewer explorer on `http://localhost:5173`.
- **The JOUST npm packages** come from npmjs.org: `npm create joust@latest` installs what it needs. Their versions
  follow JOUST's [releases](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/releases).

##### Create and build the app

1. **Create the project.**

   ```sh
   npm create joust@latest my-app
   cd my-app
   npm install
   ```

   `create-joust` writes a `Counter` contract in `.jsc` (`contracts/app/Counter.jsc`) and a Node script that calls it
   (`index.js`), and names the package after the folder. It refuses a folder that is not empty. Two options change
   what it writes (after `--`, as `npm create` passes them on):

   | Option | Values |
   |---|---|
   | `--lang` | `jsc` (the default) or `java`: the same counter in Java, `contracts/app/Counter.java` |
   | `--template` | `node` (the default): `index.js`; `web`: a browser page instead ([below](#a-browser-page)) |

   ```sh
   npm create joust@latest my-app -- --lang java
   ```

   The contract is the same in both languages:

   ```jsc title="contracts/app/Counter.jsc"
   jsc 1
   package app

   contract Counter(maxDatumBytes = 128) {
     state { count: Int, owner: Key }

     init() {
       return { count: 0, owner: caller }
     }

     action increment(by: Int) {
       require(by > 0, "increment must be positive")
       return { ...state, count: count + by }
     }

     action reset() only owner {
       return { ...state, count: 0 }
     }

     destroy close() only owner {
       pay(owner, balance)
     }

     view count(): Int = count
   }
   ```

   It is written in `.jsc`, a preview ([.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/)). Beside it, `create-joust` writes
   `Counter.abi.json`, the contract's ABI manifest: how its state and its calls are encoded on chain. A build fails
   when the manifest is missing or differs from what the contract now compiles to, so an encoding change cannot slip
   through; `npx joust build --accept-abi` accepts a change you intend, to review and commit.

   `joust build` generates the same description and the same JavaScript client from `Counter.jsc` as from
   `Counter.java`, so nothing else in the project depends on the language.

2. **Build the contract.**

   ```sh
   npm run build
   ```

   `joust build` compiles every `.java` and `.jsc` file under `contracts/` into `build/joust/`:

   ```txt
   app.Counter: … bytes, hash …, 4 transitions
   built 1 contract(s) into build/joust in … ms
   ```

   The size and hash depend on the contract, its language and the toolchain's version. The four transitions are the contract's
   four methods (`init`, `increment`, `reset`, `close`), compiled so the runtime engine can run them off chain.

3. **Deploy it on DevKit.**

   ```sh
   npm run deploy
   ```

   `joust deploy` publishes the validator as a **reference script**: a UTxO that carries the script, so later
   transactions point to it instead of including it. (A UTxO, an *unspent transaction output*, is a coin on Cardano:
   an address, a value and optional data. See the [glossary](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/glossary/).) On DevKit it pays with a key it
   makes and keeps in `.joust/devkit-wallet.json`, topped up from DevKit's faucet. It writes what it published to
   `build/joust/deployments.devkit.json`:

   ```json title="build/joust/deployments.devkit.json"
   {
     "network": "devkit",
     "networkId": 0,
     "chain": "http://localhost:8080/api/v1",
     "clock": { "zeroSlot": 0, "zeroTimeMs": 1793975371000, "slotLengthMs": 1000 },
     "contracts": {
       "app.Counter": {
         "contract": "app.Counter",
         "policy": "572399fa2a90a0452c3b29da48af6b90905ac8cfb503e1af803c942c",
         "address": "addr_test1wptj8x0692g2q3fv8v5a5j90dwgfqkkge76s8cd0sq7fgtq9nldys",
         "networkId": 0,
         "referenceScripts": ["1e4834390dae0f76de76b65d83b0f15fd99b7eb7d2e1da50e0cb1e7c10bd15c0#0"]
       }
     }
   }
   ```

4. **Run the script.**

   ```sh
   node index.js
   ```

   ```txt
   wallet      addr_test1qzsnkv3kupara60hylhrxc26ga5dn42mhc92ehmmzjzayjmdsj2justfnutk5my5a7xcdem62trnx0968tflw2mgswssjma7mj
   created     50c92ecfef4443fb9010be5e06d6a4ac24f2943a5a0f0a49ae16d239bb3247d6 tx 3c81eceba21fc5624fb0632c6268c220cba9758771e50a64b5cdb30c439560f4
   increment 5 tx bf03fd41a39d3298e6dcd5550ee2422b30477738af255552bd02dc71bb6b5670
   increment 2 tx 132896a73abd88de4f3791c821ff2ee3529132f8239ebd890af12dcde5009272
   count       7n
   refused     increment must be positive [app/Counter.jsc:22:5 (a require in increment)]
   closed      tx 9421540ed8a497c54734d29dcd0700246f5c653296d6da4fde9ab52b02ca9081
   state       null
   ```

   `npm start` runs steps 2 to 4 in one go. `index.js` is the whole app:

   ```js title="index.js (abridged)"

   import { Counter } from './build/joust/Counter.js';   // generated by `joust build`

   const rt = joustRuntime({
     chainUrl: deployed.chain, networkId: deployed.networkId, clock: deployed.clock, ttlMs: 20_000,
     contracts: read('build/joust/contracts.json'), deployments: deployed.contracts,
   });
   // A throwaway wallet, funded with 100 ADA by the DevKit's faucet.
   const wallet = devWallet({ chain: rt.chain, mnemonic: generateMnemonic(wordlist, 256) });
   await devkitTopUp(wallet.address, 100, config.networks.devkit.admin, { chain: rt.chain });

   const counter = new Counter(rt.options('app.Counter'));
   const { instance } = await counter.deploy(wallet, {});        // init: a new counter, owned by this wallet
   await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 5n });                 // anyone may call it
   console.log((await instance.state()).count);                  // read from the chain
   await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 0n });                 // throws: increment must be positive
   await instance.close(wallet);                                 // owner only; the deposit goes back to the owner
   ```

   Each call runs the contract's own code in the runtime engine to compute the next state, builds the transaction,
   signs it with the wallet's key and submits it. On chain, the validator runs the same code again and checks the
   result. `counter.deploy()` creates a counter (the contract's `init`); `joust deploy` published the contract.

5. **Run the test.**

   ```sh
   npm test
   ```

   `test/counter.test.js` makes the same calls with `node:test` and checks each result: the count is 7, an increment
   of 0 is refused, and the counter is gone after `close`.

##### The project

- contracts/
  - app/
    - Counter.jsc the contract (Counter.java with --lang java)
    - Counter.abi.json its ABI manifest (.jsc only)
- index.js the app: deploys a counter and calls it
- test/
  - counter.test.js a Node test on DevKit
- build/ written by joust build and joust deploy
  - joust/
    - generated/ the Java lowered from Counter.jsc, with its source map
    - Counter.js the typed client, with the contract's description pinned
    - Counter.d.ts its TypeScript types
    - Counter.json the description
    - Counter.plutus the compiled validator (CBOR hex)
    - contracts.json what the runtime engine needs
    - deployments.devkit.json what joust deploy published
    - joust.lock.json the versions that built it
- joust.config.json contracts, output and networks
- package.json

In `.jsc`, a contract is its `state` and its `init`, `action`, `destroy` and `view` declarations; `joust build`
lowers it to a Java contract and compiles that ([.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/)). In Java, it is a `State` record and static
methods marked `@Init`, `@Action`, `@Destroy` and `@View`, in the subset JuLC compiles
([Your first contract](https://joust.julc.dev/start/first-contract/)). `package.json` holds these scripts:

| Script | Runs | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `npm start` | `joust build && joust deploy && node index.js` | build, deploy (once per script) and run the app |
| `npm run build` | `joust build` | compile `contracts/` into `build/joust/` |
| `npm run deploy` | `joust deploy` | publish the reference scripts on the config's network (DevKit) |
| `npm test` | `node --test test/*.test.js` | the Node tests |

##### A browser page

`--template web` makes the same project with a page instead of `index.js`:

```sh
npm create joust@latest my-web-app -- --template web
cd my-web-app
npm install
```

- contracts/
  - app/
    - Counter.jsc the same contract
    - Counter.abi.json its ABI manifest
- page/
  - index.html the Counter page
  - main.js the page's code: wallet, review dialog, calls
  - engine.worker.js the runtime engine, in a Web Worker
- test/
  - counter.test.js a Node test on DevKit
- joust.config.json
- vite.config.js the page's Vite config, with @julclang/joust/vite
- package.json

The [Counter dApp tutorial](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/counter-dapp/) walks through every file. Its `package.json` has these scripts:

| Script | Runs | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `npm run build` | `joust build` | compile `contracts/` into `build/joust/` |
| `npm run deploy` | `joust deploy` | publish the reference scripts on the config's network (DevKit) |
| `npm run deploy:preview` | `joust deploy --network preview` | the same on the preview testnet |
| `npm test` | `node --test test/*.test.js` | the Node tests |
| `npm run dev` | `joust dev` | build, deploy, serve the page; rebuild and redeploy on save |
| `npm run dev:preview` | `joust dev --network preview` | the same on preview |
| `npm run build:page` | `vite build` | the page as static files in `dist/` |
| `npm run build:page:preview` | `vite build --mode preview` | the same, for preview |
| `npm run serve` | `joust serve` | serve `dist/` with the chain API at `/chain` |
| `npm run serve:preview` | `joust serve --network preview` | the same on preview |

###### Open the page

```sh
npm run dev
```

`joust dev` attaches to DevKit, builds and deploys, then serves the page at **http://127.0.0.1:5178**. It keeps
watching `contracts/`: save `Counter.jsc` and it rebuilds and redeploys.

1. Wait for the activity log to say *Runtime engine ready*. The page loads JOUST's runtime engine (about 20 MB of
   Wasm) into a Web Worker once per page load, and prepares its own transactions with it.

2. Choose **DevKit key (in this page)** and press **Connect**. Browser wallets cannot join a private devnet, so on
   DevKit the page offers a key it keeps in `localStorage`. Press **Top up 1000 ADA** to fund it from the faucet.

3. Press **Create a counter**. A dialog shows what the page checked in the prepared transaction: the redeemer is this
   call on the pinned script, what your wallet pays in all, the next state, and that nothing else is in it. Press
   **Sign in the wallet**.

4. Press **+1** a few times. Then press **+0**: the contract refuses it (`increment must be positive`) while the
   transaction is being prepared, so no wallet is ever asked to sign.

5. Press **Close**. Only the owner can close; the counter's deposit comes back to your wallet.

Each transaction hash in the log links to Yaci Viewer, DevKit's explorer.

###### Build the page as static files

```sh
npm run build:page   # vite build -> dist/
npm run serve        # dist/ at http://127.0.0.1:5178, with the chain API at /chain
```

A build is for one network: the network, its deployments, the contracts and the engine's integrity hashes are inlined
into the page, and the engine's two files are copied into `dist/joust/engine-<id>/`. `joust serve` serves `dist/` as
plain files, adds the chain API at `/chain` (and DevKit's faucet), and does nothing else: no build, no deploy, no
prepare service. See [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/).

> **Note:** 
DevKit's slot clock changes when DevKit restarts. After a restart, run `npm run deploy` and `npm run build:page`
again.

###### Use TypeScript

The page can be TypeScript. Vite compiles `.ts` files (it does not type-check them), so renaming is enough to run:

```sh
mv page/main.js page/main.ts
sed -i.bak 's#./main.js#./main.ts#' page/index.html && rm page/index.html.bak
npm install --save-dev typescript
```

The generated client is typed already: `npm run build` writes `build/joust/Counter.d.ts` beside `Counter.js`, with a
type for every state, argument and result. A call with a wrong argument name fails to compile:

```ts
await counter.at(id).increment(wallet, { amount: 1n });
// error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'amount' does not exist in type '{ by: Int; }'.
```

Two modules a page imports ship no declarations yet (`virtual:joust/network` and `@julclang/joust-runtime/page`).
Declare them in `page/joust-env.d.ts`, add a `tsconfig.json`, and type-check with `npx tsc --noEmit`: the
[TypeScript page](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/typescript/#typing-a-page) has both declarations and a typed `main.ts`, checked with
`strict` on. The template's `main.js` is plain JavaScript: under `strict` it needs parameter types before `tsc` passes.

###### Try it on preview with Eternl or Lace

Preview is a public Cardano testnet, so real browser wallets work there. You need a Blockfrost project id for
preview and a funded preview key to pay the deployment:

```sh
export BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID=preview...   # stays in the dev server; never reaches the page
export JOUST_MNEMONIC="..."                       # a funded preview key that pays the deployment
npm run dev:preview
```

Switch Eternl or Lace to preview, reload the page, choose it in the wallet list and connect. The
[Deploy to preview](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/deploy-preview/) tutorial covers this and static hosting step by step.

##### What you just used

- **The toolchain engine** (in `@julclang/joust`) compiled `.jsc` or Java to a Cardano validator, a description and a
  typed client, in Node.
- **The runtime engine** (in `@julclang/joust-runtime`) prepared each transaction from the chain, in Node for the
  script and the test, and in a Web Worker for the page. It holds no keys.
- **The page verifier** (in `@julclang/state-client`) checked every prepared transaction against the contract's
  description and the chain before the wallet was asked to sign.
- **The validator** re-ran each method on chain and checked that the new state is what the method computes.

## Tutorials: Java

### Vault: deposits, time and payouts

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/vault/

In this tutorial you walk through [`examples/vault`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/vault), a
time-locked savings vault, and run it on a local Cardano network. Anyone can deposit; only the owner can withdraw,
and only after an unlock time; the owner closes it and takes everything back.

You will learn how a contract receives money (`@Payable`), pays it out (payouts in a `Result`), restricts a method to
one key (`@OnlyOwner`) and to a time (`@ValidAfter`), and returns its deposit when it ends (`@Destroy`).

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 

JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The Java path needs JDK 25. JOUST's releases are in the
BloxBean release repository, `https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/releases` (see the
[Java quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)); nothing is on Maven Central yet.

##### Before you start

- A JOUST checkout, with JuLC built as above, and `./gradlew build` passing.
- [Yaci DevKit](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/) running with Yaci Store:

  ```sh
  yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store
  ```

  This gives a local network with Yaci Store's Blockfrost-compatible API on `localhost:8080`, an admin API on
  `:10000`, and the Yaci Viewer explorer on `:5173`.

##### Build it

1. **The state.** A vault stores who owns it, when it unlocks, and how much it holds:

   ```java title="examples/vault/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/Vault.java"
   @StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 128)
   public class Vault {

       public record State(byte[] owner, BigInteger unlockAt, BigInteger total) {}

       /** An action that pays out returns the next state and its payouts. */
       public record Result(State state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}
   ```

   `owner` is a payment key hash (28 bytes), `unlockAt` a POSIX time in milliseconds. `maxDatumBytes = 128` is plenty
   for three fields, and keeps the deposit each vault locks at 2.2 ADA. `Result` is how an action returns payouts
   along with the next state: JuLC has no generic records, so you declare the record and JOUST recognises it by its
   component names.

   **What this taught:** the state is a plain record, stored as the UTxO's datum; its size bound sets the deposit.

2. **Open the vault, with a first deposit.**

   ```java
   /** Opens a vault, optionally with a first deposit; the deployer owns it. */
   @Init
   @Payable
   public static State open(BigInteger unlockAt, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(Clock.before(ctx, unlockAt), "unlockAt must be in the future");
       return new State(ctx.caller(), unlockAt, ctx.received());
   }
   ```

   `@Payable` lets the caller add lovelace; `ctx.received()` is how much. `ctx.caller()` is the deployer's key hash,
   verified on chain by a signature check, so the deployer becomes the owner. `Clock.before(ctx, unlockAt)` holds only
   if the whole transaction happens strictly before `unlockAt`.

   **What this taught:** `Ctx` gives authenticated facts about the transaction: who, how much, when.

3. **Let anyone deposit.**

   ```java
   /** Anyone can add funds. */
   @Action
   @Payable
   public static State deposit(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "deposit must be positive");
       return new State(s.owner(), s.unlockAt(), s.total().add(ctx.received()));
   }
   ```

   No signer annotation, so any account can call it. The generated validator requires the vault's new UTxO to hold
   exactly the old lovelace plus `received`, so `total` always matches the money actually held.

   **What this taught:** an action returns the next state; the validator enforces exact value accounting around it.

4. **Withdraw: owner only, after the unlock time, with a payout.**

   ```java
   /** The owner takes funds out once the vault is unlocked. */
   @Action
   @OnlyOwner
   @ValidAfter("unlockAt")
   public static Result withdraw(State s, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
       Require.that(amount.compareTo(s.total()) <= 0, "insufficient funds");
       return new Result(new State(s.owner(), s.unlockAt(), s.total().subtract(amount)), Payouts.of(s.owner(), amount));
   }
   ```

   - `@OnlyOwner` means `@SignedBy("owner")`: the transaction must be signed by the key in the current state's
     `owner` field.
   - `@ValidAfter("unlockAt")` requires the transaction's validity interval to start at or after `unlockAt`.
   - The method returns the payout instead of building an output. The validator checks that an output pays `amount`
     to the owner's key, **tagged** with this vault's input (so no other contract in the same transaction can count
     the same output), and that the vault keeps exactly the rest.

   **What this taught:** policies are annotations checked against the current state; money leaves only as payouts
   the validator verifies.

5. **Close: return everything.**

   ```java
   /** The owner closes an unlocked vault and takes everything, deposit included. */
   @Destroy
   @OnlyOwner
   @ValidAfter("unlockAt")
   public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       return Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance());
   }

   @View
   public static BigInteger total(State s) {
       return s.total();
   }
   ```

   In a destroy, `ctx.balance()` is everything the UTxO holds, the 2.2 ADA deposit included. The validator requires
   the payouts to add up to exactly that, and the thread token to be burned. The `@View` methods become client
   getters that read the chain without a transaction.

   **What this taught:** a destroy ends the instance and must allocate all of its funds.

The same contract in `.jsc` (a language preview), which lowers to equivalent Java (the init is always named `init` there).
Its build also writes `Vault.abi.json`, which you commit beside it:

```jsc title="Vault.jsc"
jsc 1
package org.example.vault

contract Vault(maxDatumBytes = 128) {
  state { owner: Key, unlockAt: Int, total: Int }

  init(unlockAt: Int) payable {
    require(before(unlockAt), "unlockAt must be in the future")
    return { owner: caller, unlockAt, total: received }
  }

  action deposit() payable {
    require(received > 0, "deposit must be positive")
    return { ...state, total: total + received }
  }

  action withdraw(amount: Int) only owner after unlockAt {
    require(amount > 0, "amount must be positive")
    require(amount <= total, "insufficient funds")
    pay(owner, amount)
    return { ...state, total: total - amount }
  }

  destroy close() only owner after unlockAt {
    pay(owner, balance)
  }

  view held(): Int = total
}
```

##### Run it

1. **Read the app.** The processor generated `VaultValidator` and `VaultClient`. The app drives the client:

   
   
**Java:**

   ```java title="examples/vault/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/VaultApp.java"
   var runtime = DevKit.runtime();
   var alice = DevKit.fundedAccount(500);
   var bob = DevKit.fundedAccount(500);

   long unlockAt = System.currentTimeMillis() + 45_000;
   var vault = VaultClient.deploy(runtime, alice, BigInteger.valueOf(unlockAt), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
   System.out.println("vault " + vault.instanceId() + ": total " + vault.total() + ", unlocks in 45 s");

   vault.deposit(bob, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(5)));
   System.out.println("bob deposited 5 ADA -> total " + vault.total());

   try {
       vault.withdraw(alice, ADA);
   } catch (RequireException e) {
       System.out.println("withdraw before unlock rejected off-chain: " + e.getMessage());
   }
   while (System.currentTimeMillis() < unlockAt + 2_000) Thread.sleep(1_000);

   vault.withdraw(alice, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(3)));
   System.out.println("alice withdrew 3 ADA -> total " + vault.total());

   var closed = vault.close(alice);
   System.out.println("closed: paid " + closed.payouts().get(0).lovelace() + " lovelace to alice");
   ```

   `DevKit` is the examples' helper module: a runtime for the local network (with a 20-second TTL) and funded test
   accounts.

   
   
**JavaScript:**

   ```js
   // The same flow with the generated JavaScript client (see Building apps for service, chain, deployment).

   const vault = new Vault({ service, chain, deployment });
   const { instance } = await vault.deploy(alice, { unlockAt: BigInt(Date.now() + 45_000) }, { lovelace: 10_000_000n });
   await instance.deposit(bob, {}, { lovelace: 5_000_000n });
   await instance.withdraw(alice, { amount: 1_000_000n }).catch((e) => console.log(e.message));   // too early
   // … after the unlock time:
   await instance.withdraw(alice, { amount: 3_000_000n });
   await instance.close(alice);
   ```

   
   

2. **Run it against DevKit.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:vault:run
   ```

   The first run also publishes the vault's script as a reference script (lines prefixed `[joust]` come from the
   runtime). The app's own output looks like this (your instance id differs):

   ```text
   vault 5c0e…9a1f: total 10000000, unlocks in 45 s
   bob deposited 5 ADA -> total 15000000
   withdraw before unlock rejected off-chain: Vault.withdraw: too early, the time in 'unlockAt' has not been reached
   alice withdrew 3 ADA -> total 12000000
   closed: paid 14200000 lovelace to alice
   ```

   The early withdraw never reached the chain: the client checked `@ValidAfter` against the state and refused. The
   close paid 14.2 ADA: the remaining 12 ADA plus the 2.2 ADA deposit.

3. **Look at it on chain.** Open Yaci Viewer at `http://localhost:5173` and find the transactions: the deploy mints
   one token, each action spends and recreates the vault's UTxO, the withdraw and the close each add a tagged payout
   output, and the close burns the token.

4. **Run the tests.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:vault:test
   ```

   `VaultTest` evaluates the compiled validator against transactions shaped like the runtime's, runs the attack suite
   on each accepted one, and checks the refusals: a withdraw before the unlock time (`@ValidAfter`), by a stranger
   (`@OnlyOwner`), a deposit claiming more than it sent. `VaultDevnetTest` runs the client end to end when DevKit is
   up, and is skipped otherwise.

##### What you built

A contract that holds funds safely with about 40 lines of logic. You wrote no transaction-building code and no
validator: the generated validator enforces the exact value of every step, the owner's signature, the unlock time,
tagged payouts and a full payout on close; the client refuses bad calls before they are signed.

- [Escrow and crowdfunding](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/escrow-crowdfund/)
- [Ctx, funds and payouts](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/)
- [Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/)
- [Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/)

### Escrow and crowdfunding

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/escrow-crowdfund/

Two contracts from the examples, each adding something the [vault](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/vault/) did not have:

- [`examples/escrow`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/escrow): three parties, **two ways to
  end** (two `@Destroy` methods), and a rule that mixes identity and time.
- [`examples/crowdfund`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/crowdfund): many backers in a
  **`JulcMap` in the state**, kept in canonical order with `SortedMaps`, refunds paid to the caller, and a capacity
  bounded by `maxDatumBytes`.

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 

JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The Java path needs JDK 25; JOUST's releases are in the
BloxBean release repository (see the [Java quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)). Start Yaci DevKit
with `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store` before the run steps.

##### Part 1: escrow

A buyer locks the price. The buyer (or an arbiter) releases it to the seller once the goods arrive; the seller (or
the arbiter) can refund the buyer at any time, and anyone can once the deadline has passed. Either way the instance
ends and everything it holds goes to the winner.

1. **The state and the opening.** The buyer deploys and funds the escrow in one step:

   ```java title="examples/escrow/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/escrow/Escrow.java"
   @StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 192)
   public class Escrow {

       public record State(byte[] buyer, byte[] seller, byte[] arbiter, BigInteger amount, BigInteger deadline) {}

       /** The buyer deposits the price. */
       @Init
       @Payable
       public static State open(byte[] seller, byte[] arbiter, BigInteger deadline, Ctx ctx) {
           Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "the escrow must be funded");
           Require.that(Clock.before(ctx, deadline), "deadline must be in the future");
           return new State(ctx.caller(), seller, arbiter, ctx.received(), deadline);
       }
   ```

   `seller` and `arbiter` are arguments, payment key hashes. The buyer is whoever signs the deploy.

   **What this taught:** a payable `@Init` creates and funds an instance in one transaction.

2. **Release: two `@Destroy` methods.** A contract may have several ways to end. `release` pays the seller:

   ```java
   /** Buyer or arbiter: the seller delivered, pay them. */
   @Destroy
   public static JulcList<Payout> release(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       boolean allowed = ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.buyer()) || ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.arbiter());
       Require.that(allowed, "only the buyer or the arbiter can release");
       return Payouts.of(s.seller(), ctx.balance());
   }
   ```

   "Buyer or arbiter" is a choice between two keys, so it is written in the body with `ctx.caller()` (verified by a
   signature) and `ByteStringLib.equals` (never `==` on `byte[]`).

   **What this taught:** use `Ctx` and `Require` for authorisation an annotation cannot express.

3. **Refund: identity or time.**

   ```java
   /** Seller or arbiter at any time, anyone after the deadline: give the buyer their money back. */
   @Destroy
   public static JulcList<Payout> refund(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       boolean party = ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.seller()) || ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.arbiter());
       Require.that(party || Clock.after(ctx, s.deadline()), "only the seller or the arbiter can refund before the deadline");
       return Payouts.of(s.buyer(), ctx.balance());
   }
   ```

   `Clock.after(ctx, t)` holds only if the whole transaction happens at or after `t`. After the deadline the buyer,
   or anyone, can get the money back, so funds can never be stuck if the seller and arbiter disappear.

   **What this taught:** `Clock` composes with other conditions; give every contract a way out.

   
> **Note:** 

   `.jsc` allows `after(t)` and `before(t)` at the top of a `require`, alone or under `&&` or `||`, so this refund
   fits in `.jsc` too (`caller == seller` compares bytes by value):

   ```jsc
   destroy refund() open {
     require(caller == seller || caller == arbiter || after(deadline), "only the seller or the arbiter can refund before the deadline")
     pay(buyer, balance)
   }
   ```

   `open` says anyone may call a method that pays out; the body's `require` is then its only guard.

   

4. **Run it.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:escrow:run
   ```

   ```java title="examples/escrow/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/escrow/EscrowApp.java"
   var deal = EscrowClient.deploy(runtime, buyer, Keys.pkh(seller), Keys.pkh(arbiter), deadline, price);
   System.out.println("escrow " + deal.instanceId() + " holds " + deal.lovelace() + " lovelace");

   try {
       deal.release(seller);   // the seller can't pay themselves
   } catch (RequireException e) {
       System.out.println("seller release rejected off-chain: " + e.getMessage());
   }
   var r = deal.release(buyer);
   System.out.println("buyer released: seller received " + r.payouts().get(0).lovelace() + " lovelace in " + r.txHash());
   ```

   The output (ids and hashes differ):

   ```text
   escrow 8f2d…41c7 holds 27400000 lovelace
   seller release rejected off-chain: only the buyer or the arbiter can release
   buyer released: seller received 27400000 lovelace in 3b9e…d012
   ```

   The escrow holds the 25 ADA price plus its 2.4 ADA deposit, and the release pays all of it to the seller: a
   destroy must allocate everything.

##### Part 2: crowdfund

Backers contribute before a deadline. After it, if the goal was reached the creator claims everything; if not, each
backer takes their contribution back, and the creator closes the empty campaign.

1. **A map in the state.**

   ```java title="examples/crowdfund/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/crowdfund/Crowdfund.java"
   @StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 1024)
   public class Crowdfund {

       public record State(byte[] creator, BigInteger goal, BigInteger deadline, BigInteger minContribution,
                           BigInteger raised, JulcMap<byte[], BigInteger> backers) {}

       public record Result(State state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}

       @Init
       public static State launch(BigInteger goal, BigInteger deadline, BigInteger minContribution, Ctx ctx) {
           Require.that(goal.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "goal must be positive");
           Require.that(minContribution.compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(2_000_000)) >= 0, "minimum contribution is at least 2 ADA");
           Require.that(Clock.before(ctx, deadline), "deadline must be in the future");
           JulcMap<byte[], BigInteger> none = JulcMap.empty();
           return new State(ctx.caller(), goal, deadline, minContribution, BigInteger.ZERO, none);
       }
   ```

   `backers` maps each backer's key hash to what they put in. The whole map lives in the datum, so its size is
   bounded by `maxDatumBytes = 1024` (which sets a 6 ADA deposit).

   **What this taught:** collections can live in the state, and their size has a price.

2. **Contribute, keeping the map canonical.**

   ```java
   @Action
   @Payable
   public static State contribute(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(Clock.before(ctx, s.deadline()), "the campaign has ended");
       Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(s.minContribution()) >= 0, "below the minimum contribution");
       BigInteger before = SortedMaps.getOr(s.backers(), ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO);
       JulcMap<byte[], BigInteger> backers = SortedMaps.put(s.backers(), ctx.caller(), before.add(ctx.received()));
       return new State(s.creator(), s.goal(), s.deadline(), s.minContribution(), s.raised().add(ctx.received()), backers);
   }
   ```

   Why `SortedMaps` and not `JulcMap.insert`? `insert` prepends, so the map's order depends on who contributed when.
   But cardano-client-lib writes inline datums in canonical CBOR, which sorts map keys. A map out of canonical order
   would be written differently from the state the validator recomputes, and the call would fail on chain. (It did, on
   DevKit, whenever backers arrived out of key order; that is how JOUST found the problem.) `SortedMaps.put` keeps the
   keys in canonical order on the JVM and on chain alike, and the runtime refuses a non-canonical state before it
   submits anything.

   **What this taught:** state maps must be canonical; `SortedMaps` does it for `byte[]`-keyed amounts.

3. **Refund the caller.**

   ```java
   /** The goal was missed: a backer takes their contribution back. */
   @Action
   public static Result refund(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(Clock.after(ctx, s.deadline()), "the campaign is still running");
       Require.that(s.raised().compareTo(s.goal()) < 0, "the goal was reached: no refunds");
       Require.that(s.backers().containsKey(ctx.caller()), "nothing to refund");
       BigInteger amount = s.backers().get(ctx.caller());
       State next = new State(s.creator(), s.goal(), s.deadline(), s.minContribution(), s.raised().subtract(amount),
               SortedMaps.remove(s.backers(), ctx.caller()));
       return new Result(next, Payouts.of(ctx.caller(), amount));
   }
   ```

   The payout goes to `ctx.caller()`, the verified signer, so a backer can only refund themselves. `containsKey` comes
   before `get`, because `get` on a missing key aborts on chain without a message.

   **What this taught:** an action can pay the caller; check map membership before reading.

4. **Claim or close: `@SignedBy("creator")`.**

   ```java
   /** The goal was reached: the creator takes everything. */
   @Destroy
   @SignedBy("creator")
   public static JulcList<Payout> claim(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(Clock.after(ctx, s.deadline()), "the campaign is still running");
       Require.that(s.raised().compareTo(s.goal()) >= 0, "the goal was not reached");
       return Payouts.of(s.creator(), ctx.balance());
   }

   /** The goal was missed and every backer has been refunded: the creator closes the campaign. */
   @Destroy
   @SignedBy("creator")
   public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(Clock.after(ctx, s.deadline()), "the campaign is still running");
       Require.that(s.backers().isEmpty(), "backers still have funds in the campaign");
       return Payouts.of(s.creator(), ctx.balance());
   }
   ```

   `@SignedBy("creator")` names the state field whose key must sign. Two destroys again: one when the goal was met,
   one after a failed campaign is emptied.

   **What this taught:** `@SignedBy` works with any `byte[]` field, not only `owner`.

5. **Capacity.** Each backer adds an entry to the datum. With `maxDatumBytes = 1024`, the harness test fills the
   campaign with 2 ADA contributions until the next one would not fit: 27 backers. Two choices keep this safe:

   - the minimum contribution (at least 2 ADA) makes filling the campaign expensive;
   - refunds, claims and closes only shrink the state, so they never fail on size. The test checks a refund at
     capacity (286.6M CPU, 559k memory, well within limits).

   A contract that needs many more entries should use a [MerkleMap](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/).

   **What this taught:** bound growth with `maxDatumBytes`, add an economic floor, and keep the shrinking paths open.

6. **Run it.** The app runs a campaign that misses its goal:

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:crowdfund:run
   ```

   ```java title="examples/crowdfund/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/crowdfund/CrowdfundApp.java"
   long deadline = System.currentTimeMillis() + 60_000;
   var campaign = CrowdfundClient.deploy(runtime, creator, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(100)),
           BigInteger.valueOf(deadline), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TWO));
   System.out.println("campaign " + campaign.instanceId() + " launched; goal 100 ADA");

   campaign.contribute(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
   campaign.contribute(ben, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(5)));
   campaign.contribute(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(3)));
   System.out.println("raised " + campaign.raised() + "; ann " + campaign.contributionOf(Keys.pkh(ann)));

   while (System.currentTimeMillis() < deadline + 2_000) Thread.sleep(1_000);
   campaign.refund(ann);
   campaign.refund(ben);
   System.out.println("goal missed: both backers refunded; raised now " + campaign.raised());
   campaign.close(creator);
   System.out.println("creator closed the campaign");
   ```

   ```text
   campaign 1a7c…e930 launched; goal 100 ADA
   raised 18000000; ann 13000000
   goal missed: both backers refunded; raised now 0
   creator closed the campaign
   ```

   Ann's two contributions were added under one key; after the deadline each backer got their own amount back, and
   the creator closed the empty campaign and took back the 6 ADA deposit.

##### From JavaScript

The generated JavaScript clients make the same calls from a page or Node, with CIP-30 wallets:

```js
const campaign = new Crowdfund({ service, chain, deployment });
const { instance } = await campaign.deploy(creatorWallet,
  { goal: 100_000_000n, deadline: BigInt(Date.now() + 60_000), minContribution: 2_000_000n });
await instance.contribute(annWallet, {}, { lovelace: 10_000_000n });
// After the deadline:
await instance.refund(annWallet, {});
await instance.close(creatorWallet, {});
```

See [JavaScript clients](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/).

##### Test them

```sh
./gradlew :examples:escrow:test :examples:crowdfund:test
```

Each example's harness test evaluates the compiled validator for its paths and runs the attack suite on each accepted
transaction. `EscrowTest` also checks the refusals: a release by the seller, and a refund by a stranger before the
deadline (accepted after it). `CrowdfundTest` checks that contributions keep the map canonical, that a refund pays the
caller, and the capacity case above. The `…DevnetTest` classes run the clients end to end when DevKit is up, and are
skipped otherwise.

##### What you learned

- A contract can have several `@Destroy` methods, each with its own rules.
- `Ctx.caller` with `ByteStringLib.equals` expresses "one of these parties"; `@SignedBy("field")` expresses "this one".
- `Clock.after` and `Clock.before` turn deadlines into rules that hold for the whole transaction.
- A `JulcMap` in the state must stay in canonical key order: `SortedMaps`.
- `maxDatumBytes` caps growth; design the shrinking paths so they always work.

### Token balances in a MerkleMap

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/token-merklemap/

In this tutorial you run `examples/token`: a fungible token in the account model, where every holder's balance sits
in one [MerkleMap](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/). The datum stays about 100 bytes however many holders there are. You will
run it twice: from Java against Yaci DevKit, then from a browser page that prepares its own transactions and reads
balances from the map's mirror in a Web Worker.

You need [Yaci DevKit](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/) running: `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store` (Yaci Store's API
on `:8080`, the admin API on `:10000`).

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 
JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The Java part runs in a JOUST checkout with JDK 25; the
page part needs Node 22 or newer and the npm packages. Both are covered in the steps below and in the quick starts ([Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/), [npm](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/)).

##### The contract

```java title="examples/token/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/Token.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 160)
public class Token {

    public record State(byte[] admin, BigInteger supply, MerkleMap balances) {}

    @Init
    public static State create(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO, MerkleMaps.empty());
    }

    /** The admin creates new tokens for a holder. */
    @Action
    @SignedBy("admin")
    public static State mint(State s, byte[] to, BigInteger amount) {
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
        BigInteger balance = MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), to, BigInteger.ZERO);
        return new State(s.admin(), s.supply().add(amount), MerkleMaps.putInt(s.balances(), to, balance.add(amount)));
    }

    /** A holder sends tokens; an emptied balance is removed from the map. */
    @Action
    public static State transfer(State s, byte[] to, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
        BigInteger fromBalance = MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO);
        Require.that(fromBalance.compareTo(amount) >= 0, "insufficient balance");
        BigInteger left = fromBalance.subtract(amount);
        MerkleMap debited = left.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) == 0
                ? MerkleMaps.remove(s.balances(), ctx.caller())
                : MerkleMaps.putInt(s.balances(), ctx.caller(), left);
        BigInteger toBalance = MerkleMaps.getInt(debited, to, BigInteger.ZERO);   // reads the debit on a self-transfer
        return new State(s.admin(), s.supply(), MerkleMaps.putInt(debited, to, toBalance.add(amount)));
    }

    /** A holder destroys some of their tokens. */
    @Action
    public static State burn(State s, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
        BigInteger balance = MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO);
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0 && balance.compareTo(amount) >= 0, "cannot burn that much");
        BigInteger left = balance.subtract(amount);
        MerkleMap updated = left.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) == 0
                ? MerkleMaps.remove(s.balances(), ctx.caller())
                : MerkleMaps.putInt(s.balances(), ctx.caller(), left);
        return new State(s.admin(), s.supply().subtract(amount), updated);
    }

    /** The admin closes the token once everything has been burned. */
    @Destroy
    @SignedBy("admin")
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(s.supply().compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) == 0 && MerkleMaps.isEmpty(s.balances()),
                "tokens are still in circulation");
        return Payouts.of(s.admin(), ctx.balance());
    }

    @View
    public static BigInteger balanceOf(State s, byte[] holder) {
        return MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), holder, BigInteger.ZERO);
    }
}
```

Three things to notice:
- `balances` is a `MerkleMap`, a direct component of the state, created with `MerkleMaps.empty()`.
- Every read and write goes through `MerkleMaps`. The methods never look at the map's internals.
- An emptied balance is removed, so `close` can require `MerkleMaps.isEmpty(...)` and never discard live balances.

##### Part 1: from Java

1. **Check the example compiles.** From a JOUST checkout, with JDK 25:

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:token:compileJava
   ```

   The annotation processor generates `TokenValidator` (the on-chain script, compiled by JuLC) and `TokenClient` (the
   typed Java client) under `examples/token/build/generated/`. Because the state has a MerkleMap, every redeemer
   gains the map witnesses and the validator looks for the map verifier's claims.

   *What this taught:* a MerkleMap field changes what is generated, not how you write the method.

2. **Run the tests.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:token:test
   ```

   [`TokenTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/token/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/TokenTest.java)
   runs each method the way the runtime does (reads from an in-memory mirror, then proofs), evaluates the compiled
   validator against the resulting transactions, runs the attack suite on each, and attacks the map witnesses directly:
   a forged read value, a read claimed absent, a missing or reordered write. Every one is rejected. The DevKit test,
   `TokenDevnetTest`, runs too when DevKit is up.

   *What this taught:* the same `transfer` runs on the JVM and on chain, and the proofs are what tie the two together.

3. **Run the app on DevKit.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:token:run
   ```

   [`TokenApp`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/token/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/TokenApp.java)
   deploys a token, mints 1,000 to Ann and 500 to Ben, and has Ann send Ben 250:

   ```java title="examples/token/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/TokenApp.java"
   var token = TokenClient.deploy(runtime, admin);
   System.out.println("token " + token.instanceId() + " deployed (script read by reference)");
   token.mint(admin, Keys.pkh(ann), BigInteger.valueOf(1_000));
   token.mint(admin, Keys.pkh(ben), BigInteger.valueOf(500));
   token.transfer(ann, Keys.pkh(ben), BigInteger.valueOf(250));
   System.out.println("ann " + token.balanceOf(Keys.pkh(ann)) + ", ben " + token.balanceOf(Keys.pkh(ben))
           + ", supply " + token.supply());
   ```

   It prints `ann 750, ben 750, supply 1500`. Look at the transfer in Yaci Viewer (`http://localhost:5173`, under
   the contract's address): beside the token's spend there is a zero withdrawal from the map verifier, whose redeemer
   carries the two reads and two writes.
   The first map call of a network also publishes the verifier's reference script and registers its stake credential.

   *What this taught:* `balanceOf` is a `@View`, run on the JVM against the mirror with no transaction; the transfer
   carries its proofs to the shared verifier.

4. **Lose the mirror and carry on.** The runtime keeps the map in RocksDB at `./.joust/mpf` by default. A process
   that never saw this map rebuilds it from the chain. The DevKit test shows it with a fresh in-memory store:

   ```java title="examples/token/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/TokenDevnetTest.java"
   // A process that never saw this map (a restart, another machine): a fresh node store. Its mirror is rebuilt from
   // the chain history (the claims in the map-verifier redeemers, each new root checked; ADR-0015 §13.12 M4).
   var fresh = TokenClient.at(DevKit.runtime(new org.julclang.state.runtime.InMemoryNodeStore()), token.instanceId());
   assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(240), fresh.balanceOf(Keys.pkh(holders[1])), "read through the rebuilt mirror");
   fresh.transfer(holders[1], Keys.pkh(holders[0]), BigInteger.valueOf(40));
   // And the first runtime, which missed that write, catches up the same way.
   token.transfer(holders[0], Keys.pkh(holders[1]), BigInteger.valueOf(40));
   ```

   *What this taught:* the chain holds everything needed to rebuild a map; the mirror is a cache, checked against the
   root on chain.

##### Part 2: from a page

Now the same contract in a browser. The page runs JOUST's runtime engine (Wasm) in a Web Worker, which prepares each
transaction; the page verifies it before the key signs. The worker also keeps the map's mirror, in IndexedDB.

1. **Create a project.** With Node 22 or newer:

   ```sh
   npm create joust@latest token-app -- --template web --lang java
   cd token-app
   npm install
   ```

   The web template in Java holds a Counter contract (`Counter.java`), a page and a test.

2. **Swap in the token.** Delete `contracts/app/Counter.java` and `test/counter.test.js`. Copy
   `examples/token/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/Token.java` to `contracts/app/Token.java` and change
   its first line to `package app;`.

   
   - contracts
     - app
       - Token.java
   - page
     - index.html
     - main.js
     - engine.worker.js
   - joust.config.json
   - vite.config.js
   

   `npm run build` compiles it with the toolchain (no JDK) into `build/joust/`: the validator, the contract's
   description and a typed client, `Token.js`.

   *What this taught:* the npm path compiles the same Java source, through JuLC in Wasm.

3. **Write the page.** Replace `page/index.html`:

   ```html title="page/index.html"
   <!doctype html>
   <title>Token</title>
   <h1>Token</h1>
   <p>
     <button id="create">Create a token</button>
     <button id="mint">Mint 1000 to me</button>
     <button id="send">Send 250</button>
   </p>
   <p>Instance: <code id="id">none</code></p>
   <p>Mine: <b id="mine">0</b> · Theirs: <b id="theirs">0</b> · Supply: <b id="supply">0</b></p>
   <pre id="log"></pre>
   <script type="module" src="./main.js"></script>
   ```

   And `page/main.js`. `engine.worker.js` stays as the template has it (`import '@julclang/joust-runtime/worker';`).

   ```js title="page/main.js"

   const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
   const log = (line) => { $('log').textContent = line + '\n' + $('log').textContent; };

   // The chain through joust dev's /chain proxy; the engine in a worker (it holds no keys and is not trusted).
   const chain = blockfrostChain(new URL(net.chain, location.href).href);
   const service = engineWorker(new Worker(new URL('./engine.worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' }), net);
   const deployment = net.deployments['app.Token'];
   const token = new Token({ service, chain, deployment });

   // An in-page DevKit key, kept across reloads (browser wallets cannot join a DevKit).
   const mnemonic = localStorage.getItem('joust.devkitKey') ?? generateMnemonic(wordlist, 256);
   localStorage.setItem('joust.devkitKey', mnemonic);
   const me = devWallet({ chain, mnemonic, networkId: net.networkId });
   const other = 'ab'.repeat(28);   // any 28-byte key hash
   let id = localStorage.getItem('joust.token');

   /** A balance from the worker's mirror: the value is an unsigned big-endian integer; an absent key is 0. */
   async function balanceOf(root, keyHash) {
     const hex = await service.mapValue(root, keyHash, [deployment.policy + id]);
     return hex ? BigInt('0x' + hex) : 0n;
   }

   async function show() {
     if (!id) return;
     $('id').textContent = id;
     const s = await token.at(id).state();     // { admin, supply, balances: { root, reads, writes } }
     if (!s) return log('the token is closed');
     $('supply').textContent = s.supply;
     $('mine').textContent = await balanceOf(s.balances.root, me.keyHash);
     $('theirs').textContent = await balanceOf(s.balances.root, other);
   }

   async function run(what, call) {
     log(`${what}…`);
     try {
       await call();
       log(`${what}: on chain`);
       await show();
     } catch (e) {
       log(`${what}: ${e.message}`);
     }
   }

   $('create').onclick = () => run('create', async () => {
     await fetch('/dev/topup', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ address: me.address, ada: 1000 }) });
     for (let i = 0; i < 60 && !(await chain.utxosAt(me.address)).length; i++) await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1000));
     id = (await token.deploy(me, {})).instance.id;
     localStorage.setItem('joust.token', id);
   });
   $('mint').onclick = () => run('mint 1000', () => token.at(id).mint(me, { to: me.keyHash, amount: 1000n }));
   $('send').onclick = () => run('send 250', () => token.at(id).transfer(me, { to: other, amount: 250n }));

   await service.ready;
   log('engine ready');
   await show();
   ```

   Three calls do the map work:
   - `token.at(id).state()` decodes the datum. The map field is just `{ root, reads, writes }`: the datum holds only
     the root.
   - `service.mapValue(root, key, units)` asks the worker's mirror for one key under that root. `units` is the
     instance's token (policy plus instance id): if the mirror has never seen the root, it rebuilds the map from that
     token's chain history first.
   - `mint` and `transfer` look like any other call. The engine discovers the keys each method reads, asks the mirror
     for proofs, checks every proof against the on-chain root, and attaches the map verifier.

   *What this taught:* a page never needs the whole map; it asks for the keys it shows.

4. **Run it.**

   ```sh
   npm run dev
   ```

   `joust dev` builds, deploys the Token (and the map verifier) to DevKit, and serves the page at
   `http://127.0.0.1:5178`. Click **Create a token** (it tops up the in-page key first), **Mint 1000 to me**, then
   **Send 250**. The page shows `Mine: 750 · Theirs: 250 · Supply: 1000`.

5. **Reload, then try another browser profile.** Reload the page: the balances come back without reading the chain's
   history, because the worker kept the map in IndexedDB (database `joust-mirrors`).

   Now open the page in a private window, which starts with an empty IndexedDB and `localStorage`. In its console, run
   `localStorage.setItem('joust.token', '<the instance id>')` and reload. The worker has no copy of the map, so the
   first `mapValue` rebuilds it from the token's chain history, checking every claim against its root, and the page
   shows `Theirs: 250 · Supply: 1000`. `Mine` is 0: the private window made itself a new key.

   *What this taught:* mirrors are caches. The chain is the source of truth, and a second device catches up from it
   without trusting anyone.

##### What you built

- A token whose datum is constant-size, with each call proving only the balances it touches.
- The same Java contract driven from a JVM app and from a browser page with no JDK.
- Balances read from a mirror that survives reloads and rebuilds itself from the chain.

`js/joust/test/page.test.js` runs this flow in Chromium (its third test): a reload served from IndexedDB, a fresh
profile rebuilding from history, and the page built as static files.

  - [MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/)
  - [MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/)
  - [Pages: worker, Vite, static builds](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/)
  - [Bank: owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/bank-owned-objects/)

### Bank: owned objects

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/bank-owned-objects/

In this tutorial you run `examples/bank`: a bank with shared settings (an admin, a paused flag, a withdrawal limit)
and one account per customer. Each account is an [owned object](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/), its own UTxO, so two
customers can deposit and withdraw in the same block without queueing behind each other. You will see the shared
settings read without being spent, and an account closed while the bank is paused.

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 
JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The tutorial runs in a JOUST checkout with JDK 25; release
candidates for your own projects are in the BloxBean release repository (see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)).
You also need Yaci DevKit: `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`.

##### The contract

```java title="examples/bank/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/bank/Bank.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 160)
public class Bank {

    public record State(byte[] admin, boolean paused, BigInteger withdrawLimit) {}

    @Owned
    public record Account(byte[] owner, BigInteger balance) {}

    public record Withdrawal(Account state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}

    @Init
    public static State init(BigInteger withdrawLimit, Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(ctx.caller(), false, withdrawLimit);
    }

    @Action
    @SignedBy("admin")
    public static State setPaused(State s, boolean paused) {
        return new State(s.admin(), paused, s.withdrawLimit());
    }

    /** Opens an account for the caller, with a first deposit. */
    @OwnedInit
    @Payable
    public static Account open(@Shared State bank, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(!bank.paused(), "the bank is paused");
        return new Account(ctx.caller(), ctx.received());
    }

    @OwnedAction
    @Payable
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static Account deposit(Account a, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "deposit must be positive");
        return new Account(a.owner(), a.balance().add(ctx.received()));
    }

    /** Takes money out, within the bank's limit, unless the bank is paused. */
    @OwnedAction
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static Withdrawal withdraw(Account a, @Shared State bank, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(!bank.paused(), "the bank is paused");
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0 && amount.compareTo(bank.withdrawLimit()) <= 0,
                "amount outside the withdrawal limit");
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(a.balance()) <= 0, "insufficient balance");
        return new Withdrawal(new Account(a.owner(), a.balance().subtract(amount)), Payouts.of(a.owner(), amount));
    }

    /** The owner closes the account and takes everything (works even when the bank is paused). */
    @OwnedDestroy
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(Account a, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(a.owner(), ctx.balance());
    }
}
```

- `State` is the instance: one UTxO, changed only by the admin's `@Action`s.
- `Account` is `@Owned`: every `open` creates a new UTxO holding an `Account`, with a 29-byte token starting `0x4F`.
- `@Shared State bank` gives `open` and `withdraw` the bank's settings through a reference input. They read it; they
  never spend it.
- `close` takes no `@Shared` parameter. That makes it the *escape hatch*: it needs nothing from the bank, so it works
  whatever the bank's state. The processor requires one for every owned type.

##### Run it

1. **Run the harness tests.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:bank:test --tests '*BankTest'
   ```

   [`BankTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/bank/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/bank/BankTest.java)
   evaluates the compiled validator on account transactions and runs the attack suite on each. Look at the tests that
   must fail: `withdraw_byAStranger_rejected` (`@SignedBy("owner")` names the account's field),
   `sharedReadOfAnotherInstance_rejected` (a reference to another bank does not count),
   `anObjectSpentWithASharedRedeemer_rejected` (an account token cannot take an instance's redeemer) and
   `openUnderAnObjectInsteadOfAnInstance_rejected`. Then `close_escapeHatchWorksWhilePaused`, which asserts that the
   close transaction has no reference inputs at all.

   *What this taught:* the token's kind and the `Holding(instance, …)` datum are what keep objects, instances and
   other banks apart.

2. **Run the app on DevKit.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:bank:run
   ```

   ```java title="examples/bank/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/bank/BankApp.java"
   var bank = BankClient.deploy(runtime, admin, ada.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(20)));
   var acct = bank.open(ann, ada.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(30)));
   acct.withdraw(ann, ada.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
   System.out.println("account " + acct.objectId() + " balance " + acct.value().balance());
   acct.close(ann);
   System.out.println("closed");
   ```

   It deploys a bank with a 20 ADA withdrawal limit, opens Ann's account with 30 ADA, withdraws 10, and prints the
   account's id (29 bytes, so 58 hex characters starting `4f`) and a balance of `20000000` lovelace. Then it closes the
   account, and Ann gets everything back, the account's deposit included.

   *What this taught:* `bank.open` returns a typed handle (`AccountObject`) whose methods are the `@OwnedAction`s and
   `@OwnedDestroy`s.

3. **Two customers at once.** The DevKit test runs two customers from separate threads:

   ```java title="examples/bank/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/bank/BankDevnetTest.java"
   var annAcct = bank.open(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(30)));
   var benAcct = bank.open(ben, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(40)));

   // Both customers deposit and withdraw at the same time: separate UTxOs, so no contention.
   var a = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
       annAcct.deposit(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(5)));
       annAcct.withdraw(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
   });
   var b = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
       benAcct.deposit(ben, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(7)));
       benAcct.withdraw(ben, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(20)));
   });
   CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join();
   assertEquals(ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(25)), annAcct.value().balance());
   assertEquals(ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(27)), benAcct.value().balance());
   ```

   Run it with `./gradlew :examples:bank:test --tests '*BankDevnetTest'` while DevKit is up. Both threads finish
   without a contention retry: each spends only its own account, and both read the bank by reference.

   *What this taught:* reference inputs do not contend, so a shared configuration costs nothing in parallelism.

4. **Pause the bank, then close anyway.** The same test continues:

   ```java
   assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> annAcct.withdraw(ben, ADA), "not the owner");
   assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> annAcct.withdraw(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(21))), "over limit");

   bank.setPaused(admin, true);
   assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> annAcct.withdraw(ann, ADA), "paused");
   // The escape hatch: closing needs no bank state.
   var closed = annAcct.close(ann);
   ```

   The refusals come from the JVM run of the same methods, before anything is submitted: `RequireException` carries
   the `Require.that` message. The close pays Ann her 25 ADA plus the account's deposit.

   *What this taught:* an admin can stop new activity, but can never trap customers' funds.

##### From a page

The `dapp` example puts the bank in a browser page, using a typed client generated from the contract's description.
Follow [its README](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/dapp/README.md) to run it
(`./gradlew :examples:dapp:run`, then `http://localhost:8095`). Open an account, deposit, withdraw and close; every
transaction is checked by the page before the wallet signs. The calls are short:

```js title="examples/dapp/frontend/src/main.js (adapted)"
const inst = bank.at(bankId);
await inst.open(wallet, {}, { lovelace: 30_000_000n });               // @OwnedInit @Payable

const accounts = (await inst.objects()).filter((o) => o.value.owner === myKeyHash);
const acct = inst.account(accounts[0].id);                           // a handle per owned type
await acct.deposit(wallet, {}, { lovelace: 5_000_000n });
await acct.withdraw(wallet, { amount: 10_000_000n });
await acct.close(wallet);
```

`inst.objects()` lists every owned object of the instance on chain, each with its id, type, decoded value and
lovelace.

##### What you built

- Per-customer state with no contention between customers.
- Shared settings read by reference, so the admin can pause new activity.
- An escape hatch that keeps every customer's funds reachable.

##### Going further

- **Several owned types and moves.** `examples/guild` has heroes and items, and moves a hero to another guild with
  `@Into` and `@Admits`; see [Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/#moving-an-object-to-another-instance).
- **Maps inside objects.** `Armory` in the same example gives each player a vault with a MerkleMap inventory.
- **Objects holding tokens.** The [DEX tutorial](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/dex-assets/) ends with a marketplace whose listings hold
  their NFT.
