### Pool: batched intents

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/pool-batched-intents/

In this tutorial you run `examples/pool`: anyone donates to a pool, and anyone buys a ticket whose price rises by a
step with every sale. Both write the same shared state, so if users called the pool directly they would collide on its
one UTxO. Instead they lock [intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/) concurrently, and a batcher applies them together.
You will lock six intents at once, cancel one, watch the batch skip an expired one, and see the order-dependent price
protected by a bound.

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 
JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The tutorial runs in a JOUST checkout with JDK 25; release
candidates for your own projects are in the BloxBean release repository (see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)).
You also need Yaci DevKit: `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`.

##### The contract

```java title="examples/pool/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/pool/Pool.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 192)
public class Pool {

    public record State(byte[] admin, BigInteger donated, BigInteger sold, BigInteger price, BigInteger step) {}

    public record Sale(State state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}

    @Init
    public static State init(BigInteger price, BigInteger step, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(price.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0 && step.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) >= 0, "bad pricing");
        return new State(ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO, BigInteger.ZERO, price, step);
    }

    @Action
    @Batched
    @Payable
    public static State donate(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(1_000_000)) >= 0, "donate at least 1 ADA");
        return new State(s.admin(), s.donated().add(ctx.received()), s.sold(), s.price(), s.step());
    }

    @Action
    @Batched(only = true)
    @Payable
    public static Sale buy(State s, BigInteger maxPrice, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(s.price().compareTo(maxPrice) <= 0, "price above the buyer's bound");
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(s.price()) >= 0, "pays less than the price");
        BigInteger change = ctx.received().subtract(s.price());
        State next = new State(s.admin(), s.donated(), s.sold().add(BigInteger.ONE), s.price().add(s.step()), s.step());
        if (change.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0) {
            return new Sale(next, Payouts.of(ctx.caller(), change));
        }
        return new Sale(next, Payouts.none());
    }

    @Action
    @SignedBy("admin")
    public static Sale withdraw(State s, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0 && amount.compareTo(ctx.balance()) <= 0, "bad amount");
        return new Sale(s, Payouts.of(s.admin(), amount));
    }
}
```

- `donate` is `@Batched`: it runs as an intent, or as a direct call.
- `buy` is `@Batched(only = true)`: intents only, so nobody can spend the pool with a direct buy and invalidate the
  batch being built.
- `buy` depends on order: each ticket costs more than the last. The buyer can't know the price when the batch runs, so
  they pay a ceiling, bound it with `maxPrice`, and get the change back as a payout.
- Inside a batch, `ctx.caller()` is the intent's owner and `ctx.received()` its payment. `withdraw` is the admin's
  ordinary direct call.

##### Run it

1. **Run the harness tests.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:pool:test --tests '*PoolTest'
   ```

   [`PoolTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/pool/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/pool/PoolTest.java)
   builds a batch of three (a donation and two buys), checks that the on-chain fold gives the same state as the JVM
   fold (5 ADA donated, 2 sold, price 12 ADA), and runs the attack suite on it. Then come the attacks specific to
   batches: a step's change paid to someone else, a direct redeemer on the instance, an intent left out, one past its
   deadline, a cancel composed with the batch, a refund to another stake key, an intent of another instance riding
   along, wrong redeemer kinds, an empty batch. `buyIsIntentOnly` checks that no direct `Buy` redeemer even exists.
   `batchCost_growsWithTheNumberOfIntents` prints the cost of batches of 1, 5, 10 and 15 donations.

   *What this taught:* the batch is the same method folded on chain, and every way to cheat an intent's owner is a
   rejected transaction.

2. **Run the DevKit flow.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:pool:test --tests '*PoolDevnetTest'
   ```

   [`PoolDevnetTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/pool/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/pool/PoolDevnetTest.java)
   deploys a pool at 10 ADA a ticket, rising by 1 ADA, then has six users lock intents at the same time:

   ```java title="examples/pool/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/pool/PoolDevnetTest.java"
   var pool = PoolClient.deploy(runtime, admin, ada(10), ada(1));
   Instant later = Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(30));

   // Six users lock intents at the same time: each spends only their own UTxOs, so nobody contends.
   futures.add(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> switch (k) {
       case 0, 1 -> pool.donateIntent(u, ada(5 + k), later);
       // Buyers accept up to 20 ADA and pay 20: the change comes back as a payout.
       case 2, 3, 4 -> pool.buyIntent(u, ada(20), ada(20), later);
       // Expires before any batch window could end (the batch window is about 20 s).
       default -> pool.donateIntent(u, ada(3), Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofSeconds(5)));
   }));
   ```

   All six land: each intent spends only its owner's UTxOs. `pool.pendingIntents()` lists six.

   *What this taught:* locking an intent never touches the pool's UTxO, so users never contend.

3. **Cancel one.**

   ```java
   intents.get(1).cancel(users.get(1));
   assertFalse(intents.get(1).isPending());
   ```

   Only the owner can cancel: the cancel burns the intent token and returns everything it held.

4. **Batch.** Any account can be the batcher:

   ```java
   var result = pool.batch(batcher, 8);
   System.out.println("[pool batch] " + result.txHash() + " applied " + result.applied().size() + " skipped " + result.skipped());
   ```

   The batch applies four intents (one donation of 5 ADA, three buys) and skips the one whose deadline passed, with
   the reason in `skipped`. The pool ends at `donated` 5 ADA, `sold` 3 and `price` 13 ADA: the tickets cost 10, 11 and
   12 in ledger order, and each buyer got their change back in an output tagged with their own intent.

   *What this taught:* the batcher picks which intents to include and when, but each intent's bound (`maxPrice`) and
   deadline still hold.

5. **Clean up.** The expired intent stays pending until its owner takes it back, and the admin's direct call still
   works:

   ```java
   assertTrue(intents.get(5).isPending());
   intents.get(5).cancel(users.get(5));
   var w = pool.withdraw(admin, ada(5));
   ```

##### The same flow in JavaScript

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Pool)"
const pool = await contract('Pool', admin);
const p = pool.at((await pool.deploy(admin, { price: 10n * ADA, step: ADA })).instance);
const d0 = (await p.intent(u0, 'donate', {}, { lovelace: 5n * ADA })).intent;
const d1 = (await p.intent(u1, 'donate', {}, { lovelace: 6n * ADA })).intent;
// buy is batch-only (@Batched(only = true)): the buyer pays 20 and accepts up to 20; the change is paid out.
await p.intent(u2, 'buy', { maxPrice: 20n * ADA }, { lovelace: 20n * ADA });
await p.intent(u3, 'buy', { maxPrice: 20n * ADA }, { lovelace: 20n * ADA });
await assert.rejects(async () => p.call(u2, 'buy', { maxPrice: 1n }, { lovelace: ADA }), /no action/);   // batch-only
await assert.rejects(p.cancelIntent(u0, d1));                  // only its owner withdraws it
await p.cancelIntent(u1, d1);
const b = await p.batch(batcher);
assert.equal(b.applied.length, 3, 'a donation and two buys');
const s = await p.state();                                     // donated 5 ADA, sold 2, price 12 ADA
```

The test also tampers with every engine-built intent lock and batch, and checks that each is refused before the
wallet is asked to sign. With a generated client (`npm run build` in a JOUST project), `instance.donate(wallet, {}, pay)`
locks an intent, and `pool.contract.at(id)` gives `pendingIntents`, `cancelIntent` and `batch`.

##### What you built

- A shared total and an order-dependent price that many users write at once, without contention.
- Users protected against the batcher's choices by their own bounds and deadlines.
- A batch that anyone can run, paying only the fee.

> **Limits to remember:** 
About 8 intents fit in one batch (memory bound); the batcher halves the batch when it cannot build one. Batched
actions cannot yet be combined with MerkleMaps or native assets. See [Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/#limits).

##### Next steps

  - [Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/)
  - [DEX: native assets and LP tokens](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/dex-assets/)
  - [Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/)
  - [.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/)

### DEX: native assets and LP tokens

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/dex-assets/

In this tutorial you run `examples/dex`: a constant-product automated market maker (AMM) for one ADA/token pair. The
pool holds both reserves in its UTxO, mints LP (liquidity provider) tokens under the contract's own policy, and swaps
both ways with a 0.3% fee and a minimum-output bound. Every piece of
[native assets, mints and sends](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/) appears: `Funds`, `accepted`, `mint` and `Send`. At
the end you look at `examples/market`, an NFT marketplace whose listings are owned objects holding their NFT.

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 
JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The tutorial runs in a JOUST checkout with JDK 25; release
candidates for your own projects are in the BloxBean release repository (see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)).
You also need Yaci DevKit: `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`.

##### The contract

1. **The state and the reserves.**

   ```java title="examples/dex/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/dex/Dex.java"
   @StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 256, assetSlots = 2)
   public class Dex {

       public record Pool(byte[] admin, byte[] tokenPolicy, byte[] tokenName, byte[] lpName, BigInteger lpSupply) {}

       public record Moved(Pool state, JulcList<Payout> payouts, JulcList<Send> sends, Value mint, Value accepted) {}
       public record Closed(JulcList<Payout> payouts, JulcList<Send> sends) {}
   ```

   The state does not store the reserves. They are what the UTxO holds: `ctx.balance()` is the lovelace above the
   deposit, and `funds.held()` the native assets (without the thread token). State and funds cannot drift apart.
   `assetSlots = 2` sizes the deposit for the two assets the UTxO may hold.

   *What this taught:* let the value be the source of truth for amounts; keep only what the value cannot say in the
   state.

2. **Opening a pool.**

   ```java
   /** Opens an empty pool for {@code (tokenPolicy, tokenName)}; its LP token is named after the pool id. */
   @Init
   public static Pool open(byte[] tokenPolicy, byte[] tokenName, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
       Require.that(tokenPolicy.length == 28, "token policy must be 28 bytes");
       return new Pool(ctx.caller(), tokenPolicy, tokenName, CryptoLib.blake2b_224(funds.self()), BigInteger.ZERO);
   }
   ```

   `funds.self()` is the new instance's id. Naming the LP token `blake2b_224(self)` (28 bytes: a user-kind name, not
   a reserved one) gives each pool its own LP token, so one pool's LP tokens can never redeem another's reserves.

3. **Adding liquidity: accept, mint, send.**

   ```java
   @Action @Payable
   public static Moved addLiquidity(Pool p, BigInteger tokenIn, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
       BigInteger adaIn = ctx.received();
       Require.that(adaIn.signum() > 0 && tokenIn.signum() > 0, "add both ADA and tokens");
       BigInteger reserveAda = ctx.balance();
       BigInteger reserveToken = Assets.quantity(funds.held(), p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName());
       BigInteger minted = p.lpSupply().signum() == 0 ? adaIn
               : adaIn.multiply(p.lpSupply()).divide(reserveAda).min(tokenIn.multiply(p.lpSupply()).divide(reserveToken));
       Require.that(minted.signum() > 0, "deposit too small");
       Value lp = Assets.of(funds.policy(), p.lpName(), minted);
       Pool next = new Pool(p.admin(), p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName(), p.lpName(), p.lpSupply().add(minted));
       return new Moved(next, Payouts.none(), Sends.of(wallet(ctx.caller()), lp, new OutputDatum.NoOutputDatum()), lp,
               Assets.of(p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName(), tokenIn));
   }
   ```

   The result says exactly what happens to value: `accepted` is the `tokenIn` tokens the provider puts in (the
   validator requires it to equal what was offered, so nobody can slip junk tokens in), `mint` is the new LP tokens,
   and `sends` delivers them to the provider's enterprise address. The validator checks the state output's value is
   exactly the input plus the ADA and tokens received, plus the mint, minus the send.

4. **Swaps with slippage bounds.**

   ```java
   /** Swaps {@code ctx.received()} lovelace for at least {@code minOut} tokens. */
   @Action @Payable
   public static Moved swapAdaForToken(Pool p, BigInteger minOut, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
       BigInteger out = amountOut(ctx.received(), ctx.balance(), Assets.quantity(funds.held(), p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName()));
       Require.that(out.signum() > 0 && out.compareTo(minOut) >= 0, "slippage: output below minOut");
       return new Moved(p, Payouts.none(),
               Sends.of(wallet(ctx.caller()), Assets.of(p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName(), out), new OutputDatum.NoOutputDatum()),
               Assets.none(), Assets.none());
   }

   /** Output of a swap of {@code in} into reserves {@code (reserveIn, reserveOut)}, after the 0.3 % fee. */
   public static BigInteger amountOut(BigInteger in, BigInteger reserveIn, BigInteger reserveOut) {
       BigInteger inWithFee = in.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(997));
       return reserveOut.multiply(inWithFee).divide(reserveIn.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(1000)).add(inWithFee));
   }
   ```

   `amountOut` is plain static Java: the off-chain client calls it to quote a swap, and the validator runs the same
   code. The swap state is unchanged (the reserves are the value), and `minOut` protects the trader if another swap
   lands first. `swapTokenForAda` is the mirror image: it accepts tokens and pays ADA with a `Payout`.

5. **Removing liquidity: burn.** `removeLiquidity` accepts the LP tokens (`accepted = lpTokens`) and burns them
   (`mint = Assets.subtract(Assets.none(), lpTokens)`), paying out the provider's share of both reserves. `close`
   requires `lpSupply` zero and sends any leftover token dust to the admin.

   *What this taught:* minting is a negative or positive `Value` in the result; the policy only lets the transition
   that declared it mint, exactly that much.

##### Run it

1. **Harness tests.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:dex:test --tests '*DexTest'
   ```

   `DexTest` opens a pool, adds the first liquidity (LP minted to the provider), swaps both ways and removes liquidity
   (LP burned), each through the compiled validator, the mint policy and the output verifier, with the attack suite:
   a foreign token added to the state output, a send short by one unit, a send's claim missing or duplicated, one LP
   token too many minted, a `ByAction` naming another input.

2. **The DevKit flow.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:dex:test --tests '*DexDevnetTest'
   ```

   ```java title="examples/dex/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/dex/DexDevnetTest.java"
   byte[] name = "HOSKY".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
   byte[] policy = HexUtil.decodeHexString(DevKit.mintToken(lp, "HOSKY", 1_000_000));

   var dex = DexClient.deploy(runtime, admin, policy, name);
   Value tokens = Assets.of(policy, name, BigInteger.valueOf(100_000));
   dex.addLiquidity(lp, BigInteger.valueOf(100_000), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(100)), tokens);

   // ADA -> token, with slippage protection.
   BigInteger expect = Dex.amountOut(ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(100)),
           BigInteger.valueOf(100_000));
   assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> dex.swapAdaForToken(trader, expect.add(BigInteger.ONE),
           ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), Assets.none()), "minOut above the quote");
   dex.swapAdaForToken(trader, expect, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), Assets.none());
   ```

   The test mints a token on DevKit, opens a pool, and adds 100 ADA and 100,000 HOSKY: the provider receives 100,000,000
   LP tokens (the first deposit mints its lovelace). A 10 ADA swap quotes 9,066 HOSKY; asking for one more is refused
   on the JVM before anything is submitted; asking for the quote succeeds. The trader then sells half back, the
   provider removes all liquidity (every LP token burned), and the admin closes the empty pool.

   In the Java client an asset-aware method takes its arguments, then the lovelace paid, then the native assets
   offered (`funds.received`).

   *What this taught:* the quote and the check are one function; the bound is what makes a swap safe to sign.

3. **From JavaScript.** The npm runtime runs the same flow in Node:

   ```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Dex)"
   const { policy } = await devkitMint(CSL, rt.chain, lp, 'HOSKY', 1_000_000n);
   const name = Buffer.from('HOSKY').toString('hex');
   const dex = await contract('Dex', admin);
   const d = dex.at((await dex.deploy(admin, { tokenPolicy: policy, tokenName: name })).instance);
   await d.call(lp, 'addLiquidity', { tokenIn: 100_000n }, { lovelace: 100n * ADA, assets: [[policy, [[name, 100_000n]]]] });
   const pool = await d.state();
   const lpUnit = dex.deployment.policy + pool.lpName;

   // ADA -> token, with slippage protection: amountOut(in, reserveIn, reserveOut) with the 0.3% fee.
   const amountOut = (i, rIn, rOut) => (i * 997n * rOut) / (rIn * 1000n + i * 997n);
   const expect = amountOut(10n * ADA, 100n * ADA, 100_000n);
   await assert.rejects(d.call(trader, 'swapAdaForToken', { minOut: expect + 1n }, { lovelace: 10n * ADA }));
   await d.call(trader, 'swapAdaForToken', { minOut: expect }, { lovelace: 10n * ADA });

   // The provider takes its liquidity out: LP burned.
   const all = (await d.state()).lpSupply;
   await d.call(lp, 'removeLiquidity', { lp: all }, { lovelace: 0n, assets: [[dex.deployment.policy, [[pool.lpName, all]]]] });
   ```

   A payment with assets is `{ lovelace, assets: [[policy, [[name, quantity]]]] }`, all hex and `bigint`.

##### A look at the marketplace

`examples/market` combines assets with [owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/). Each listing is an owned object
that holds the NFT it sells, so listings never contend:

```java title="examples/market/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/market/Market.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 384, assetSlots = 1)
public class Market {

    public record Config(byte[] admin, BigInteger feeBps, Address royaltyVault, BigInteger royaltyBps, boolean paused) {}

    @Owned
    public record Listing(byte[] seller, byte[] nftPolicy, byte[] nftName, BigInteger price) {}

    /** Buys a listing: pays exactly its price, receives the NFT. */
    @OwnedDestroy @Payable
    public static Sold buy(Listing l, @Shared Config c, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
        Require.that(!c.paused(), "the market is paused");
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(l.price()) == 0, "pay exactly the price");
        Require.that(!ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), l.seller()), "the seller cannot buy their own listing");
        BigInteger fee = l.price().multiply(c.feeBps()).divide(BigInteger.valueOf(10_000));
        BigInteger royalty = l.price().multiply(c.royaltyBps()).divide(BigInteger.valueOf(10_000));
        // The seller gets the price less fee and royalty, plus the listing's deposit (ctx.balance()).
        JulcList<Payout> payouts = Payouts.of(l.seller(), l.price().subtract(fee).subtract(royalty).add(ctx.balance()));
        JulcList<Payout> withFee = fee.signum() > 0 ? Payouts.add(payouts, c.admin(), fee) : payouts;
        JulcList<Send> nft = Sends.of(wallet(ctx.caller()), funds.held(), new OutputDatum.NoOutputDatum());
        JulcList<Send> sends = royalty.signum() > 0
                ? Sends.add(nft, c.royaltyVault(), Assets.lovelace(royalty),
                        Datum.inline(royalty(l)))
                : nft;
        return new Sold(withFee, sends, Assets.none());
    }
}
```

- `offer` is a `@Payable` `@OwnedInit` that accepts exactly one NFT (`accepted`): a junk token alongside is refused
  (`offer_withAJunkTokenAlongside_rejected`).
- `buy` is a `@Payable` owned destroy: the buyer pays the price, the seller is paid with a payout, the NFT goes to the
  buyer with a send, and the royalty goes to a script address with an inline `Royalty` datum. A royalty output that
  is really a spent script's continuing output is refused (`royaltyClaimedByASpentVaultContinuation_rejected`).
- `cancel` reads no market state, so the seller can always take the NFT back, even from a paused market.
- `relist` moves a listing, NFT included, into another market, which admits it with `@Admits enlist`.

Run it with `./gradlew :examples:market:test`. On DevKit the seller receives 92.5% of a 100 ADA price plus the
listing's deposit, the buyer gets the NFT, and 5% goes to the royalty script.

##### What you built

- A pool whose reserves are its value, with LP tokens minted and burned by its own policy.
- Swaps that the trader bounds, quoted with the same function the validator runs.
- A marketplace where each listing holds its NFT and every output counts for exactly one obligation.

  - [Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/)
  - [Oracle and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/oracle-composition/)
  - [Fees and script size](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/)

### Multisig treasury

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/multisig-treasury/

This tutorial walks through [`examples/treasury`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/treasury), a
multisig treasury, and runs it on Yaci DevKit. A council of keys decides by quorum; a guardian fixed at deploy time
can freeze the treasury; every state keeps a reachable quorum; and payments and council changes emit events that
indexers can trust.

You will use five features from [ADR-0009](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-option-i-params-auth-invariants-events.md):
`@Params`, `@Quorum`, `@AuthorizedBy` with a script, `@Invariant`, and events.

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 

JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The Java path needs JDK 25; JOUST's releases are in the
BloxBean release repository (see the [Java quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)). For the DevKit run,
start Yaci DevKit with `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`.

##### Build it

1. **Deploy-time parameters.** The guardian and the payout cap are fixed when the treasury is deployed:

   ```java title="examples/treasury/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/Treasury.java"
   @StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 640)
   public class Treasury {

       @Params
       public record Config(Credential guardian, BigInteger maxPayout) {}

       public record State(JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, boolean frozen) {}
   ```

   `@Params` values are applied to the script itself, so each `Config` gives a different script hash, policy id and
   address. Nobody can change them later, and no action can swap the guardian. `guardian` is a `Credential`: a key
   or a script. The council and quorum live in the state, because the council can rotate.

   **What this taught:** put what must never change in `@Params`; what may change, in the state.

2. **Open and fund.**

   ```java
   @Init @Payable
   public static State open(Config cfg, JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, Ctx ctx) {
       return new State(council, quorum, false);
   }

   @Action @Payable
   public static State fund(State s, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(ctx.received().signum() > 0, "fund with some ADA");
       return s;
   }
   ```

   The params come first in `@Init` (there is no state yet), right after the state elsewhere. `fund` returns the
   state unchanged: the validator's exact value check still requires the treasury's UTxO to grow by exactly
   `received`.

   **What this taught:** a method declares the params record to read them; callers never pass it.

3. **Pay by quorum, and emit an event.**

   ```java
   public sealed interface Event permits Paid, CouncilChanged, Frozen {}
   public record Paid(byte[] to, BigInteger amount) implements Event {}
   public record CouncilChanged(BigInteger members, BigInteger quorum) implements Event {}
   public record Frozen(boolean frozen) implements Event {}

   public record Spent(State state, JulcList<Payout> payouts, JulcList<Event> events) {}
   public record Changed(State state, JulcList<Event> events) {}

   /** Pays {@code amount} to {@code to}; needs a quorum of the council. */
   @Action @Quorum(keys = "council", threshold = "quorum")
   public static Spent pay(State s, Config cfg, byte[] to, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
       Require.that(!s.frozen(), "the treasury is frozen");
       Require.that(amount.signum() > 0 && amount.compareTo(cfg.maxPayout()) <= 0, "amount out of range");
       Require.that(amount.compareTo(ctx.balance()) <= 0, "not enough funds");
       JulcList<Event> none = JulcList.empty();
       return new Spent(s, Payouts.of(to, amount), none.prepend(new Paid(to, amount)));
   }
   ```

   - `@Quorum(keys = "council", threshold = "quorum")` requires at least `quorum` of the transaction's signers to be
     in the **current** council.
   - `Spent` has three components the processor recognises by name: `state`, `payouts` and `events`.
   - The events travel in the redeemer, and the validator requires them to equal what the method returned. An event
     read from a valid JOUST transaction is therefore exactly what the contract emitted.

   **What this taught:** an M-of-N rule is one annotation; events are part of the checked result.

4. **Rotate the council, guarded by an invariant.**

   ```java
   /** Replaces the council; needs a quorum of the current one. The new council must keep a reachable quorum. */
   @Action @Quorum(keys = "council", threshold = "quorum")
   public static Changed rotate(State s, JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum) {
       JulcList<Event> none = JulcList.empty();
       return new Changed(new State(council, quorum, s.frozen()),
               none.prepend(new CouncilChanged(BigInteger.valueOf(council.size()), quorum)));
   }

   /** A quorum the council can reach (the generated check also requires distinct, sorted 28-byte keys). */
   @Invariant
   public static boolean reachable(State s) {
       return s.quorum().signum() > 0 && s.quorum().compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(s.council().size())) <= 0;
   }
   ```

   The quorum check reads the **input** state, so a rotation needs the current council's approval and cannot
   authorise itself. The `@Invariant` runs on every state the validator accepts as an output (and in the client,
   first), so no rotation can leave a quorum nobody can reach. Because the contract uses `@Quorum`, the validator
   also checks that council keys are strictly ascending and 28 bytes each.

   **What this taught:** invariants protect the contract from transitions that would lock it.

5. **Freeze through a guardian script.**

   ```java
   /** The guardian freezes or unfreezes the treasury. */
   @Action @AuthorizedBy("params.guardian")
   public static Changed freeze(State s, boolean frozen) {
       JulcList<Event> none = JulcList.empty();
       return new Changed(new State(s.council(), s.quorum(), frozen), none.prepend(new Frozen(frozen)));
   }

   /** Ends the treasury, paying everything to {@code to}; needs a quorum. */
   @Destroy @Quorum(keys = "council", threshold = "quorum")
   public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, byte[] to, Ctx ctx) {
       return Payouts.of(to, ctx.balance());
   }
   ```

   `@AuthorizedBy("params.guardian")` needs the guardian's approval. On DevKit the guardian is a **script**, a
   withdraw-zero governor: a transaction that withdraws zero lovelace from the script's reward account makes the
   ledger run it. The governor's redeemer must list `Approval(policy, target, action)` naming this treasury, this
   instance and the `freeze` action, so one approval cannot be reused elsewhere:

   ```java title="examples/treasury/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/Guardian.java"
   @WithdrawValidator
   public class Guardian {

       @Param static byte[] owner;

       @Entrypoint
       public static boolean validate(PlutusData redeemer, ScriptContext ctx) {
           boolean rewarding = ctx.scriptInfo() instanceof ScriptInfo.RewardingScript;
           return rewarding && ContextsLib.signedBy(ctx.txInfo(), owner);
       }
   }
   ```

   `Guardian` approves when its owner signs, and refuses any other purpose, so nobody can deregister it. A real
   governor would decide by votes or another contract's state.

   **What this taught:** another script can authorise an action, bound to exactly that action.

##### Run it

The treasury has no app class; its DevKit test plays the whole flow.

1. **Read the flow.**

   
   
**Java:**

   ```java title="examples/treasury/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/TreasuryDevnetTest.java"
   Account[] members = {DevKit.fundedAccount(300), DevKit.fundedAccount(300), DevKit.fundedAccount(300)};
   Arrays.sort(members, Comparator.comparing(a -> HexUtil.encodeHexString(Keys.pkh(a))));   // keys ascending
   var a = members[0];
   var b = members[1];
   var owner = DevKit.fundedAccount(100);
   var bob = DevKit.fundedAccount(10);

   // The guardian script, with its owner applied, and its stake credential registered once.
   var guardian = JulcScriptLoader.load(Guardian.class, new BytesPlutusData(Keys.pkh(owner)));
   String reward = DevKit.registerScriptStake(guardian, owner);
   var cfg = new Treasury.Config(new Credential.ScriptCredential(new ScriptHash(guardian.getScriptHash())),
           ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(50)));
   JulcList<byte[]> council = JulcList.empty();
   for (int i = members.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) council = council.prepend(Keys.pkh(members[i]));

   var t = TreasuryClient.deploy(runtime, cfg, a, council, BigInteger.TWO, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(200)));
   assertEquals(TreasuryClient.policyIdFor(cfg), t.instance().contract().policyId(), "the params pin the script");

   // 2 of 3: a calls, b co-signs. The Paid event comes back with the result.
   var paid = t.pay(a, Keys.pkh(bob), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), b);
   paid.events(Treasury.Paid.class).get(0).amount();          // 10 ADA
   assertThrows(RuntimeException.class, () -> t.pay(a, Keys.pkh(bob), ADA), "one signature is not a quorum");

   // The guardian freezes: a zero withdrawal from its script, with an Approvals redeemer for this action (tag 3).
   byte[] policy = HexUtil.decodeHexString(t.instance().contract().policyId());
   byte[] id = HexUtil.decodeHexString(t.instanceId());
   JulcList<Approval> approvals = JulcList.<Approval>empty().prepend(new Approval(policy, id, BigInteger.valueOf(3)));
   var frozen = t.freeze(owner, true, Authorization.script(reward, guardian, new Approvals(approvals), owner));
   assertThrows(RuntimeException.class, () -> t.pay(a, Keys.pkh(bob), ADA, b), "frozen");
   t.freeze(owner, false, Authorization.script(reward, guardian, new Approvals(approvals), owner));

   // Rotate to a council of two, then close by quorum.
   t.rotate(a, JulcList.<byte[]>empty().prepend(Keys.pkh(b)).prepend(Keys.pkh(a)), BigInteger.TWO, a, b);
   t.close(a, Keys.pkh(a), b);
   ```

   The generated client takes `@Quorum` co-signers as trailing `Account`s, and an `Authorization` for
   `@AuthorizedBy`. `DevKit.registerScriptStake` is the examples' helper that registers the governor's stake
   credential.

   
   
**JavaScript:**

   ```js
   // The same calls with the generated JavaScript client and CIP-30 wallets.
   const treasury = new Treasury({ service, chain, deployment });     // deployment: one applied Config
   const { instance } = await treasury.deploy(walletA, { council, quorum: 2n }, { lovelace: 200_000_000n });

   const paid = await instance.pay(walletA, { to: bobKeyHash, amount: 10_000_000n }, { cosigners: [walletB] });
   paid.report.events;   // [{ $variant: 'Paid', to: bobKeyHash, amount: 10000000n }]

   await instance.freeze(walletA, { frozen: true }, { governor: { governor, signers: [ownerWallet] } });
   ```

   Each co-signer's wallet signs the same transaction, after the page has verified it.

   
   

2. **Run the tests.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:treasury:test
   ```

   With DevKit up, `TreasuryDevnetTest > quorumGuardianEvents()` runs the flow above on the local network and passes.
   Without DevKit it is skipped, and the harness tests still run. Gradle lists each test as `PASSED`.

3. **See what the harness proved.** `TreasuryTest` evaluates the compiled validator against each transaction and runs
   the attack suite on every accepted one. Beyond the happy paths, it checks that the validator refuses:

   - a council with duplicate keys, or a quorum above the council's size, at creation;
   - a payment signed by one of three, or by one member and a stranger;
   - forged events in the redeemer;
   - a rotation to duplicate or unsorted keys;
   - a freeze with no guardian withdrawal, an approval for another instance or another action, or another script's
     withdrawal;
   - a close with one signature.

   A payment over `maxPayout` is refused by the method itself, on the JVM (`RequireException`).

   Run `./gradlew :examples:treasury:test --info` to see the lines the tests print, including each transaction's
   budget and how many attacks it rejected.

##### What you built

A treasury where:

- spending needs a quorum of the council, checked against the council **before** the call;
- the council can change, but never into one that cannot reach its quorum;
- an independent script can freeze it, with an approval bound to one instance and one action;
- the guardian and the payout cap are fixed by the script hash;
- every payment and council change is recorded as an event the validator checked.

About 70 lines of contract code; every one of those guarantees is generated.

- [Params, invariants and events](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/)

### Oracle and composition

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/oracle-composition/

In this tutorial you run `examples/oracle`: an `Oracle` contract that a publisher updates with a price, and a `Shop`
that sells credits at that price. The shop reads the oracle's state with [`@Reads`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/),
checked on chain, without spending it. Then you compose a purchase and another oracle's update into one transaction,
and see `Compose` refuse a transaction that would spend the same instance twice.

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 
JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The tutorial runs in a JOUST checkout with JDK 25; release
candidates for your own projects are in the BloxBean release repository (see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)).
You also need Yaci DevKit: `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`.

##### The two contracts

1. **The oracle** stores a price and when it was set:

   ```java title="examples/oracle/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/Oracle.java"
   @StateContract
   public class Oracle {

       public record State(byte[] publisher, BigInteger price, BigInteger updatedAt) {}

       @Init
       public static State open(BigInteger price, Ctx ctx) {
           Require.that(price.signum() > 0, "price must be positive");
           return new State(ctx.caller(), price, ctx.validFrom());
       }

       @Action @SignedBy("publisher")
       public static State post(State s, BigInteger price, Ctx ctx) {
           Require.that(price.signum() > 0, "price must be positive");
           return new State(s.publisher(), price, ctx.validFrom());
       }
   }
   ```

   `updatedAt` is `ctx.validFrom()`, the start of the transaction's validity window, which the ledger enforces. A
   reader can then tell how old the price is.

2. **The shop pins the oracle in its params:**

   ```java title="examples/oracle/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/Shop.java"
   @StateContract
   public class Shop {

       @Params
       public record Config(ForeignInstance oracle, BigInteger maxAgeMs) {}

       public record State(byte[] owner, BigInteger sold) {}

       @Init
       public static State open(Config cfg, Ctx ctx) {
           return new State(ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO);
       }

       /** Buys {@code qty} credits, paying {@code qty * price} at a price no older than {@code maxAgeMs}. */
       @Action @Payable
       public static State buy(State s, Config cfg, @Reads("params.oracle") Oracle.State price, BigInteger qty, Ctx ctx) {
           Require.that(qty.signum() > 0, "buy at least one credit");
           Require.that(ctx.validFrom().subtract(price.updatedAt()).compareTo(cfg.maxAgeMs()) <= 0, "stale price");
           Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(qty.multiply(price.price())) == 0, "pay exactly qty * price");
           return new State(s.owner(), s.sold().add(qty));
       }
   }
   ```

   `ForeignInstance(policy, instance)` names one oracle instance of one oracle script. Because it is in `@Params`,
   it is applied to the shop's script at deploy: a different oracle means a different shop script and address.
   `@Reads("params.oracle") Oracle.State price` hands `buy` that oracle's current state.

   *What this taught:* the trusted source is part of the reader's identity, never something a caller supplies.

3. **What the shop's validator checks.** For `price`, the transaction must carry a reference input that holds exactly
   one token of the oracle's policy, named with the 32-byte instance id, at the oracle's script address, with an
   inline datum shaped like `Oracle.State`. Freshness is not automatic: a reference input does not run the oracle's
   validator, so an old state stays readable. That is why `buy` checks `updatedAt` against `maxAgeMs`.

##### Run it

1. **Harness tests: spoofed oracles.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:oracle:test --tests '*ShopTest'
   ```

   [`ShopTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/oracle/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/ShopTest.java)
   buys at a fresh price, then tries every way to feed the shop a price it should not trust:

   ```java title="examples/oracle/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/ShopTest.java"
   h.assertRejected(buy(fresh(), null), "no oracle reference input");
   // ... the oracle's token at a key address; another policy's token; two tokens of the policy;
   // a datum of another shape
   h.assertRejected(buy(stale, oracleInput(oracleAddress(), oracleValue(), stale)), "stale price");
   ```

   Each is refused by the validator.

   *What this taught:* `@Reads` checks where the state comes from; your method checks whether it is recent enough.

2. **Deploy an oracle, then a shop that reads it.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:oracle:test --tests '*OracleDevnetTest'
   ```

   ```java title="examples/oracle/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/OracleDevnetTest.java"
   var oracle = OracleClient.deploy(runtime, publisher, BigInteger.valueOf(3_000_000));
   var cfg = new Shop.Config(new ForeignInstance(HexUtil.decodeHexString(oracle.instance().contract().policyId()),
           HexUtil.decodeHexString(oracle.instanceId())), BigInteger.valueOf(600_000));
   var shop = ShopClient.deploy(runtime, cfg, shopOwner);

   shop.buy(buyer, BigInteger.TWO, BigInteger.valueOf(6_000_000));
   assertEquals(BigInteger.TWO, shop.state().sold());
   assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> shop.buy(buyer, BigInteger.ONE, BigInteger.valueOf(2_000_000)),
           "pays less than the oracle price");
   ```

   The oracle starts at 3 ADA. Two credits cost exactly 6 ADA; one credit for 2 ADA is refused by the JVM run before
   anything is submitted. The client finds the oracle's UTxO and adds it as a reference input: `buy` takes only the
   quantity and the payment.

   *What this taught:* reading another contract costs the caller nothing extra to write.

3. **Compose a purchase with another contract's call.**

   ```java
   // A second oracle (another instance of the same contract) posts while the shop sells: one transaction.
   var oracle2 = OracleClient.deploy(runtime, publisher2, BigInteger.valueOf(1_000_000));
   String tx = Compose.of(runtime, buyer)
           .add(() -> shop.buy(buyer, BigInteger.ONE, BigInteger.valueOf(3_000_000)))
           .add(() -> oracle2.post(publisher2, BigInteger.valueOf(5_000_000)))
           .submit();
   assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(3), shop.state().sold());
   assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(5_000_000), oracle2.state().price());
   ```

   Inside `add`, each call is an ordinary client call. `Compose` runs it in capture mode, so it writes into one shared
   transaction instead of submitting: the shop's spend with the first oracle as a reference input, the second oracle's
   spend, both redeemers, and the signatures of the buyer and `publisher2`. It picks a validity window both calls
   accept, runs both methods in it, checks every output after balancing, and submits once. Both happen, or neither.

   *What this taught:* composition is a runtime feature; each validator still checks only its own transition.

4. **Watch a composition be refused.**

   ```java
   assertThrows(JoustException.class, () -> Compose.of(runtime, buyer)
           .add(() -> shop.buy(buyer, BigInteger.ONE, BigInteger.valueOf(3_000_000)))
           .add(() -> shop.buy(buyer, BigInteger.ONE, BigInteger.valueOf(3_000_000)))
           .submit(), "the same instance spent twice is refused before submitting");
   ```

   Two calls on one instance would spend the same UTxO twice. `Compose` refuses before building, as it does for two
   mints under one policy, an empty common window, or one key signing for two calls without `allowSharedSigners()`.

##### From JavaScript

The npm runtime runs the same contracts, and composes the same way:

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Oracle and Shop)"
const oracle = await contract('Oracle', publisher);
const o = oracle.at((await oracle.deploy(publisher, { price: 3_000_000n })).instance);
await o.call(publisher, 'post', { price: 3_000_000n });
await assert.rejects(o.call(other, 'post', { price: 1n }));          // not the publisher
// The shop's script carries its oracle (@Params); buy reads the oracle's state as a reference input (@Reads).
const shop = await contract('Shop', shopOwner, { oracle: { policy: oracle.deployment.policy, instance: o.id }, maxAgeMs: 600_000n });
const sh = shop.at((await shop.deploy(shopOwner, {})).instance);
await sh.call(buyer, 'buy', { qty: 2n }, { lovelace: 6_000_000n });
await assert.rejects(sh.call(buyer, 'buy', { qty: 1n }, { lovelace: 2_000_000n }), /pay exactly/);
```

To compose, pass steps to `rt.compose(wallet, steps)`, each `{ contract, method, instance, args, pay }`. A composed
transaction is verified call by call and as a whole before the wallet signs; see
[Reads and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/).

##### What you built

- A reader whose trusted source is fixed in its script, checked on chain by token, address and datum shape.
- A freshness rule, written by you, on top of that.
- One transaction that calls two contracts, all or nothing.

  - [Reads and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/)
  - [Deposits](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/)
  - [Upgrading a contract](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/upgrades/)
  - [Staked vault and governance](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/staked-vault/)

### Staked vault and governance

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/staked-vault/

In this tutorial you run `examples/staking`: a vault whose state UTxOs are staked to its own script, so the ADA they
lock earns rewards. A council of three, two of whom must sign, decides where the stake is delegated and where the
rewards go, can vote as a script DRep, and a guardrail caps treasury withdrawals. Along the way you see how the
non-spending [script purposes](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/staking-and-governance/) work and why each handler is governed by params.

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 
JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The tutorial runs in a JOUST checkout with JDK 25; release
candidates for your own projects are in the BloxBean release repository (see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)).
You also need Yaci DevKit: `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`.

##### The contract

1. **Staked state and params.**

   ```java title="examples/staking/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/staking/StakedVault.java"
   @StateContract(stakeSelf = true)
   public class StakedVault {

       @Params
       public record Config(JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, byte[] pool, byte[] payee, BigInteger cap) {}

       public record State(BigInteger deposits) {}

       @Init @Payable
       public static State open(Config cfg, Ctx ctx) {
           return new State(ctx.received());
       }

       @Action @Payable
       public static State deposit(State s, Ctx ctx) {
           Require.that(ctx.received().signum() > 0, "deposit some ADA");
           return new State(s.deposits().add(ctx.received()));
       }

       @Destroy @Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")
       public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Config cfg, Ctx ctx) {
           return Payouts.of(cfg.payee(), ctx.balance());
       }
   ```

   `stakeSelf = true` puts every state UTxO at a base address whose stake credential is this script. The council, the
   quorum, the one pool it may delegate to, the payee of rewards and the guardrail's cap are deploy-time
   [params](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/): they are applied to the script, so changing them means a new
   script.

2. **The purpose handlers.**

   ```java
   /** Rewards go only to the payee. */
   @Withdraw @Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")
   public static JulcList<Send> collect(Config cfg, BigInteger amount) {
       return amount.signum() == 0 ? Sends.none()
               : Sends.of(wallet(cfg.payee()), Assets.lovelace(amount), new OutputDatum.NoOutputDatum());
   }

   /** Registration, and delegation of stake only (no vote delegation) to the pool in the params; nothing else. */
   @Certify @Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")
   public static boolean certificate(Config cfg, TxCert cert) {
       return Certs.isRegistration(cert) || Certs.delegatesOnlyTo(cert, cfg.pool()) || Certs.isDRepLifecycle(cert);
   }

   /** The council votes as the script DRep: a quorum signing is the decision. */
   @Votes @Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")
   public static boolean vote(Config cfg, Voter voter, GovernanceActionId action, Vote vote) {
       return true;
   }

   /** Guardrail: no treasury withdrawal above the cap in total. */
   @Propose
   public static boolean proposal(Config cfg, ProposalProcedure p) {
       return switch (p.governanceAction()) {
           case GovernanceAction.TreasuryWithdrawals t -> totalOf(t).compareTo(cfg.cap()) <= 0;
           default -> true;
       };
   }
   ```

   These run when the ledger runs the script for a withdrawal, a certificate, a vote or a proposal. No instance is
   spent, so they see the params, not any instance's state. That is why `@Quorum` names `params.council`: the
   processor refuses an ungoverned `@Withdraw`, `@Certify` or `@Votes`.

   *What this taught:* rewards, delegation and votes belong to the contract type and its params, shared by all its
   instances.

3. **The build flag.** The example compiles with `-Ajulc.blueprint=false`, because JuLC's pinned CIP-57 revision has
   no vocabulary for vote and propose handlers yet:

   ```groovy title="examples/staking/build.gradle"
   tasks.named('compileJava') { options.compilerArgs += ['-Ajulc.blueprint=false'] }
   ```

##### Run it

1. **Harness tests: every handler, every way to cheat.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:staking:test --tests '*StakingTest'
   ```

   [`StakingTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/staking/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/staking/StakingTest.java)
   covers:
   - the staked address (open and deposit, with the attack suite);
   - withdrawals: one signature, a wrong amount, a wrong marker, rewards sent to someone else, a send not claimed in
     the output registry, all refused;
   - certificates: delegation to another pool, a stake-and-vote delegation to an attacker's DRep, stake and DRep
     unregistration, a committee certificate and a single signature, all refused;
   - votes: one signature, and no votes for this voter, refused;
   - the guardrail: a treasury withdrawal over the cap, refused.

   *What this taught:* `Certs.delegatesOnlyTo` refuses a delegation that would also move the vote, which a hand-written
   check can easily miss.

2. **Deploy at a staked address.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:staking:test --tests '*StakingDevnetTest'
   ```

   ```java title="examples/staking/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/staking/StakingDevnetTest.java"
   Account[] council = {DevKit.fundedAccount(300), DevKit.fundedAccount(300), DevKit.fundedAccount(300)};
   Arrays.sort(council, Comparator.comparing(a -> HexUtil.encodeHexString(Keys.pkh(a))));
   var payee = DevKit.fundedAccount(5);
   JulcList<byte[]> keys = JulcList.empty();
   for (int i = council.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) keys = keys.prepend(Keys.pkh(council[i]));
   String pool = DevKit.poolId();
   var cfg = new StakedVault.Config(keys, BigInteger.TWO, HexUtil.decodeHexString(pool), Keys.pkh(payee),
           ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(1000)));

   var vault = StakedVaultClient.deploy(runtime, cfg, council[0], ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(100)));
   String address = vault.instance().contract().address();
   assertTrue(address.startsWith("addr_test1x"), "a base address staked to the script: " + address);
   vault.deposit(council[1], ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(20)));
   ```

   Quorum keys must be strictly ascending, so the test sorts the council first. The vault's address starts
   `addr_test1x`: a base address with a script payment credential and a script stake credential.

3. **Register and delegate by quorum.**

   ```java
   var handle = StakedVaultClient.contract(runtime, cfg);
   handle.registerStake(council[0]);
   handle.delegateTo(pool, council[0], council[1]);
   assertThrows(RuntimeException.class, () -> handle.delegateTo(pool, council[2]), "one signature is not a quorum");
   ```

   Registration is the legacy kind, which needs no script witness: anyone may register the credential, harmlessly.
   Delegation runs `@Certify` on chain, so it needs two council signatures; one is refused.

   *What this taught:* the ledger runs your handler for every certificate of the script's credential, and the
   built-in filter refuses unregistration before your method is even asked.

4. **Collect the rewards, then close.**

   ```java
   // Rewards take epochs to accrue on DevKit; withdrawing whatever is there (zero now) runs @Withdraw.
   StakedVaultClient.collect(runtime, cfg, council[0], council[2]);
   vault.close(council[1], council[2]);
   ```

   `collect` withdraws the whole reward balance (the ledger allows nothing else) through `@Withdraw`, and the sends the
   handler returns are claimed in the output registry so no other obligation can count them. On a DevKit run the
   balance is zero, since rewards take epochs; the handler still runs. `close` needs a quorum too, and pays everything
   to the payee.

##### From JavaScript

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (StakedVault)"
const council = (await wallets(3)).sort((x, y) => (x.keyHash < y.keyHash ? -1 : 1));
const [a, b, c] = council;
const pool = (await (await fetch(STORE + '/pools/registrations?page=0&count=1')).json())[0].pool_id;
const params = { council: council.map((m) => m.keyHash), quorum: 2n, pool, payee: payee.keyHash, cap: 1000n * ADA };
const vault = await contract('StakedVault', a, params);
const v = vault.at((await vault.deploy(a, {}, { lovelace: 100n * ADA })).instance);
await v.call(b, 'deposit', {}, { lovelace: 20n * ADA });

await vault.registerStake(a);
await assert.rejects(vault.delegate(a, pool));                                  // one signature is not a quorum
await assert.rejects(vault.delegate(a, 'ab'.repeat(28), { cosigners: [b] }));    // another pool: @Certify refuses
await vault.delegate(a, pool, { cosigners: [b] });

const amount = await rt.chain.rewards(vault.rewardAddress);
await vault.collect(a, { amount, cosigners: [c] });
await v.call(b, 'close', {}, {}, { cosigners: [c] });
```

Co-signers are other wallets: each signs the same transaction after the page verifies it. The test also tampers with
every engine-built delegation and collection, and checks that each is refused before any wallet is asked.

> **Registration on Yaci Store:** 
Yaci Store answers the same for registered and unknown stake credentials, so the client cannot tell whether
registration is needed. `registerStake` registers anyway and resolves to `null` when the chain refuses it as already
registered.

##### Votes and the guardrail

The clients do not cast votes or submit proposals, and DevKit would need an enacted constitution and live governance
actions to exercise them. `StakingTest` covers both in the harness: `votes_asAScriptDRep_byQuorum` checks that the
script's vote needs the quorum and that a transaction with no votes for this voter is refused, and
`guardrail_capsTreasuryWithdrawals` checks that a treasury withdrawal over `cap` fails the guardrail.

##### What you built

- A vault whose locked ADA earns rewards for a council to direct.
- Delegation restricted to one pool, by quorum, with every other certificate refused.
- Rewards that can only go to the payee, each output counted once.

### Upgrading a contract

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/upgrades/

A deployed script cannot change. To ship a new version you deploy a new contract and move each live instance into
it. In this tutorial you run [`examples/upgrade`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/upgrade): a
`CounterV1` instance, with a count and some funds, migrates into `CounterV2`, which adds a step size. Both
validators check the move in one transaction, so the funds can only go where both sides agree.

> **Experimental, pre-release:** 

JOUST is experimental and pre-release (not for production). The Java path needs JDK 25; JOUST's releases are in the
BloxBean release repository (see the [Java quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/)). For the DevKit run,
start Yaci DevKit with `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`.

##### Build it

1. **Version 1 names its successor.** `CounterV1` holds an admin, a successor policy (empty at first) and a count:

   ```java title="examples/upgrade/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/upgrade/CounterV1.java"
   @StateContract
   public class CounterV1 {

       public record State(byte[] admin, byte[] successor, BigInteger count) {}

       @Init @Payable
       public static State open(Ctx ctx) {
           return new State(ctx.caller(), new byte[]{}, BigInteger.ZERO);
       }

       @Action
       public static State increment(State s) {
           return new State(s.admin(), s.successor(), s.count().add(BigInteger.ONE));
       }

       @Action @SignedBy("admin")
       public static State setSuccessor(State s, byte[] successor) {
           return new State(s.admin(), successor, s.count());
       }
   ```

   Only the admin can set `successor`. If you are writing a v1 today and may want to upgrade later, this is the hook
   to add: a field for the successor's policy id, and an admin-only setter.

   **What this taught:** an upgradeable contract plans for it; the admin is trusted to name the successor.

2. **Version 1 migrates out.**

   ```java
       /** Ends v1 by migrating: nothing is paid out, everything moves to the successor's new instance. */
       @Destroy @SignedBy("admin") @MigrateTo("successor")
       public static JulcList<Payout> upgrade(State s, Ctx ctx) {
           return Payouts.none();
       }
   }
   ```

   `@MigrateTo("successor")` turns this destroy into a migration. Instead of paying `ctx.balance()` out, its
   validator requires that the policy in `successor` mints a token named `blake2b_256(this state UTxO)`, that one
   output at that policy's script address holds it, and that this output holds at least everything the instance held.

   **What this taught:** the old side lets its funds go only into the successor it names.

3. **Version 2 adopts.** `CounterV2` pins v1 in its `@Params` and adopts its state:

   ```java title="examples/upgrade/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/upgrade/CounterV2.java"
   @StateContract
   public class CounterV2 {

       @Params
       public record Config(byte[] previous) {}

       public record State(byte[] admin, BigInteger count, BigInteger step) {}

       @Init
       public static State open(Config cfg, Ctx ctx) {
           return new State(ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO, BigInteger.ONE);
       }

       @Migrate(from = "params.previous")
       public static State adopt(Config cfg, CounterV1.State old) {
           return new State(old.admin(), old.count(), BigInteger.ONE);
       }

       @Action
       public static State increment(State s) {
           return new State(s.admin(), s.count().add(s.step()), s.step());
       }

       @Action @SignedBy("admin")
       public static State setStep(State s, BigInteger step) {
           return new State(s.admin(), s.count(), step);
       }

       @Destroy @SignedBy("admin")
       public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
           return Payouts.of(s.admin(), ctx.balance());
       }
   }
   ```

   `adopt` takes the params and **v1's state record**, and maps it to v2's: the admin and count carry over, the new
   `step` starts at 1. Its validator checks that the seed is a genuine v1 state UTxO (v1's 32-byte token at v1's
   address, with a datum shaped like `CounterV1.State`), that v1's token is burned in the same transaction, and that
   the new instance holds exactly v1's lovelace.

   Why does v2 pin v1 in params while v1 names v2 in its state? If both used params, each script hash would depend on
   the other's: a cycle. So one side must use a state field.

   **What this taught:** the new side accepts only an instance of the predecessor it names, and only if that
   instance ends.

##### Run the migration

1. **Read the flow.** The DevKit test plays the whole migration:

   ```java title="examples/upgrade/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/upgrade/UpgradeDevnetTest.java"
   var runtime = DevKit.runtime();
   var admin = DevKit.fundedAccount(200);
   var v1 = CounterV1Client.deploy(runtime, admin, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
   v1.increment(admin);
   v1.increment(admin);
   BigInteger lovelace = v1.lovelace();

   // v2's params pin v1's policy; v1's admin names v2's policy.
   var cfg = new CounterV2.Config(HexUtil.decodeHexString(v1.instance().contract().policyId()));
   String v2Policy = CounterV2Client.policyIdFor(cfg);
   v1.setSuccessor(admin, HexUtil.decodeHexString(v2Policy));

   // One transaction: v1's migrating destroy and v2's adoption.
   var adopted = new CounterV2Client[1];
   String tx = Compose.of(runtime, admin)
           .add(() -> v1.upgrade(admin))
           .add(() -> adopted[0] = CounterV2Client.adopt(runtime, cfg, admin, v1.instance()))
           .submit();

   var v2 = CounterV2Client.at(runtime, cfg, adopted[0].instanceId());
   assertEquals(BigInteger.TWO, v2.state().count(), "the count moved");
   assertEquals(lovelace, v2.lovelace(), "the funds moved");
   assertThrows(InstanceNotFoundException.class, v1::state, "v1 ended");
   v2.increment(admin);
   assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(3), v2.state().count());
   ```

   `CounterV2Client.policyIdFor(cfg)` computes v2's policy id from its params before anything is deployed, so v1's
   admin can name it. `Compose` captures the two client calls and builds **one** transaction from them; on its own,
   neither half is valid. `adopt` refuses to run outside a `Compose`.

2. **Run it.**

   ```sh
   ./gradlew :examples:upgrade:test
   ```

   With DevKit up, `UpgradeDevnetTest > v1MigratesToV2()` passes: the v1 counter (count 2, 10 ADA plus its deposit)
   becomes a v2 counter with the same count and exactly the same lovelace, v1's instance is gone, and v2's
   `increment` works. Without DevKit it is skipped, and the harness test still runs.

3. **See what the harness proved.** `UpgradeTest` builds the migration transaction and evaluates it with **both**
   contracts' harnesses (v1's spend and burn, v2's adoption). It then checks the handshake against tampering:

   - v1 refuses a successor its admin did not name;
   - both sides refuse when the new instance holds less than the old;
   - v1 refuses when no successor token is minted;
   - v2 refuses to adopt when v1's token is not burned.

> **A new id:** 

The migrated instance has a new id: `blake2b_256` of v1's state UTxO reference. Keep `adopted[0].instanceId()`. The
old instance is gone: `v1.state()` throws `InstanceNotFoundException`.

##### What you learned

- A migration is a handshake: `@MigrateTo` on the old side's `@Destroy`, `@Migrate` on the new side's creation.
- The old side names the successor in an admin-set state field; the new side pins the predecessor in `@Params`.
- Both halves must be in one transaction, built with `Compose`.
- State moves through a plain Java function from the old record to the new one; funds move exactly.
- Not yet supported for contracts with MerkleMaps, owned objects or native assets.

- [Oracle and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/oracle-composition/)
- [Params, invariants and events](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/)
