## Tutorials: JavaScript

### A counter dApp in the browser

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/counter-dapp/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

In this tutorial you build the Counter dApp that `npm create joust` gives you, and read every file that makes it work.
At the end you have a page, served on Yaci DevKit, that creates counters, increments them and closes them, with each
transaction prepared in the page itself, checked by the page and signed by a wallet.

You will learn:

- how one Java method becomes both a validator and the code that builds the transaction;
- what the generated client (`Counter.js`, `Counter.d.ts`) contains;
- how the page runs the runtime engine in a Web Worker and gets its network from `virtual:joust/network`;
- how the page connects CIP-30 wallets, and shows each call for review before signing;
- what the page verifier checks, and why a bad call never reaches the wallet.

##### Set up

1. Start Yaci DevKit with Yaci Store:

   ```sh
   yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store
   ```

2. Create the app and install it:

   ```sh
   npm create joust@latest counter-dapp -- --template web --lang java
   cd counter-dapp
   npm install
   ```

   `--template web` makes the page version of the app; `--lang java` writes the contract in Java, as this tutorial
   reads it (the default is `.jsc`, with the same generated client).

3. Start the dev server. It builds and deploys the contract first:

   ```sh
   npm run dev
   ```

   Leave it running; the page is at http://127.0.0.1:5178. The rest of this tutorial explains what you are looking
   at.

##### 1. The contract

```java title="contracts/app/Counter.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 128)
public class Counter {

    /** The state, stored as the inline datum of the state UTxO. */
    public record State(BigInteger count, byte[] owner) {}

    /** The deployer becomes the owner. */
    @Init
    public static State init(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, ctx.caller());
    }

    /** Anyone can increment by a positive amount (no Ctx: no signature needed, cheaper). */
    @Action
    public static State increment(State s, BigInteger by) {
        Require.that(by.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "increment must be positive");
        return new State(s.count().add(by), s.owner());
    }

    /** Only the owner can reset. */
    @Action
    @OnlyOwner
    public static State reset(State s) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, s.owner());
    }

    /** Only the owner can close the counter; the deposit goes back to them. */
    @Destroy
    @OnlyOwner
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance());
    }

    /** Read-only view (off-chain, no transaction). */
    @View
    public static BigInteger count(State s) {
        return s.count();
    }
}
```

Each counter lives in one UTxO at the contract's address. The UTxO holds a **thread token** that names the instance,
and its **datum** (the data attached to the UTxO) is the `State` record. Calling an action spends that UTxO with a
**redeemer** (the call and its arguments) and creates the next one. (These terms are in the
[glossary](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/glossary/).)

- `@Init` creates an instance; `ctx.caller()` is the key that signed the transaction, so the creator owns it.
- `increment` takes no `Ctx`, so it needs no signature: anyone can call it. `Require.that` refuses a non-positive
  amount, on chain and off.
- `@OnlyOwner` makes the validator require the `owner` field's key to sign.
- `@Destroy` ends the instance: its thread token is burned and `close` says where its value goes.

The contract chapters cover all of this in depth: [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/),
[Authorization](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/), [Require and errors](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/require-and-errors/).

##### 2. What `joust build` writes

`joust dev` ran `joust build` first. Its output, in `build/joust/`:

- build/joust/
  - Counter.json the description: CIP-57 schemas plus JOUST's `x-joust` section
  - Counter.plutus the compiled validator, CBOR hex
  - Counter.js the client, with the description inlined
  - Counter.d.ts its types
  - contracts.json description, script and transition programs, for the runtime engine
  - joust.lock.json the toolchain version and each contract's script hash
  - deployments.devkit.json written by joust deploy

The **description** is the contract's interface: its state, every call and its redeemer, its arguments' schemas, and
the policies the validator enforces. Both the runtime engine and the page work from it. See the
[description format](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/description-format/).

The generated client wraps `JoustContract` from `@julclang/state-client`, with the description pinned in the module:

```js title="build/joust/Counter.js (abridged)"
// GENERATED by joust-gen from app.Counter. Do not edit.
// The description is pinned here: the page verifies every prepared transaction against it (ADR-0013 D2).
import { JoustContract } from '@julclang/state-client';

export const description = {"preamble":{"title":"app.Counter", /* ... */ }};

export class Counter {
  /** @param o { deployment, service, chain, limits?, onReview? } */
  constructor(o) { this.contract = new JoustContract({ ...o, description }); }
  /** init Counter.init. */
  async deploy(wallet, args = {}) {
    const r = await this.contract.deploy(wallet, args);
    return { ...r, instance: this.at(r.instance) };
  }
  /** An instance by its id (the thread token's name, hex). */
  at(instanceId) { return new CounterInstance(this.contract.at(instanceId)); }
}

export class CounterInstance {
  constructor(i) { this.i = i; this.id = i.id; }
  read() { return this.i.read(); }
  state() { return this.i.state(); }
  /** action Counter.increment. */
  increment(wallet, args = {}) { return this.i.call(wallet, "increment", args); }
  /** action Counter.reset; signed by owner. */
  reset(wallet, args = {}) { return this.i.call(wallet, "reset", args); }
  /** destroy Counter.close; signed by owner. */
  close(wallet, args = {}) { return this.i.call(wallet, "close", args); }
}
```

And its types, from the same description:

```ts title="build/joust/Counter.d.ts (abridged)"
export type CounterState = { "count": bigint; "owner": Hex };
export type CounterStateIn = { "count": Int; "owner": Hex };

export declare class Counter {
  constructor(o: JoustOptions);
  readonly contract: JoustContract;
  deploy(wallet: Cip30Api, args: Record<string, never>): Promise<CallResult & { instance: CounterInstance }>;
  at(instanceId: Hex): CounterInstance;
}
export declare class CounterInstance {
  readonly id: Hex;
  read(): Promise<{ ref: string; state: CounterState; lovelace: bigint } | null>;
  state(): Promise<CounterState | null>;
  increment(wallet: Cip30Api, args: { "by": Int }): Promise<CallResult>;
  reset(wallet: Cip30Api, args?: Record<string, never>): Promise<CallResult>;
  close(wallet: Cip30Api, args?: Record<string, never>): Promise<CallResult>;
}
```

Integers come back as `bigint`; you may pass them as `bigint`, a safe `number` or a decimal string (`Int`). Bytes
are lowercase hex. [TypeScript](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/typescript/) explains the mapping.

##### 3. The engine in a worker

The page prepares its own transactions. The runtime engine (Wasm, about 20 MB) runs in a module worker, which is two
lines:

```js title="page/engine.worker.js"
// The runtime engine, in a worker: the page prepares its own transactions with it (see main.js).
import '@julclang/joust-runtime/worker';
```

`page/main.js` starts it and wraps it as a **prepare service**, the object a client asks for transactions:

```js title="page/main.js"
import { blockfrostChain, walletView, VerificationError, toJson } from '@julclang/state-client';
import { engineWorker } from '@julclang/joust-runtime/page';
import { Wallet, NetworkType } from '@cardano-foundation/cardano-connect-with-wallet-core';
import { Counter } from '../build/joust/Counter.js';
// The network, deployments, contracts and engine: from joust dev while developing, inlined in a build.
import net from 'virtual:joust/network';

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const chain = blockfrostChain(new URL(net.chain, location.href).href);
const deployment = net.deployments['app.Counter'];
const service = engineWorker(new Worker(new URL('./engine.worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' }), {
  engine: net.engine, chain: net.chain, clock: net.clock, networkId: net.networkId, ttlMs: net.ttlMs,
  deployments: net.deployments, contracts: net.contracts, validators: net.validators,
});
const counter = new Counter({ service, chain, deployment, onReview: review });
```

- **`virtual:joust/network`** comes from the Vite plugin, `@julclang/joust/vite`. Under `joust dev` it fetches
  `/joust/network.json` and the contracts when the page loads, so a redeploy after a save is picked up on reload. In
  `vite build` it is inlined for one network. Its `chain` is `/chain`: the dev server's proxy, so a Blockfrost
  project id never reaches the page.
- **`chain`** is the page's own view of the chain. The verifier reads from it, independently of the engine.
- **`engineWorker`** sends the engine's URL, its integrity hashes and the network to the worker, and returns a
  service with `prepare(request)`. `service.ready` resolves once the engine has loaded.
- **`new Counter({ service, chain, deployment, onReview })`**: the deployment (policy, address, reference scripts) is
  pinned; the service builds; the page checks.

The page logs how long the engine took to load:

```js title="page/main.js"
const started = performance.now();
const entry = log('Loading the runtime engine (in a worker)…');
service.ready.then(() => entry.ok(`Runtime engine ready in ${((performance.now() - started) / 1000).toFixed(1)} s: this page prepares its own transactions`),
  (e) => entry.bad(`The runtime engine did not load: ${reason(e)}`));
```

[Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/) covers the worker, the plugin and static builds in depth.

##### 4. Connecting a wallet

A dApp talks to browser wallets through **CIP-30**, the standard API that wallet extensions (Eternl, Lace, and
others) inject as `window.cardano.<name>`. The page lists them, and on DevKit adds an in-page key, since browser
wallets cannot join a private devnet:

```js title="page/main.js"
function walletChoices() {
  const sel = $('wallet-choice');
  const current = sel.value;
  const injected = Object.entries(window.cardano ?? {}).filter(([, w]) => w && typeof w.enable === 'function');
  sel.replaceChildren(...injected.map(([key, w]) => el('option', { value: `cip30:${key}` }, w.name ?? key)),
    ...(net.network === 'devkit' ? [el('option', { value: 'dev' }, 'DevKit key (in this page)')] : []));
  // ...
}
```

Connecting uses the Cardano Foundation's connector to enable the extension with a network check, or makes the
in-page key:

```js title="page/main.js"
if (choice === 'dev') {
  const { devWallet } = await import('@julclang/state-client/devwallet');
  const { generateMnemonic } = await import('@scure/bip39');
  const { wordlist } = await import('@scure/bip39/wordlists/english');
  const mnemonic = localStorage.getItem('joust.devkitKey') ?? generateMnemonic(wordlist, 256);
  localStorage.setItem('joust.devkitKey', mnemonic);
  app.api = devWallet({ chain, mnemonic, networkId: net.networkId });
} else {
  const key = choice.slice('cip30:'.length);
  await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    Wallet.connect(key, net.networkId === 1 ? NetworkType.MAINNET : NetworkType.TESTNET, resolve, reject).catch(reject);
  });
  app.api = await window.cardano[key].enable();
}
app.view = await walletView(app.api);
if (app.view.networkId !== net.networkId) throw new Error(`the wallet is on network ${app.view.networkId}; this app is on ${net.network}`);
```

Either way, `app.api` is a CIP-30 API object. Everything after this line works the same with the DevKit key or with
Eternl. Extensions inject themselves after load, some late, so the page also listens:

```js title="page/main.js"
Wallet.addEventListener('installedWalletExtensions', walletChoices);
Wallet.startInjectWalletListener();
```

The **Top up** button posts the wallet's address to the dev server's `/dev/topup`, which funds it from DevKit's
faucet. See [Wallets](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/).

##### 5. Calling the contract

Each button calls the generated client with the wallet's CIP-30 API:

```js title="page/main.js"
$('create').addEventListener('click', () => act('create', async () => {
  const r = await counter.deploy(app.api, {});
  remember(r.instance.id);
  return r;
}));

// per counter, in renderCounters():
const inst = counter.at(id);
const r = await inst.read();                 // { ref, state: { count, owner }, lovelace } or null
el('button', { onclick: () => act('increment(1)', () => inst.increment(app.api, { by: 1n })) }, '+1');
el('button', { onclick: () => act('increment(0)', () => inst.increment(app.api, { by: 0n })) }, '+0');
el('button', { disabled: !mine, onclick: () => act('reset', () => inst.reset(app.api)) }, 'Reset');
el('button', { disabled: !mine, onclick: () => act('close', () => inst.close(app.api)) }, 'Close');
```

One call such as `inst.increment(app.api, { by: 1n })` does all of this:

1. Encodes the arguments with the description's schemas, and reads the wallet: its addresses, keys and the UTxOs it
   reports.
2. Asks the service (the worker) to **prepare** the transaction. The engine fetches what it needs from the chain,
   runs `increment` as a compiled transition program to get the next state, and builds the unsigned transaction from
   the wallet's own UTxOs.
3. **Verifies** the transaction in the page, against the pinned description and deployment, the wallet and the chain.
4. Calls `onReview`, which shows the review dialog.
5. Asks the wallet to sign (`signTx(cbor, true)`), adds the witness to the original bytes, checks the hash, and
   submits through the wallet.
6. Waits until the chain shows the transaction, and returns `{ txHash, report }`.

`act` wraps each call, logs the outcome and links the transaction to the network's explorer:

```js title="page/main.js"
async function act(label, fn) {
  const entry = log(`${label}…`);
  try {
    const r = await fn();
    entry.ok(`${label}: on chain, tx `, txLink(r.txHash));
    await refresh();
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof VerificationError) entry.bad(`${label}: refused by this page's verifier; the wallet was not asked to sign`, e.problems);
    else entry.bad(`${label}: ${reason(e)}`);
  }
}

const txLink = (hash) => (net.explorer
  ? el('a', { href: net.explorer.replace('{tx}', hash), target: '_blank', rel: 'noopener' }, short(hash))
  : short(hash));
```

`net.explorer` is the network's `explorer` from `joust.config.json`, with `{tx}` standing for the hash. DevKit's
default is Yaci Viewer, `http://localhost:5173/transactions/{tx}`.

##### 6. The review dialog

`onReview` receives `{ contract, call, report, txHash }` after the transaction has passed verification and before the
wallet is asked. Resolve to go on; throw to cancel. The template shows what the page checked:

```js title="page/main.js"
function review({ contract, call, report }) {
  const args = Object.keys(call.args ?? {}).length ? JSON.stringify(toJson(call.args)) : '';
  $('review-body').replaceChildren(
    el('h3', {}, `${contract}.${call.meta.name}(${args})`),
    el('ul', {},
      el('li', {}, `The redeemer is exactly this call, on the pinned script ${short(deployment.policy)}`),
      el('li', {}, report.walletNet > 0n ? `Your wallet pays ${ada(report.walletNet)} in all (fee ${ada(report.fee)})`
        : `Your wallet receives ${ada(-report.walletNet)} net of the ${ada(report.fee)} fee`),
      el('li', {}, report.next ? `The next state: ${JSON.stringify(toJson(report.next))}` : 'The counter ends; its deposit comes back to you'),
      el('li', {}, 'No other spends, mints, certificates, withdrawals or signers; it expires within minutes')),
  );
  const dlg = $('review');
  dlg.returnValue = '';
  dlg.showModal();
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => dlg.addEventListener('close',
    () => (dlg.returnValue === 'sign' ? resolve() : reject(new Error('cancelled before signing'))), { once: true }));
}
```

`report.walletNet` is what the wallet loses in lovelace, fee included (negative when it gains, as when `close` pays
the deposit back). `report.next` is the next state, decoded from the new datum.

##### 7. What the page verifier checks

Neither the engine nor the chain API is trusted. Before `onReview` runs, `verifyPrepared` (in
[`js/state-client/src/verify.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/state-client/src/verify.js))
checks the transaction against what the page knows itself. For a Counter call that means:

| Check | Refused when |
|---|---|
| Inputs | anything but the wallet's own UTxOs and this counter's UTxO is spent |
| Redeemer | it is not exactly the call the page asked for, with the page's arguments, on the counter's input |
| Script | the counter's UTxO is not at the pinned address, or a reference input is not a pinned one |
| Continuation | there is not exactly one new counter UTxO with the token, an inline datum that decodes as `State` |
| Mint | an action mints anything; `close` burns anything but its own token; a creation mints more than its new token |
| Wallet's loss | the wallet loses more than it pays, plus the fee (plus the new UTxO's minimum ADA for a creation) |
| Others | an output gives anyone else more than the script releases |
| Extras | certificates, withdrawals, votes, metadata, other required signers, another network |
| Fee | above what the protocol asks for this size and budget (times 1.2, plus 0.5 ADA), or above 3 ADA |
| Collateral | not the wallet's, not returned to the wallet, or more than 5 ADA at risk |
| Validity | it ends more than 900 slots (15 minutes) from now, or starts later than 60 slots from now |
| Plan | the engine's plan of the transaction differs from the one the page derives from the bytes |

What the page does not check, the validator does: that the next state is what `increment` computes, that `close`
pays the owner, and that the script's value is conserved. Together, the wallet risks nothing beyond the call it was
shown. A refusal throws `VerificationError`, whose `problems` the page lists; the wallet is never opened.

##### 8. The `+0` refusal

Press **+0** on a counter. The activity log marks `increment(0)` as failed, with the contract's own message:
`increment must be positive`.

This refusal does not come from the page verifier. When the engine prepares the call, it runs `increment` itself,
compiled from the same Java method, and `Require.that` fails with the contract's own message. No transaction is built,
so no wallet is asked. The validator would refuse the same call on chain for the same reason; JOUST finds it before
anything is signed or paid.

The Node test checks the same thing:

```js title="test/counter.test.js"
await assert.rejects(instance.increment(wallet, { by: 0n }), /increment must be positive/);
```

##### 9. Try it

With `npm run dev` running, open http://127.0.0.1:5178 and:

1. Choose **DevKit key (in this page)**, **Connect**, then **Top up 1000 ADA**.
2. **Create a counter** and review it: your wallet pays the fee and the counter's deposit.
3. Press **+1** twice. The count shows 2; each review shows the next state.
4. Press **+0**: refused before signing.
5. **Reset**, then **Close**. Close's review shows your wallet receiving the deposit back, net of the fee.
6. Change `increment` in `Counter.java` (for example, also refuse amounts over 100) and save. The dev server
   rebuilds and redeploys a new script; reload the page and the new rule holds. Counters made by the old script stay
   with it.

##### What you learned

- A JOUST contract is a state record and pure methods. `joust build` turns it into a validator, a description and a
  typed client, and `joust deploy` publishes the validator as a reference script.
- The page prepares transactions in a Web Worker with the runtime engine, which runs the contract's own methods. A
  contract refusal surfaces there, before any wallet is involved.
- The page verifies every transaction against the pinned description and deployment before `onReview` and the wallet
  see it. The validator enforces the rest on chain.
- CIP-30 wallets and the DevKit key are interchangeable: the client only needs the CIP-30 API.

### Deploy to preview

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/deploy-preview/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

Yaci DevKit is private and fast, but browser wallets cannot join it. **Preview** is a public Cardano testnet: its ADA
(tADA) is free from a faucet, and Eternl, Lace and other CIP-30 wallets work there. In this tutorial you deploy the
template's Counter on preview, use it with a real wallet, then build the page as static files you can host anywhere.

You need the app from the [Counter dApp tutorial](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/counter-dapp/) or the
[npm quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/), built with `npm run build`.

##### What changes on preview

`preview` is a built-in network: you do not need to add it to `joust.config.json`. Its definition, from
[`js/joust/src/config.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/joust/src/config.js):

```js title="js/joust/src/config.js"
preview: {
  chain: 'https://cardano-preview.blockfrost.io/api/v0', projectIdEnv: 'BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID', networkId: 0,
  clock: { zeroSlot: 0, zeroTimeMs: 1666656000000, slotLengthMs: 1000 },
  explorer: 'https://preview.cardanoscan.io/transaction/{tx}',
},
```

| | DevKit | preview |
|---|---|---|
| Chain API | Yaci Store, `http://localhost:8080/api/v1` | Blockfrost, with your project id |
| Slot clock | read from DevKit's admin API | preview's genesis: slot 0 at 1666656000 s, one-second slots |
| Deployer key | made by `joust deploy`, funded from the faucet | yours, from `JOUST_MNEMONIC` |
| Page wallets | the in-page DevKit key | Eternl, Lace, any CIP-30 wallet |
| Transaction TTL (pages) | 20 s | 180 s |
| Explorer links | Yaci Viewer | Cardanoscan (preview) |

##### 1. Credentials

1. **A Blockfrost project for preview.** Create one at [blockfrost.io](https://blockfrost.io) and export its id:

   ```sh
   export BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID=preview...
   ```

   JOUST reads it from the environment only, never from `joust.config.json`. `joust dev` and `joust serve` keep it in
   the server and proxy the chain API to the page at `/chain`, so it never reaches a browser.

2. **A funded deployer key.** `joust deploy` pays for publishing the reference script with the key in
   `JOUST_MNEMONIC`, a BIP39 mnemonic:

   ```sh
   export JOUST_MNEMONIC="word1 word2 ... word24"
   ```

   It pays from the mnemonic's first base address (payment key `m/1852'/1815'/0'/0/0`, as cardano-client-lib derives
   it). Print that address, then send it tADA from the Cardano testnet faucet:

   ```sh
   node --input-type=module -e "

   console.log(deriveAccount(process.env.JOUST_MNEMONIC, 0, 0).address);"
   ```

   The deployment locks ADA in the reference-script output (its minimum ADA grows with the script's size), plus the
   fee.

> **Keep deployer keys apart:** 
Use a key made for preview, holding test ADA only. Never put a mainnet mnemonic in `JOUST_MNEMONIC`, in a shell
history or in a CI log.

##### 2. Deploy

```sh
npm run build
npm run deploy:preview      # joust deploy --network preview
```

For each contract, `joust deploy` asks the runtime engine for its deployment. If the reference script is not on chain
yet, it has the engine build the publishing transaction, checks that it pays only the contract's address (with the
script) and the deployer, signs it with `JOUST_MNEMONIC`'s key and submits it. Then it writes
`build/joust/deployments.preview.json`: the contract's policy (its script hash), address and reference script, the
network id, the chain URL and the clock.

```txt
app.Counter: addr_test1w... (reference script 9a3c...#0)
wrote .../build/joust/deployments.preview.json
```

Running it again publishes nothing: the script is found at the contract's address. A changed contract has another
script hash, so it is published as a new deployment.

> **Note:** 
`joust deploy` stops with `set JOUST_MNEMONIC to deploy on preview` when the key is missing, and with
`network preview reads its chain API's project id from BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID: set it` when the project id is.

##### 3. Run the page with a browser wallet

```sh
npm run dev:preview         # joust dev --network preview
```

`joust dev` attaches to Blockfrost, builds, deploys (a no-op when nothing changed) and serves the page at
http://127.0.0.1:5178, with the chain at `/chain`.

1. Install Eternl or Lace, and switch it to the **preview** network. Fund its address from the faucet.

2. Reload the page. The wallet appears in the list (the page watches for extensions that inject late). Choose it and
   press **Connect**, then approve in the wallet. The connector checks that the wallet is on a test network, and the
   page checks its network id against the deployment's.

3. **Create a counter.** The page prepares the transaction in its worker, from the UTxOs your wallet reports, verifies
   it and shows the review dialog. Press **Sign in the wallet**: the wallet shows its own prompt, signs, and submits.

4. Press **+1**, then **Close**. Each transaction hash links to Cardanoscan's preview explorer.

###### What a call costs on preview

ADR-0015 §13.11 records a maintainer's run of this page on preview with a browser wallet. The fees were:

| Call | Fee |
|---|---|
| Create a counter | 303,656 lovelace |
| `increment(1)` | 292,146 lovelace |
| Close | 309,674 lovelace |

So a Counter call costs about 0.29 tADA in fees. Each fee is the protocol's fixed part (by size), the reference-script
fee (by the size of the script the transaction references; 29% of an increment's fee, issue #34) and the script's
execution budget. The fees also overpay by one vkey witness, 4,563 lovelace (issue #33). Creating a counter also
locks its minimum ADA in the counter's UTxO, which `close` pays back to the owner.

##### 4. Build the page as static files

`joust dev` serves a page that reads its network from the dev server. For hosting, build it instead:

```sh
npm run build:page:preview  # vite build --mode preview
npm run serve:preview       # joust serve --network preview
```

`vite build --mode preview` selects the `preview` network (Vite's mode names it). The Vite plugin then inlines into
the page:

- the network, its id, clock, TTL and explorer;
- `deployments.preview.json` and `contracts.json` (run `deploy:preview` first: the build reads no chain);
- the runtime engine's sha384 hashes.

It copies the engine's two files into `dist/joust/engine-<id>/`. `joust serve` then serves `dist/` as plain static
files, plus the chain proxy at `/chain`. It builds, deploys and bundles nothing. Open http://127.0.0.1:5178 and repeat
the wallet run: it behaves exactly as under `joust dev`.

##### 5. Host it

`dist/` can go on any static host. The page needs one thing the host must give it: a chain API.

**A /chain proxy (default):**

By default a built page reads the chain at `/chain` on its own origin. Put a proxy there that forwards to Blockfrost
and adds the project id, as `joust serve` does
([`js/joust/src/routes.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/joust/src/routes.js)):

| The page sends | The proxy forwards |
|---|---|
| `GET /chain/<path>?<query>` | `GET https://cardano-preview.blockfrost.io/api/v0/<path>?<query>` with the header `project_id: <your id>` |
| `POST /chain/tx/submit` (body: CBOR, `content-type: application/cbor`) | the same `POST` to `.../tx/submit`, body and content type unchanged, with `project_id` |

Return the upstream status, content type and body unchanged. `joust serve` also keeps Blockfrost's load-balancer
affinity cookie (`__cflb`) for every upstream request, so its reads all reach one Blockfrost backend: worth doing in
your own proxy too, since Blockfrost's backends can be a moment apart.

**A public chain API (pageChain):**

If you have a Blockfrost-compatible API that a browser may call directly (it needs no secret), name it as the
network's `pageChain` and build again:

```json title="joust.config.json"
{
  "networks": {
    "preview": { "pageChain": "https://chain.example.org/api/v0" }
  }
}
```

The network is merged over the built-in `preview`, so only `pageChain` changes. The page then needs no proxy.

The page and its worker resolve the chain URL and the engine's URL against the page's address, not the worker's
script. The default `/chain` is therefore at the root of the page's origin. To host the page under a sub-path, set
Vite's `base`: the plugin builds the engine's URL from it.

###### Integrity of the engine

The page's own code pins the engine's sha384 hashes. Its worker fetches the engine's script with
`fetch(url, { integrity })`, and adds the Wasm module's hash to the one request that loads it. A browser then refuses
an engine whose bytes differ, wherever it is served from. A tampered copy fails to start, and the page logs that the
engine does not match its integrity hash. You can put the 20 MB engine on a CDN without trusting the CDN.

And whatever builds a transaction, the page verifies it before the wallet signs. Neither the host, the CDN, the engine
nor the chain API can make the wallet sign something other than the call the page shows.

##### What you learned

- `preview` is built in: a Blockfrost project id and a funded deployer key are all it needs.
- `joust deploy --network preview` publishes reference scripts once and writes `deployments.preview.json`, which
  pages pin.
- The same page runs with Eternl or Lace: the client only needs the CIP-30 API.
- A built page is static files for one network. It needs a chain API: a `/chain` proxy that keeps the project id
  secret, or a `pageChain`. The engine is checked by its hashes wherever it is served.

  - [Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/)
  - [Pages: worker, Vite, static builds](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/)
  - [Wallets](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/)

## Writing contracts

### State and lifecycle

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/

A JOUST contract is a **state record** plus **pure static methods** that create, change, read and end it. This page
covers that core: the `@StateContract` options, the four method kinds and their exact signatures, how an instance is
identified, how big the state may grow, and how to keep maps and lists in the state so the chain and the JVM agree.

Every other feature (payments, authorisation, time, maps, objects) builds on what is here.

##### The model in one picture

On Cardano, data lives in **UTxOs** (unspent transaction outputs): each holds some value and, optionally, a piece of
data called a **datum**. A script guards the UTxOs at its address; spending one runs the script with a **redeemer**
(the argument of the call). See the [glossary](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/glossary/) for these terms.

JOUST maps your contract onto that model:

- An **instance** of your contract is one UTxO at the contract's script address. Its inline datum is your state
  record, as is (no envelope), and it holds one **thread token** that names the instance.
- `@Init` creates an instance: the transaction mints the thread token and creates the state UTxO.
- `@Action` spends the state UTxO and creates the next one, with the new state.
- `@Destroy` spends the state UTxO, burns the token and pays everything out. The instance is gone.
- `@View` reads the current state. It runs only off chain and builds no transaction.

![An instance's life on chain: create, actions, destroy](../../../assets/diagrams/lifecycle.svg)

The same method runs twice: on the JVM (or in the npm engine) to compute the next state and build the transaction,
and on chain, where the generated validator re-runs it and checks that the output datum equals its result.

##### A complete contract

**Java:**

```java title="examples/counter/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/counter/Counter.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 128)
public class Counter {

    /** The state, stored as the inline datum of the state UTxO. */
    public record State(BigInteger count, byte[] owner) {}

    /** The deployer becomes the owner. */
    @Init
    public static State init(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, ctx.caller());
    }

    /** Anyone can increment by a positive amount (no Ctx: no signature needed, cheaper). */
    @Action
    public static State increment(State s, BigInteger by) {
        Require.that(by.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "increment must be positive");
        return new State(s.count().add(by), s.owner());
    }

    /** Only the owner can reset. */
    @Action
    @OnlyOwner
    public static State reset(State s) {
        return new State(BigInteger.ZERO, s.owner());
    }

    /** Only the owner can close the counter; the deposit goes back to them. */
    @Destroy
    @OnlyOwner
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance());
    }

    /** Read-only view (off-chain, no transaction). */
    @View
    public static BigInteger count(State s) {
        return s.count();
    }
}
```

**.jsc:**

```jsc title="Counter.jsc"
jsc 1
package org.example.counter

// A counter anyone can increment and only its owner can reset or close.
contract Counter(maxDatumBytes = 128) {
  state { count: Int, owner: Key }

  init() {
    return { count: 0, owner: caller }
  }

  action increment(by: Int) {
    require(by > 0, "increment must be positive")
    return { ...state, count: count + by }
  }

  action reset() only owner {
    return { ...state, count: 0 }
  }

  destroy close() only owner {
    pay(owner, balance)
  }

  view current(): Int = count
}
```

`state { … }` declares the components of the generated `State` record, in order. `init` returns the first state,
every field given; an action returns the next one, `{ ...state, … }` keeping the fields it does not change.
`only owner` lowers to `@SignedBy("owner")`. See [.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/).

**JavaScript:**

```js title="test/counter.test.js (from the create-joust template)"
import { Counter } from '../build/joust/Counter.js';   // generated by joust-gen from the contract description

const counter = new Counter(rt.options('app.Counter')); // or new Counter({ service, chain, deployment })
const { instance } = await counter.deploy(wallet, {});   // @Init
await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 5n });            // @Action
await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 2n });
(await instance.state()).count;                          // 7n
await instance.close(wallet);                            // @Destroy
await instance.state();                                  // null: the instance is gone
```

See [JavaScript clients](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/) for `service`, `chain` and `deployment`.

From this one file the JOUST annotation processor generates `CounterValidator` (compiled to UPLC by JuLC) and
`CounterClient` (the typed Java client) in the same package.

##### `@StateContract` options

`@StateContract` marks the class. The class must be top-level and public. JuLC treats
`@StateContract` exactly like its own `@OnchainLibrary` (a fixed alias), so JuLC compiles the class for on-chain use
without a second annotation.

| Element | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `maxDatumBytes` | `512` | Largest serialised state the validator accepts, between 16 and 8192. A transition whose result is larger is rejected, so no call can grow the state UTxO beyond what `minAda` covers. |
| `minAda` | `0` (derived) | Lovelace locked in the state UTxO as its min-ADA deposit, on top of the contract's funds. `0` derives it: `4310 × (160 + 200 + maxDatumBytes + 80 × assetSlots)`, rounded up to 0.1 ADA. An explicit value below that is a compile error. |
| `maxValidityMs` | `3_600_000` (1 h) | Widest validity interval, in POSIX milliseconds, that a call reading `Ctx` may use. At least 60,000. See [Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/). |
| `assetSlots` | `-1` | Native assets a state UTxO may hold, for the deposit (about 80 bytes each). `-1` means 4 for contracts that handle native assets, 0 otherwise. Between 0 and 64. See [native assets](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/). |
| `stakeSelf` | `false` | Stake the state UTxOs to the contract's own script. Needs `@Withdraw` and `@Certify` handlers. See [staking](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/staking-and-governance/). |

Derived deposits for lovelace-only contracts (`assetSlots` 0), as the generated clients record them:

| `maxDatumBytes` | `minAda` | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 128 | 2,200,000 (2.2 ADA) | counter, vault |
| 192 | 2,400,000 (2.4 ADA) | escrow |
| 512 (default) | 3,800,000 (3.8 ADA) | upgrade |
| 640 | 4,400,000 (4.4 ADA) | treasury |
| 1024 | 6,000,000 (6.0 ADA) | crowdfund |

The deposit stays in the state UTxO for the instance's whole life. Actions cannot spend it; a `@Destroy` pays it out.

##### The state record

The state type is defined by the return type of the `@Init` method. It must be a record. Its components can be any
type JuLC can encode as Plutus data:

- `BigInteger`, `byte[]` and `boolean`;
- records and sealed interfaces declared in the contract;
- `JulcList<T>`, `JulcMap<K, V>` and `Optional<T>`;
- `MerkleMap` for unbounded maps (top-level components only; see [MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/)).

The datum on chain is the record itself, readable with the contract's CIP-57 schema. Framework data (the instance
id, the deposit) comes from the UTxO (its token name and value), not from the datum.

> **The JuLC subset:** 

The whole class, views included, must stay inside JuLC's subset of Java, because JuLC compiles it as a library:
`BigInteger` (never `int` or `long`: the processor rejects fixed-width numbers, which would make the JVM and the chain
disagree), records and sealed interfaces only, no generic records, immutable locals except loop accumulators, no
`throw` (use [`Require.that`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/require-and-errors/)), and `byte[]` compared with `ByteStringLib.equals`,
never `==` or `.equals`. See [Java](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/java/).

##### Method kinds and signatures

`S` is the state type. Arguments are any encodable types (as above). `Ctx` is optional, and when present it is the
last parameter (or the last before `Funds`). Every method is `public static` and not generic, and names are unique
among the annotated methods (no overloading).

| Kind | Shape | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| `@Init` | `public static S name(args… [, Ctx])` | Exactly one per contract. Its return type is the state type. Parameter names `seed`, `ctx` and `instance` are reserved. |
| `@Action` | `public static S name(S s, args… [, Ctx])` or `public static R name(S s, args… [, Ctx])` | `R` is a result record (below) with a `state` component. |
| `@Destroy` | `public static JulcList<Payout> name(S s, args…, Ctx ctx)` | `Ctx` is required: it must pay out `ctx.balance()`. May also return a result record without `state`. A contract may have several (escrow has `release` and `refund`). |
| `@View` | `public static T name(S s, args…)` | No `Ctx`. Runs only off chain; becomes a client getter. Must return a value. |

A method that takes deploy-time parameters declares the `@Params` record right after the state (first in `@Init`);
see [Params, invariants and events](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/).

###### Result records

JuLC rejects generic records, so there is no `Result<S>`. A method that returns more than the next state declares
its own record, and the processor recognises it **by its component names**:

```java title="examples/vault/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/Vault.java"
/** An action that pays out returns the next state and its payouts. */
public record Result(State state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}
```

| Component | Type | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `state` | the state type | required in actions, forbidden in destroys |
| `payouts` | `JulcList<Payout>` | lovelace to key hashes ([Ctx, funds and payouts](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/)) |
| `sends` | `JulcList<Send>` | any output, native assets included ([assets](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/)) |
| `mint` | `Value` | tokens under the contract's own policy |
| `accepted` | `Value` | native assets a `@Payable` method with `Funds` takes in |
| `deposits` | `JulcList<Deposit>` | payments into another instance ([deposits](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/)) |
| `events` | `JulcList<E>` | authenticated events ([events](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/)) |

Any other component name is a compile error. A destroy's record needs at least one of `payouts`, `sends`, `mint`
or `deposits`.

###### Names

Each action or destroy becomes a redeemer variant named after the method, capitalised (`increment` →
`Increment`). The processor reports a compile error when a method or parameter name clashes with something it
generates: the client's members (`deploy`, `at`, `contract`, `state`, `instance`, `instanceId`, `lovelace`,
`fullValue`, `params`, `policyIdFor`, …), the parameter names `ctx` and `maps`, or the generated types.

##### Instances and their ids

There is **one script per contract type**, not one per instance. The validator is a JuLC `@MultiValidator` with a
MINT and a SPEND side, and its hash is at once the policy id of the thread tokens and the payment credential of the
address. All instances of a contract live at that one **enterprise** script address (no stake credential, unless
`stakeSelf`).

An instance is named by its thread token:

```text
instanceId = blake2b_256(seedTxId ‖ seedIndex as 2 bytes)
```

The **seed** is any UTxO the deployer spends in the creating transaction. Each UTxO can be spent once, so each seed
gives one instance, forever. The id is 32 bytes, shown as hex.

**Java:**

```java
var vault = VaultClient.deploy(runtime, alice, BigInteger.valueOf(unlockAt), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
String id = vault.instanceId();                 // 64 hex characters

var again = VaultClient.at(runtime, id);        // reconnect later, from anywhere
BigInteger total = again.total();               // a @View: no transaction
Vault.State s = again.state();                  // the decoded datum
BigInteger held = again.lovelace();             // what the UTxO holds, deposit included
```

**JavaScript:**

```js
const { instance, txHash } = await vault.deploy(wallet, { unlockAt }, { lovelace: 10_000_000n });
const id = instance.id;                          // hex thread-token name

const again = vault.at(id);
const { state, lovelace } = await again.read();  // null once destroyed
```

> **Authenticate instances by policy and id:** 

Ids are unique per policy only: one seed can create one instance of each contract type in the same transaction. A
dApp that trusts an instance must check both the policy id (the contract) and the instance id. Anyone can also create
an instance of your contract with any `@Init` arguments (for example naming a victim as the seller of an escrow), so a
front end should show who created an instance and with what arguments.

A contract without a `@Destroy` compiles with a warning: an instance can never end, so its deposit is locked forever.

##### Datum size and capacity

`maxDatumBytes` bounds the serialised state. The validator checks it on every state it accepts as an output: the
initial state and every action's result. The runtime checks it first and refuses the call with a `RequireException` of this form:

```text
<Contract>.<method>: the new state is <n> bytes, over <Contract>'s maxDatumBytes (<max>)
```

Why it exists: the deposit (`minAda`) is fixed when the instance is created. If a call could grow the datum past
what that deposit covers, the next state UTxO would be below the ledger's minimum and the instance would be stuck.

The cap creates a capacity limit. An action anyone can call that grows a collection lets anyone fill it: about 13
entries of `key hash → amount` fit in the default 512 bytes. Size `maxDatumBytes` for your use, and add an economic
floor. Crowdfund sets `maxDatumBytes = 1024` and a minimum contribution of at least 2 ADA; its harness test fills the
campaign (27 backers with 2 ADA each) and checks that a refund still succeeds at capacity. Make sure the paths that
**shrink** the state (refunds, claims, destroys) always remain possible.

For maps without a practical bound, use a [MerkleMap](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/): only a 32-byte root lives in the datum.

##### Lists and maps in the state

`JulcList` and `JulcMap` are JuLC's immutable collections. They work in the state, with a few rules that come from
how they behave on chain.

###### `JulcList`

The treasury keeps its council as a list of key hashes:

```java title="examples/treasury/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/Treasury.java"
public record State(JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, boolean frozen) {}
```

Build lists with `JulcList.empty()` and `prepend`, and iterate with `for (var x : list)`. Order is part of the data:
two lists with the same elements in a different order are different states.

###### `JulcMap` and `SortedMaps`

A `JulcMap` is an ordered association list:

- `insert` **prepends**; an existing key stays, so a map can hold duplicates. Update with `delete(k)` then
  `insert(k, v)`.
- `get` aborts on chain when the key is missing: check `containsKey` first.
- `getOrDefault` has no on-chain form.

There is one more trap. cardano-client-lib writes inline datums in **canonical CBOR**, which sorts map keys (shorter
key first, then byte-wise). If a state map is not already in that order, the datum written on chain differs from the
state the validator recomputes, and the call fails on chain. So keep state maps in canonical order. For the common
`JulcMap<byte[], BigInteger>`, `SortedMaps` does it on the JVM and on chain alike:

| Method | Does |
|---|---|
| `SortedMaps.put(m, k, v)` | `m` with `k` set to `v`, keeping canonical order |
| `SortedMaps.remove(m, k)` | `m` without `k` (order kept) |
| `SortedMaps.getOr(m, k, otherwise)` | the value for `k`, or `otherwise` |
| `SortedMaps.before(a, b)` | true if `a` sorts before `b` in canonical CBOR order |

```java title="examples/crowdfund/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/crowdfund/Crowdfund.java"
@Action
@Payable
public static State contribute(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(Clock.before(ctx, s.deadline()), "the campaign has ended");
    Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(s.minContribution()) >= 0, "below the minimum contribution");
    BigInteger before = SortedMaps.getOr(s.backers(), ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO);
    JulcMap<byte[], BigInteger> backers = SortedMaps.put(s.backers(), ctx.caller(), before.add(ctx.received()));
    return new State(s.creator(), s.goal(), s.deadline(), s.minContribution(), s.raised().add(ctx.received()), backers);
}
```

The runtime refuses to submit a state whose maps are out of order, before anything reaches the chain:

```text
Crowdfund.contribute: the new Crowdfund state contains a map whose keys are not in canonical order, so the datum
written on chain would differ from the one the validator recomputes. Keep state maps ordered with
org.julclang.state.api.SortedMaps
```

> **Tip:** 

`SortedMaps` covers `byte[]` keys and `BigInteger` values. For other maps in the state, insert in canonical key order
yourself, or use a MerkleMap. In `.jsc`, a `Map<K, V>` is an inline map that the generated code keeps canonical, and a `BigMap<K, V>`
is a MerkleMap.

##### What the generated validator checks

The validator wraps your methods with the invariants of [ADR-0001](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-option-a-single-utxo-state-machine.md) §4. For the lifecycle:

**Create (MINT):**
- the seed named in the redeemer is spent by the transaction;
- exactly one token is minted under the policy, named `blake2b_256(seed)`, with quantity 1, and nothing else;
- exactly one output carries it, at the contract's enterprise script address, with no reference script;
- its inline datum equals `init(args, ctx)` and fits `maxDatumBytes`;
- its value is exactly the deposit plus what the caller paid in, plus the token;
- `Ctx` matches the transaction, with `balance` 0.

**Action (SPEND):**
- the spent UTxO holds exactly one thread token of the policy (UTxOs without one are junk and can never be spent);
- exactly one output carries the token, at the **same address**, with an inline datum equal to the method's result,
  within `maxDatumBytes`, and no reference script;
- its value is exactly `{lovelace: in + received − payouts, token: 1}`: no token dust, no skimming;
- that lovelace is at least `minAda`: actions never spend the deposit.

**Destroy (SPEND + MINT):**
- the thread token is burned (−1);
- the payouts add up to **everything** the UTxO holds, deposit included;
- the burn redeemer only burns.

The checks for `Ctx`, payouts, authorisation and time are on their own pages. [Security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/)
lists them all.

##### Pitfalls

- **Forgetting `Ctx` in a destroy.** It is a compile error: a destroy must pay out `ctx.balance()`.
- **Growing the state without a floor.** Anyone-callable growth plus `maxDatumBytes` is a griefing vector. Add a
  minimum amount or a signer.
- **Map order.** A `JulcMap` built with plain `insert` fails on chain as soon as keys arrive out of order. Use
  `SortedMaps`.
- **Comparing bytes.** `a == b` and `a.equals(b)` compare references on the JVM and bytes on chain. Use
  `ByteStringLib.equals(a, b)`.
- **Reading `count` from a view in a transaction.** Views never run on chain. A method that needs a value computes it
  from the state itself.

##### Reference

- [Annotations](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/) and [State API](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/state-api/)
- Sources: [`StateContract.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/StateContract.java),
  [`SortedMaps.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/SortedMaps.java),
  [`ContractReader.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-processor/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/processor/ContractReader.java) (every rule the processor enforces)
- ADR-0001: D1 (annotations), D2 (method shapes), D6 (the datum), D8 (instance identity), §10 (capacity), §15 F13 (canonical maps)

### Ctx, funds and payouts

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/

A contract that holds money needs three things: to know who is calling, to take payments in, and to pay funds out
safely. In JOUST these are a parameter (`Ctx`), an annotation (`@Payable`) and a return value (`Payout`s). This page
explains each, and exactly what the generated validator checks so that the numbers your method sees are the real
ones.

##### `Ctx`: transaction facts your method may read

A method that needs facts about the transaction declares `Ctx` as its last parameter:

```java title="julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Ctx.java"
public record Ctx(byte[] caller, BigInteger received, BigInteger balance, BigInteger validFrom, BigInteger validTo) {}
```

The client fills it in; the validator **verifies every field** against the transaction before it calls your method.
Your method can therefore trust each value, on the JVM and on chain.

| Field | Meaning | How the validator verifies it |
|---|---|---|
| `caller` | Payment key hash (28 bytes) of the party calling | The transaction is signed by that key |
| `received` | Lovelace this call adds to the contract | `received ≥ 0` if the method is `@Payable`, else `received == 0`; the exact value check then forces the state output to hold it |
| `balance` | Funds the call may allocate | In an `@Action`: the state UTxO's lovelace before the call **minus** the `minAda` deposit. In a `@Destroy`: **everything** the UTxO holds, deposit included. In `@Init`: 0 |
| `validFrom` | Start of the validity interval (POSIX ms, inclusive) | Equal to the transaction's finite lower bound |
| `validTo` | End of the validity interval (POSIX ms, exclusive) | Equal to the transaction's finite upper bound, and `validTo − validFrom ≤ maxValidityMs` |

Time has its own page: [Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/).

###### When to declare `Ctx`

Declare it when the method reads any of these facts. It has a cost:

- the transaction must be signed by `caller`, and carry a finite validity interval;
- the redeemer carries five more values (bigger transaction, higher size fee).

A method without `Ctx` gets no caller signature and no time bounds. The counter's `increment` has no `Ctx`, so anyone
can call it cheaply:

```java title="examples/counter/.../Counter.java"
@Action
public static State increment(State s, BigInteger by) {
    Require.that(by.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "increment must be positive");
    return new State(s.count().add(by), s.owner());
}
```

Without `Ctx` the contract's value must stay unchanged, unless the method returns payouts (then nothing can be paid
in). `@Payable` and `@Destroy` both require `Ctx`; the processor reports an error otherwise.

###### Who the caller is

The caller is the account (Java) or wallet (JavaScript) you pass to the client call. Its payment key hash becomes
`ctx.caller()`, and the transaction lists it as a required signer. Compare it with stored keys through
`ByteStringLib.equals`:

```java title="examples/escrow/.../Escrow.java"
@Destroy
public static JulcList<Payout> release(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    boolean allowed = ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.buyer()) || ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.arbiter());
    Require.that(allowed, "only the buyer or the arbiter can release");
    return Payouts.of(s.seller(), ctx.balance());
}
```

For checks that only compare the caller with a state field, the annotations on [Authorization](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/)
are shorter and are checked before your method runs.

##### `@Payable`: taking lovelace in

`@Payable` on an `@Init` or `@Action` lets the caller add lovelace. The method sees the amount in `ctx.received()`
and decides what to do with it. Without `@Payable`, `received` must be zero. A destroy may be `@Payable` too, to take a
price it pays on (the market example's `buy` is a payable owned destroy); its payouts must then allocate what the UTxO
held plus what was paid in.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/vault/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/Vault.java"
/** Opens a vault, optionally with a first deposit; the deployer owns it. */
@Init
@Payable
public static State open(BigInteger unlockAt, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(Clock.before(ctx, unlockAt), "unlockAt must be in the future");
    return new State(ctx.caller(), unlockAt, ctx.received());
}

/** Anyone can add funds. */
@Action
@Payable
public static State deposit(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "deposit must be positive");
    return new State(s.owner(), s.unlockAt(), s.total().add(ctx.received()));
}
```

**.jsc:**

```jsc
init(unlockAt: Int) payable {
  require(before(unlockAt), "unlockAt must be in the future")
  return { owner: caller, unlockAt, total: received }
}

action deposit() payable {
  require(received > 0, "deposit must be positive")
  return { ...state, total: total + received }
}
```

`received` is `ctx.received()`; a method that uses it gets a `Ctx` parameter in the lowered Java. A destroy cannot be
`payable` in `.jsc`.

**JavaScript:**

```js
// A payable call takes the payment as its last argument: { lovelace, assets? }.
const { instance } = await vault.deploy(wallet, { unlockAt }, { lovelace: 10_000_000n });
await instance.deposit(wallet, {}, { lovelace: 5_000_000n });
```

The generated Java client adds a `BigInteger payLovelace` parameter to every payable call:

```java title="examples/vault/.../VaultApp.java"
var vault = VaultClient.deploy(runtime, alice, BigInteger.valueOf(unlockAt), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
vault.deposit(bob, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(5)));
```

Native assets come in through a second trailing parameter, `Funds`, and an `accepted` result component. That is
covered in [Native assets, mints and sends](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/).

##### Payouts: paying funds out

Your method never builds outputs. It **returns** what the contract owes, and the generated validator checks that the
transaction pays it. A payout is lovelace to a payment key hash:

```java title="julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Payout.java"
public record Payout(byte[] to, BigInteger lovelace) {}
```

Build lists with `Payouts`:

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `Payouts.none()` | an empty list |
| `Payouts.of(to, lovelace)` | a list with one payout |
| `Payouts.add(payouts, to, lovelace)` | `payouts` with one more (prepended) |
| `Payouts.total(payouts)` | the sum of the amounts |

An action that pays out returns a result record with the next state and the payouts:

```java title="examples/vault/.../Vault.java"
public record Result(State state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}

/** The owner takes funds out once the vault is unlocked. */
@Action
@OnlyOwner
@ValidAfter("unlockAt")
public static Result withdraw(State s, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
    Require.that(amount.compareTo(s.total()) <= 0, "insufficient funds");
    return new Result(new State(s.owner(), s.unlockAt(), s.total().subtract(amount)), Payouts.of(s.owner(), amount));
}
```

In `.jsc`, `pay(owner, amount)` adds a payout (a zero amount pays nothing; a negative one fails); payouts are in source
order.

###### What the validator checks for payouts

For every payout list a method returns:

- each payout's `lovelace` is greater than zero, and its `to` is 28 bytes;
- for each recipient `r`, the outputs that pay `r`'s key **and carry this instance's input reference as their inline
  datum** add up to at least what the payouts owe `r` (several payouts to one key are added up);
- in an action, the continuing state output holds exactly `in + received − total(payouts)`, and that is at least
  `minAda`.

The runtime pays one output per recipient, tagged as above, and tops an amount below the ledger's minimum UTxO up
from the fee payer. The check is "paid ≥ owed", so a top-up is accepted.

###### Why payouts are tagged

Without the tag, a transaction could spend two instances that each owe Alice 10 ADA and pay her once: both validators
would look at the same 10 ADA output and be satisfied. This is **double satisfaction**. The tag (the inline datum of
the payout output equals the spent state UTxO's reference) ties each payout to exactly one instance, so two
instances, of this or any other JOUST contract, can never count the same output.

> **Payouts go to keys:** 

A `Payout` pays lovelace to a public-key payment credential. The Java runtime pays a key-holding caller at its
enterprise address (cardano-client-lib's builder takes the fee from outputs at the fee payer's address, which would
shrink the payout), a wallet caller at its wallet's address, and other recipients at an address from the runtime's
address book, or else at their enterprise address. To pay a script, pay native assets, or set a datum, return
a `Send` instead: see [Native assets, mints and sends](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/).

##### The deposit, `balance` and `minAda`

Every state UTxO holds the contract's `minAda` deposit (see [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/))
plus its funds:

```text
state UTxO lovelace = minAda + funds
ctx.balance() in an action  = funds          (the deposit is not yours to spend)
ctx.balance() in a destroy  = minAda + funds (everything: the instance ends)
```

So an action can never pay out the deposit: the validator requires the continuing lovelace to be at least `minAda`,
and the runtime refuses the call first with `<Contract>.<method>: payouts exceed the contract's funds`.

##### Returning everything on `@Destroy`

A destroy ends the instance, so nothing may stay behind. Its payouts must allocate **exactly** `ctx.balance()`, the
whole UTxO including the deposit:

```java title="examples/counter/.../Counter.java"
/** Only the owner can close the counter; the deposit goes back to them. */
@Destroy
@OnlyOwner
public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    return Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance());
}
```

The validator checks that the payouts total exactly what the state UTxO holds, that the thread token is burned, and
that every payout is paid and tagged. The runtime checks the total before building:

```text
Counter.close: a destroy must pay out everything the instance holds (2200000 lovelace, ctx.balance()), but pays …
```

Split it however your rules say. Crowdfund's `claim` gives everything to the creator; a destroy could equally pay
several parties with `Payouts.add`, as long as the amounts add up to `ctx.balance()`.

##### `@Receives`: payments from other contracts

A plain action refuses value added by anyone other than its caller: the exact value check fails. An action that takes
**deposits** from other JOUST contracts in the same transaction declares `@Receives` and a `Funds` parameter, and sees
each deposit in `funds.deposits()`. That is covered in [Deposits](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/).

##### Pitfalls

- **Trusting the client's numbers.** You do not need to: every `Ctx` field is checked against the transaction. But
  only if the method declares `Ctx`; values passed as ordinary arguments are whatever the caller chose.
- **Tracking funds in the state.** A field like the vault's `total` is your bookkeeping. The validator's exact value
  check keeps the UTxO's lovelace equal to `minAda + received − payouts` at every step, so bookkeeping that adds
  `received` and subtracts payouts stays equal to the funds held.
- **Paying out more than `ctx.balance()`.** Check it with `Require.that` for a clear message (the treasury does:
  `"not enough funds"`); otherwise the runtime refuses the call with its own message.
- **A destroy that pays only the funds.** It must pay the deposit too: use `ctx.balance()` in the destroy, not a
  state field.

##### Reference

- [State API](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/state-api/): `Ctx`, `Payout`, `Payouts`, `Funds`
- Sources: [`Ctx.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Ctx.java),
  [`Payouts.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Payouts.java),
  [`Payable.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Payable.java)
- ADR-0001: D3 (`Ctx`), D4 and D5 (payouts), D9 (I3 value, I7 payouts, I14 deposit); ADR-0007 (assets and sends)

- [Authorization](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/)

### Authorization

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/

By default anyone can call any method. Authorisation is how you restrict that: to one key stored in the state, to a
quorum of a council, or to another script's decision. Each form is a check the generated validator runs on chain,
against the **current** state, before your method's result is accepted. The client runs the same check first and
refuses a call that would fail.

##### The options at a glance

| You need | Use | Checked against |
|---|---|---|
| The caller's identity inside your logic | `Ctx` and `ctx.caller()` | The transaction is signed by `caller` |
| One key stored in the state | `@SignedBy("field")` | A `byte[]` field of the current state |
| The key in a field named `owner` | `@OnlyOwner` | Same as `@SignedBy("owner")` |
| M of N keys | `@Quorum(keys = "…", threshold = "…")` | A `JulcList<byte[]>` and a `BigInteger` field |
| A key or a script (a DAO, a governor) | `@AuthorizedBy("field")` | A `Credential` field of the state or the params |

##### Caller identity: `Ctx.caller`

A method that declares [`Ctx`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/) receives `ctx.caller()`, the payment key hash of the party
calling. The validator checks that the transaction is signed by that key, so the value is authenticated: it is
JOUST's `msg.sender`.

Use it when the rule is more than "this one field":

```java title="examples/escrow/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/escrow/Escrow.java"
/** Seller or arbiter at any time, anyone after the deadline: give the buyer their money back. */
@Destroy
public static JulcList<Payout> refund(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    boolean party = ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.seller()) || ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.arbiter());
    Require.that(party || Clock.after(ctx, s.deadline()), "only the seller or the arbiter can refund before the deadline");
    return Payouts.of(s.buyer(), ctx.balance());
}
```

and to record who did something (`new State(ctx.caller(), …)` in an `@Init` makes the deployer the owner).

> **Caution:** 

Compare keys with `ByteStringLib.equals(a, b)`. On the JVM, `a == b` and `a.equals(b)` compare array references and
are almost always false; on chain they compare bytes. Shared code must give the same answer on both sides.

##### `@SignedBy` and `@OnlyOwner`

`@SignedBy("field")` requires the transaction to be signed by the key hash held in the named `byte[]` field of the
**current** state. `@OnlyOwner` is shorthand for `@SignedBy("owner")`.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/crowdfund/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/crowdfund/Crowdfund.java"
/** The goal was reached: the creator takes everything. */
@Destroy
@SignedBy("creator")
public static JulcList<Payout> claim(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(Clock.after(ctx, s.deadline()), "the campaign is still running");
    Require.that(s.raised().compareTo(s.goal()) >= 0, "the goal was not reached");
    return Payouts.of(s.creator(), ctx.balance());
}
```

**.jsc:**

```jsc
destroy claim() only creator {
  require(after(deadline), "the campaign is still running")
  require(raised >= goal, "the goal was not reached")
  pay(creator, balance)
}
```

`only <field>` lowers to `@SignedBy("<field>")` and needs a `Key` field. A `.jsc` action or destroy that pays out must
say who may call it: `only <field>`, or `open` if anyone may (the body's `require`s are then the only guard).
Otherwise it does not compile.

**JavaScript:**

```js
// Nothing extra: the caller's wallet signs. A wallet whose key is not the creator's is refused
// before it is asked to sign.
await campaign.at(id).claim(creatorWallet, {});
```

Rules and behaviour:

- The field must be a `byte[]` component of the state record. It is read from the current state, not the method's
  result, so an action cannot authorise itself by changing the field.
- The method does not need `Ctx`. The counter's `reset` has none: `@OnlyOwner` alone makes the client add the
  owner's key as a required signer.
- It cannot go on an `@Init` (there is no current state yet): use `Ctx` and `Require.that` in the body.
- It cannot go on a `@Batched` action: the batcher, not the intent's owner, signs a batch.
- The Java client checks the caller first and throws
  `RequireException("Vault.withdraw: must be called by the key in 'owner'")`.

On chain the generated check is one line, `ContextsLib.signedBy(tx, current.owner())`.

##### `@Quorum`: M-of-N signatures

`@Quorum(keys = "council", threshold = "quorum")` requires at least `threshold` of the transaction's signers to be
among `keys`. Both name fields: `keys` a `JulcList<byte[]>` of key hashes, `threshold` a `BigInteger`, in the state,
in the owned record, or in the `@Params` record (`"params.x"`).

```java title="examples/treasury/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/Treasury.java"
public record State(JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, boolean frozen) {}

/** Pays {@code amount} to {@code to}; needs a quorum of the council. */
@Action @Quorum(keys = "council", threshold = "quorum")
public static Spent pay(State s, Config cfg, byte[] to, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(!s.frozen(), "the treasury is frozen");
    Require.that(amount.signum() > 0 && amount.compareTo(cfg.maxPayout()) <= 0, "amount out of range");
    Require.that(amount.compareTo(ctx.balance()) <= 0, "not enough funds");
    JulcList<Event> none = JulcList.empty();
    return new Spent(s, Payouts.of(to, amount), none.prepend(new Paid(to, amount)));
}

/** Replaces the council; needs a quorum of the current one. The new council must keep a reachable quorum. */
@Action @Quorum(keys = "council", threshold = "quorum")
public static Changed rotate(State s, JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum) { … }
```

What the validator checks:

- **The count.** The transaction's signatories that appear in `keys` number at least `threshold`, and `threshold`
  is at least 1. The ledger's signatory set has no repeats. The cost grows with signatories × keys.
- **The current state.** The check reads the input state, never the method's result. `rotate(council = [attacker],
  quorum = 1)` cannot authorise itself.
- **Every output keeps a reachable quorum.** On every state the validator accepts as an output (creation and every
  action), and on the params at creation, it checks that the keys are **strictly ascending** (so distinct), each 28
  bytes, and `1 ≤ threshold ≤ number of keys`. No rotation can lock the contract.

So **sort the keys** before you deploy or rotate. The treasury's DevKit test sorts the members by key hash first:

```java title="examples/treasury/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/TreasuryDevnetTest.java"
Account[] members = {DevKit.fundedAccount(300), DevKit.fundedAccount(300), DevKit.fundedAccount(300)};
Arrays.sort(members, Comparator.comparing(a -> HexUtil.encodeHexString(Keys.pkh(a))));
JulcList<byte[]> council = JulcList.empty();
for (int i = members.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) council = council.prepend(Keys.pkh(members[i]));
```

###### Co-signers

The caller's signature counts toward the quorum. The other members sign the same transaction as co-signers:

**Java:**

```java
// The generated client takes the co-signers as trailing Accounts.
var paid = t.pay(a, Keys.pkh(bob), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), b);   // a calls, b co-signs: 2 of 3
t.close(a, Keys.pkh(a), b);
```

**JavaScript:**

```js
// A @Quorum call takes { cosigners: [...] }: each co-signer's wallet signs the same transaction.
await treasury.at(id).pay(walletA, { to: bobKeyHash, amount: 10_000_000n }, { cosigners: [walletB] });
```

A method may combine `@Quorum` with `@SignedBy`, and `ctx.caller()` may be one of the keys. When several calls are
composed into one transaction, a signature counts for every call that requires it; `Compose` refuses that unless
you call `allowSharedSigners()` (see [Reads and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/)).

##### `@AuthorizedBy`: a key or a script

`@AuthorizedBy("field")` needs the approval of a **credential** held in a `Credential` field of the state, the owned
record, or the params (`"params.guardian"`). A credential is either a key or a script, and the check differs:

- **Key credential:** the key signed the transaction.
- **Script credential `h`:** script `h` ran in the transaction, for a **withdrawal** from its reward account. This is
  the withdraw-zero pattern: withdrawing zero lovelace from a script's reward account makes the ledger run that
  script, so the transaction proves the script approved it. The validator requires:
  - `h` is in the transaction's withdrawals (native scripts count too);
  - `h` is not this contract's own script, nor JOUST's map verifier or output verifier, which approve any withdrawal;
  - if `h` has a Rewarding redeemer (every Plutus script does), it is an `Approvals` list containing
    `Approval(policy, target, action)`: this contract's policy id, this instance's (or object's) token name, and this
    method's redeemer tag.

```java title="julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Approval.java"
public record Approval(byte[] policy, byte[] target, BigInteger action) {}
public record Approvals(JulcList<Approval> approvals) {}
```

The binding means one approval never authorises another instance, another action or another contract. The action
tag is the method's constructor index in the generated `Calls` redeemer: the actions first, then the destroys (then
any owned methods), each in declaration order. The treasury's `fund`, `pay`, `rotate`, `freeze` and `close` are 0 to 4,
so `freeze` is 3. The contract
[description](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/description-format/) lists each method's index.

```java title="examples/treasury/.../Treasury.java"
@Params
public record Config(Credential guardian, BigInteger maxPayout) {}

/** The guardian freezes or unfreezes the treasury. */
@Action @AuthorizedBy("params.guardian")
public static Changed freeze(State s, boolean frozen) {
    JulcList<Event> none = JulcList.empty();
    return new Changed(new State(s.council(), s.quorum(), frozen), none.prepend(new Frozen(frozen)));
}
```

###### Writing a governor

A governor is a plain JuLC withdraw validator. The example's `Guardian` approves whatever its redeemer lists when its
owner signs, and refuses any purpose other than Rewarding:

```java title="examples/treasury/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/Guardian.java"
@WithdrawValidator
public class Guardian {

    @Param static byte[] owner;

    @Entrypoint
    public static boolean validate(PlutusData redeemer, ScriptContext ctx) {
        boolean rewarding = ctx.scriptInfo() instanceof ScriptInfo.RewardingScript;
        return rewarding && ContextsLib.signedBy(ctx.txInfo(), owner);
    }
}
```

A governor's obligations:

- list only the approvals its own rules grant (votes, another contract's state, a signature);
- refuse certificates (the Certifying purpose), so nobody can deregister its stake credential and block every
  `@AuthorizedBy` call;
- have its stake credential **registered** once, so withdrawals from it are possible.

###### Calling with a governor

**Java:**

```java title="examples/treasury/.../TreasuryDevnetTest.java"
var guardian = JulcScriptLoader.load(Guardian.class, new BytesPlutusData(Keys.pkh(owner)));
String reward = DevKit.registerScriptStake(guardian, owner);   // the example's helper: register once

byte[] policy = HexUtil.decodeHexString(t.instance().contract().policyId());
byte[] id = HexUtil.decodeHexString(t.instanceId());
JulcList<Approval> approvals = JulcList.<Approval>empty().prepend(new Approval(policy, id, BigInteger.valueOf(3)));
var frozen = t.freeze(owner, true, Authorization.script(reward, guardian, new Approvals(approvals), owner));
```

For a key credential, pass `Authorization.key(account)`.

**JavaScript:**

```js
// A key credential: the key's wallet co-signs (or calls).
await treasury.at(id).freeze(walletA, { frozen: true }, { cosigners: [guardianWallet] });

// A script credential: a governor built by `joust build`, registered once (see @julclang/joust-runtime).
await treasury.at(id).freeze(walletA, { frozen: true }, { governor: { governor, signers: [ownerWallet] } });
```

> **Note:** 

`@Quorum` and `@AuthorizedBy` read the current state, so neither can go on an `@Init` or `@Migrate` creation. Neither
can go on a `@Batched` action: an intent's owner is the caller. `.jsc` gets `quorum` and `authorized` in milestone M2;
until then write those contracts in Java.

##### Which to use when

- **One fixed party** (an owner, an admin, a creator): `@SignedBy("field")` or `@OnlyOwner`. Cheapest, and the
  client checks it before anything is built.
- **A choice among parties, or a rule that mixes identity and time** (escrow's "seller or arbiter, or anyone after
  the deadline"): `Ctx` and `Require.that` with `ByteStringLib.equals`.
- **A committee**: `@Quorum`. Keep the council in the state if it must change (with a quorum-guarded `rotate`), or
  in `@Params` if it is fixed for the deployment.
- **Another contract's or a DAO's decision**: `@AuthorizedBy` with a script credential, kept in `@Params` so the
  governor is fixed by the script hash and cannot be swapped by an action.
- **Anyone**: no annotation. The method's `Require`s are then the only guard, so make sure they are enough,
  especially for anything that pays out.

##### Pitfalls

- **Unsorted council keys.** `@Quorum` rejects any state whose keys are not strictly ascending, at creation too.
- **An admin field changed by an unguarded action.** `@SignedBy` protects the method it is on, not the field. Guard
  every action that writes the field.
- **A governor that accepts anything.** `@AuthorizedBy` trusts the script's rules completely. Bind its approvals to
  real conditions, and pin it in `@Params`.
- **Forgetting to register the governor's stake credential.** Without registration the zero withdrawal is invalid,
  and no `@AuthorizedBy` call can succeed.

##### Reference

- [Annotations](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/): `@SignedBy`, `@OnlyOwner`, `@Quorum`, `@AuthorizedBy`
- Sources: [`SignedBy.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/SignedBy.java),
  [`Quorum.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Quorum.java),
  [`AuthorizedBy.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/AuthorizedBy.java),
  [`examples/treasury`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/treasury)
- ADR-0001 D3 and I11 (`@SignedBy`); [ADR-0009](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-option-i-params-auth-invariants-events.md) D2 (`@Quorum`, I32) and D3 (`@AuthorizedBy`, I33)
