### Time

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/

A script on Cardano cannot ask "what time is it now?". It sees the transaction's **validity interval**: the range of
time in which the transaction may be included in a block. The ledger refuses the transaction outside that range, so a
contract can reason about time by reasoning about the interval. This page shows how JOUST exposes it, the two safe
ways to write a deadline, and the limits that come with it.

##### The validity interval

Every JOUST call that needs time runs in a window `[validFrom, validTo)`, in POSIX milliseconds: inclusive at the
start, exclusive at the end (the Conway ledger's rule). The client chooses the window when it builds the
transaction:

- it starts at the current chain tip;
- it lasts `min(TTL, maxValidityMs)`;
- it is chosen in **slots** first, and the milliseconds are derived from the network's slot configuration, so the JVM
  run and the on-chain run see identical numbers.

Your method sees the window through [`Ctx`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/):

| Field | Meaning | Verified on chain |
|---|---|---|
| `ctx.validFrom()` | Start of the window (POSIX ms, inclusive) | Equal to the transaction's lower bound, which must be finite |
| `ctx.validTo()` | End of the window (POSIX ms, exclusive) | Equal to the transaction's upper bound, which must be finite |
| | | `validTo − validFrom ≤ @StateContract(maxValidityMs)` (default one hour) |

Because the window contains the moment of inclusion, the real time is somewhere in `[validFrom, validTo)`. You do not
know where.

##### Deadlines with `Clock`

`Clock` turns that into the two questions you can answer safely, true for **every** moment the transaction could be
valid:

| Method | True when | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `Clock.after(ctx, t)` | `ctx.validFrom() ≥ t`: the call happens at or after `t` | "not before": unlocks, refunds after a deadline |
| `Clock.before(ctx, t)` | `ctx.validTo() ≤ t`: the call happens strictly before `t` | "not after": contributions before a deadline, a deadline in the future at creation |

```java title="examples/crowdfund/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/crowdfund/Crowdfund.java"
@Init
public static State launch(BigInteger goal, BigInteger deadline, BigInteger minContribution, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(goal.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "goal must be positive");
    Require.that(minContribution.compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(2_000_000)) >= 0, "minimum contribution is at least 2 ADA");
    Require.that(Clock.before(ctx, deadline), "deadline must be in the future");
    JulcMap<byte[], BigInteger> none = JulcMap.empty();
    return new State(ctx.caller(), goal, deadline, minContribution, BigInteger.ZERO, none);
}

/** The goal was missed: a backer takes their contribution back. */
@Action
public static Result refund(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(Clock.after(ctx, s.deadline()), "the campaign is still running");
    …
}
```

`Clock` works anywhere: in combination with other conditions, on any value (a state field, an argument, a computed
time). The escrow lets the seller or the arbiter refund at any time, and anyone once the deadline has passed:

```java title="examples/escrow/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/escrow/Escrow.java"
boolean party = ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.seller()) || ByteStringLib.equals(ctx.caller(), s.arbiter());
Require.that(party || Clock.after(ctx, s.deadline()), "only the seller or the arbiter can refund before the deadline");
```

> **Don't compare validFrom and validTo yourself the other way round:** 

`ctx.validTo() > t` does **not** mean "after `t`": part of the window may still be before `t`. And
`!Clock.before(ctx, t)` does not mean "after `t`" either. Use `Clock.after` for "after" and `Clock.before` for
"before", and nothing else, unless you have worked out the interval yourself.

##### `@ValidAfter` and `@ValidBefore`

When the time is a state field, an annotation says it without code. `@ValidAfter("field")` requires the window to
start at or after the `BigInteger` time in that field of the current state; `@ValidBefore("field")` requires it to
end at or before it.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/vault/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/Vault.java"
/** The owner takes funds out once the vault is unlocked. */
@Action
@OnlyOwner
@ValidAfter("unlockAt")
public static Result withdraw(State s, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
    Require.that(amount.compareTo(s.total()) <= 0, "insufficient funds");
    return new Result(new State(s.owner(), s.unlockAt(), s.total().subtract(amount)), Payouts.of(s.owner(), amount));
}
```

**.jsc:**

```jsc
// Modifiers name a state field (an Int): after <field>, before <field>.
action withdraw(amount: Int) only owner after unlockAt {
  require(amount > 0, "amount must be positive")
  require(amount <= total, "insufficient funds")
  pay(owner, amount)
  return { ...state, total: total - amount }
}

// Functions take any Int: after(t), before(t). validFrom and validTo are the window's bounds.
action contribute() payable {
  require(before(deadline), "the campaign has ended")
  return { ...state, total: total + received }
}

// The escrow's refund: the seller or the arbiter at any time, anyone after the deadline.
destroy refund() open {
  require(caller == seller || caller == arbiter || after(deadline), "only the seller or the arbiter can refund before the deadline")
  pay(buyer, balance)
}
```

`after(t)` and `before(t)` hold for the whole window, so `.jsc` allows them only at the top of a `require`, alone or
as an operand of `&&` or `||`: never negated, in an `if` or a `?:`, in a `const`, a `fn` or a lambda. And `.jsc`
goes further: a value computed from `validFrom` or `validTo` never decides anything and never makes an operation
fail; it may only flow into amounts and state, with a warning ([the time rule](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc-reference/#time-d11)).

**JavaScript:**

```js
// Nothing to pass: the engine picks the window, as the Java runtime does.
await vault.at(id).withdraw(ownerWallet, { amount: 3_000_000n });
// Too early: the promise rejects with "...too early, the time in 'unlockAt' has not been reached".
```

The annotation and `Clock` check the same thing on chain. The differences:

| | `@ValidAfter` / `@ValidBefore` | `Clock.after` / `Clock.before` |
|---|---|---|
| Time comes from | a `BigInteger` field of the current state | any expression |
| Needs `Ctx` | no | yes |
| Combines with other conditions | no (always required) | yes |
| On `@Init` | not allowed (no current state) | allowed |
| On `@Batched` | not allowed | allowed |
| Client behaviour | picks a window that satisfies it, or refuses with a clear message | runs your method; a failed `Require` refuses the call |

The client's handling is the practical reason to prefer the annotation for state-field deadlines. With
`@ValidBefore("deadline")` it **shortens** the window so that it ends no later than the deadline, and refuses with
`too late, the deadline in 'deadline' has passed` only when no window fits. With `@ValidAfter("unlockAt")` it refuses
with `too early, the time in 'unlockAt' has not been reached`. `Clock.before` in a method body gets the default window,
which may run past the deadline and make the call fail (see below).

###### What the validator checks

For `@ValidAfter(f)`: the lower bound is finite and at least `current.f`. For `@ValidBefore(f)`: the upper bound is
finite and at most `current.f`; the upper bound is exclusive, so the call happens strictly before `f`. An unbounded
side never passes. The generated code pattern-matches the bound type itself rather than calling
`IntervalLib.finiteLowerBound`, for the reason below.

> **IntervalLib returns -1 for an infinite bound:** 

If you read the validity range yourself (in a hand-written JuLC validator, such as a governor), note that JuLC's
`IntervalLib.finiteLowerBound` and `IntervalLib.finiteUpperBound` return `-1` for an infinite bound and ignore whether
the bound is inclusive. A check like `finiteLowerBound(range) >= deadline` then fails safe, but
`finiteUpperBound(range) <= deadline` **passes** for a transaction with no upper bound. Pattern-match
`IntervalBoundType.Finite` first. In JOUST contract code, use `Ctx` and `Clock`, which never have this problem.

##### TTL, `maxValidityMs` and the trust radius

Two settings decide how wide the window is:

- **The TTL** is the runtime's: how long a built transaction stays valid. The Java `StateRuntime` defaults to 10
  minutes (`StateRuntime.builder(backend).ttl(Duration)` changes it); the examples' DevKit runtime uses 20 seconds.
  Pages built with `@julclang/joust` use `dev.ttlMs` from `joust.config.json`, by default 20 seconds on a DevKit and
  3 minutes on other networks; the npm runtime takes a `ttlMs` option.
- **`maxValidityMs`** is the contract's: the widest window it accepts from a call that reads `Ctx` (default one hour,
  at least one minute). The client uses `min(TTL, maxValidityMs)`.

`maxValidityMs` bounds the **trust radius of time**. `validFrom` can be up to `maxValidityMs` in the past at the
moment the transaction lands, and `validTo` up to that far in the future. A contract that stores "now" inherits that
skew. The oracle example records `ctx.validFrom()` as the time of a price, and the shop that reads it checks the age
the same way:

```java title="examples/oracle/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/Shop.java"
Require.that(ctx.validFrom().subtract(price.updatedAt()).compareTo(cfg.maxAgeMs()) <= 0, "stale price");
```

If your contract accrues by time (interest, vesting), lower `maxValidityMs` to what the business can tolerate.

##### Short horizons and near deadlines

Two practical limits follow from the window:

1. **The ledger's horizon.** The ledger converts a validity bound to time only within its stability window. On Yaci
   DevKit that is a few minutes, and a 10-minute TTL fails with `PastHorizon`. Keep the TTL short on DevKit (the
   examples and the page defaults use 20 seconds).
2. **`Clock.before` needs the whole window before the deadline.** With a 10-minute TTL, a call 5 minutes before the
   deadline fails `Clock.before(ctx, deadline)` even though "now" is before it. Use a TTL shorter than the shortest
   deadline gap you care about, or put the deadline in a state field and use `@ValidBefore`, which shortens the
   window for you.

`Clock.after` and `@ValidAfter` depend on the window's start, which is the chain tip's slot: a call made just after the
deadline is refused until the tip has passed it. The examples wait a couple of seconds past a deadline before calling.

##### Pitfalls

- **Using `ctx.validTo()` as "now"** for something that must not be early, or `validFrom` for something that must not
  be late. Pick the bound that is safe for the rule.
- **Deadlines in seconds.** All times are POSIX **milliseconds**, as `BigInteger`. `System.currentTimeMillis()` in
  Java, `Date.now()` in JavaScript.
- **A long TTL on DevKit.** `PastHorizon`, or refusals near deadlines. 20 seconds works.
- **Time annotations on `@Init`.** Not allowed: there is no current state. Use `Clock` in the body.

- [State API](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/state-api/): `Clock`, `Ctx`; [Annotations](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/): `@ValidAfter`, `@ValidBefore`
- Sources: [`Clock.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Clock.java),
  [`Ctx.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Ctx.java),
  [`Window.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-runtime/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/runtime/Window.java) (how the client picks the window)

### Require and errors

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/require-and-errors/

Contract rules are written as `Require.that(condition, "message")`. The same line refuses the call on the JVM (with
the message, before anything is built or signed) and fails the script on chain. This page shows how to write rules,
where each kind of failure surfaces, and how to find out why a transaction was rejected.

##### `Require.that`

**Java:**

```java title="examples/vault/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/Vault.java"
@Action
@OnlyOwner
@ValidAfter("unlockAt")
public static Result withdraw(State s, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
    Require.that(amount.compareTo(s.total()) <= 0, "insufficient funds");
    return new Result(new State(s.owner(), s.unlockAt(), s.total().subtract(amount)), Payouts.of(s.owner(), amount));
}
```

**.jsc:**

```jsc
action withdraw(amount: Int) only owner after unlockAt {
  require(amount > 0, "amount must be positive")
  require(amount <= total, "insufficient funds")
  pay(owner, amount)
  return { ...state, total: total - amount }
}
```

`require(condition, "message")` lowers to `Require.that`. The message is a required string literal.

`Require` has two implementations that fail on exactly the same inputs (a test asserts it):

| Where | What `Require.that(false, msg)` does |
|---|---|
| JVM (`julc-state-api/src/main/java`) | throws `RequireException(msg)` |
| On chain (`julc-state-api/src/onchain/java`, bundled for JuLC) | traces `msg`, then fails the script |

This is the one place where the JVM and on-chain sources of the state API differ, and it is four lines. JuLC rejects
`throw` in contract code, so `Require.that` is how a contract fails. `Builtins.error()` also works, but carries no
message.

###### Writing good rules

- **One rule, one message.** The message is what the user sees. Say what is wrong in the user's terms:
  `"deposit must be positive"`, `"the campaign has ended"`.
- **Check before you compute.** A `JulcMap.get` on a missing key aborts on chain with no message; guard it with
  `Require.that(m.containsKey(k), "nothing to refund")` first, as crowdfund's `refund` does.
- **Keep messages short.** Each message is stored in the compiled script, and every transaction pays 15 lovelace per
  byte of the script it references. ADR-0008 measured 100 to 300 bytes of messages per contract and chose to keep
  them, for the failure reasons they give.
- **Don't validate what the validator already guarantees.** `Ctx` fields, the payment amount, payout tags, the
  signer of `@SignedBy` are all checked by generated code.

##### Where a refusal surfaces

A JOUST call fails at the first of these that refuses it. Most failures happen on your machine, before anything is
signed.

1. **The client's policy checks.** Before running your method, the client checks the annotations against the
   current state: `@SignedBy`/`@OnlyOwner`, `@ValidAfter`/`@ValidBefore` (choosing a window). Messages name the
   contract, the method and the field:

   ```text
   Vault.withdraw: must be called by the key in 'owner'
   Vault.withdraw: too early, the time in 'unlockAt' has not been reached
   <Contract>.<method>: too late, the deadline in '<field>' has passed
   ```

2. **Your method, on the JVM.** The client runs the method with the real state and `Ctx`. A failing `Require.that`
   throws `RequireException` with your message, unchanged:

   ```text
   only the buyer or the arbiter can release
   ```

3. **The runtime's checks on the result.** The next state's size and map order, the `@Invariant`s, payouts within the
   funds, a destroy paying everything:

   ```text
   invariant reachable                       (an @Invariant failed: "invariant <method name>")
   Vault.withdraw: payouts exceed the contract's funds
   Counter.close: a destroy must pay out everything the instance holds (…)
   ```

4. **Building and evaluating the transaction.** The runtime balances the transaction and evaluates every script in it
   with JuLC's evaluator, as the node will. A script that fails here fails the call with a `SubmitException`
   (`…: could not build the transaction: …`). Nothing was submitted.

5. **The node.** The node validates the transaction again. A rejection raises
   `SubmitException("…: the node rejected the transaction: …")` with the node's answer.

Steps 1 to 3 throw `RequireException` (from `org.julclang.state.api`). Steps 4 and 5 throw subclasses of the runtime's
`JoustException` (from `org.julclang.state.runtime`):

| Exception | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `RequireException` | A contract rule failed on the JVM. Nothing was built or submitted |
| `SubmitException` | The transaction could not be built (a script failed evaluation) or the node definitely rejected it |
| `ContentionException` | Another transaction kept moving the state UTxO; the runtime re-ran the method against each new state and gave up |
| `PendingTransactionException` | The outcome is unknown (a timeout, an unclear submit answer). `txHash()` names the transaction; nothing is resubmitted |
| `InstanceNotFoundException` | No state UTxO holds the instance's token (wrong id, or destroyed) |

When the node rejects a call because the state moved (another call landed first), the runtime reads the new state,
re-runs your method and tries again. It never resubmits a transaction the node accepted.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/vault/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/VaultApp.java"
try {
    vault.withdraw(alice, ADA);
} catch (RequireException e) {
    System.out.println("withdraw before unlock rejected off-chain: " + e.getMessage());
}
```

**JavaScript:**

```js
// The engine runs the same Java method; a refusal rejects the promise with the same message.
await assert.rejects(instance.increment(wallet, { by: 0n }), /increment must be positive/);

// In a page: a VerificationError means the page's own verifier refused the prepared transaction,
// and the wallet was never asked to sign.
try {
  await instance.increment(api, { by: 1n });
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof VerificationError) show(e.problems);   // what the verifier found
  else show(e.message);                                    // a contract rule, or a chain error
}
```

##### On chain: traces

When a script fails on chain (or in the runtime's evaluation), the node's error carries the script's **trace**. A
failing `Require.that` traces its message, so you see the reason.

The generated checks around your method (value, datum, `Ctx`, payouts) are boolean conjunctions and trace nothing by
default: a failure says only that the script failed. To find which check failed, compile with the processor option
`-Ajoust.traces=true`. Each failing check then traces where it is and its name, for example
`Withdraw: after_unlockAt` or `Withdraw: paid` (the redeemer variant, then the check). It makes the scripts larger and changes their hashes: use it for debugging only.

Some examples wire it to a Gradle property:

```groovy title="examples/treasury/build.gradle"
// -Pjoust.traces: each failing validator check traces its name (debugging only; larger scripts).
if (project.hasProperty('joust.traces')) {
    tasks.named('compileJava') { options.compilerArgs += ['-Ajoust.traces=true'] }
}
```

```sh
./gradlew :examples:treasury:test -Pjoust.traces
```

Add the same block to your own `build.gradle`. The `joust` CLI has no switch for it yet.

##### Debugging a failed transaction

Work from the cheapest evidence to the most expensive.

1. **Read the exception type and message.** A `RequireException` is a rule (yours, or an annotation's), with the
   reason. Fix the input, the caller, or the time. You are done.

2. **A `SubmitException` saying "could not build the transaction".** The JVM run passed but a script refused the
   transaction in evaluation. Usually a generated check: rebuild with `-Ajoust.traces=true` and call again to see its
   name. Common causes:
   - a state map out of canonical order (the runtime normally catches this first; see
     [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/));
   - a validity window the ledger cannot convert (`PastHorizon`): the TTL is too long for the network
     ([Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/));
   - code that behaves differently on the JVM and on chain (`==` on `byte[]`, a fixed-width number the lint missed).

3. **Reproduce it in the harness.** `StateHarness` (from `julc-state-testkit`) builds the same transaction shape the
   runtime submits and evaluates the compiled validator. Its verdict prints each script's result, budget and traces:

   ```java title="examples/vault/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/VaultTest.java"
   final StateHarness<Vault.State> h = StateHarness.of(VaultClient.SPEC);

   var live = h.live(new Vault.State(OWNER, LATER, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN)), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
   Ctx ctx = h.ctx(OWNER, BigInteger.ZERO, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
   var r = Vault.withdraw(live.state(), ADA, ctx);
   h.assertRejected(h.act(live, new VaultValidator.Withdraw(ADA, ctx), r.state(), r.payouts(), OWNER, ctx), "@ValidAfter");
   ```

   See [Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/).

4. **Keep the transaction.** Run with the system property `-Djoust.dumpTx=<dir>`, and the runtime writes each signed
   transaction it submits to `<dir>/<txHash>.cbor` (hex). In this repository's Gradle build, `-Pjoust.dumpTx=<dir>`
   passes it to the tests. Inspect it with any CBOR or transaction decoder.

5. **Let the node evaluate.** As a last resort, `-Djoust.debug.nodeEvaluates=true` skips the local script-cost
   evaluation, so the node evaluates the transaction and reports the full script context it saw. It is a diagnostic
   only: never use it for normal runs.

> **Tip:** 

A transaction whose scripts pass but which the node still rejects is usually about value or time, not your rules:
an output below the ledger's minimum, an expired window, inputs already spent. The node's message names the ledger
rule (`ValueNotConservedUTxO`, `OutsideValidityIntervalUTxO`, …).

### Params, invariants and events

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/

Three features from [ADR-0009](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-option-i-params-auth-invariants-events.md)
that hand-written validators often need:

- **`@Params`**: values fixed when the contract is deployed (a guardian, a fee rate, another contract's policy),
  baked into the script itself;
- **`@Invariant`**: rules every state must satisfy, checked on chain after every transition;
- **events**: records a method emits, carried in the redeemer and checked by the validator, so indexers can trust
  them.

All three appear in [`examples/treasury`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/treasury), a multisig
treasury. This page uses it throughout. `.jsc` has none of them yet (`.jsc` gets them in
milestone M2): write these contracts in Java.

##### `@Params`: deploy-time parameters

Mark one nested record with `@Params`:

```java title="examples/treasury/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/Treasury.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 640)
public class Treasury {

    @Params
    public record Config(Credential guardian, BigInteger maxPayout) {}

    public record State(JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, boolean frozen) {}
    …
}
```

A method receives the parameters by declaring a parameter of that type:

- right after the state, in actions, destroys and views;
- first, in the `@Init` (there is no state yet);
- right after the `@Shared` state, in [owned methods](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/).

```java
@Init @Payable
public static State open(Config cfg, JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, Ctx ctx) {
    return new State(council, quorum, false);
}

@Action @Quorum(keys = "council", threshold = "quorum")
public static Spent pay(State s, Config cfg, byte[] to, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(!s.frozen(), "the treasury is frozen");
    Require.that(amount.signum() > 0 && amount.compareTo(cfg.maxPayout()) <= 0, "amount out of range");
    …
}
```

The parameter is not part of the redeemer: callers cannot choose it.

###### How it works

The parameters are **applied to the script** (JuLC's partial application of `@Param` fields). So:

- each set of parameters is a different script, with its own hash, so its own policy id and its own address;
- the parameters are public and fixed by that hash: nobody can change them for a deployed script;
- whoever deploys chooses them, as with any parameterised validator.

The generated validator declares `@Param static PlutusData PARAMS` and reads it through a **typed local** before any
accessor:

```java title="TreasuryValidator.java (generated)"
static boolean onPay(Pay r, Treasury.State current, TxInfo tx, TxInInfo own, byte[] policy, byte[] id, BigInteger inLovelace) {
    Treasury.Config params = (Treasury.Config) (Object) PARAMS;
    …
    Treasury.Spent result = Treasury.pay(current, params, r.to(), r.amount(), r.ctx());
```

JuLC needs a typed receiver before an accessor call (`params.guardian()`, not `((Config) PARAMS).guardian()`). Your
contract code never sees `PARAMS`: it gets the typed record as a parameter. Keep the idiom in mind when you write
plain JuLC validators with `@Param` fields, and for accessors on call results in general (`f(x).field()` needs a
typed local first).

###### Naming params in annotations

Annotations that name a field accept `params.<component>`:

| Annotation | Example |
|---|---|
| `@AuthorizedBy` | `@AuthorizedBy("params.guardian")` |
| `@Quorum` | `@Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")` |
| `@Reads` | `@Reads("params.oracle") Oracle.State price` ([composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/)) |
| `@Migrate` | `@Migrate(from = "params.previous")` ([upgrades](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/upgrades/)) |
| `@MigrateTo` | `@MigrateTo("params.next")` |

Put anything a caller must not be able to change after deployment in the params: a governor credential, an oracle's
policy, a cap. A state field can be changed by an action; a parameter cannot.

###### Clients and pinning

**Java:**

```java title="examples/treasury/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/treasury/TreasuryDevnetTest.java"
var cfg = new Treasury.Config(new Credential.ScriptCredential(new ScriptHash(guardian.getScriptHash())),
        ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(50)));

var t = TreasuryClient.deploy(runtime, cfg, a, council, BigInteger.TWO, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(200)));
assertEquals(TreasuryClient.policyIdFor(cfg), t.instance().contract().policyId(), "the params pin the script");

var again = TreasuryClient.at(runtime, cfg, t.instanceId());   // reconnecting needs the params too
```

**JavaScript:**

```js
// A deployment is one applied script: the params are fixed in deployment.policy and address.
const treasury = new Treasury({ service, chain, deployment });
const { instance } = await treasury.deploy(walletA, { council, quorum: 2n }, { lovelace: 200_000_000n });
```

**Pin the policy id.** Anyone can deploy the same contract with other parameters, and its types would look the same.
A front end that trusts a deployment should know its expected policy id (`policyIdFor(params)`) and check it.

Limits:

- at most one `@Params` record per contract, and it cannot hold MerkleMaps;
- `@Batched` methods cannot take the params yet;
- the runtime refuses an applied script over 15,000 bytes, which could not be published as a reference script.

##### `@Invariant`: rules every state keeps

An invariant is a `public static boolean` method that takes the state (or an owned record), optionally followed by
the `@Params` record, and nothing else:

```java title="examples/treasury/.../Treasury.java"
/** A quorum the council can reach (the generated check also requires distinct, sorted 28-byte keys). */
@Invariant
public static boolean reachable(State s) {
    return s.quorum().signum() > 0 && s.quorum().compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(s.council().size())) <= 0;
}
```

Where it is checked:

- **On chain**, on every state the validator accepts as an output: the initial state, every action's result (plain
  and asset-aware, shared and owned), and every owned object's creation. A destroy has no output to check.
- **On the JVM**, by the generated client, before anything is built. It throws `RequireException("invariant reachable")`.

So a call that would break the invariant is refused off chain, and could not pass on chain anyway. In the treasury,
`rotate` to a council of two with a quorum of three is refused both ways.

```java title="TreasuryValidator.java (generated)"
boolean invariant_0 = Treasury.reachable(next);
boolean quorumShape_1 = quorumWellFormed(next.council(), next.quorum());
return quorum && continues && paid && invariant_0 && quorumShape_1 && eventsOk;
```

The second line is not yours: every contract with `@Quorum` gets a generated well-formedness check (strictly
ascending, 28-byte keys, `1 ≤ threshold ≤ n`) on the same outputs. See [Authorization](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/).

Rules and limits:

- an invariant is not also an `@Init`, `@Action`, `@Destroy` or `@View`;
- not with `@Batched` actions: a batch passes through intermediate states that are not checked;
- not over MerkleMap state: on chain only the opened entries are visible, so the JVM and the chain would disagree;
- an instance whose state already breaks an invariant (deployed by an older version, say) can only be destroyed.

> **Tip:** 

Invariants cost execution on every call. Keep them to rules that guard against locking or draining the contract
(a reachable quorum, a total that matches its parts), and keep them cheap.

##### Events: authenticated, in the redeemer

Cardano scripts cannot see transaction metadata, so events written there are unauthenticated: anyone can put anything
in. JOUST carries events in the **redeemer** instead, where the validator checks them.

A method emits events by returning an `events` component: a `JulcList<E>`, where `E` is a record or a sealed interface
of the contract.

```java title="examples/treasury/.../Treasury.java"
public sealed interface Event permits Paid, CouncilChanged, Frozen {}
public record Paid(byte[] to, BigInteger amount) implements Event {}
public record CouncilChanged(BigInteger members, BigInteger quorum) implements Event {}
public record Frozen(boolean frozen) implements Event {}

public record Spent(State state, JulcList<Payout> payouts, JulcList<Event> events) {}
public record Changed(State state, JulcList<Event> events) {}

@Action @AuthorizedBy("params.guardian")
public static Changed freeze(State s, boolean frozen) {
    JulcList<Event> none = JulcList.empty();
    return new Changed(new State(s.council(), s.quorum(), frozen), none.prepend(new Frozen(frozen)));
}
```

The redeemer carries `events` as its last field, and the validator requires it to equal the method's result
(`listData(redeemer.events) == listData(result.events)`). A client cannot add, drop or alter an event.

Events are allowed on actions and destroys, shared and owned. Not on `@Init` or `@Batched` actions yet. They cost
redeemer bytes, so size-based fees.

###### Reading events

**Java:**

```java title="examples/treasury/.../TreasuryDevnetTest.java"
var paid = t.pay(a, Keys.pkh(bob), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), b);
BigInteger amount = paid.events(Treasury.Paid.class).get(0).amount();
```

`CallResult.events(Class)` returns the events of a call the client submitted.

**JavaScript:**

```js
const paid = await treasury.at(id).pay(walletA, { to: bobKeyHash, amount: 10_000_000n }, { cosigners: [walletB] });
paid.report.events;   // [{ $variant: 'Paid', to: bobKeyHash, amount: 10000000n }]
```

###### When an event is authentic

An indexer reading events from the chain must apply the provenance rule. Events are authentic only if:

- the transaction is phase-2 valid (a transaction with `isValid = false` is on chain, but none of its scripts ran);
- the redeemer is the **Spending** redeemer of the input holding the `(policy, id)` token of the instance or object
  being followed;
- `policy` is the expected applied script hash: with `@Params`, every parameter set is its own script, and anyone can
  deploy one, so pin `policyIdFor(params)`;
- the instance's lineage goes back to a deploy you know.

Deduplicate by `(txHash, input, eventIndex)`. An indexer integration that applies the rule to chain data is planned,
not built.

### MerkleMaps

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/

A `MerkleMap` is a state field that holds a map of any size while the datum keeps only a 32-byte root. Use one when a
contract tracks something per user or per key with no fixed bound: token balances, loyalty points, an allow-list, a
registry. Each call proves only the keys it reads and writes, so the cost of a call depends on the keys it touches,
not on how many entries the map holds.

The `token` example keeps every holder's balance in one:

```java title="examples/token/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/Token.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 160)
public class Token {

    public record State(byte[] admin, BigInteger supply, MerkleMap balances) {}

    @Init
    public static State create(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO, MerkleMaps.empty());
    }

    /** The admin creates new tokens for a holder. */
    @Action
    @SignedBy("admin")
    public static State mint(State s, byte[] to, BigInteger amount) {
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
        BigInteger balance = MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), to, BigInteger.ZERO);
        return new State(s.admin(), s.supply().add(amount), MerkleMaps.putInt(s.balances(), to, balance.add(amount)));
    }

    @View
    public static BigInteger balanceOf(State s, byte[] holder) {
        return MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), holder, BigInteger.ZERO);
    }
}
```

The datum stays about 100 bytes however many holders there are (ADR-0002 D8).

##### When to use a MerkleMap

JOUST gives you several ways to keep many entries. Pick by size and by who writes.

| You need | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A small map, read whole on every call | `JulcMap` in the state, kept sorted with `SortedMaps` | Cheapest per call, but the datum caps it: the crowdfund example fits 27 backers in 1 KB |
| An unbounded map, written by one call at a time | `MerkleMap` (this page) | Constant datum size; each call proves only the keys it touches |
| Per-user state that users change in parallel | [Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/) | One UTxO per user, so users never contend |
| Entries unique by key, each updated on its own (names, ballots) | [Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/) | One UTxO per key in a sorted on-chain list: uniqueness without writing the instance, no mirror |
| Many writers to one hot total | [Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/) | Users lock requests; a batcher applies them together |

A MerkleMap does not remove contention: every write still spends the instance's one UTxO, so writes to one instance
go one after another. If many users write at once, owned objects (which can hold their own MerkleMaps) are the
better fit.

##### The API

You read and change a map only through the static helpers of `MerkleMaps`
([source](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/MerkleMaps.java)).
Keys and values are `byte[]`; the `Int` helpers store non-negative `BigInteger` values.

| Method | Returns | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `MerkleMaps.empty()` | `MerkleMap` | A new, empty map. Use it in `@Init` (or `@OwnedInit`) |
| `MerkleMaps.contains(m, key)` | `boolean` | Whether `key` is in the map |
| `MerkleMaps.get(m, key, otherwise)` | `byte[]` | The value, or `otherwise` when absent |
| `MerkleMaps.getInt(m, key, otherwise)` | `BigInteger` | The value as an unsigned big-endian integer, or `otherwise` |
| `MerkleMaps.put(m, key, value)` | `MerkleMap` | Sets `key` to `value` |
| `MerkleMaps.putInt(m, key, value)` | `MerkleMap` | Sets `key` to a non-negative integer (fails on a negative value) |
| `MerkleMaps.remove(m, key)` | `MerkleMap` | Deletes `key` |
| `MerkleMaps.isEmpty(m)` | `boolean` | True if the map was empty before this call and this call wrote nothing |

Writes return a new `MerkleMap`: put it in the state you return, as you would any other field. A lookup sees this
call's own writes first (latest first), then what was in the map, so a method can read back what it just wrote. The
token's `transfer` relies on this for a transfer to yourself:

```java title="examples/token/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/Token.java"
/** A holder sends tokens; an emptied balance is removed from the map. */
@Action
public static State transfer(State s, byte[] to, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
    BigInteger fromBalance = MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO);
    Require.that(fromBalance.compareTo(amount) >= 0, "insufficient balance");
    BigInteger left = fromBalance.subtract(amount);
    MerkleMap debited = left.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) == 0
            ? MerkleMaps.remove(s.balances(), ctx.caller())
            : MerkleMaps.putInt(s.balances(), ctx.caller(), left);
    BigInteger toBalance = MerkleMaps.getInt(debited, to, BigInteger.ZERO);   // reads the debit on a self-transfer
    return new State(s.admin(), s.supply(), MerkleMaps.putInt(debited, to, toBalance.add(amount)));
}
```

> **Zero is present:** 
`putInt(m, key, BigInteger.ZERO)` stores the empty byte string, and the key is still present. To drop a key, call
`remove`. The token removes a holder whose balance reaches zero, which keeps the map (and its proofs) small.

##### In `.jsc`

In [`.jsc`](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/), a `BigMap<K, Int>` or `BigMap<K, Bytes>` state field is a MerkleMap (keys are
`Bytes`, `Key` or `Hash` of at most 64 bytes). `m[k]` reads an `Int` entry, `0` when absent; `m.get(k)` and `m.has(k)`
read any entry. A write is the field's own value in the next state, `{ ...state, points: points.set(k, v) }`:
`set(k, 0)` removes an `Int` entry, a value can never go negative, and `delete(k)` removes any entry. `m.isEmpty`
(empty before the call) is read in a destroy. A method reads its own writes through the chain, as `give` does.

**Java:**

```java
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 160)
public class Token {
    public record State(byte[] admin, BigInteger supply, MerkleMap balances) {}

    @Action
    @SignedBy("admin")
    public static State mint(State s, byte[] to, BigInteger amount) {
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "amount must be positive");
        BigInteger balance = MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), to, BigInteger.ZERO);
        return new State(s.admin(), s.supply().add(amount), MerkleMaps.putInt(s.balances(), to, balance.add(amount)));
    }
}
```

**.jsc:**

```jsc title="Points.jsc"
jsc 1
package org.example.points

// Loyalty points in a BigMap<Key, Int> (a Merkle map: any number of holders, a 32-byte root on chain).
contract Points(maxDatumBytes = 160) {
  state { admin: Key, supply: Int, points: BigMap<Key, Int> }

  init() {
    return { admin: caller, supply: 0, points: BigMap.empty() }
  }

  action award(to: Key, n: Int) only admin {
    require(n > 0, "award a positive amount")
    return { ...state, points: points.set(to, points[to] + n), supply: supply + n }
  }

  // Spending everything removes the holder: set(k, 0) removes the entry.
  action spend(n: Int) {
    const have = points[caller]
    require(n > 0 && have >= n, "not enough points")
    return { ...state, points: points.set(caller, have - n), supply: supply - n }
  }

  // A transfer reads the recipient through the debit, so giving to yourself keeps your balance.
  action give(to: Key, n: Int) {
    require(n > 0 && points[caller] >= n, "not enough points")
    const left = points[caller] - n
    return { ...state, points: points.set(caller, left).set(to, points.set(caller, left)[to] + n) }
  }

  destroy close() only admin {
    require(supply == 0 && points.isEmpty, "points are still out")
    pay(admin, balance)
  }

  view pointsOf(who: Key): Int = points[who]
}
```

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Token)"
const token = await contract('Token', admin);          // a JoustContract for the deployed Token
const t = token.at((await token.deploy(admin, {})).instance);
await t.call(admin, 'mint', { to: ann.keyHash, amount: 1000n });
await t.call(ann, 'transfer', { to: ben.keyHash, amount: 250n });
await t.call(ann, 'burn', { amount: 750n });
```

The call looks like any other. The runtime engine finds the keys the method reads, asks the map mirror for their
proofs, and attaches the map verifier. See [MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/).

`.jsc` `BigMap` values are `Int` or `Bytes`. For other value shapes, write the contract in Java.

##### How a call works

A MerkleMap in the datum is just `(root, [], [])`. The `reads` and `writes` lists exist only while a method runs.

1. **Off chain, the runtime runs your method** with the map's mirror bound behind it. Every key the method looks up
   is answered from the mirror and recorded. That set of keys becomes the call's *read set*.
2. **It builds proofs** for the read set against the current root, and folds the method's net writes (the latest write
   of each key, in order) over the trie to get the new root.
3. **It replays your method** against exactly the proven reads, with any other lookup disabled, and must get the same
   result. Then it builds the transaction: the state spend, plus a zero withdrawal from the map verifier carrying the
   proofs.
4. **On chain, your method runs again** inside the contract's validator, on the proven reads, and the verifier checks
   the proofs.

The same `MerkleMaps` code runs on both sides. The JVM source and the on-chain source differ only in what happens when
a key is not in the read set: the JVM reads it from the mirror; on chain the script fails. An honest client always
puts every key the method reads in the read set, so it never hits that failure.

###### The map verifier

A validator that carried the Merkle Patricia Forestry (MPF) code itself would be 18 to 19 KB, above the 16 KB
transaction limit. So proofs are checked once per transaction by a shared script,
[`MapVerifier`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-verifier/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/verifier/MapVerifier.java)
in `julc-state-verifier`. It is a *withdraw-zero* script: a transaction withdraws 0 ADA from its stake credential,
which makes the ledger run it, and its redeemer carries the claims (ADR-0002 D9).

- **The verifier's redeemer** is `MapClaims`: one `MapClaim(policy, owner, field, oldRoot, reads, writes, newRoot)`
  per map per instance. It checks each claim's reads against `oldRoot` (unique keys, an empty value when absent) and
  applies its writes in order to `oldRoot`, which must give `newRoot`.
- **The claim key** is `(policy, owner, field)`: the contract's script hash, the input the map belongs to (the
  instance's or object's input, or the seed when creating), and the field's index. Creations use fields -1, -2, …, so
  they never collide with a spend in the same transaction (ADR-0014 D1). A claim made for one contract can never be
  read by another.
- **Your contract's validator** finds the verifier's redeemer among the transaction's redeemers, takes its own claim,
  and requires:
  - `oldRoot` equals the root in the current datum;
  - your method, given the claimed reads, writes exactly the claimed writes, in order, with the same keys and values;
  - the next datum stores the claim's `newRoot`, with empty `reads` and `writes`;
  - the result map's root is still the opened root, so a method cannot swap in another map.

The runtime publishes the verifier's reference script and registers its stake credential once per network, the first
time a map contract needs it.

| Invariant | Meaning (ADR-0002 D7) |
|---|---|
| I15 | Every value a method reads is proven against the pre-call root (inclusion, or exclusion when absent) |
| I16 | The next root is exactly the old root with the method's net writes applied, each proven at its step |
| I17 | A method cannot replace a map; the datum stores `(root, [], [])` only |

The attack suite (`Attacks`, in `julc-state-testkit`) adds forged read values, reads claimed present when absent and
the reverse, missing, extra, reordered and renamed write witnesses, a wrong root, and non-empty `reads`/`writes` in the
output datum. The token's tests run all of them.

##### Rules and limits

The processor enforces these; most of them close a way to read a value that nobody proved.

- **Top-level components only.** A `MerkleMap` must be a direct component of the state record, or of an `@Owned`
  record. A map nested inside another record, held in `@Params`, or passed as a method argument is a compile error.
- **Never construct one or look inside.** `new MerkleMap(...)` and `new MapEntry(...)` are rejected in a contract, and
  so are `.reads()`, `.writes()` and `.root()` on a map. Use `MerkleMaps.empty()` and the helpers.
- **`maps` is a reserved parameter name.** The generated redeemers use it for the witnesses.
- **Not combined yet** (each is a compile error):
  - `@Batched` actions in a contract with map state (each step of a batch would need its own claim);
  - an `@Invariant` that reads a state or owned record holding maps (on chain only the read set is visible);
  - `@Reads` of another contract whose state holds maps;
  - `@Migrate` and `@MigrateTo`;
  - maps in the shared state of a contract with `@Owned` objects. Put them in the owned records instead (see
    [Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/#merklemaps-inside-objects)).
- **Bytes and integers only.** Keys and values are `byte[]`; the integer helpers store non-negative values.
- **Proof cost grows with the keys touched,** and slowly with the map's size. There is no per-call cap besides the
  transaction budget.

> **A destroy discards the map:** 
When an instance ends, its map ends with it. The processor warns on every contract with maps and a `@Destroy` (and on
every `@OwnedDestroy` of a record with maps). Check `MerkleMaps.isEmpty(...)` in the destroy's rules unless losing the
contents is what you want. The token refuses to close while tokens are out:

```java
@Destroy
@SignedBy("admin")
public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(s.supply().compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) == 0 && MerkleMaps.isEmpty(s.balances()),
            "tokens are still in circulation");
    return Payouts.of(s.admin(), ctx.balance());
}
```

A destroy still opens the maps, so it needs a verifier withdrawal and a claim even when it reads nothing. A call that
reads and writes no entry builds that claim from the root alone, without the mirror (ADR-0012 r4).

##### MerkleMaps with native assets

A contract may hold native assets and MerkleMaps together (ADR-0014 D2): maps live in the datum, assets in the value,
and each is checked as usual. The `locker` example holds one token for many users and keeps each user's balance in a
map:

```java title="examples/locker/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/locker/Locker.java"
@StateContract(assetSlots = 2)
public class Locker {

    public record State(byte[] admin, byte[] tokenPolicy, byte[] tokenName, BigInteger total, MerkleMap balances) {}

    public record Locked(State state, Value accepted) {}

    /** Locks {@code qty} of the token for the caller. */
    @Action
    @Payable
    public static Locked lock(State s, BigInteger qty, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
        Require.that(qty.signum() > 0, "lock a positive amount");
        Require.that(ctx.received().signum() == 0, "the locker takes the token, not ADA");
        BigInteger had = MerkleMaps.getInt(s.balances(), ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO);
        return new Locked(new State(s.admin(), s.tokenPolicy(), s.tokenName(), s.total().add(qty),
                MerkleMaps.putInt(s.balances(), ctx.caller(), had.add(qty))), Assets.of(s.tokenPolicy(), s.tokenName(), qty));
    }
}
```

> **Watch the script size:** 
A contract with maps and assets carries both sets of generated helpers. The examples come to 14.3 KB (an instance)
and 14.4 KB (owned objects), under the 16 KB reference-script limit but close to it (ADR-0014 §3). See
[Fees and script size](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/).

##### Off chain: the mirror

To call a map contract, the runtime needs the map's contents: the *mirror*, an off-chain MPF whose root matches the
datum. You rarely touch it directly.

- **On the JVM** the default node store is RocksDB at `./.joust/mpf`. Set another with `StateRuntime.Builder.mapStore`
  or `mapStorePath`; tests use `-Djoust.mapStore=memory`. A runtime that has never seen a map rebuilds it from the
  chain history: the claims in the instance's verifier redeemers, replayed from the empty root, each new root checked.
  The token's DevKit test calls the map from a fresh in-memory store to show it.
- **In JavaScript** the mirror uses Aiken's MPF library, cached with `level` (LevelDB in Node, IndexedDB in a page),
  and is rebuilt from history the same way. The runtime engine takes proofs from it and checks every one against the
  on-chain root.

[MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/) covers stores, caching and rebuilding in detail.

###### Views and tests

A `@View` on map state runs on the JVM with the mirror bound, without a transaction: `token.balanceOf(pkh)` in the
generated Java client. Outside a JOUST call no mirror is bound, so calling a map method directly in a plain unit test
throws `IllegalStateException` ("no ReadSource is bound"). Run it through `MerkleSupport` or the harness, as
[`TokenTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/token/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/TokenTest.java)
does:

```java title="examples/token/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/token/TokenTest.java"
/** Runs {@code method} on {@code current} as the runtime does: reads from the mirror, then witnesses. */
MerkleSupport.Prepared<Token.State> call(Token.State current, Function<Token.State, Token.State> method) {
    var ms = new MerkleSupport(store);
    Token.State next = ms.run(() -> method.apply(current));
    return ms.prepare(h.policy(), Token.State.class, current, next, StateHarness.LIVE_REF);
}
```

##### Costs

From the harness (examples/README.md), per script execution. The token's validator is 11,718 bytes; the shared
`MapVerifier` is 4,700 bytes and read by reference.

| Token call | Scripts | CPU | Memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| create | MINT + verifier | 121.2M + 32.0M | 366k + 138k |
| mint (1 read, 1 write) | SPEND + verifier | 156.2M + 336.5M | 483k + 1,277k |
| transfer (2 reads, 2 writes) | SPEND + verifier | 218.4M + 502.3M | 707k + 1,901k |
| transfer, 203 holders in the map | SPEND + verifier | 218.4M + 742.4M | 707k + 2,923k |

A transaction may use 10,000M CPU and 14M memory on mainnet.

##### Pitfalls

- **Forgetting to remove emptied keys.** A zero stays present. Remove it, or `isEmpty` never becomes true and a
  destroy guarded by it can never run.
- **Assuming parallel writers.** Two users writing the same instance at once still contend. Use owned objects with
  their own maps, or shard across instances.
- **Comparing keys with `==` or `.equals`.** Use `ByteStringLib.equals` for `byte[]` in contract code; the helpers
  already do.
- **Losing the mirror on the JVM.** A missing store is rebuilt from the chain, but that takes one history read per
  map. Keep the RocksDB directory in production.

  [Architecture decisions](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/)

### Owned objects

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/

An *owned object* is a record that lives in its own UTxO under a contract instance: one bank account, one game hero,
one marketplace listing. Owned methods spend only the object's UTxO, never the instance's, so two users acting on their
own objects never wait for each other. The instance keeps the shared settings, and an owned method can read them
without spending them.

Use owned objects whenever state belongs to one user and many users act at the same time. Cardano's UTxO model fits
this directly: each object is its own output, much as Sui's owned objects skip the global sequence (ADR-0003).

##### A bank with one account per customer

```java title="examples/bank/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/bank/Bank.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 160)
public class Bank {

    public record State(byte[] admin, boolean paused, BigInteger withdrawLimit) {}

    @Owned
    public record Account(byte[] owner, BigInteger balance) {}

    public record Withdrawal(Account state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}

    @Init
    public static State init(BigInteger withdrawLimit, Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(ctx.caller(), false, withdrawLimit);
    }

    @Action
    @SignedBy("admin")
    public static State setPaused(State s, boolean paused) {
        return new State(s.admin(), paused, s.withdrawLimit());
    }

    /** Opens an account for the caller, with a first deposit. */
    @OwnedInit
    @Payable
    public static Account open(@Shared State bank, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(!bank.paused(), "the bank is paused");
        return new Account(ctx.caller(), ctx.received());
    }

    @OwnedAction
    @Payable
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static Account deposit(Account a, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0, "deposit must be positive");
        return new Account(a.owner(), a.balance().add(ctx.received()));
    }

    /** Takes money out, within the bank's limit, unless the bank is paused. */
    @OwnedAction
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static Withdrawal withdraw(Account a, @Shared State bank, BigInteger amount, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(!bank.paused(), "the bank is paused");
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0 && amount.compareTo(bank.withdrawLimit()) <= 0,
                "amount outside the withdrawal limit");
        Require.that(amount.compareTo(a.balance()) <= 0, "insufficient balance");
        return new Withdrawal(new Account(a.owner(), a.balance().subtract(amount)), Payouts.of(a.owner(), amount));
    }

    /** The owner closes the account and takes everything (works even when the bank is paused). */
    @OwnedDestroy
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(Account a, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(a.owner(), ctx.balance());
    }
}
```

The instance holds `State` (the admin, a paused flag, a limit). Each customer's `Account` is an object. `deposit`
spends only the account. `withdraw` also reads the bank's state through `@Shared`, as a reference input, so it does not
spend the bank either.

##### The annotations

| Annotation | On | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| `@Owned` | a nested record | Marks a record as an owned object type. A contract may declare several |
| `@OwnedInit` | a method | `R name([@Shared S shared,] args... [, Ctx] [, Funds])`: creates an object under an instance. Returns the record, or a result record with `state` (and `accepted` with `Funds`) |
| `@OwnedAction` | a method | `R name(R object, [@Shared S shared,] [@Into S destination,] args... [, Ctx] [, Funds])`: changes one object. Returns the record or a result record (`state`, `payouts`, `sends`, …) |
| `@OwnedDestroy` | a method | `name(R object, [@Shared S shared,] args..., Ctx [, Funds])`: ends an object, burns its token. Returns `JulcList<Payout>` or a result record, and must pay out everything it holds |
| `@Shared` | a parameter | The instance's state, read-only, through a reference input. Must have the state type and come right after the owned record |
| `@Into` | a parameter | The destination of a move (see [Moving objects](#moving-an-object-to-another-instance)) |
| `@Admits` | an `@Action` | The destination's consent to a move |

The owned type of a method is its first parameter (or, for `@OwnedInit`, its return type). `@SignedBy`, `@ValidAfter`
and `@ValidBefore` on an owned method name fields of the **owned** record: `@SignedBy("owner")` above checks
`Account.owner`. `@Payable`, `Ctx` and `Funds` work as on instance methods, with the object's own balance and deposit.
See [Ctx, funds and payouts](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/) and [Authorization](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/).

##### Calling objects

The generated clients give each owned type a handle, and the instance a lookup per type.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/bank/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/bank/BankDevnetTest.java"
var bank = BankClient.deploy(runtime, admin, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(20)));
var annAcct = bank.open(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(30)));     // an AccountObject
var benAcct = bank.open(ben, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(40)));

// Both customers deposit and withdraw at the same time: separate UTxOs, so no contention.
var a = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
    annAcct.deposit(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(5)));
    annAcct.withdraw(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
});
var b = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
    benAcct.deposit(ben, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(7)));
    benAcct.withdraw(ben, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(20)));
});
CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join();

bank.setPaused(admin, true);
annAcct.close(ann);    // the escape hatch: closing needs no bank state
```

`bank.account(objectId)` reconnects to an existing object; `annAcct.value()` reads it.

**JavaScript:**

```js title="examples/dapp/frontend/src/main.js (adapted)"
const bank = new Bank(options);                        // the generated client (joust-gen)
const inst = bank.at(bankId);
const { object } = await inst.open(wallet, {}, { lovelace: 30_000_000n });
await object.deposit(wallet, {}, { lovelace: 5_000_000n });
await object.withdraw(wallet, { amount: 10_000_000n });

// Every account of this bank on chain, then a handle for one of them.
const mine = (await inst.objects()).filter((o) => o.value.owner === myKeyHash);
const acct = inst.account(mine[0].id);
await acct.close(wallet);
```

##### What an object is on chain

An object is a UTxO at the contract's address holding:
- **The object token** `(policy, objectId)`, quantity 1. `objectId = 0x4F ‖ blake2b_224(seedTxId ‖ I2OSP(seedIndex, 2))`:
  29 bytes starting with `0x4F`, derived from a UTxO the creation spends.
- **An inline datum** `Holding(instance, value)`: the id of the instance it belongs to, and your record. With several
  owned types it is `Holding_<Type>(instance, value)`, one constructor per type.
- **An exact value:** `minAda` plus the object's funds plus its token, as for instances.

Token names tell kinds apart, and every spend arm checks the kind first:

| Kind | Token name |
|---|---|
| Instance | 32 bytes |
| Owned object | 29 bytes, first byte `0x4F` |
| Intent ([batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/)) | 29 bytes, first byte `0x49` |

###### What the validator checks

- **Creation** (MINT, `CreateObject`): the seed is spent; exactly one token is minted, named `objectId(seed)`; a
  reference input holds the instance token, so the instance exists, and gives the `@Shared` state; one output carries
  the object at the script address with `Holding(instance, …)` equal to your method's result and the exact value.
- **Owned spends:** the spent UTxO must hold an object token (I21); with several types, the datum's constructor tag
  must be the method's type, checked before decoding (I42). Then the usual checks apply to the object: one continuing
  output with its token, the datum equal to your method's result, an exact value, payouts tagged, signatures and time.
  The `instance` in `Holding` never changes, except through a move (I19, I43).
- **`@Shared` reads:** the reference input must hold the 32-byte token of exactly the object's instance, at the state
  address, with an inline datum (I20).
- **Owned destroys** burn the token and must allocate everything the object holds.

| Invariant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| I18 | An object token is minted only by `CreateObject`, from a spent seed, under an existing instance |
| I19 | An object's datum keeps its instance (except through an admitted move); owned actions never spend the instance |
| I20 | A `@Shared` read is the current state of exactly the object's instance |
| I21 | A token's kind decides which redeemers it accepts |
| I42 | An owned method runs only on an object of its own type |
| I43 | An object changes instance only by a move its destination admits in the same transaction |

##### Rules the processor enforces

- **An escape hatch for every owned type.** Each `@Owned` type needs an `@OwnedDestroy` without `@Shared`, so an owner
  can always close their object whatever the instance's state. The bank's `close` works while the bank is paused.
- **No instance `@Destroy`** in a contract with owned objects: objects that read `@Shared` state would be stranded.
- **Every `@Owned` type needs an `@OwnedInit`.**
- **A warning** for an owned method without `@SignedBy`: anyone could call it on anyone's object.
- **`@Shared` comes right after the owned record**, and has the state type. The state reaches an owned method only
  through it.
- **No MerkleMaps in the shared state** of a contract with owned objects. Put them in the owned records.

> **One mint redeemer per policy:** 
The ledger allows one mint redeemer per policy in a transaction. So one transaction cannot create two objects of a
contract, or create one and burn another, under the same policy. Use separate transactions.

##### Several owned types

Declare as many `@Owned` records as you need. The `guild` example has heroes and items:

```java title="examples/guild/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/guild/Guild.java"
@Owned
public record Hero(byte[] owner, BigInteger level) {}

@Owned
public record Item(byte[] owner, BigInteger power) {}

@OwnedInit
public static Hero recruit(@Shared State guild, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(guild.open(), "the guild is closed");
    return new Hero(ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ONE);
}

@OwnedAction
@SignedBy("owner")
public static Hero levelUp(Hero h) {
    return new Hero(h.owner(), h.level().add(BigInteger.ONE));
}

@OwnedDestroy
@SignedBy("owner")
public static JulcList<Payout> retire(Hero h, Ctx ctx) {
    return Payouts.of(h.owner(), ctx.balance());
}

// ... forge, enchant and scrap for Item

@Invariant
public static boolean itemPower(Item i) {
    return i.power().compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(100)) <= 0;
}
```

With more than one type, the datum becomes a sealed `Holding` with one `Holding_<Type>` constructor per type, and each
spend arm checks the constructor tag before decoding, so `levelUp` can never run on an item. Each type gets its own
handle (`HeroObject`, `ItemObject`) and lookup in the clients, and its own invariants. A contract with one owned type
keeps the plain `Holding(instance, value)`.

##### Moving an object to another instance

An object can move to another instance of the same contract, for example a hero joining another guild. A move is a
handshake in one transaction: the object's `@OwnedAction` names the destination with `@Into`, and the destination
consents through an `@Action` marked `@Admits`.

```java title="examples/guild/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/guild/Guild.java"
/** Moves the hero to {@code destination}, which must admit it; only from an open guild, and only from level 2. */
@OwnedAction
@SignedBy("owner")
public static Hero transfer(Hero h, @Shared State source, @Into State destination, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(source.open(), "the source guild is closed");
    Require.that(h.level().compareTo(BigInteger.TWO) >= 0, "a hero moves from level 2");
    return new Hero(h.owner(), h.level());
}

/** Admits a hero moving in from another guild. It sees the arriving hero, read on-chain from the hero's own input. */
@Action
@Admits("Hero")
public static State admit(State s, byte[] heroId, Hero hero, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(s.open(), "the guild is closed");
    Require.that(hero.level().compareTo(s.minLevel()) >= 0, "the hero's level is too low for this guild");
    return new State(s.master(), s.open(), s.arrivals().add(BigInteger.ONE), s.minLevel());
}
```

- **The object's side:** the destination instance is *spent* in the same transaction with an `@Admits` action whose
  first argument is this object's id. The continuing `Holding` names the destination, which must differ from the
  source. The method gets the destination's state as it was before, and may also read the source with `@Shared`, so a
  closed source can stop objects leaving.
- **The destination's side:** its validator requires the object to be spent with a move naming this instance. Its
  method decides whether to admit, and may update its own state. It may take the arriving object as the parameter
  right after its id (`Hero hero` above): it is read from the object's input, not from the redeemer.
- **Typed admits:** `@Admits("Hero")` names the owned type it admits, so a hero cannot arrive through an item's admit.
  The name may be left out when only one owned type has moves.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/guild/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/guild/GuildDevnetTest.java"
var a = GuildClient.deploy(runtime, master, BigInteger.ONE);
var b = GuildClient.deploy(runtime, other, BigInteger.TWO);
var hero = a.recruit(ann);
hero.levelUp(ann);

// A move needs the destination's consent in the same transaction: alone, it is refused.
assertThrows(JoustException.class, () -> hero.transfer(ann, b));
var moved = hero.transferAdmitted(ann, b);     // the move and b's admit, composed

// Nested: the move-and-admit joins an outer composition with another call, in one transaction.
Compose.of(runtime, ann).allowSharedSigners()
        .add(() -> moved.transferAdmitted(ann, c))
        .add(() -> sword.enchant(ann, BigInteger.ONE))
        .submit();
```

When the contract has one `@Admits` action taking only the object id (and optionally the arriving object), the client
gets `<move>Admitted(caller, destination, …)`, which composes both calls for you.

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Guild)"
const move = [
  { contract: guild, method: 'transfer', instance: a, object: hero, into: b, args: {} },
  { contract: guild, method: 'admit', instance: b, args: { heroId: hero } },
];
await rt.compose(ann, move);     // one transaction, one signature
```

Moves run only inside a [composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/). A destination has one redeemer per
transaction, so it admits one move per transaction. A move cannot take `@Reads`, and `@Admits` cannot be `@Batched`.
With native assets, a move carries the object's full value: the `market` example relists a listing, NFT included,
into another market (`relist`/`enlist`).

##### MerkleMaps inside objects

An owned record may have [MerkleMap](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/) components, so each user's object can hold a map of any
size. The `Armory` contract gives each player a vault with an inventory:

```java title="examples/guild/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/guild/Armory.java"
/** A player's vault: an inventory (item name -> count) of any size, in a MerkleMap (ADR-0012 D2). */
@Owned
public record Vault(byte[] owner, BigInteger kinds, MerkleMap inventory) {}

@OwnedInit
public static Vault openVault(@Shared State armory, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(armory.open(), "the armory is closed");
    return new Vault(ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO, MerkleMaps.empty());
}

@OwnedAction
@SignedBy("owner")
public static Vault stash(Vault v, byte[] item, BigInteger count) {
    Require.that(count.signum() > 0, "stash a positive count");
    BigInteger have = MerkleMaps.getInt(v.inventory(), item, BigInteger.ZERO);
    BigInteger kinds = have.signum() == 0 ? v.kinds().add(BigInteger.ONE) : v.kinds();
    return new Vault(v.owner(), kinds, MerkleMaps.putInt(v.inventory(), item, have.add(count)));
}

/** Closes an empty vault (no @Shared: it works whatever the armory's state). */
@OwnedDestroy
@SignedBy("owner")
public static JulcList<Payout> closeVault(Vault v, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(v.kinds().signum() == 0, "empty the vault first");
    return Payouts.of(v.owner(), ctx.balance());
}
```

An object's map claims are keyed by the object's input (or its creation's seed), exactly as an instance's are, and
the runtime keeps a mirror per object. The processor warns that an `@OwnedDestroy` discards the object's maps; the
vault above counts its kinds so `closeVault` can require an empty inventory. An `@Invariant` cannot read an owned
record that holds maps.

##### Size

Owned types, moves and maps each add generated code. Measured (ADR-0012 §5):

| Validator | Size |
|---|---|
| Bank (one owned type) | 7.9 KB |
| Guild (two owned types, both movable, two admits, invariants) | 11.1 KB |
| Armory (an owned type with a MerkleMap) | 12.4 KB |
| Hero, Item and a MerkleMap Vault in one contract, with moves | 16.7 KB: over the limit |

That last one is why `Armory` is a second contract. If yours grows past about 14 KB, split it the same way. See
[Fees and script size](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/).

##### Pitfalls

- **Writes to shared state still contend.** Owned methods cannot change the instance's state. A total that every
  deposit updates is a hot shared write: use [batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/).
- **`@Shared` couples objects to instance writes.** An owned call reads the instance as of its reference input; if the
  instance changes first, the call fails and the runtime retries. Keep shared writes rare and gated.
- **Ownership is a field.** Transferring an object means an owned action that changes its owner field.
- **Objects are not unique by any field.** Two users can create objects with the same name or owner. When at most one
  object per key matters (one ballot per voter, unique names), use [keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/).
- **Gating creation** is your method's job: check the `@Shared` state with `Require`, as `open` checks `paused`.

- [Annotations](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/), [State API](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/state-api/)
- ADR-0003 (owned objects) and ADR-0012 (several types, maps in objects, moves):
  [Architecture decisions](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/)
