### Keyed objects

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/

A *keyed object* is an [owned object](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/) with a key: one ballot per voter, one name in a
registry, one position per account. Like any owned object it is its own UTxO, so updates to different keys never
wait for each other. Unlike a plain owned object, the chain guarantees that an instance holds **at most one object per
key**, and anyone can find an object by its key without knowing who created it.

Use a keyed type when uniqueness by key matters and the objects are updated independently. Use a
[MerkleMap](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/) when the entries are small and you want them in the instance's own state (every
write then goes through the one instance UTxO), and a plain owned type when nothing needs to be unique.

##### Why plain owned objects cannot be unique

A plain owned object is named by the seed UTxO it was created from (`0x4F` followed by a hash of the seed). A minting
policy cannot see tokens minted in earlier transactions, so no validator can tell whether an object already exists
for a given key. Minting a token whose name is derived from the key does not help either: a second transaction could
mint the same name again.

Keyed objects solve this with a **sorted linked list on chain** (ADR-0016 §1, the linked-list pattern):

- Each object is a node: its own UTxO holding one token, whose datum has the object's value and the **next key** in
  the list.
- Each keyed type of an instance has a **head**, an empty-key node created with the instance itself.
- To insert key `k`, a transaction spends the node just before it (the *anchor*) and checks that
  `anchor.key < k < anchor.next`. It then relinks the anchor to `k` and creates the new node pointing at the anchor's
  old `next`.

Two objects with one key would need two places in a strictly increasing list, so the neighbours prove uniqueness. The
minting policy checks every insert and every removal, and the list stays well formed whatever a transaction builder
tries (ADR-0016 I47; `ListIntegrityTest` checks it with random operations and mutated transactions).

| | Plain owned object | Keyed object |
|---|---|---|
| Unique per key | No | Yes, per instance and type |
| Find it by | Its object id (from the seed) | Its key |
| Token name | `0x4F` + `blake2b_224(seed)` | `0x4B` + `blake2b_224(instance ‖ typeId ‖ key)` (29 bytes) |
| Creation spends | A seed UTxO of the creator | The predecessor in the list (the anchor) |
| Updates | Only the object's UTxO | Only the object's UTxO |
| Leaves by | `@OwnedDestroy`: burns the token | Removing (frees the key) or retiring (keeps it) |

##### A registry: one ballot per voter, unique names

The [`registry`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/examples/#registry) example has two keyed types. `Ballot` allows one ballot per voter,
ever. `Entry` is a name registry: a name can be released (and claimed again) or retired (kept for good), and guardians
can recover it.

```java title="examples/registry/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/registry/Registry.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 384)
public class Registry {

    public record State(byte[] admin, boolean open) {}

    /** One ballot per voter, ever (only a retiring exit). */
    @Owned(key = "voter", maxKeyBytes = 28, signedKey = true)
    public record Ballot(byte[] voter, BigInteger choice) {}

    @Owned(key = "name", maxKeyBytes = 64)
    public record Entry(byte[] name, byte[] owner, BigInteger stake, BigInteger tier, JulcList<byte[]> guardians,
                        BigInteger needed) {}

    public record Withdrawal(Entry state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}

    @Init
    public static State init(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(ctx.caller(), true);
    }

    // ---- ballots

    @OwnedInit
    public static Ballot cast(@Shared State s, byte[] voter, BigInteger choice, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(s.open(), "voting is closed");
        Require.that(choice.signum() >= 0 && choice.compareTo(BigInteger.TEN) < 0, "choose 0 to 9");
        return new Ballot(voter, choice);
    }

    @OwnedAction
    @SignedBy("voter")
    public static Ballot change(Ballot b, BigInteger choice) {
        Require.that(choice.signum() >= 0 && choice.compareTo(BigInteger.TEN) < 0, "choose 0 to 9");
        return new Ballot(b.voter(), choice);
    }

    /** The voter leaves with everything but the deposit; the ballot stays retired, so the voter can never vote again. */
    @OwnedDestroy(retire = true)
    @SignedBy("voter")
    public static JulcList<Payout> leave(Ballot b, Ctx ctx) {
        return ctx.balance().signum() > 0 ? Payouts.of(b.voter(), ctx.balance()) : Payouts.none();
    }

    // ---- names

    /** Claims a free name for the caller, staking what the call pays. */
    @OwnedInit
    @Payable
    public static Entry claim(byte[] name, BigInteger tier, JulcList<byte[]> guardians, BigInteger needed, Ctx ctx) {
        return new Entry(name, ctx.caller(), ctx.received(), tier, guardians, needed);
    }

    /** Guardians hand the entry to a new owner (the old owner can still retire or release first). */
    @OwnedAction
    @Quorum(keys = "guardians", threshold = "needed")
    public static Entry recover(Entry e, byte[] newOwner) {
        return new Entry(e.name(), newOwner, e.stake(), e.tier(), e.guardians(), e.needed());
    }

    /** Releases the name: the entry is removed from the list and the name can be claimed again. */
    @OwnedDestroy
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static JulcList<Payout> release(Entry e, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(e.owner(), ctx.balance());
    }

    /** Retires the name: the owner leaves with the stake, the name stays taken for good. */
    @OwnedDestroy(retire = true)
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static JulcList<Payout> retire(Entry e, Ctx ctx) {
        return ctx.balance().signum() > 0 ? Payouts.of(e.owner(), ctx.balance()) : Payouts.none();
    }

    @Invariant
    public static boolean tierInRange(Entry e) {
        return e.tier().signum() >= 0 && e.tier().compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(3)) <= 0;
    }
}
```

The full file also has the admin's `setOpen`, an admin-only `grant`, and the owner's `upgrade` and `withdraw`.
Everything you already know from owned objects applies: `@OwnedInit` creates, `@OwnedAction` updates,
`@OwnedDestroy` ends, `@Shared` reads the instance's state by reference, `@Invariant` is checked on every result.

##### Declaring a keyed type

Name a `byte[]` component of an `@Owned` record as its key:

| Element of `@Owned` | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `""` (not keyed) | The `byte[]` component that keys the object. It never changes for the object's life |
| `maxKeyBytes` | 32 | The longest key, 1 to 64 bytes |
| `signedKey` | `false` | The key is a 28-byte key hash that must sign the insert (needs `maxKeyBytes` of at least 28) |
| `linkCooldownMs` | 60,000 | The least time between two relinks of a node: 0 (written explicitly), or 60,000 to 3,600,000 |
| `linkWindowMs` | `min(120,000, maxValidityMs)` | The widest validity window of a transaction that relinks a node: 20,000 to `min(900,000, maxValidityMs)` |

`@OwnedDestroy(retire = true)` marks a retiring exit. The source is
[`Owned.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Owned.java)
and [`OwnedDestroy.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/OwnedDestroy.java).

##### The four kinds of call

**Insert** (`@OwnedInit`). The runtime finds the key's predecessor, the anchor, and builds one transaction that spends
the anchor, relinks it to the new key and mints the new node's token. The policy checks the anchor's place
(`anchor.key < key < anchor.next`), the key's length, the anchor's cooldown, that exactly one token is minted, and the
new node: at the state address, its datum the method's result, its value exactly `minAda` plus what the call paid.
With `signedKey`, the key must be a signer of the transaction. Every insert variant is its own redeemer
(`Insert_<method>`), so a type may have several initializers, as `Entry` has `claim` and `grant`.

**Keyed action** (`@OwnedAction`). Spends only the object's UTxO, as a plain owned action does. The validator also
checks that the node keeps its token, its instance, its key and its place in the list (`next` and the time of its last
relink). Every keyed action must be authorized: `@SignedBy`, `@Quorum` or `@AuthorizedBy`.

**Remove** (`@OwnedDestroy`). Frees the key. The transaction spends the node and its predecessor, burns the node's
token and relinks the predecessor past it. The method must pay out everything the node holds, deposit included, as a
plain owned destroy does. A removing exit is optional.

**Retire** (`@OwnedDestroy(retire = true)`). Leaves without touching any neighbour. The node stays in the list as a
retired node, holding its token and its deposit (`minAda`), so the key stays taken for good. The method sees
`ctx.balance()` as everything but the deposit, and its payouts must total exactly that. A retired node takes no more
calls; it can still be an anchor for inserts next to it.

Every keyed type needs a retiring exit, because it is the one exit nobody else can block (see
[Cooldown and window](#cooldown-and-window)). A type whose only exits retire gives "once ever" uniqueness, as `Ballot`
does: a voter who leaves can never vote again.

> **What the retire may carry:** 
The retiring exit must carry `@SignedBy` (unsigned, anyone could retire anyone's object, and its key, for good), and
nothing a third party controls: `@Shared`, `@Reads`, `@Payable`, `@Quorum`, `@AuthorizedBy`, `@ValidAfter` and
`@ValidBefore` are errors on it.

##### Calling keyed objects from Java

The processor generates, per keyed type, a list accessor, a lookup by key, one insert method per `@OwnedInit`, and an
object class with the keyed actions, removes and retires. Adapted from the registry's DevKit test,
[`RegistrySmokeDevnetTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/registry/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/registry/devnet/RegistrySmokeDevnetTest.java)
(comments added, assertions shortened):

```java
var reg = RegistryClient.deploy(runtime, admin);                     // the instance and both list heads
var ballot = reg.cast(ann, Keys.pkh(ann), BigInteger.TWO);           // insert a Ballot keyed by Ann's key hash
var b = reg.claim(ann, new byte[]{0x62}, BigInteger.ONE, JulcList.<byte[]>empty().prepend(Keys.pkh(ann)),
        BigInteger.ONE, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(5)));         // insert an Entry, paying 5 ADA of stake
assertTrue(reg.entryExists(new byte[]{0x62}));
b.upgrade(ann, BigInteger.TWO, ADA);                                 // a keyed action
b.withdraw(ann, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TWO));
b.release(ann);                                                      // remove: the name is free again
assertFalse(reg.entryExists(new byte[]{0x62}));
ballot.leave(ann);                                                   // retire: the ballot stays, retired
assertTrue(reg.ballot(Keys.pkh(ann)).retired());
```

| Generated member (for `Entry`) | What it does |
|---|---|
| `claim(Account, args... [, payLovelace])`, `grant(...)` | Inserts with that `@OwnedInit`; returns an `EntryObject`. Refused on the JVM if the key is taken |
| `entry(byte[] key)` | The object of a key, live or retired. Fails when the provider returned nothing |
| `entryExists(byte[] key)` | The key is taken, live or retired |
| `entryKeys()` | Every key in list order (`KeyedList.Entry`: `key()`, `retired()`, `keyHex()`), walked from the head |
| `entryList()` | The underlying `KeyedList`: `find`, `get`, `exists`, `keys`, `unit`, `insert` |
| `EntryObject` | `key()`, `value()`, `retired()`, `lovelace()`, `object()`, and one method per keyed action, remove and retire |

A lookup by key computes the token name and asks the provider for the UTxO holding it: one query on Yaci Store and
Blockfrost. Every answer is validated (policy, address, datum, instance, key). "Not found" means the provider returned
nothing, not that the key is provably free. An insert or a remove lists the whole state address to find the
neighbour, so its cost grows with the number of UTxOs there.

A keyed contract's `deploy` mints the instance token and one head per keyed type in the same transaction. The heads
live as long as the contract: a contract with owned objects cannot be destroyed, and a keyed one cannot be migrated,
so a keyed registry is permanent.

###### The designated input and retries

A keyed call can be rejected for ordinary reasons: another insert took the gap first, or the neighbour moved. The
runtime then builds the call again. Building again is dangerous when an earlier attempt might still land: a relay
that said "rejected" could be wrong, and two different attempts could both be included.

So before the first attempt of a keyed operation, the runtime **designates one ordinary UTxO of the wallet** (the
largest ADA-only UTxO of at least 5 ADA) and spends it in **every** attempt of that operation. Any two attempts then
share an input, and at most one of them can ever land, whatever relays or providers claim. In plain words:

- Each attempt is a different transaction, but they all spend the same coin of yours, so only one can be included.
- The runtime never replaces that coin while the operation runs, even when it looks spent: an earlier attempt may
  have landed.
- When it cannot tell (a timeout, an unknown answer), it stops and throws `PendingTransactionException`, naming every
  attempt (`attempts()`) and the designated input (`designatedInput()`). Look the attempts up: if one landed, the
  operation happened; if none did once their windows have passed and the input is unspent, a new call is safe.
- After a definite rejection it rebuilds everything (the window, the method's result, the anchor) up to `maxRetries`
  times, then throws `ContentionException`.

The wallet needs an ADA-only UTxO of at least 5 ADA free for each keyed operation running at once. Designations are
per JVM: two processes sharing one wallet should use separate UTxOs or separate wallets.

`StateRuntime.Builder` has options for keyed calls: `relays(List<Relay>)` sends every attempt to several submit
endpoints (`Relay.of(backend)` wraps a CCL backend), `relayTimeout` (60 s), `settlementSlots` (2),
`topUpAllowance` (10 ADA), and `pageLimits(maxStartSlots, maxValiditySlots)`. See the
[Java runtime API](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/java-runtime-api/#keyed-objects).

###### In a composition

Inserts, removes, retires and keyed actions can run inside [`Compose`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/) with other
calls. The runtime refuses, before building, two structural operations (inserts or removes) of one contract in one
transaction, a structural operation beside another mint of the same policy, and a call on an input that the insert or
remove already spends. A composition with a keyed call designates one input and retries as a whole.

##### Cooldown and window

An insert or a remove spends a neighbour, so someone could keep your node busy: insert a throwaway key next to it,
remove it, insert again, every block. Two rules on every relink (ADR-0016 D9) stop this:

- **Window.** A transaction that relinks a node has a finite validity window of at most `linkWindowMs` (`W`). The node
  records the window's upper bound as `linkedAt`.
- **Cooldown.** The next relink of that node must start at least `linkCooldownMs` (`C`) after `linkedAt`.

So between two relinks of a node, its owner has at least `C` in which only their own calls touch it. With the
defaults (`C` = 60 s, `W` = 120 s) an honest call that finds a fresh relink waits at most `W + C`, about three
minutes. The runtime does this for you: it moves the window's start to the end of the cooldown and submits then.

Throughput follows from it: each gap between two keys takes at most one insert or remove per `C` plus the window.
An empty registry has one gap, so a launch fills slowly at first (about one insert per 80 s with `C` = 60 s and a
20 s window); capacity grows with the number of keys. Keys that grow monotonically (sequence numbers, timestamps)
always insert at the tail and contend there: key by a hash of the value instead. `linkCooldownMs = 0` removes the
cooldown, and the processor warns: the retiring exit is then no longer guaranteed against churn.

##### What the validator checks

| Invariant | Rule |
|---|---|
| I44 | Keyed and head tokens are 29 bytes, `0x4B` + a hash of instance, type and key; the name is reserved |
| I45 | One head per instance and keyed type, minted only with the instance; heads never burn |
| I46 | A keyed token is minted only by an insert, alone under the policy, after a `Link`-spent anchor in the right place |
| I47 | List integrity: from the head, keys strictly increase, and the list holds exactly the type's tokens, each once |
| I48 | A node is relinked only by the insert or remove that names it; only `next` and `linkedAt` change, and its lovelace never goes down |
| I49 | A keyed token burns only by a remove, which relinks the predecessor past it |
| I50 | A keyed action keeps the node's token, instance, key, `next` and `linkedAt` |
| I51 | A node's token name matches its datum's instance and key |
| I52 | Token kinds decide arms: keyed tokens take only keyed arms, plain owned and instance tokens never take them |
| I53 | With `signedKey`, the key signed the insert |
| I54 | Cooldown and window, on every relink |
| I55 | A retire keeps the token and the deposit, and pays out exactly the rest |

The full list, with the proof that every transaction keeps the list sorted, is ADR-0016 §3 and §3.1. The registry's
attack suite (`RegistryAttacksTest`) requires each attack to be refused by a script, not by the ledger's first phase.

##### Rules and limits

The processor refuses:

- keyed types in a contract that handles native assets (any `Funds`, sends, mints, accepted assets, deposits or a
  `@Withdraw` handler), and keyed types in contracts with MerkleMaps, `@Batched` actions or migration;
- `@Into` moves of keyed objects;
- a keyed type without a retiring `@OwnedDestroy(retire = true)` signed by `@SignedBy` and without `@Shared`;
- a keyed `@OwnedAction` without `@SignedBy`, `@Quorum` or `@AuthorizedBy`;
- `maxDatumBytes` above 2048 in a contract with keyed types, more than 16 keyed types, two keyed types with one simple
  name, and contract names that clash with generated ones (`Link`, `Remove_*`, `Insert_*`, `anchor`, `removed`).

It warns when a keyed `@OwnedInit` does not bind the key to the caller (neither `signedKey` nor every return being
`new T(...)` with the key argument `ctx.caller()`): anyone could then take a name someone else wants first. The
registry's `claim` and `grant` warn, by design: a free name goes to whoever claims it.

Other limits:

- **Script size.** The registry's validator is 14,717 bytes, close to the 15,000-byte limit for a reference script.
  About 11 minimal keyed types fit in one contract today, not 16. Traces (`-Pjoust.traces`) push the registry over.
- **Arguments.** The runtime refuses initializer and `@Init` arguments over 4,096 serialised bytes in a keyed
  contract.
- **Locked deposits.** Heads and retired nodes keep their deposits for good, and retired nodes accumulate: the state
  address grows with every key ever retired, and so does the listing behind each insert and remove.
- **Maps in a keyed value.** A value holding a Plutus map must keep its keys unique and in canonical order, or relinks
  next to it are refused.
- **Pages.** A page runs keyed calls one at a time and never in a composition; see
  [Keyed objects in JavaScript](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/keyed-objects-js/).
- **`.jsc`.** `.jsc` has no owned objects, so no keyed types (`.jsc` gets them in milestone M3); write keyed
  contracts in Java.

##### Costs

Measured on the ledger model with every script of the transaction summed, at the size caps (64-byte keys, datums at
their limit). Limits per transaction: 10,000M CPU and 14M memory on mainnet.

| Transaction | CPU | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| Insert (policy and the anchor's `Link`) | 387.1M | 1,212,522 |
| Remove (policy, the predecessor's `Link`, the node's destroy) | 426.2M | 1,405,297 |
| Retire | 190.8M | 655,308 |
| Keyed action (`upgrade`) | 229.2M | 712,127 |
| Instance creation with two heads | 382.7M | 1,230,285 |

Source: ADR-0016, "Implementation notes (M1)". On Yaci DevKit, an insert with both datums at 2,048 bytes and 4,096
bytes of arguments makes a 9,142-byte transaction, under the 16,384-byte limit.

##### Testing

`examples/registry` tests keyed contracts at every level: the JVM, the harness with its ledger model (`Ledger` in
`julc-state-testkit`), the attack suite, the list-integrity test with mutated transactions, and DevKit tests for
concurrency, contested gaps, hostile neighbours, cooldowns, compositions and submission across relays. Run them with
`./gradlew :examples:registry:test` (the DevKit tests skip themselves without DevKit). See [Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/).

##### Reference

- [ADR-0016: Keyed objects](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0016-keyed-objects.md): the threat
  model, decisions D1 to D11, the invariants, and the implementation notes of M1 to M3.
- [Annotations: `@Owned`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/#owned) and [`@OwnedDestroy`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/#owneddestroy).
- [`examples/registry`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/registry).

  - [Keyed objects in JavaScript](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/keyed-objects-js/)

### Batched intents

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/

Some state is hot and shared: a donation total, a ticket price that rises with each sale, an AMM's reserves. Every
call spends the instance's one UTxO, so when many users call at once, all but one fail and retry. Owned objects do not
help, because the total itself is shared.

`@Batched` solves this the way Cardano DEXes do. A user locks an *intent* (a request, with its payment) in a UTxO of
their own, which contends with nobody. Anyone can then run a *batcher* that applies many intents to the instance in
one transaction. The action's code is the same method you would call directly (ADR-0004).

##### When to use it

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Many users change one shared value at the same time | `@Batched` (this page) |
| Each user changes only their own state | [Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/): no batcher, one transaction per call |
| Each key may exist at most once (names, ballots) | [Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/) |
| Few writers (an admin, a publisher) | A plain `@Action` |

The cost is latency: every operation takes two transactions (lock, then batch), and something must run the batcher.

##### Declaring batched actions

```java title="examples/pool/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/pool/Pool.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 192)
public class Pool {

    public record State(byte[] admin, BigInteger donated, BigInteger sold, BigInteger price, BigInteger step) {}

    public record Sale(State state, JulcList<Payout> payouts) {}

    @Action
    @Batched
    @Payable
    public static State donate(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(1_000_000)) >= 0, "donate at least 1 ADA");
        return new State(s.admin(), s.donated().add(ctx.received()), s.sold(), s.price(), s.step());
    }

    /**
     * Buys one ticket at the current price, if it is at most {@code maxPrice}; the change goes back to the buyer. Only as
     * an intent ({@code only = true}): nobody can spend the pool with a direct buy and so invalidate pending batches.
     */
    @Action
    @Batched(only = true)
    @Payable
    public static Sale buy(State s, BigInteger maxPrice, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(s.price().compareTo(maxPrice) <= 0, "price above the buyer's bound");
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(s.price()) >= 0, "pays less than the price");
        BigInteger change = ctx.received().subtract(s.price());
        State next = new State(s.admin(), s.donated(), s.sold().add(BigInteger.ONE), s.price().add(s.step()), s.step());
        if (change.compareTo(BigInteger.ZERO) > 0) {
            return new Sale(next, Payouts.of(ctx.caller(), change));
        }
        return new Sale(next, Payouts.none());
    }
}
```

- `@Batched` lets the action run as an intent **and** as a direct call.
- `@Batched(only = true)` drops the direct call. Nobody can then spend the instance with that action directly, which
  would invalidate the batches being built against it. Use it for actions users race on.

In `.jsc` the modifier is `batched` (and `batched only` for intent-only). In `.jsc` a batched action that pays
says `open` ([the rules](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc-reference/#modifiers)):

**Java:**

```java
@Action
@Batched
@Payable
public static State donate(State s, Ctx ctx) {
    Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(1_000_000)) >= 0, "donate at least 1 ADA");
    return new State(s.admin(), s.donated().add(ctx.received()), s.sold(), s.price(), s.step());
}
```

**.jsc:**

```jsc title="examples/dsl/src/main/jsc/org/julclang/state/examples/dsl/Pool.jsc"
action donate() payable batched {
  require(received >= 1 ada, "donate at least 1 ADA")
  return { ...state, donated: donated + received }
}
```

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Pool)"
const p = pool.at((await pool.deploy(admin, { price: 10n * ADA, step: ADA })).instance);
const d0 = (await p.intent(u0, 'donate', {}, { lovelace: 5n * ADA })).intent;
await p.intent(u2, 'buy', { maxPrice: 20n * ADA }, { lovelace: 20n * ADA });
```

In a generated client, a batched action's method (`instance.donate(wallet, {}, pay)`) locks an intent.

###### What `Ctx` means inside a batch

A batched action needs a `Ctx` parameter. In a batch:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `ctx.caller()` | The intent's owner, who signed when creating it |
| `ctx.received()` | The lovelace the intent carries for the action |
| `ctx.balance()` | The contract's balance at that point of the fold |
| `ctx.validFrom()`, `ctx.validTo()` | The batch transaction's bounds |

Because the batcher, not the user, signs the batch, a batched action cannot use `@SignedBy`, `@OnlyOwner`,
`@ValidAfter` or `@ValidBefore`. Authorise with `ctx.caller()` in the body, and check time with
[`Clock`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/).

##### The flow

**Java:**

```java title="examples/pool/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/pool/PoolDevnetTest.java"
var pool = PoolClient.deploy(runtime, admin, ada(10), ada(1));
Instant later = Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(30));

// Users lock intents: each spends only their own UTxOs, so nobody contends.
IntentHandle<Pool.State> d0 = pool.donateIntent(u0, ada(5), later);
IntentHandle<Pool.State> d1 = pool.donateIntent(u1, ada(6), later);
pool.buyIntent(u2, ada(20), ada(20), later);    // accepts a price up to 20 ADA, pays 20

d1.cancel(u1);                                  // one user changes their mind

var result = pool.batch(batcher, 8);            // anyone can batch
System.out.println(result.applied().size() + " applied, skipped " + result.skipped());
```

`pool.pendingIntents()` lists what is waiting; `pool.intent(id)` reconnects to one. An `IntentHandle` has
`isPending()`, `data()` and `cancel(owner)`.

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Pool)"
const d1 = (await p.intent(u1, 'donate', {}, { lovelace: 6n * ADA })).intent;
await p.intent(u3, 'buy', { maxPrice: 20n * ADA }, { lovelace: 20n * ADA });
assert.equal((await p.pendingIntents()).length, 4);
await p.cancelIntent(u1, d1);                   // only its owner withdraws it
const b = await p.batch(batcher);               // up to 8 intents; pays only the fee
console.log(b.applied, b.skipped);
```

`intent(wallet, name, args, pay, { deadline })` takes the deadline in milliseconds (default: 30 minutes from now).
With a generated client, these methods are on `pool.contract.at(id)`.

###### Intents

An intent is a UTxO at the contract's address holding:
- **The intent token** `(policy, 0x49 ‖ blake2b_224(seedTxId ‖ I2OSP(seedIndex, 2)))`: 29 bytes starting with `0x49`.
  Instance tokens are 32 bytes and object tokens start with `0x4F`, so no kind can pass for another.
- **An inline datum** `Intent(instance, owner, refund, deadline, received, call)`: the instance it targets, the owner,
  the full refund address, the deadline, the payment for the action and the action's arguments.
- **At least `received + 2 ADA`.** The surplus pays for the refund output and comes back to the owner.

Creating an intent does not reference the instance: the instance moves with every batch, and a reference would make
intent creation contend again. An intent for an instance that does not exist can never be batched; its owner cancels
it.

###### The batch

The batcher's transaction spends the instance with a `Batch(validFrom, validTo)` redeemer and the intents with
`InBatch`. The validator walks the transaction's inputs in ledger order (by transaction id, then index) and, for every
intent of this instance:

1. builds `Ctx(owner, received, balance, validFrom, validTo)`;
2. runs your method on the current state, on chain;
3. updates the balance (`+ received − payouts`), which must never go negative;
4. requires `validTo ≤ deadline`;
5. requires the intent spent with `InBatch` and its token burned;
6. requires the **refund** (`L − received`) at exactly the intent's refund address, tagged `IntentRefund(ref)`;
7. requires each **payout** tagged with that intent's own input, so two steps can never share one output.

At least one intent must be applied. The continuing output holds the final state and exactly the final balance plus
the deposit, with all the usual single-UTxO checks.

###### Cancel and expiry

- **Cancel:** the owner signs a `CancelIntent`, the token is burned and the funds go back. Only the owner can cancel.
- **Expiry:** an intent past its deadline can no longer be batched. The batcher skips it and reports it in
  `skipped`; its owner cancels it to get the funds back.

###### The batcher

Batching is permissionless: any account can run `batch`. The runtime's batcher:
1. scans the contract's address for `0x49` tokens of this instance;
2. opens a validity window first, then drops intents whose deadline falls before its end;
3. folds the intents on the JVM with the validator's exact rules, skipping (and reporting) any whose action throws or
   that would make the balance negative;
4. builds the transaction (refunds and payouts topped up to the ledger minimum), checks it after balancing, submits;
5. if the transaction cannot be built, for example because it is over budget, retries with half as many intents.

The batcher pays the fee and signs nothing on the owners' behalf. There is no batcher fee yet.

| Invariant | Meaning (ADR-0004 D4) |
|---|---|
| I22 | An intent token is minted only with its owner's signature, under a 32-byte instance id, with `received ≥ 0` (0 unless payable) and at least `received + 2 ADA` |
| I23 | An intent is consumed only by its owner's cancel or by a batch of its own instance |
| I24 | A batch applies, in ledger order, every intent of its instance among the inputs; refunds go to the exact refund address, payouts are tagged per intent, the balance never goes negative |
| I25 | Every applied intent's token is burned, and the instance continues exactly |

##### Limits

- **About 8 intents per batch.** The cost grows a little faster than linearly, and memory runs out first:

  | Batch | CPU | Memory |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 intent (all scripts) | 0.46 B | 1.6 M |
  | 5 | 1.9 B | 6.2 M |
  | 10 | 5.0 B | 15.5 M |

  With a 14 to 16.5 M memory limit per transaction, about 8 donations fit (`Batcher.DEFAULT_MAX = 8`). The JS
  `batch` also defaults to 8.
- **Not combined yet** (compile errors): MerkleMap state; native assets (`Funds`, sends, mint); `@Params` or `@Reads`
  in the batched action; `@Quorum`, `@AuthorizedBy` or events; `@Invariant`.
- **Two transactions per operation.**

##### Ordering, MEV and standing authorisations

> **An intent runs against whatever state the batch finds:** 
The batcher chooses which intents to include and, through the validity range, when they run. It cannot reorder the
intents it includes, but anyone can grind transaction ids to place their own. So an order-sensitive action must take
a bound as an argument and check it: `buy(maxPrice)` refuses if the price has risen above what the buyer accepts.

- An intent authorises its action until its deadline, against any future state. Keep deadlines short, and gate
  anything admin-like on more than `ctx.caller()`.
- Anyone can deploy another instance of the same contract. Clients pin the instance id, and intents name it.

- ADR-0004: [Architecture decisions](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/)

### Native assets, mints and sends

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/

By default a JOUST state UTxO holds lovelace and its own thread token, and an action pays lovelace to key hashes. That
covers counters and vaults, but not a DEX that holds a token reserve, a marketplace that holds the NFT it sells, or a
treasury that pays a royalty script with a datum. This page covers the four pieces that make those possible
(ADR-0007):

- **`Funds`**: the native assets a method sees (received, held) and the contract's own policy id;
- **`accepted`**: exactly which assets a method takes in;
- **`mint`**: user tokens minted or burned by the contract's own policy;
- **`Send`**: an output to any address, key or script, with any datum and any value.

A *native asset* (or token) on Cardano is identified by a *policy id* (the hash of the script that controls minting)
and a token name; a *value* is lovelace plus any number of these. See the [glossary](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/glossary/).

##### A constant-product AMM

The `dex` example is one ADA/token pool. Its reserves are what its UTxO holds, so state and funds can never drift
apart: lovelace above the deposit (`ctx.balance()`) and the token (`funds.held()`).

```java title="examples/dex/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/dex/Dex.java"
@StateContract(maxDatumBytes = 256, assetSlots = 2)
public class Dex {

    public record Pool(byte[] admin, byte[] tokenPolicy, byte[] tokenName, byte[] lpName, BigInteger lpSupply) {}

    public record Moved(Pool state, JulcList<Payout> payouts, JulcList<Send> sends, Value mint, Value accepted) {}

    /** Opens an empty pool for {@code (tokenPolicy, tokenName)}; its LP token is named after the pool id. */
    @Init
    public static Pool open(byte[] tokenPolicy, byte[] tokenName, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
        Require.that(tokenPolicy.length == 28, "token policy must be 28 bytes");
        return new Pool(ctx.caller(), tokenPolicy, tokenName, CryptoLib.blake2b_224(funds.self()), BigInteger.ZERO);
    }

    /** Adds {@code ctx.received()} lovelace and {@code tokenIn} tokens; mints LP tokens to the caller. */
    @Action @Payable
    public static Moved addLiquidity(Pool p, BigInteger tokenIn, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
        BigInteger adaIn = ctx.received();
        Require.that(adaIn.signum() > 0 && tokenIn.signum() > 0, "add both ADA and tokens");
        BigInteger reserveAda = ctx.balance();
        BigInteger reserveToken = Assets.quantity(funds.held(), p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName());
        BigInteger minted = p.lpSupply().signum() == 0 ? adaIn
                : adaIn.multiply(p.lpSupply()).divide(reserveAda).min(tokenIn.multiply(p.lpSupply()).divide(reserveToken));
        Require.that(minted.signum() > 0, "deposit too small");
        Value lp = Assets.of(funds.policy(), p.lpName(), minted);
        Pool next = new Pool(p.admin(), p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName(), p.lpName(), p.lpSupply().add(minted));
        return new Moved(next, Payouts.none(), Sends.of(wallet(ctx.caller()), lp, new OutputDatum.NoOutputDatum()), lp,
                Assets.of(p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName(), tokenIn));
    }

    /** The enterprise address of a key: never the caller's fee-paying base address (ADR-0007 D6). */
    static Address wallet(byte[] key) {
        return new Address(new Credential.PubKeyCredential(new PubKeyHash(key)), Optional.empty());
    }
}
```

`addLiquidity` takes ADA and tokens in (`accepted`), mints LP tokens under the contract's own policy (`mint`), and
sends them to the provider (`sends`), all in one result record. The [DEX tutorial](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/dex-assets/) walks
through the whole contract.

##### `Funds`

Declare `Funds` as the last parameter, after `Ctx` if there is one. The client fills it in; the validator checks
every field.

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `policy` | This contract's policy id (its script hash). Name your own tokens with it |
| `self` | The token name of what the method acts on: the instance id, or the object id in an owned method |
| `received` | Native assets the caller adds in this call. No lovelace entry (that is `ctx.received()`); positive amounts; empty unless the method is `@Payable` |
| `held` | Native assets the UTxO holds before the call, without lovelace and without its own thread token; empty when creating |
| `deposits` | Deposits from other contracts in this transaction, for a `@Receives` action only (see [Deposits](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/)) |

Only `received` travels in the redeemer. The validator computes `policy`, `self` and `held` from the transaction.

##### The result record

A method that does more than return the state returns a record whose components are recognised by name and type:

| Component | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `state` | the state or owned record | The next state. Required for actions and inits; forbidden for destroys |
| `payouts` | `JulcList<Payout>` | Lovelace to key hashes, tagged with this input (cheapest) |
| `sends` | `JulcList<Send>` | Outputs to any address with any datum and value |
| `mint` | `Value` | User tokens this contract's policy mints (positive) or burns (negative) |
| `accepted` | `Value` | Exactly the native assets this call takes in |

`deposits` and `events` are covered in [Deposits](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/) and
[Params, invariants and events](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/). A destroy may still return a bare
`JulcList<Payout>`. `@Init` and `@OwnedInit` may take `Funds` and return `accepted`, but cannot mint, send or pay out.

##### `Assets`: values in contract code

`Value` arithmetic goes through
[`Assets`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Assets.java).
It has the same API on the JVM and on chain: the JVM body works on maps, the on-chain body
(`julc-state-api/src/onchain/java`) uses the Plutus V3 native value builtins. Every value it returns is canonical (sorted,
no zero quantities), as the ledger requires.

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `Assets.none()` | The empty value |
| `Assets.of(policy, name, quantity)` | `quantity` of one asset (empty if zero) |
| `Assets.lovelace(quantity)` | Lovelace as a value |
| `Assets.add(a, b)`, `Assets.subtract(a, b)` | Entry-wise sum or difference (negative entries stay) |
| `Assets.quantity(v, policy, name)` | One asset's quantity, zero if absent |
| `Assets.lovelaceOf(v)` | The lovelace in `v` |
| `Assets.withoutLovelace(v)` | `v` without its lovelace |
| `Assets.isEmpty(v)` | Whether `v` holds nothing |
| `Assets.covers(a, b)` | Whether `a` holds at least `b` of every entry (both non-negative) |

The JVM also has `Assets.check(v, what)`, which the runtime and the harness run on every value a method returns, so a
JVM test never passes on a value the chain would reject.

##### `accepted`: no unwanted tokens

A `@Payable` method with `Funds` must return `accepted`, and the validator requires `funds.received == accepted`
exactly. This stops a caller pushing junk tokens into your UTxO, which could make it unspendable through its min-ADA or
the size of its value. A method that takes anything says so by returning `funds.received()`.

```java title="examples/market/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/market/Market.java"
/** Offers one NFT at {@code price}: the listing takes the NFT in. */
@OwnedInit @Payable
public static Listed offer(@Shared Config c, byte[] nftPolicy, byte[] nftName, BigInteger price, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
    Require.that(!c.paused(), "the market is paused");
    Require.that(price.compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(2_000_000)) >= 0, "price below 2 ADA");
    Require.that(ctx.received().signum() == 0, "a listing takes the NFT, not ADA");
    return new Listed(new Listing(ctx.caller(), nftPolicy, nftName, price), Assets.of(nftPolicy, nftName, BigInteger.ONE));
}
```

`@Payable` governs both `ctx.received()` and `funds.received()`: without it, both must be zero.

##### `mint`: tokens of your own policy

The contract's policy mints its lifecycle tokens (instances, objects, intents) and can also mint **user tokens**. The
token name decides which is which:

- **reserved:** 32 bytes (an instance), or 29 bytes starting with `0x4F` (an object) or `0x49` (an intent);
- **user:** any other name, 0 to 31 bytes.

Return `mint` from an action: positive amounts mint, negative burn. The dex burns LP tokens on the way out:

```java title="examples/dex/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/dex/Dex.java"
/** Burns {@code lp} LP tokens; pays the provider its share of both reserves. */
@Action @Payable
public static Moved removeLiquidity(Pool p, BigInteger lp, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
    Require.that(lp.signum() > 0 && lp.compareTo(p.lpSupply()) <= 0, "bad LP amount");
    BigInteger adaOut = ctx.balance().multiply(lp).divide(p.lpSupply());
    BigInteger tokenOut = Assets.quantity(funds.held(), p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName()).multiply(lp).divide(p.lpSupply());
    Value lpTokens = Assets.of(funds.policy(), p.lpName(), lp);
    Pool next = new Pool(p.admin(), p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName(), p.lpName(), p.lpSupply().subtract(lp));
    return new Moved(next, Payouts.of(ctx.caller(), adaOut),
            Sends.of(wallet(ctx.caller()), Assets.of(p.tokenPolicy(), p.tokenName(), tokenOut), new OutputDatum.NoOutputDatum()),
            Assets.subtract(Assets.none(), lpTokens), lpTokens);
}
```

The caller sends the LP tokens in (`accepted = lpTokens`) and the method burns them (`mint = −lpTokens`).

**How minting is checked.** The transaction's mint redeemer for the policy is `ByAction(by)`, naming the state input
whose method mints. The minting policy checks that the input at `by` sits at the state address, holds a reserved token
and is spent with a method that can mint. That method's validator checks the mint redeemer names its own input, that
every declared entry has a user-kind name under the own policy and a non-zero amount, and that the whole mint under the
policy equals the declared mint exactly (I28). One transition per transaction owns the policy's mint. A method whose
`mint` is empty needs no mint redeemer, and requires that nothing is minted under the policy.

Name per-instance tokens after the instance, as the dex does with `blake2b_224(funds.self())`: one name per pool, so
one pool's LP tokens can never redeem another's reserves.

##### `Send`: outputs to anyone

`Send(Address to, Value value, OutputDatum datum)` asks for an output at any address, key or script, with any datum
(none, a hash or inline) and at least `value`. Build lists with `Sends.none()`, `Sends.of(to, value, datum)` and
`Sends.add(sends, to, value, datum)`, and datums with `Datum.inline(data)` or `Datum.none()`. `Payout` stays the cheap
form for lovelace to a key.

The `market`'s `buy` pays the seller with a payout, delivers the NFT with a send, and pays a royalty to a script
address with an inline datum:

```java title="examples/market/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/market/Market.java"
JulcList<Send> nft = Sends.of(wallet(ctx.caller()), funds.held(), new OutputDatum.NoOutputDatum());
JulcList<Send> sends = royalty.signum() > 0
        ? Sends.add(nft, c.royaltyVault(), Assets.lovelace(royalty), Datum.inline(royalty(l)))
        : nft;

/** The royalty datum, {@code Royalty(nftPolicy, nftName, price)} as data (built so it also runs on the JVM). */
public static PlutusData royalty(Listing l) {
    return Builtins.constrData(0, Builtins.mkCons(Builtins.bData(l.nftPolicy()), Builtins.mkCons(Builtins.bData(l.nftName()),
            Builtins.mkCons(Builtins.iData(l.price()), Builtins.mkNilData()))));
}
```

> **Build datums with Builtins, not casts:** 
`(PlutusData) (Object) record` works on chain but throws on the JVM. Build a datum with `Builtins.constrData`,
`bData`, `iData` and `mkCons`, which run on both: a record `R(a, b)` is
`constrData(0, mkCons(a, mkCons(b, mkNilData())))`.

###### The output verifier

A send cannot be tagged with the sender's input, because its datum belongs to the recipient. Without a tag, one output
could satisfy two obligations: two instances owing Bob 10 ADA with the same datum would both accept a single 10 ADA
output (*double satisfaction*). So sends are claimed in a transaction-wide registry, kept by a shared withdraw-zero
script,
[`OutputVerifier`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-verifier/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/verifier/OutputVerifier.java)
in `julc-state-verifier` (ADR-0007 D5):

- **The verifier** runs as a withdrawal; its redeemer lists `OutputClaim(output, by)` with output indices strictly
  increasing and in range. So each output is claimed at most once.
- **Each transition with sends** reads the registry from the transaction's redeemers, takes its own claims (those with
  `by` equal to its input), and requires exactly one claim per send, in order.
- **A claimed output must** sit at `send.to`, carry exactly `send.datum`, have no reference script and hold at least
  `send.value`. It may **not** sit at the payment credential of any input the transaction spends, so a continuing
  output (of this or any script) never passes as a send. And its inline datum may not equal any input's reference or
  `IntentRefund` of one, so it can never also count as a JOUST payout or refund.

The runtime publishes and registers the verifier once per network, adds the withdrawal with the claims, and re-checks
every send after balancing.

##### What the validator checks: the exact value

A contract is *asset-aware* if any method takes `Funds` or returns `sends` or `mint`. Every transition of an
asset-aware contract checks, over full multi-asset values (I26):

```
out.value == in.value + lovelace(ctx.received) + accepted + mint − Σ payouts − Σ sends.value
```

For a creation, the input is the deposit plus the minted thread token. For a destroy there is no output: everything
except the burned token must be allocated. Contracts that are not asset-aware keep the cheaper lovelace-only check.

| Invariant | Meaning (ADR-0007 §3) |
|---|---|
| I26 | The state output's value is exactly the input plus what was received and minted, less what was paid and sent; a destroy allocates everything |
| I27 | Only reserved-kind names are lifecycle tokens; lifecycle redeemers never mint or burn user tokens |
| I28 | User tokens are minted or burned only through `ByAction(by)`, by the transition at `by`, exactly as declared |
| I29 | Every send has its own claim in the output registry; each output is claimed at most once |
| I30 | A claimed output is never at a spent input's payment credential and never carries a JOUST payout or refund tag |
| I31 | `funds.received` equals `accepted`; no reserved-kind token of the own policy is received, sent or minted |

##### Calling asset-aware methods

**Java:**

```java title="examples/dex/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/dex/DexDevnetTest.java"
var dex = DexClient.deploy(runtime, admin, policy, name);
Value tokens = Assets.of(policy, name, BigInteger.valueOf(100_000));
// args..., then the lovelace paid, then the native assets offered (funds.received)
dex.addLiquidity(lp, BigInteger.valueOf(100_000), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(100)), tokens);
dex.swapAdaForToken(trader, expect, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), Assets.none());
```

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Dex)"
const d = dex.at((await dex.deploy(admin, { tokenPolicy: policy, tokenName: name })).instance);
// pay: lovelace, and assets as [[policy, [[name, quantity]]]]
await d.call(lp, 'addLiquidity', { tokenIn: 100_000n }, { lovelace: 100n * ADA, assets: [[policy, [[name, 100_000n]]]] });
await d.call(trader, 'swapAdaForToken', { minOut: expect }, { lovelace: 10n * ADA });
```

##### Rules and limits

- `Funds` is the last parameter. `@Payable` with `Funds` requires `accepted` in the result; `accepted` without
  `@Payable` and `Funds` is an error.
- `@StateContract(assetSlots)` (default 4 for asset-aware contracts, 0 otherwise; 0 to 64) sizes the min-ADA deposit
  for the assets a state UTxO may hold, about 80 bytes each. Set it to what you expect: the dex uses 2.
- One minting transition per transaction per policy, and no user minting at init.
- An asset-aware contract cannot have `@Batched` actions: intents carry only lovelace.
- The 32-byte CIP-68 shape (label plus a 28-byte hash) is a reserved name under your own policy; such tokens need their
  own minting policy.
- Asset-aware contracts pay for full-value accounting, and a transaction with sends runs the output verifier too. The
  dex validator is 12,008 bytes plus the 703-byte output verifier, shared (examples/README.md).

##### Pitfalls

> **Send to the enterprise address, not the fee payer's:** 
The runtime's transaction builder (QuickTx, from cardano-client-lib) may take the fee from an output at the fee
payer's address. A send there could be eaten by the fee, so the runtime refuses it before submitting with an error that says
so. Send to the recipient's enterprise address (payment key, no stake part), as the examples' `wallet(key)` helpers
do. Payouts go to enterprise addresses already.

- **Do not take a `Value` method argument.** JuLC decodes a redeemer field typed `Value` as a constructor, and it
  fails. Take quantities as `BigInteger` and names as `byte[]` (as the dex does), or `PlutusData` if you must. Values a
  method builds (`Send.value`, `mint`) are fine.
- **A `Value` cannot be a loop accumulator** in JuLC. Use recursion.
- **Datums must be canonical.** cardano-client-lib writes inline datums in canonical CBOR, map keys sorted. A datum or
  memo with a map must already be in key order (`SortedMaps`), or the on-chain equality fails.
- **A send with no datum to a script address locks its funds.** The runtime warns.
- **Off-chain code of your own:** a QuickTx `ScriptTx` balances only lovelace from the fee payer. The JOUST runtime
  collects the UTxOs holding the offered assets for you; code that builds its own transactions must do the same.
- **Debugging a refusal:** build with `-Pjoust.traces` (`-Ajoust.traces=true`) so every failing check traces its
  name.

- [State API: `Assets`, `Funds`, `Send`, `Sends`, `Datum`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/state-api/)
- ADR-0007: [Architecture decisions](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/)

### Reads and composition

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/

Contracts work together. A shop prices its goods from an oracle; a market pays into a fee pot; a counter migrates to
its next version. On Cardano this happens at the transaction level: one transaction spends several scripts' UTxOs,
and each script checks its own part. JOUST gives you two tools for it (ADR-0011):

- **`@Reads`**: a method parameter that reads another JOUST contract's state, through a reference input, checked on
  chain;
- **`Compose`**: one transaction built from several ordinary client calls, all or nothing.

A *reference input* is a UTxO a transaction reads without spending it: its datum is visible to the scripts, and its
own validator does not run.

##### `@Reads`: another contract's state

The `oracle` example has a price feed and a shop that sells at the feed's price:

```java title="examples/oracle/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/Oracle.java"
/** A price feed (ADR-0011): the publisher posts a price with the time it was set (the call's validity start). */
@StateContract
public class Oracle {

    public record State(byte[] publisher, BigInteger price, BigInteger updatedAt) {}

    @Action @SignedBy("publisher")
    public static State post(State s, BigInteger price, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(price.signum() > 0, "price must be positive");
        return new State(s.publisher(), price, ctx.validFrom());
    }
}
```

```java title="examples/oracle/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/Shop.java"
@StateContract
public class Shop {

    @Params
    public record Config(ForeignInstance oracle, BigInteger maxAgeMs) {}

    public record State(byte[] owner, BigInteger sold) {}

    /** Buys {@code qty} credits, paying {@code qty * price} at a price no older than {@code maxAgeMs}. */
    @Action @Payable
    public static State buy(State s, Config cfg, @Reads("params.oracle") Oracle.State price, BigInteger qty, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(qty.signum() > 0, "buy at least one credit");
        Require.that(ctx.validFrom().subtract(price.updatedAt()).compareTo(cfg.maxAgeMs()) <= 0, "stale price");
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(qty.multiply(price.price())) == 0, "pay exactly qty * price");
        return new State(s.owner(), s.sold().add(qty));
    }
}
```

###### The rules

- **The source is pinned in params.** `@Reads("params.x")` names a `ForeignInstance(byte[] policy, byte[] instance)`
  field of the contract's `@Params` record. Params are applied to the script at deploy, so the trusted contract and
  instance are fixed then. A state field could be changed by an action; a param cannot. See
  [Params, invariants and events](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/).
- **The parameter's type is the other contract's state record**, here `Oracle.State`.
- **Placement:** the `@Params` record parameter comes right after the state, and `@Reads` parameters right after it.
- **Not yet:** `@Reads` in a creation, in a move or an `@Admits` action, or in a `@Batched` action; and foreign state
  holding MerkleMaps (a reference input has no proof path for map reads).

###### What the validator checks

For each `@Reads` parameter, the reference input must:
- hold exactly one token of `policy`, named `instance`, which is 32 bytes (an instance, not an object or intent);
- sit at an address whose payment credential is the script `policy`;
- carry an inline datum, decoded as the foreign state after a shape check (constructor 0 and the record's number of
  fields), which refuses another version's layout.

This is invariant I39. The runtime finds the reference input and adds it for you: the call looks like any other.

> **Freshness is your rule:** 
A reference input's validator does not run, so an old oracle state stays readable. Give the source state a timestamp
and check it, as `Shop.buy` checks `updatedAt` against `ctx.validFrom()` and `maxAgeMs`. See [Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/).

###### Deploying a reader

The reader's params name the source's policy and instance, so deploy the source first:

**Java:**

```java title="examples/oracle/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/OracleDevnetTest.java"
var oracle = OracleClient.deploy(runtime, publisher, BigInteger.valueOf(3_000_000));
var cfg = new Shop.Config(new ForeignInstance(HexUtil.decodeHexString(oracle.instance().contract().policyId()),
        HexUtil.decodeHexString(oracle.instanceId())), BigInteger.valueOf(600_000));
var shop = ShopClient.deploy(runtime, cfg, shopOwner);

shop.buy(buyer, BigInteger.TWO, BigInteger.valueOf(6_000_000));   // reads the oracle by reference
```

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Oracle and Shop)"
const oracle = await contract('Oracle', publisher);
const o = oracle.at((await oracle.deploy(publisher, { price: 3_000_000n })).instance);
// The shop's script carries its oracle (@Params); buy reads the oracle's state as a reference input (@Reads).
const shop = await contract('Shop', shopOwner, { oracle: { policy: oracle.deployment.policy, instance: o.id }, maxAgeMs: 600_000n });
const sh = shop.at((await shop.deploy(shopOwner, {})).instance);
await sh.call(buyer, 'buy', { qty: 2n }, { lovelace: 6_000_000n });
```

`contract(name, payer, params)` is the test's helper around `rt.ensureDeployment(title, wallet, params)`. With
`joust deploy`, params go in `joust.config.json` under `"params"`; see [joust.config.json](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/config/).

If the source contract later migrates to a new version, a reader whose params pin it must migrate too.

##### `Compose`: several calls, one transaction

`Compose` runs ordinary client calls inside one composition and submits them as one transaction: every call's checks
pass, or nothing happens. On chain nothing changes: each validator checks only its own transition, so composing adds
no new trust.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/oracle/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/oracle/OracleDevnetTest.java"
// A second oracle posts while the shop sells: one transaction.
String tx = Compose.of(runtime, buyer)
        .add(() -> shop.buy(buyer, BigInteger.ONE, BigInteger.valueOf(3_000_000)))
        .add(() -> oracle2.post(publisher2, BigInteger.valueOf(5_000_000)))
        .submit();
```

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Compose.of(runtime, payer)` | Starts a composition; `payer` pays the fee |
| `add(Runnable call)` | Adds any client call: an action, a destroy, a deploy, an owned call |
| `allowSharedSigners()` | Lets one key's signature count for several calls (refused by default) |
| `submit()` | Builds, checks, submits and confirms; returns the transaction hash |
| `prepare()` | Builds and checks it for a wallet to sign, without signing ([Wallets](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/)) |

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Fees)"
await rt.compose(buyer, [
  { contract: stall, method: 'sell', instance: stallId, args: { price: 10n * ADA }, pay: { lovelace: 10n * ADA } },
  { contract: pot, method: 'collect', instance: potId, args: {} },
]);
```

Each step is `{ contract, method, args, pay, instance, object, into, cosigners }`, where `contract` is a
`JoustContract` (a generated client's `.contract`). `rt.compose(wallet, steps)` is the runtime's shortcut for
`runComposed({ service, chain, api, steps })`: the engine prepares the transaction, the page verifies each call and the
whole, and one wallet signature covers it. See [JavaScript clients](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/).

###### How it builds the transaction

The calls run in *capture mode*: instead of submitting, each client call writes its inputs, outputs, redeemers and
signers into one shared transaction.

1. **Windows first.** A first pass learns every call's validity window. The second pass runs every call in their
   intersection, so each method's `Ctx` equals the final bounds. A call whose result depends on time is never reused
   with another window.
2. **Shared verifiers.** Each verifier withdrawal (map, output) appears once, with every call's claims merged, and the
   output registry is rebuilt from the final output order.
3. **Checks after balancing.** Every state output, payout and send is verified after balancing, before submission.

**Refused before building:**
- the same UTxO spent by two calls (for example two calls on one instance);
- two calls minting under one policy (the ledger allows one mint redeemer per policy);
- an empty common window;
- a key that signs for more than one call, unless you call `allowSharedSigners()`.

> **Why shared signers are opt-in:** 
A signature on a transaction counts for every `@SignedBy` and `@Quorum` check in it. If Ann signs for her own call,
her signature also satisfies a second call's `@SignedBy("ann")`. That is how the ledger works, so `Compose` asks you
to say you mean it.

A composition can be nested: a call that composes internally (such as an owned move's `<move>Admitted`) joins the
outer transaction. Owned-object moves and [deposits](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/) run only inside a composition.

##### Migration is a composition

Moving an instance to a new contract version is two calls in one transaction: the old version's `@Destroy
@MigrateTo(...)` and the new version's `@Migrate` creation. Each side names the other, and the funds move only into
the named successor (I41).

**Java:**

```java title="examples/upgrade (CounterV1 to CounterV2)"
var adopted = new CounterV2Client[1];
String tx = Compose.of(runtime, admin)
        .add(() -> v1.upgrade(admin))
        .add(() -> adopted[0] = CounterV2Client.adopt(runtime, cfg, admin, v1.instance()))
        .submit();
```

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Upgrade)"
const steps = [
  { contract: v1, method: 'upgrade', instance: old.id },
  { contract: v2, method: 'adopt', instance: old.id },
];
const r = await rt.compose(admin, steps);
const adopted = r.report.calls[1].created;    // the new instance's id
```

Migration is not supported yet for contracts with MerkleMaps, owned objects or native assets.
[Upgrades and migration](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/upgrades/) covers the design.

##### Limits

- **One transaction's limits apply:** 16 KB of transaction, and the CPU and memory budget (10,000M CPU, 14M memory on
  mainnet). Each contract adds its reference script's size fee and its execution.
- **One mint per policy per transaction,** so two calls that both mint under one contract cannot compose.
- **Foreign validators** that ignore JOUST's payout tags and output registry can still be double-satisfied by a JOUST
  output. `Compose` with them needs care (ADR-0007 D5).

- [Java runtime API: `Compose`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/java-runtime-api/), [@julclang/joust-runtime](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/joust-runtime/),
  [Annotations: `@Reads`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/)
- ADR-0011: [Architecture decisions](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/)

### Deposits

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/

A *deposit* moves value from one JOUST contract's call into another contract's instance, in the same transaction: a
market stall sends 5% of each sale into a fee pot, a vault forwards interest into a treasury. A
[`Send`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/) cannot do this, because a send may never land on a spent script's continuing
output (invariant I30), and the receiving instance is exactly that. Deposits are the safe path (ADR-0011 D3).

Both sides take part:
- **the depositor** returns `deposits`, and its validator subtracts them from its own value;
- **the receiver** declares an action `@Receives`, sees the deposits in `funds.deposits()`, and decides what to credit.

The two calls run in one [composed](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/) transaction.

##### The `fees` example

A `Stall` sells for a price and deposits a fee into a `Pot` instance fixed in its params:

```java title="examples/fees/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/fees/Stall.java"
@StateContract
public class Stall {

    @Params
    public record Config(ForeignInstance pot, BigInteger feeBps) {}

    public record State(byte[] owner, BigInteger sales) {}

    public record Sale(State state, JulcList<Deposit> deposits) {}

    /** Sells for {@code price} lovelace: the stall keeps the price less the fee, the pot gets the fee. */
    @Action
    @Payable
    public static Sale sell(State s, Config cfg, BigInteger price, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(ctx.received().compareTo(price) == 0 && price.compareTo(BigInteger.valueOf(2_000_000)) >= 0,
                "pay exactly the price, at least 2 ADA");
        BigInteger fee = price.multiply(cfg.feeBps()).divide(BigInteger.valueOf(10_000));
        Require.that(fee.compareTo(BigInteger.ONE) >= 0, "the fee rounds to zero");
        return new Sale(new State(s.owner(), s.sales().add(price.subtract(fee))),
                Deposits.of(cfg.pot(), Assets.lovelace(fee), Builtins.bData(ctx.caller())));
    }
}
```

```java title="examples/fees/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/fees/Pot.java"
@StateContract
public class Pot {

    public record State(byte[] owner, BigInteger collected, BigInteger deposits) {}

    /** Takes in every deposit made to this pot in the transaction; anyone may call it, but only with deposits. */
    @Action
    @Receives
    public static State collect(State s, Ctx ctx, Funds funds) {
        BigInteger got = Deposits.lovelace(funds.deposits());
        Require.that(got.signum() > 0, "nothing deposited");
        return new State(s.owner(), s.collected().add(got),
                s.deposits().add(BigInteger.valueOf(funds.deposits().size())));
    }

    /** Hands the pot to a new owner. Not @Receives: a deposit claimed on its output makes it fail (I40). */
    @Action
    @SignedBy("owner")
    public static State handOver(State s, byte[] newOwner) {
        return new State(newOwner, s.collected(), s.deposits());
    }
}
```

##### The API

| Type or method | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Deposit(policy, instance, value, memo)` | A payment of `value` into instance `instance` of contract `policy`. `memo` is any data the receiver may read: a beneficiary, an order id |
| `Deposits.none()` | No deposits |
| `Deposits.of(target, value, memo)` | One deposit into a `ForeignInstance` |
| `Deposits.add(deposits, target, value, memo)` | One more |
| `deposits` result component | `JulcList<Deposit>`, returned by the depositor's method |
| `@Receives` | On an `@Action` or `@OwnedAction` that takes deposits. Needs a `Funds` parameter; cannot be `@Batched` |
| `funds.deposits()` | `JulcList<DepositClaim>`: the deposits claimed on this call's continuing output, in registry order |
| `DepositClaim(output, by, value, memo)` | One deposit: the output index it lands on, the input that made it, its value and memo |
| `Deposits.lovelace(claims)` | The total lovelace of a receiver's deposits |

##### Calling it

A deposit needs its receiver in the same transaction, so a lone `sell` is refused before anything is built.

**Java:**

```java title="examples/fees/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/fees/FeesDevnetTest.java"
var pot = PotClient.deploy(runtime, owner);
var config = new Stall.Config(new ForeignInstance(HexUtil.decodeHexString(PotClient.contract(runtime).policyId()),
        HexUtil.decodeHexString(pot.instanceId())), BigInteger.valueOf(500));
var stall = StallClient.deploy(runtime, config, owner);

// A deposit needs its receiver in the same transaction.
assertThrows(JoustException.class, () -> stall.sell(buyer, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN)));

Compose.of(runtime, buyer).allowSharedSigners()
        .add(() -> stall.sell(buyer, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN)))
        .add(() -> pot.collect(buyer))
        .submit();
```

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (Fees)"
const pot = await contract('Pot', owner);
const potId = (await pot.deploy(owner, {})).instance;
const stall = await contract('Stall', owner, { pot: { policy: pot.deployment.policy, instance: potId }, feeBps: 500n });
const stallId = (await stall.deploy(owner, {})).instance;

await rt.compose(buyer, [
  { contract: stall, method: 'sell', instance: stallId, args: { price: 10n * ADA }, pay: { lovelace: 10n * ADA } },
  { contract: pot, method: 'collect', instance: potId, args: {} },
]);
```

The receiver may come first or last in the composition. The runtime runs the calls in two passes: in the first, a
receiver sees the deposits made so far, and if one placed before its depositors refuses, the pass is rerun with the
deposits found; in the second, every receiver sees every deposit.

##### What the validators check

Deposit claims sit in the same output registry as sends, kept by the shared
[output verifier](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/#the-output-verifier), in their own list.

**The output verifier** requires each deposit claim's value to be canonical, non-empty, strictly positive and free of
reserved-kind token names under any policy; each `by` to be an input of the transaction; output indices in range and
non-decreasing (several claims may name one output).

**The depositor's validator:**
- subtracts the deposits in its value equation, like sends;
- requires each deposit to target a distinct instance with a 32-byte id, whose token an input holds, so the
  receiver's validator runs;
- requires one claim by its own input on the target's unique continuing output, with the same value and memo;
- requires the number of claims naming its input to equal its number of deposits, so no claim can be attributed to it
  falsely.

**The receiver's validator:**
- adds every claim on its continuing output to its value equation, each counted once:
  `out = in + received + accepted + Σ deposits + mint − payouts − sends`;
- gives the method exactly that list as `funds.deposits()`.

**Every other continuing transition** of a contract with `@Receives` refuses a deposit claim on its output. That is
why `Pot.handOver` fails if anyone tries to deposit through it.

| Invariant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| I40 | A deposit is counted only by its receiver, which runs in the same transaction and counts each claimed deposit exactly once in its value equation |

##### Rules

> **The target must be a @Receives contract, fixed in params:** 
A depositor checks that the target is spent and that its claim exists; it cannot check what the target's validator
does. A contract generated before deposits existed, a plain contract or a foreign script could take the value without
counting it. So choose the target when you write the depositor, and fix it in `@Params` (a `ForeignInstance`), never in
an argument a caller supplies.

- A contract may not deposit into itself.
- **`by` is not authenticated** beyond naming an input of the transaction. A receiver that credits by depositor must
  check the input at `by` itself. A memo is whatever the depositor's method wrote: trust it as far as you trust the
  depositor contract.
- **Memos must be canonical.** A memo with a map built out of key order would be reordered by serialisation and fail
  the depositor's check; the runtime refuses it. Keep maps sorted (`SortedMaps`).
- **Reserved names cannot be deposited,** under any policy: an NFT named by a 32-byte hash cannot be a deposit. Send it
  instead.
- `@Receives` needs `Funds` and goes on an action or owned action, never a creation or destroy.

##### Cost

From ADR-0011 §7, for one sale: the stall 280.7M CPU and 895k memory, the pot 209.6M and 669k, the output verifier
41.7M and 135k. Pot is 8.6 KB and Stall 9.4 KB.

- [State API: `Deposit`, `Deposits`, `DepositClaim`, `Funds`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/state-api/),
  [Annotations: `@Receives`](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/)
- ADR-0011 D3 and §7: [Architecture decisions](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/)
