### Staking and governance

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/staking-and-governance/

A Plutus V3 script can run for six *purposes*: minting, spending, rewarding (withdrawals), certifying (stake and DRep
certificates), voting and proposing. Every JOUST contract uses the first two. This page covers the other four, and
`stakeSelf`, which lets the funds a contract locks earn staking rewards (ADR-0010).

By default a state UTxO sits at an *enterprise address*: a payment credential with no stake part, so the ADA it holds
earns nothing and carries no delegation. With `@StateContract(stakeSelf = true)`, state and object UTxOs sit at a
*base address* whose stake credential is the contract's own script, and four handlers decide what happens to that
credential.

| Handler | Purpose | Shape | Decides |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@Withdraw` | Rewarding | `(Params cfg, BigInteger amount, args... [, Ctx])` returns `JulcList<Send>` | Where withdrawn rewards go |
| `@Certify` | Certifying | `(Params cfg, TxCert cert)` returns `boolean` | Which certificates of the credential are allowed |
| `@Votes` | Voting | `(Params cfg, Voter voter, GovernanceActionId action, Vote vote)` returns `boolean` | How the script votes as a DRep |
| `@Propose` | Proposing | `(Params cfg, ProposalProcedure p)` returns `boolean` | Whether a proposal complies (a constitution guardrail) |

##### A staked vault

```java title="examples/staking/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/staking/StakedVault.java"
@StateContract(stakeSelf = true)
public class StakedVault {

    @Params
    public record Config(JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, byte[] pool, byte[] payee, BigInteger cap) {}

    public record State(BigInteger deposits) {}

    @Init @Payable
    public static State open(Config cfg, Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(ctx.received());
    }

    @Action @Payable
    public static State deposit(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        Require.that(ctx.received().signum() > 0, "deposit some ADA");
        return new State(s.deposits().add(ctx.received()));
    }

    @Destroy @Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Config cfg, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(cfg.payee(), ctx.balance());
    }

    /** Rewards go only to the payee. */
    @Withdraw @Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")
    public static JulcList<Send> collect(Config cfg, BigInteger amount) {
        return amount.signum() == 0 ? Sends.none()
                : Sends.of(wallet(cfg.payee()), Assets.lovelace(amount), new OutputDatum.NoOutputDatum());
    }

    /** Registration, and delegation of stake only (no vote delegation) to the pool in the params; nothing else. */
    @Certify @Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")
    public static boolean certificate(Config cfg, TxCert cert) {
        return Certs.isRegistration(cert) || Certs.delegatesOnlyTo(cert, cfg.pool()) || Certs.isDRepLifecycle(cert);
    }

    /** The council votes as the script DRep: a quorum signing is the decision. */
    @Votes @Quorum(keys = "params.council", threshold = "params.quorum")
    public static boolean vote(Config cfg, Voter voter, GovernanceActionId action, Vote vote) {
        return true;
    }

    /** Guardrail: no treasury withdrawal above the cap in total. */
    @Propose
    public static boolean proposal(Config cfg, ProposalProcedure p) {
        return switch (p.governanceAction()) {
            case GovernanceAction.TreasuryWithdrawals t -> totalOf(t).compareTo(cfg.cap()) <= 0;
            default -> true;
        };
    }
}
```

The council is a list of key hashes in the params; [`@Quorum`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/) requires `quorum` of them to
sign. The staking tutorial runs it: [Staked vault and governance](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/staked-vault/).

##### Handlers are governed by params

These purposes spend no input of the contract, so a handler sees no instance state. It sees the deploy-time
[`@Params`](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/), which must be its first parameter. Every instance of a deployment
shares one reward account, governed by rules fixed at deploy.

- `@Withdraw`, `@Certify` and `@Votes` **must** carry `@Quorum` or `@AuthorizedBy`, naming `params.*` fields. An open
  handler would let anyone drain the rewards, redelegate the stake or cast the script's votes; the processor refuses
  it. `@Propose` is a predicate and needs none.
- At most one handler per purpose; a handler cannot also be `@Init`, `@Action`, `@View` or an owned method.
- A purpose without a handler fails. So no certificate can touch the script's credential, and no vote can be cast,
  unless a handler allows it.
- `stakeSelf = true` requires both `@Withdraw` and `@Certify`, or the rewards and the credential would be
  unreachable.

> **One reward account, shared:** 
All instances' funds earn rewards, and carry delegation weight, for whoever governs the params. Tell the users of a
multi-owner contract. Per-instance rewards would need one stake credential per instance, which a script hash cannot
give.

##### `@Withdraw`: rewards

The ledger only allows withdrawing a reward account's whole balance. The generated validator:
- requires `amount` to equal the transaction's withdrawal from the script's credential;
- requires the sends your method returns to total exactly `amount`;
- claims each send in the shared [output registry](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/#the-output-verifier) by
  `RewardRef(own)` (a reference no real input can have), so no other payout or send can count the same output (I37).

The redeemer starts with an integer marker, so it can never be read as an `Approvals` list. Inside a withdrawal,
`Ctx.caller` must sign, the validity bounds are checked, `ctx.balance()` is the amount and `ctx.received()` is 0. Make
the sends depend only on the params and the amount: the reward account can also receive proposal deposit refunds and
treasury withdrawals.

##### `@Certify`: certificates

Before your method runs, the generated code requires that the certificate is for the script's own credential and is
one of: stake registration (with or without a deposit), stake delegation, registration with delegation, DRep
registration, DRep update. Unregistration (stake or DRep), committee and pool certificates are refused outright: an
unregistration refund would enter the transaction with no destination the script could pin.

Your method then decides, with the exact helpers in
[`Certs`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Certs.java):

| Helper | True for |
|---|---|
| `Certs.isRegistration(cert)` | A stake registration |
| `Certs.delegatesOnlyTo(cert, pool)` | A stake delegation (alone or with registration) to exactly `pool`, with no vote delegation |
| `Certs.delegatesVoteTo(cert, drep)` | A vote delegation (alone or with registration) to exactly `drep`, with no stake delegation |
| `Certs.isDRepLifecycle(cert)` | A DRep registration or update of the own credential |

Prefer these to matching certificate variants yourself: a delegation that also moves the vote is easy to miss.

##### `@Votes`: the script as a DRep

The contract can register as a DRep (through `@Certify` with `isDRepLifecycle`) and vote. The generated code takes
exactly this script's entry among the transaction's votes, fails if there is none, and calls your method for every
`(action id, vote)` pair: each must be allowed. The method sees the governance action's id, not its content, so the
decision is usually the quorum's signatures, as above.

##### `@Propose`: a guardrail

A constitution can name a script as its *guardrail*. The ledger then runs it for parameter-change and
treasury-withdrawal proposals. `@Propose` gets the proposal procedure and returns whether it complies. This is meant
for a standalone guardrail contract; the vault's cap is an example of the shape.

##### `@AuthorizedBy` outside spends

When a purpose handler uses `@AuthorizedBy` with a script governor, the approval is bound to exactly this certificate,
vote, proposal or withdrawal: its `target` is `blake2b_224` of the serialised script info, and its `action` is
1000 plus the purpose's tag. One approval can never authorise a different certificate or purpose. See
[Authorization](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/).

##### Using it

**Java:**

```java title="examples/staking/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/staking/StakingDevnetTest.java"
var vault = StakedVaultClient.deploy(runtime, cfg, council[0], ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(100)));
vault.deposit(council[1], ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(20)));

var handle = StakedVaultClient.contract(runtime, cfg);
handle.registerStake(council[0]);                          // legacy registration: no script witness
handle.delegateTo(pool, council[0], council[1]);           // runs @Certify, signed by a quorum

// Withdraws the whole reward balance through @Withdraw (zero until rewards accrue).
StakedVaultClient.collect(runtime, cfg, council[0], council[2]);
vault.close(council[1], council[2]);
```

`handle.rewardAddress()` and `handle.rewardBalance()` read the reward account.

**JavaScript:**

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js (StakedVault)"
const params = { council: council.map((m) => m.keyHash), quorum: 2n, pool, payee: payee.keyHash, cap: 1000n * ADA };
const vault = await contract('StakedVault', a, params);
const v = vault.at((await vault.deploy(a, {}, { lovelace: 100n * ADA })).instance);

await vault.registerStake(a);
await vault.delegate(a, pool, { cosigners: [b] });          // @Certify by quorum
const amount = await rt.chain.rewards(vault.rewardAddress);
await vault.collect(a, { amount, cosigners: [c] });         // @Withdraw
```

`delegate` takes a pool id as 28 bytes of hex or `pool1…` bech32. `collect` reads the balance itself when `amount` is
left out.

The clients cover registration, delegation and reward withdrawal. Votes and proposals are exercised in the harness
(`StakingTest`): on DevKit they need an enacted constitution and live governance actions.

##### Build and network notes

> **-Ajulc.blueprint=false for @Votes and @Propose:** 
JuLC's pinned CIP-57 (blueprint) revision has no vocabulary for the vote and propose purposes yet. A contract with
`@Votes` or `@Propose` compiles with the blueprint off:

```groovy title="examples/staking/build.gradle"
tasks.named('compileJava') { options.compilerArgs += ['-Ajulc.blueprint=false'] }
```

- **Registration on Yaci Store.** Yaci Store answers the same for registered and unknown stake credentials, so a client
  cannot tell whether registration is needed. Register anyway and treat "already registered" as success: the JS
  `registerStake` resolves to `null` in that case.
- **Rewards on DevKit** take epochs to accrue, so a test collects a zero balance. That still runs `@Withdraw`.
- **Addresses.** A staked contract's state address is a base address (`addr_test1x…` on a test network). Its min-ADA
  deposit includes the 28 extra bytes. `stakeSelf` changes the script hash and every address of the contract.

| Invariant | Meaning (ADR-0010 D3) |
|---|---|
| I36 | A state UTxO's address is exactly (own script, the configured stake credential) |
| I37 | A withdrawal is fully allocated by `@Withdraw`'s sends, each claimed in the output registry |
| I38 | Every certificate, vote and proposal the script runs for passes its handler (after the built-in certificate filter); a purpose without a handler fails |

##### Cost

StakedVault's validator is 12 KB with all six purposes. From the harness (ADR-0010 §6): a 5 ADA withdrawal by quorum
81.3M CPU / 278k memory; a delegation 18.6M / 80k; a vote 25.9M / 97k; the guardrail 12.0M / 40k; a deposit at the
staked address 117.8M / 377k.

- ADR-0010: [Architecture decisions](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/)

### Upgrades and migration

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/upgrades/

A deployed script never changes: its hash is its identity. To ship a new version of a contract you deploy a new
script and **migrate** each instance into it. JOUST makes migration a two-sided handshake, checked by both validators
in one transaction:

- the **old** contract ends the instance with a `@Destroy` marked `@MigrateTo`, which may send its funds only into the
  successor it names;
- the **new** contract creates the replacement with a `@Migrate` method, which adopts only an instance of the
  predecessor it names, and only if that instance ends in the same transaction.

Neither side alone can move funds. The example is [`examples/upgrade`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/upgrade):
`CounterV1` migrates into `CounterV2`, which adds a step size and keeps the admin, the count and the funds.

##### The old side: `@MigrateTo`

`@MigrateTo("field")` goes on an instance `@Destroy`. The field is a `byte[]` holding the successor's policy id: a
state field an admin sets, or `params.<component>`.

```java title="examples/upgrade/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/upgrade/CounterV1.java"
@StateContract
public class CounterV1 {

    public record State(byte[] admin, byte[] successor, BigInteger count) {}

    @Init @Payable
    public static State open(Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(ctx.caller(), new byte[]{}, BigInteger.ZERO);
    }

    @Action
    public static State increment(State s) {
        return new State(s.admin(), s.successor(), s.count().add(BigInteger.ONE));
    }

    @Action @SignedBy("admin")
    public static State setSuccessor(State s, byte[] successor) {
        return new State(s.admin(), successor, s.count());
    }

    /** Ends v1 by migrating: nothing is paid out, everything moves to the successor's new instance. */
    @Destroy @SignedBy("admin") @MigrateTo("successor")
    public static JulcList<Payout> upgrade(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.none();
    }
}
```

A migrating destroy does not pay out `ctx.balance()`: the funds go to the successor instead. What its validator
checks, besides the usual destroy checks (the method's rules, `@SignedBy`, `Ctx`, its own token burned, payouts
paid and tagged):

- exactly one token is minted under the **successor policy**, named `blake2b_256(own input)`: the instance id the
  successor derives from this state UTxO;
- exactly one output holds that token, at an address whose payment credential is the successor script;
- that output holds at least this instance's lovelace, plus what was paid in, minus the method's payouts.

So the funds can only move into an instance of the contract the field names.

##### The new side: `@Migrate`

`@Migrate(from = "params.previous")` marks a creation method that adopts an instance of the previous version. `from`
must name a `byte[]` component of the new contract's `@Params` record, holding the previous policy id. The method
takes the params, then the **previous contract's state record**, then any arguments and an optional `Ctx`, and
returns the new state:

```java title="examples/upgrade/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/examples/upgrade/CounterV2.java"
/** Version 2: adds a step size; adopts v1 instances, keeping their admin, count and funds (ADR-0011 D4). */
@StateContract
public class CounterV2 {

    @Params
    public record Config(byte[] previous) {}

    public record State(byte[] admin, BigInteger count, BigInteger step) {}

    @Init
    public static State open(Config cfg, Ctx ctx) {
        return new State(ctx.caller(), BigInteger.ZERO, BigInteger.ONE);
    }

    @Migrate(from = "params.previous")
    public static State adopt(Config cfg, CounterV1.State old) {
        return new State(old.admin(), old.count(), BigInteger.ONE);
    }

    @Action
    public static State increment(State s) {
        return new State(s.admin(), s.count().add(s.step()), s.step());
    }

    @Action @SignedBy("admin")
    public static State setStep(State s, BigInteger step) {
        return new State(s.admin(), s.count(), step);
    }

    @Destroy @SignedBy("admin")
    public static JulcList<Payout> close(State s, Ctx ctx) {
        return Payouts.of(s.admin(), ctx.balance());
    }
}
```

The adoption's validator (its MINT side, with its own `Adopt` redeemer) checks:

- the seed it names is a state UTxO of the previous policy: one 32-byte token of that policy, at that policy's script
  address, with an inline datum;
- the datum has the shape of the previous state record: constructor 0 and the record's number of fields (JuLC's casts
  are unchecked, so this is what refuses another layout);
- the previous instance's token is **burned** (−1) in the same transaction, so the old instance ends;
- exactly one new token is minted, named `blake2b_256(seed)`, and one output holds it at the new contract's state
  address, without a reference script;
- the output's datum equals `adopt(params, old)` and fits `maxDatumBytes`;
- its value is **exactly** the old UTxO's lovelace plus the new token, and at least the new `minAda`.

##### Why the old side names its successor in the state

Both sides pin each other. If both did it through `@Params`, each script hash would depend on the other's: v1's
params would hold v2's hash and v2's params v1's. That is circular, so the example splits it:

- **v2** pins v1 in its params (`Config(previous)`), fixed when v2 is deployed;
- **v1** names v2 in a state field, `successor`, that only its admin may set (`setSuccessor`, `@SignedBy("admin")`).

This puts trust in v1's admin: the admin decides where every instance may migrate. Users of v1 should know that. A
contract that must never move needs no `@MigrateTo` at all.

##### The migration transaction

The two halves must be in **one** transaction: v1's destroy is only valid if v2 mints the successor, and v2's
adoption is only valid if v1's token burns. The Java runtime builds it with `Compose`, which runs several client
calls into one transaction:

```java title="examples/upgrade/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/upgrade/UpgradeDevnetTest.java"
var v1 = CounterV1Client.deploy(runtime, admin, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
v1.increment(admin);
v1.increment(admin);

// v2's params pin v1; v1's admin names v2.
var cfg = new CounterV2.Config(HexUtil.decodeHexString(v1.instance().contract().policyId()));
String v2Policy = CounterV2Client.policyIdFor(cfg);
v1.setSuccessor(admin, HexUtil.decodeHexString(v2Policy));

// One transaction: v1's migrating destroy and v2's adoption.
var adopted = new CounterV2Client[1];
String tx = Compose.of(runtime, admin)
        .add(() -> v1.upgrade(admin))
        .add(() -> adopted[0] = CounterV2Client.adopt(runtime, cfg, admin, v1.instance()))
        .submit();

var v2 = CounterV2Client.at(runtime, cfg, adopted[0].instanceId());
v2.state().count();   // 2: the count moved
v2.lovelace();        // the funds moved
```

The generated `CounterV2Client.adopt(runtime, params, caller, prior)` takes the old instance's `StateInstance`. Called
outside a `Compose`, it refuses: `adopt runs inside a Compose, together with the old instance's migrating destroy`.

> **The instance id changes:** 

The new instance's id is `blake2b_256` of the old **state UTxO's** reference, not the old id. Store the new id
(`adopted[0].instanceId()`). Anything that refers to the old instance by `(policy, id)`, including other contracts
that read it through `@Reads` pinned in their params, must migrate too.

##### Rules and limits

- At most one `@Migrate` per contract. `@Migrate` is its own kind of creation: no other lifecycle annotation on the
  same method, and no `@Quorum` or `@AuthorizedBy`.
- `@MigrateTo` goes only on an instance `@Destroy`, and names a `byte[]`.
- Not supported yet with **MerkleMaps**, **owned objects** or **native assets**, on either side. The processor reports
  an error.
- A migrating destroy should return `Payouts.none()`: the new side requires the new instance to hold exactly the
  old UTxO's lovelace, so nothing can be paid out of it.
- Migration is an atomic transaction of two contracts, so both reference scripts' fees and both executions count
  toward one transaction's limits (see [Fees and script size](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/)).

##### What the harness tests

`examples/upgrade/src/test/.../UpgradeTest.java` evaluates the migration transaction with each contract's harness and
checks that the handshake holds:

- v1 refuses a successor its admin did not name;
- both sides refuse when the new instance holds less than the old;
- v1 refuses when no successor token is minted;
- v2 refuses to adopt when the old token is not burned.

##### Reference

- [Annotations](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/): `@MigrateTo`, `@Migrate`; [Java runtime API](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/java-runtime-api/): `Compose`
- Sources: [`MigrateTo.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/MigrateTo.java),
  [`Migrate.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-api/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/api/Migrate.java),
  [`examples/upgrade`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/tree/main/examples/upgrade)
- [ADR-0011](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0011-option-k-composition.md) D4 (I41), §6 (why the old side uses a state field)

### Fees and script size

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/

Every JOUST call is a Cardano transaction, and its fee is set by the ledger's rules, not by JOUST. But the generated
validator's size and cost are a large part of that fee, and they decide what fits in one transaction. This page
explains the fee, gives the measured numbers for the examples, and lists what you can do to keep a contract small.

##### What a call costs

A Cardano transaction pays three things (mainnet parameters, as [ADR-0008](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0008-option-h-fees-and-size.md) uses them):

| Part | Rule | What drives it in JOUST |
|---|---|---|
| **Size fee** | 155,381 lovelace plus 44 per byte of the transaction | inputs, outputs, the inline datum (your state), the redeemer (arguments, `Ctx`, events), collateral, witnesses |
| **Execution** | 0.0577 lovelace per memory unit and 0.0000721 per CPU step | the generated checks plus your method, for every script that runs |
| **Reference scripts** | 15 lovelace per byte of every reference script the transaction reads (the first 25,600-byte tier; more costs more per byte) | the size of the compiled validator, and of any shared verifier the call uses |

A **reference script** is a script stored in a UTxO on chain (CIP-33). A transaction that reads it does not carry the
script's bytes, but since Conway it pays for them by size. JOUST validators are always read by reference, so their
size is a fixed charge on every call.

What a call costs, from ADR-0008 (mainnet parameters, a transaction of about 1.2 KB):

| Call | Size fee | Execution | Reference script | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| counter increment | 0.208 | 0.018 | 0.084 | **0.310 ADA** |
| market buy | about 0.25 | 0.106 | 0.170 + 0.011 | **about 0.54 ADA** |

For a simple call the size fee is now the largest part; the reference-script fee is next.

##### Reference scripts in JOUST

JOUST publishes each contract's validator once, as a reference script at the contract's own address, and every
transaction reads it from there:

- the Java runtime publishes it on the first `deploy` of a contract type (`StateContractHandle.ensureReferenceScript`),
  and finds it on chain afterwards;
- on the npm path, `joust deploy` publishes it and records it in `build/joust/deployments.<network>.json`.

The reference-script UTxO holds no thread token, so the validator never lets it be spent (junk UTxOs at a script
address are never spendable). Its min-ADA deposit, about 4.3 lovelace per script byte plus a margin, stays locked
with it for good.

Shared scripts (the MerkleMap verifier, the output verifier) are published the same way, once per network, and are
read only by calls that use them.

##### Measured sizes and budgets

Exact bytes of each compiled script, and per-script execution budgets from the harness tests, after the ADR-0008
optimisations. Compiled by JuLC for `plutus-v3-pv11` with the `pv11-safe` optimisation. For scale: a transaction may
use at most 10,000M CPU steps and 14M memory units on mainnet (16.5M memory on DevKit).

| Contract | Script size | Call | CPU | Mem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Counter | 5,631 B | increment | 73.4M | 213k |
| | | close (spend + burn) | 94.1M + 17.6M | 317k + 64k |
| Vault | 6,273 B | deposit | 99.4M | 303k |
| | | withdraw | 140.6M | 445k |
| Escrow | 5,688 B | release / refund (spend + burn) | 92.1M + 17.6M | 309k + 64k |
| Crowdfund | 7,976 B | contribute | 132.8M | 385k |
| | | refund, 27 backers (at capacity) | 286.6M | 559k |
| Bank | 7,920 B | withdraw (owned, `@Shared` read) | 171.4M | 547k |
| Pool | 9,586 B | batch of 10 donations (all scripts) | 4,629.8M | 13,976k |
| Token | 11,718 B (+ MapVerifier 4,700 B) | transfer (spend + verifier) | 218.4M + 502.3M | 707k + 1,901k |
| Dex | 12,008 B (+ OutputVerifier 703 B) | swapAdaForToken (spend + verifier) | 221.6M + 21.2M | 688k + 86k |
| Market | 11,325 B | buy (spend + mint + verifier) | 345.7M + 24.0M + 35.3M | 1,127k + 100k + 145k |

The full table, every call of every example, is in [`examples/README.md`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/README.md#script-sizes-and-budgets).
Other measured sizes: Treasury 9.1 KB before its params are applied (ADR-0009), CounterV1 5.9 KB and CounterV2 6.9 KB
(ADR-0011), Pot 8.6 KB and Stall 9.4 KB (ADR-0011 §7). Maps and native assets together reach about 14.3 KB.

Two observations from these numbers:

- **The generated checks dominate execution**, not your logic. A counter `increment` and `reset` cost almost the
  same.
- **Size grows with features.** Each feature a contract uses (assets, maps, owned objects, moves) adds generated code
  to its one validator.

##### What ADR-0008 changed

ADR-0008 cut the generated checks' cost by 30 to 60 % for plain contracts and the scripts by about 2.4 KB, with no
source change and no change to what is checked. The main moves:

- the exact value check (I3) became a single Data equality against the canonical value, built directly, instead of
  generic value arithmetic and comparison;
- token lookups walk only one policy's map (`ledgerTokensOf`) instead of flattening whole values;
- the mint checks and the unique-output search became one-pass loops;
- asset-aware transitions share one settlement helper.

Two ideas were measured and rejected: JuLC's `pv11-costed` profile gave byte-identical scripts, and stripping
`Require` messages saved only 100 to 300 bytes per contract at the cost of every failure reason.

##### Limits

| Limit | Value | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Transaction size | 16 KB (16,384 bytes) | everything in the transaction, reference scripts excluded, must fit |
| Reference script the runtime publishes | 15,000 bytes | the runtime refuses an applied script larger than this |
| Execution per transaction | 10,000M CPU, 14M memory (mainnet) | bounds batches (about 8 intents) and compositions |
| State size | `maxDatumBytes` | see [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/) |

Composition adds up: a transaction that touches several contracts pays every reference script it reads and every
script it runs, within one transaction's limits.

##### Keeping scripts small and calls cheap

- **Skip `Ctx` where you don't need it.** A method without `Ctx` has no caller signature, no validity interval and a
  smaller redeemer. Counter's `increment` has none.
- **Use annotations for simple policies.** `@SignedBy` and `@ValidAfter` are one generated check each, and the client
  checks them before building.
- **Keep the state small.** The datum is paid for in every transaction that writes it (size fee), and it sets the
  deposit. Store hashes or roots for large data ([MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/)).
- **Keep `Require` messages short.** Each is in the script.
- **Use only the features you need.** Native assets, MerkleMaps and owned objects each add generated code; a contract
  that uses three owned types plus moves plus maps has exceeded 16 KB.
- **Move heavy logic into a shared withdraw-zero script** when a contract nears the size limit. This helps with the
  16 KB transaction limit only: the transaction still reads that script, and pays for its bytes.
- **Compose calls.** Several calls in one transaction share the fixed part of the size fee
  ([Reads and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/)).

##### Known issues

> **Open work:** 

- **Script size** ([#34](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/issues/34)). The reference-script fee is charged on every
  call, so every kilobyte removed saves 15,000 lovelace per transaction. The issue plans a size report per generated
  function, trimming unused generated helpers per contract, and possibly moving creation and closing out of the spend
  script (an ADR-level change). Any change to the generated validators changes script hashes and addresses.
- **Fee estimate for wallet-prepared transactions** ([#33](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/issues/33)).
  Transactions prepared for a CIP-30 wallet (pages, `joust dev`) are estimated with one more key witness than the
  wallet adds, so they overpay by the size of one witness (a few thousand lovelace). It never underpays. The fix is
  planned in cardano-client-lib.

##### Reference

- [ADR-0008](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0008-option-h-fees-and-size.md): the optimisations and the cost tables
- [`examples/README.md`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/examples/README.md): sizes and budgets of every example
- [`StateContractHandle.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-runtime/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/runtime/StateContractHandle.java): reference-script publishing and the 15,000-byte check

### Security model

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/

JOUST's security rests on one rule: **the chain only accepts what the generated validator checks**. Your method
decides the next state and the payouts; the validator re-runs it on chain and enforces a fixed set of invariants
around it. Everything off chain (the Java client, the npm engine, a prepare service, a page) is there to build
transactions that pass, and to refuse early those that would not. None of it can make the chain accept a transaction
the validator refuses.

This page lists what is enforced, how it is tested, and what each off-chain part is trusted with.

##### Trust at a glance

| Part | Trusted for | Not trusted for |
|---|---|---|
| The generated validator (on chain) | every state transition, every lovelace moved | |
| Your contract methods | the business rules you write | nothing else: the invariants below hold whatever they return |
| The client or engine (JVM or Wasm) | building a transaction that passes, early refusals | correctness on chain: the validator checks again |
| A prepare service | nothing a page signs: the page verifies every transaction | |
| A chain API | availability | data: answers feeding a transaction are checked by the verifier and the ledger |
| A governor script (`@AuthorizedBy`) | its own approvals | anything beyond the approval it names |
| The deployer | choosing `@Init` arguments and `@Params` | |

##### What the generated validator enforces

The invariants come from [ADR-0001](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-option-a-single-utxo-state-machine.md)
§4 (I1 to I14) and the later ADRs. Each is a check you could write by hand, emitted around your method.

###### Identity: one-shot thread tokens

| ID | Invariant |
|---|---|
| I1 | One seed gives one instance: the seed is consumed, exactly one token is minted under the policy, named `blake2b_256(seed)` |
| I9 | The burn redeemer only burns |
| I10 | A UTxO at the script address without exactly one thread token of the policy is never spendable (junk is inert) |
| I12 | State outputs sit at the contract's own script address, with no reference script attached |

Because the token can only be minted once per seed, and only leaves a state UTxO through the contract's own SPEND
checks, holding the token proves a UTxO is a genuine instance. Other dApps authenticate an instance by its
`(policy, id)` pair.

###### Exact state and value

| ID | Invariant |
|---|---|
| I2 | The initial datum equals `init(args, ctx)` |
| I3 | Exact value accounting: the continuing output holds exactly `{lovelace: in + received − payouts, token: 1}`. No token dust can be added, no lovelace skimmed |
| I4 | Exactly one continuing output carries the token, at the same address, with an inline datum equal to the method's result |
| I13 | The serialised state never exceeds `maxDatumBytes`, so no call can make the instance outgrow its deposit |
| I14 | Actions never spend the deposit: the continuing lovelace is at least `minAda` |

Asset-aware contracts generalise I3 to full multi-asset values (`out = in + received + accepted + mint − payouts −
sends`), and the reserved tokens of the contract's own policy never move (ADR-0007).

###### Verified `Ctx`

| ID | Invariant |
|---|---|
| I5 | `ctx.caller` signed the transaction |
| I6 | `received`, `balance`, `validFrom` and `validTo` match the transaction; the interval is finite on both sides and at most `maxValidityMs` wide |
| I11 | `@SignedBy`, `@ValidAfter` and `@ValidBefore` hold against the **current** state, with finite bounds |

Your method can trust every `Ctx` field: a client that lies about one is refused. See
[Ctx, funds and payouts](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/).

###### Payouts and destroy

| ID | Invariant |
|---|---|
| I7 | Every payout is paid: for each recipient, outputs to its key **tagged** with this instance's input reference add up to at least what is owed |
| I8 | A destroy burns the token and its payouts allocate the whole balance, deposit included |

The tag (the payout output's inline datum is the spent state UTxO's reference) prevents **double satisfaction**: two
instances spent in one transaction, of this or any other JOUST contract, can never count the same payout output.

###### Later invariants

Each later layer adds its own, specified in its ADR. Among them: map claims checked against the root (ADR-0002, the
shared MerkleMap verifier), owned objects and their kinds (ADR-0003, ADR-0012), batched intents (ADR-0004), assets,
sends and the output-claim registry (ADR-0007, I26 to I31), quorum, script approval, invariants and events (ADR-0009,
I32 to I35), reads, deposits and migration (ADR-0011, I39 to I41).

##### How it is tested: the attack suite

Every example runs **the attack suite** (`Attacks` in `julc-state-testkit`, ADR-0001 D16). Given a transaction the
harness accepts, it lists every mutation the invariants forbid that applies to it, evaluates each against the compiled
validator, and fails if any is accepted:

- a wrong datum; an extra token in the output; one lovelace skimmed or added;
- the thread token missing, sent elsewhere, or two continuing outputs;
- the caller not signed; `received`, `balance`, `validFrom` or `validTo` lied about;
- a payout untagged, underpaid or paid to someone else;
- a destroy without a burn; spending a junk UTxO;
- for creations: the seed not consumed, two tokens minted, a wrong token name;
- a stake credential added to the state address, a reference script attached, a datum hash instead of an inline datum;
- a validity bound not equal to `Ctx`, an unbounded side, a window wider than `maxValidityMs`;
- payouts exceeding the balance, a state grown past `maxDatumBytes`.

On top of these, composed transactions: two instances sharing one payout output (double satisfaction), duplicate
payouts to one recipient, a create and a burn under one policy.

```java title="examples/vault/src/test/java/org/julclang/state/examples/vault/VaultTest.java"
var tx = h.act(live, new VaultValidator.Deposit(ctx), Vault.deposit(live.state(), ctx), BOB, ctx);
System.out.println("[deposit] " + h.assertAccepted(tx) + "  attacks rejected: " + Attacks.assertAllRejected(h, tx));
```

Run it on every transaction your tests accept. See [Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/).

##### Off chain: the client runs the method first

The Java client (and the npm engine, which runs the same Java code compiled to WebAssembly) does, for every call:

1. read the current state from the chain;
2. check the policy annotations (`@SignedBy`, time) against it;
3. run your method on the JVM with the real `Ctx`: a failing rule refuses the call here;
4. check the result: datum size, canonical maps, invariants, payouts within the funds;
5. build and balance the transaction, evaluate every script, and verify that the balanced transaction still has
   exactly the expected state output and payouts;
6. submit, then wait for **that** transaction. It never resubmits one the node accepted.

This catches mistakes early and gives clear messages. It adds no trust: if the client were wrong, the validator would
refuse the transaction.

##### Pages: verify before signing

A browser page signs with the user's CIP-30 wallet. Whoever builds the transaction (a prepare service, or the engine
in the page's worker) chooses what the user signs, and wallets show transactions poorly. A malicious builder could add
an output draining the wallet, a certificate delegating the user's stake, or a collateral return it controls.

So the page **verifies every transaction before the wallet is asked to sign** (ADR-0015 I5). The verifier in
`@julclang/state-client` works from the contract description bundled in the page, never from values the builder
sends. It checks, among other things:

- the inputs are the wallet's own UTxOs and the target instance; the redeemer is exactly the call the page asked for,
  on the pinned script and thread token;
- `ctx.caller` is a wallet key and `ctx.received` the payment;
- the wallet's net outflow is at most the expected payment plus the fee;
- no certificates, votes, proposals or donation; no withdrawals except JOUST's verifiers' (and a named governor's);
  no mint except the expected one;
- `isValid` is true, the collateral return goes to the user, total collateral is bounded, and the network id is
  right.

A refused transaction raises `VerificationError` with its problems, and the wallet never sees it. The verifier is
covered by **tamper tests**: the JavaScript suites build real transactions, mutate them in every way they know, and
require each mutation to be refused before any wallet is asked to sign (for example every tampering of a co-signed
treasury payment, and of a governor's registration). See [Wallets](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/).

###### The engine is pinned with SRI

A page that prepares its own transactions runs the runtime engine (Wasm) in a worker. The page's own code pins the
engine's sha384 hashes, and the worker fetches the engine with Subresource Integrity, so a browser refuses an engine
whose bytes differ, wherever it is served from. Even so, the engine is not trusted with the user's funds: its output
goes through the verifier like a service's. See [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/).

##### MerkleMaps: proofs are checked, mirrors are rebuilt

A [MerkleMap](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/) keeps only a 32-byte root in the state. Every read and write a call makes comes
with a proof, and the shared map verifier checks each against the root on chain, so a wrong value or a forged proof
fails the transaction.

Off chain, the proofs come from a **mirror** of the map. Mirrors are untrusted too:

- the engine checks each supplied proof against the on-chain root with the validator's own logic, and computes new
  roots itself;
- a mirror rebuilt from chain history replays every map claim from the transactions' redeemers, checking each
  write's proof and each new root, and is accepted only if the final root equals the on-chain datum's. A history
  source that drops, alters or invents anything stops matching.

See [MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/).

##### What JOUST does not protect against

> **Caution:** 

- **Your rules.** If a method lets anyone withdraw, the validator enforces exactly that. Review who can call each
  method, especially those that pay out.
- **Hostile `@Init` arguments.** Anyone can create an instance with any arguments (for example naming a victim as
  an escrow's seller). Front ends should show who created an instance and with what arguments.
- **Junk at the script address.** UTxOs sent there without a thread token can never be spent, by anyone.
- **Parameterised clones.** Anyone can deploy your contract with other `@Params`. Pin the expected policy id.
- **Governor scripts and admins.** `@AuthorizedBy` trusts the script's rules; a `@MigrateTo` field set by an admin
  trusts the admin.
- **Foreign validators.** A non-JOUST script in the same transaction that ignores JOUST's tags can still be
  double-satisfied by a JOUST output.
- **Stale reads.** A reference input does not run its validator: check an oracle's freshness yourself.

##### Reference

- [ADR-0001](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-option-a-single-utxo-state-machine.md) §4 (invariants), D16 (attack suite), §10 (limits)
- [ADR-0013](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0013-option-m-wallets-and-js.md) D2 and §9 (the page verifier)
- [ADR-0015](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0015-option-n-javascript-developer-experience.md) §5 (threat model), I5, §13.12 (mirrors)
- Sources: [`Attacks.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-testkit/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/testkit/Attacks.java),
  [`verify.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/state-client/src/verify.js),
  [`ValidatorGenerator.java`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/julc-state-processor/src/main/java/org/julclang/state/processor/gen/ValidatorGenerator.java)

### Testing

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/

A JOUST contract is one class, but it runs in three places: your methods on the JVM, the compiled validator on
chain, and the client building real transactions. Each example in the repository tests all three, at increasing
cost:

| Level | Tool | Needs | Catches |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain Java | JUnit | Nothing | Wrong business logic, `Require` messages |
| On-chain harness | `StateHarness` (`julc-state-testkit`) | The build's compiled validator | What the validator accepts and rejects; script budgets |
| Attack suite | `Attacks` | An accepted harness transaction | Every mutation the invariants forbid must be rejected |
| End to end | The generated client on Yaci DevKit | DevKit running | Building, balancing, submitting, confirming, contention |
| JavaScript | `node --test`, Playwright | DevKit, built JS packages | JS clients, the runtime engine, the page verifier, pages in a browser |

Add the test kit to your build (it brings JUnit 5 with it):

```groovy
testImplementation "org.julclang:julc-state-testkit:$joustVersion"   // in the JOUST build: project(':julc-state-testkit')
```

##### Plain Java: test the methods

Your methods are pure static functions, so test them directly. `StateHarness.ctx(caller, received, balance)` makes
a `Ctx` with a fixed validity window, `[StateHarness.T0, T0 + WINDOW_MS)`:

```java title="examples/counter/.../CounterTest.java"
static final byte[] ALICE = StateHarness.fill(28, 0x11);    // a 28-byte key hash

final StateHarness<Counter.State> h = StateHarness.of(CounterClient.SPEC);

@Test
void incrementResetClose() {
    var s0 = Counter.init(h.ctx(ALICE, BigInteger.ZERO, BigInteger.ZERO));
    var s1 = Counter.increment(s0, BigInteger.valueOf(5));
    var s2 = Counter.increment(s1, BigInteger.TWO);
    assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(7), Counter.count(s2));
    assertEquals(BigInteger.ZERO, Counter.reset(s2).count());
}

@Test
void rulesFailOnTheJvmWithTheirMessage() {
    var s = Counter.init(h.ctx(ALICE, BigInteger.ZERO, BigInteger.ZERO));
    var e = assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> Counter.increment(s, BigInteger.ZERO));
    assertEquals("increment must be positive", e.getMessage());
}
```

This is where most of your tests belong: they are fast, and they exercise exactly the code the validator runs.

##### The compiled validator: StateHarness

`StateHarness` evaluates the generated validator **as compiled by your build** (loaded from
`META-INF/plutus/<Name>Validator.plutus.json`) in JuLC's VM, against transactions shaped like the ones the runtime
submits. A transaction is accepted when every script it triggers accepts: SPEND for each state input, MINT if it
mints or burns under the policy, and the shared verifiers when the contract uses them.

The pattern: compute the next state on the JVM (as the client would), build the matching transaction, and assert:

```java title="examples/counter/.../CounterTest.java"
@Test
void increment_byAnyone() {
    var live = h.live(new Counter.State(BigInteger.valueOf(3), ALICE), BigInteger.ZERO);
    var next = Counter.increment(live.state(), BigInteger.TEN);          // the client computes this on the JVM
    var tx = h.act(live, new CounterValidator.Increment(BigInteger.TEN), next, null, null);
    System.out.println("[increment] " + h.assertAccepted(tx));
    System.out.println("  attacks rejected: " + Attacks.assertAllRejected(h, tx));
}

@Test
void increment_wrongResult_rejected() {
    var live = h.live(new Counter.State(BigInteger.valueOf(3), ALICE), BigInteger.ZERO);
    var cheat = new Counter.State(BigInteger.valueOf(999), ALICE);
    h.assertRejected(h.act(live, new CounterValidator.Increment(BigInteger.TEN), cheat, null, null), "wrong next state");
}

@Test
void increment_hugeNumberCannotOutgrowTheDatum() {
    var live = h.live(new Counter.State(BigInteger.valueOf(3), ALICE), BigInteger.ZERO);
    var by = BigInteger.TEN.pow(400);    // ~170 bytes, over maxDatumBytes = 128
    var next = Counter.increment(live.state(), by);
    h.assertRejected(h.act(live, new CounterValidator.Increment(by), next, null, null), "datum over maxDatumBytes");
}
```

The redeemers are the generated validator's records: `<Name>Validator.CreateInstance`, `BurnInstance`, and one per
action or destroy (`Increment`, `Reset`, `Close`), with `Ctx` as their last field when the method declares it.

**The ledger's value rules come first.** Before any script runs, `evaluate` refuses a transaction the ledger itself
would refuse for its values: an output holding a negative quantity or more than 2^64 − 1 of anything, or a mint entry
of zero or outside Int64. The verdict then has one entry, `LEDGER`, and no script result. This catches a method that
sends or burns more than the instance holds: the value equation can still balance (the continuing output would hold a
negative quantity), so the validator alone would accept it. A test that measures scripts at quantities no output may
hold (a worst-case budget) can turn the check off with `h.ledgerRules(false)`; use it for that run only. The rest of
the ledger (the minimum lovelace per output, fees, balance, conservation) is not modelled here: the testkit's `Ledger`
(the full transaction model, used for keyed objects) checks those and refuses non-positive output quantities, but not
yet the 2^64 − 1 and Int64 bounds. The two share no code yet (issue #86).

###### Creating, acting, destroying

| Method | Builds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `StateHarness.of(SPEC [, params])` | A harness for a contract (and its params) | `SPEC` is the generated client's |
| `ctx(caller, received, balance)` | A `Ctx` over `[T0, T0 + WINDOW_MS)` | `T0` is 1,800,000,000,000 ms, `WINDOW_MS` 120,000 |
| `seed()` | The seed `TxOutRef` a create spends | Pass it to `CreateInstance` |
| `live(state, funds)` | An instance on chain: `Live(ref, state, lovelace)` | `lovelace` = min-ADA + `funds` |
| `create(createRedeemer, initial, ctx)` | A deploy: consumes the seed, mints the token, locks `initial` | |
| `act(live, redeemer, next, payouts, signer, ctx)` | An action: spends, continues with `next`, pays out | `signer`: the key that signs, or null; `ctx`: the method's `Ctx`, or null. There is a form without `payouts` |
| `destroy(live, redeemer, burnRedeemer, payouts, signer, ctx)` | A destroy: spends, burns, pays out | |
| `evaluate(tx)` | A `Verdict`: one result per script, with CPU and memory | `accepted()` |
| `assertAccepted(tx)` | Fails with every script's result unless all accept | Returns the `Verdict`; print it for budgets |
| `assertRejected(tx, what)` | Fails if every script accepts | `what` names the rule, for the failure message |
| `fill(len, byte)` | A test bytestring | `fill(28, 0x11)` for a key hash |

The harness also builds transactions for owned objects (`liveObject`, `createObject`, `actObject`,
`destroyObject`), native assets (`held`, `funds`, `createWith`, `stepWith`), intents and batches (`liveIntent`,
`createIntent`, `cancelIntent`, `batch`), and the staking purposes (`withdrawTx`, `evaluateWithdraw`,
`evaluateCertify`, `evaluateVote`, `evaluatePropose`). The examples show each: `bank`, `dex`, `pool`, `staking`.

###### Time, signers and payouts

Pick deadlines relative to `T0` so the harness window is before or after them, and pass the payouts your method
returned:

```java title="examples/vault/.../VaultTest.java"
static final BigInteger UNLOCK = StateHarness.T0.subtract(BigInteger.valueOf(60_000));   // already unlocked
static final BigInteger LATER = StateHarness.T0.add(BigInteger.valueOf(3_600_000));      // still locked

@Test
void withdraw_afterUnlock() {
    var live = h.live(new Vault.State(OWNER, UNLOCK, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN)), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
    Ctx ctx = h.ctx(OWNER, BigInteger.ZERO, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
    var r = Vault.withdraw(live.state(), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(3)), ctx);
    var tx = h.act(live, new VaultValidator.Withdraw(ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(3)), ctx), r.state(), r.payouts(), OWNER, ctx);
    System.out.println("[withdraw] " + h.assertAccepted(tx) + "  attacks rejected: " + Attacks.assertAllRejected(h, tx));
}

@Test
void withdraw_beforeUnlock_rejectedOnChain() {
    var live = h.live(new Vault.State(OWNER, LATER, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN)), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
    Ctx ctx = h.ctx(OWNER, BigInteger.ZERO, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));
    var r = Vault.withdraw(live.state(), ADA, ctx);
    h.assertRejected(h.act(live, new VaultValidator.Withdraw(ADA, ctx), r.state(), r.payouts(), OWNER, ctx), "@ValidAfter");
}
```

`Ctx` must tell the truth, as the client's does: `balance` is the lovelace above the deposit in an action and
everything in a destroy (`live.lovelace()`), and `received` must match what the transaction adds. The vault tests
also check that a lying `Ctx` is rejected:

```java title="examples/vault/.../VaultTest.java"
Ctx claimed = h.ctx(BOB, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN), ADA);       // says 10 ADA, the output only gets 1
Ctx actual = h.ctx(BOB, ADA, ADA);
var tx = h.act(live, new VaultValidator.Deposit(claimed), Vault.deposit(live.state(), claimed), BOB, actual);
h.assertRejected(tx, "ctx.received must match the value added");
```

##### The attack suite

`Attacks.assertAllRejected(h, tx)` takes a transaction the harness accepts, applies every mutation the invariants of
[ADR-0001 §4](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-option-a-single-utxo-state-machine.md) (and
of the later ADRs) forbid that applies to it, and fails listing any mutation the validator accepted. It returns how
many it tried. Call it on every accepted transaction in your tests.

A mutation applies only where it makes sense: removing a signer only if the call needed one, range attacks only if
the transaction has a validity range, payout attacks only if it pays out. What it tries includes:

| Invariant | Mutations |
|---|---|
| I1, I9 | Seed not consumed; two thread tokens minted; an extra token under the policy |
| I2, I4 | Datum replaced; datum hash instead of inline datum; state output dropped |
| I3 | Token dust added; one lovelace skimmed; one lovelace added |
| I4, I12 | Thread token sent to a key address; stake credential on the state address; reference script on the state output |
| I5, I11 | Required signer missing |
| I6, I11 | Upper or lower bound unbounded; range shifted by 1 ms; range wider than `maxValidityMs` |
| I7 | A payout untagged, tagged with another input, under-paid by one lovelace, paid to someone else, or to a script with the same hash |
| I8 | Destroy without burning the token |
| I10 | A junk UTxO (no thread token) spent as the state |
| ADR-0007 | Native tokens skimmed; sends under-filled, redirected, re-tagged or unclaimed; user mints off by one |

Double satisfaction across two instances needs two transactions, so it is its own helper:

```java title="examples/counter/.../CounterTest.java"
var txA = h.destroy(a, new CounterValidator.Close(ctx), new CounterValidator.BurnInstance(),
        Counter.close(a.state(), ctx), ALICE, ctx);
var txB = h.destroy(b, new CounterValidator.Close(ctx), new CounterValidator.BurnInstance(),
        Counter.close(b.state(), ctx), ALICE, ctx);
h.assertRejected(Attacks.sharedPayouts(txA, txB), "one payout output satisfying two instances");
```

The attack suite tests the **generated** checks. Your own rules (who may call, what amounts are allowed) are yours
to test with `assertRejected`, as the examples above do.

##### The description

JavaScript clients encode calls from the contract's description. One line checks that the description matches the
generated validator, constructor by constructor:

```java title="examples/counter/.../DescriptionTest.java"
@Test
void descriptionsMatchTheValidators() {
    Descriptions.assertMatches(Counter.class, CounterValidator.class);
}
```

##### End to end on Yaci DevKit

The last level runs the generated client against a live local network. The examples tag these tests `devnet` and
skip them when DevKit is not reachable, so `./gradlew build` works anywhere:

```java title="examples/counter/.../CounterDevnetTest.java"
@Tag("devnet")
class CounterDevnetTest {

    @BeforeAll
    static void devkit() {
        assumeTrue(DevKit.isReachable(), "Yaci DevKit not reachable");
    }

    @Test
    void lifecycle() {
        var runtime = DevKit.runtime();
        var alice = DevKit.fundedAccount(500);
        var bob = DevKit.fundedAccount(500);

        var counter = CounterClient.deploy(runtime, alice);
        assertEquals(BigInteger.ZERO, counter.count());
        assertArrayEquals(Keys.pkh(alice), counter.state().owner());
        assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(CounterClient.SPEC.minAda()), counter.lovelace());

        counter.increment(bob, BigInteger.valueOf(5));
        counter.increment(alice, BigInteger.TWO);
        assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(7), counter.count());

        // Rejected on the JVM before anything is submitted.
        assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> counter.increment(bob, BigInteger.ZERO));
        assertThrows(RequireException.class, () -> counter.reset(bob));

        // Reconnect by id from a fresh client.
        var again = CounterClient.at(runtime, counter.instanceId());
        again.reset(alice);
        assertEquals(BigInteger.ZERO, counter.count());

        var closed = counter.close(alice);
        assertEquals(1, closed.payouts().size());
        assertThrows(InstanceNotFoundException.class, counter::state);
    }
}
```

```sh
yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store
./gradlew :examples:counter:test       # runs the devnet test too, now that DevKit answers
```

`DevKit` (in `examples/devkit`) builds a runtime for DevKit and funds fresh accounts from its faucet; the
[quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/#run-it-on-devkit) shows a trimmed copy for your own project. Use fresh
accounts per test, keep the TTL short (DevKit's time horizon is minutes), and expect each call to take a few seconds.

The JOUST build adds two switches for these tests:

| Property | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-PjoustFixtures` | Records every transaction the examples' tests build, with the chain reads behind it, into `fixtures/m0/<example>` (the oracle the JavaScript runtime is checked against; ADR-0015 M0). DevKit must be running |
| `-Pjoust.dumpTx=<dir>` | Writes each submitted transaction's CBOR to `<dir>` |

##### When a test fails

- **`assertAccepted` fails:** the message lists each script, `ok` or `REJECTED`, with its CPU and memory, the
  traces and the error. `Require` messages appear in the traces.
- **Which generated check failed?** Build with the processor option `-Ajoust.traces=true`: every failing check then
  traces its name (larger scripts; for debugging only). For example:

  ```groovy
  tasks.named('compileJava', JavaCompile) {
      options.compilerArgs += ['-Ajoust.traces=true']
  }
  ```

- **`-Pjoust.failedTerm`** (JOUST build) adds the failing UPLC term to the harness output.
- **The JVM accepts, the validator rejects** (or the reverse) on the same input: that is a divergence between the two
  runs. Look for `byte[]` compared with `.equals`, or arithmetic outside `BigInteger`; see [Java](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/java/).

##### JavaScript tests

The npm side is tested with Node's built-in runner, `node --test`, against DevKit.

**Your npm project:**

A project made by `create-joust` has `test/counter.test.js`. Build and deploy first, then run it:

```sh
npm run build
npm run deploy
npm test          # node --test test/*.test.js
```

```js title="test/counter.test.js"
const counter = new Counter(rt.options('app.Counter'));
const { instance } = await counter.deploy(wallet, {});
await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 5n });
await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 2n });
assert.equal((await instance.state()).count, 7n);
await assert.rejects(instance.increment(wallet, { by: 0n }), /increment must be positive/);
await instance.close(wallet);
assert.equal(await instance.state(), null);
```

**JOUST's own packages:**

```sh
(cd js/state-client && npm install && npm test)      # codec and verifier; CI runs these
(cd js/joust-runtime && npm install && npm test)     # the runtime engine on DevKit, Blockfrost and Ogmios providers
(cd js/joust && npm install && npm test)             # joust dev/serve, and the template's page in Chromium
```

`js/joust-runtime/test/devkit.test.js` runs Counter and Bank from Node with no JVM, and checks that every
tampered variant of an engine-built transaction is refused before the wallet is asked to sign.

###### Pages in a browser

Node tests cannot catch a page that fails to load. `js/joust/test/page.test.js` drives the template's page in
Chromium with Playwright, on DevKit: it connects the in-page DevKit key, tops it up, creates a counter, increments
it, sees the contract refuse `+0`, and closes it, with every transaction prepared in the page's worker and verified
before signing. It also runs the built page as static files (with its engine checked against the hashes pinned in
the page) and a MerkleMap contract whose mirror survives a reload. The tests skip themselves when DevKit is not
reachable. If Playwright has no browser yet, install Chromium with `npx playwright install chromium`.

The dApp example runs its page flows from Gradle: `DappDevnetTest` drives `examples/dapp/frontend/e2e/run.mjs` in
Node on DevKit, including a malicious prepare service whose every transaction the page must refuse.

> **Tip:** 

A good test file for a new contract has, for each method: a JVM test of the happy path and of each `Require`; a
harness test that is accepted and runs `Attacks.assertAllRejected`; a harness test per rule the validator must
enforce (`assertRejected`); and one DevKit test of the whole lifecycle.

## Building apps: Java

### Java off-chain runtime

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/apps/java-runtime/

`julc-state-runtime` is the off-chain half of JOUST for Java applications. The processor generates a typed
`<Name>Client` per contract; the client fills in a call and the runtime does the rest: it finds the instance's state
UTxO, runs your method on the JVM, builds the transaction with cardano-client-lib (CCL) QuickTx, checks it, signs,
submits, waits for it on chain, and retries if the state moved under it.

This page shows how to use it. Every class and method named here is listed in the
[Java runtime API reference](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/java-runtime-api/).

##### Configure a StateRuntime

A `StateRuntime` holds everything a client needs to talk to a network. It is immutable and shared by every client;
build one per network with `StateRuntime.builder(backend)`.

Against a local Yaci DevKit, the way the examples' `DevKit.runtime()` does it:

```java title="examples/devkit/.../DevKit.java (abridged)"
BackendService backend = new BFBackendService("http://localhost:8080/api/v1/", "dummy-key");   // Yaci Store
SlotChainTime time = new SlotChainTime(0, startSec * 1000, Math.round(slotLengthSec * 1000), backend);
StateRuntime runtime = StateRuntime.builder(backend)
        .network(Networks.testnet())
        .chainTime(time)
        .ttl(Duration.ofSeconds(20))
        .evaluator(new JulcTransactionEvaluator(
                new DefaultUtxoSupplier(backend.getUtxoService()),
                new DefaultProtocolParamsSupplier(backend.getEpochService()),
                new DefaultScriptSupplier(backend.getScriptService()),
                new SlotConfig(time.zeroSlot(), time.zeroTimeMs(), time.slotLengthMs())))
        .log(msg -> System.out.println("  [joust] " + msg))
        .build();
```

`startSec` and `slotLengthSec` come from DevKit's admin API
(`GET http://localhost:10000/local-cluster/api/admin/devnet`, fields `startTime` and `slotLength`); the
[quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/#run-it-on-devkit) has a complete helper.

Against the preview testnet through Blockfrost, the clock is preview's genesis (system start 1666656000, one-second
slots from slot 0, as `js/joust/src/config.js` pins it):

```java
String projectId = System.getenv("BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID");
BackendService backend = new BFBackendService(Constants.BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_URL, projectId);
StateRuntime runtime = StateRuntime.builder(backend)
        .network(Networks.preview())
        .chainTime(new SlotChainTime(0, 1_666_656_000_000L, 1000, backend))
        .build();
```

`Constants` is `com.bloxbean.cardano.client.backend.blockfrost.common.Constants`, from
`cardano-client-backend-blockfrost`. Without an evaluator, QuickTx asks the backend to compute script budgets.

What the options mean:

| Builder method | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `chainTime(ChainTime)` | required | Slot and POSIX time conversion, and the chain tip. The runtime picks slots first and derives the milliseconds `Ctx` carries from them |
| `network(Network)` | `Networks.testnet()` | Addresses are built for this network |
| `evaluator(TransactionEvaluator)` | none (the backend evaluates) | Computes script budgets; the examples use JuLC's local evaluator |
| `ttl(Duration)` | 10 minutes | The validity window of calls that read `Ctx` or time annotations, clamped to the contract's `maxValidityMs`. Must stay inside the network's time horizon: about 36 h on mainnet, minutes on DevKit |
| `maxRetries(int)` | 3 | How often a call is rebuilt when the node rejected it because the state moved |
| `confirmTimeout(Duration)` | 90 s | How long to wait for a submitted transaction to appear on chain |
| `address(byte[] pkh, String bech32)` | none | Pay this key hash at this address instead of its enterprise address |
| `log(Consumer<String>)` | silent | Progress messages (`submitted ...`, retries) |
| `referenceScript(Utxo)` | none | A known reference-script UTxO, so contracts skip scanning their address for it |
| `onBuilt(Consumer<BuiltTx>)` | none | Observes every transaction the runtime builds |
| `mapStore`, `mapStorePath`, `mapProver` | RocksDB at `./.joust/mpf` | Where [MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/) keep their nodes |

##### Deploy and call

Every generated client has the same shape. For the counter:

```java title="examples/counter/.../CounterApp.java"
CounterClient counter = CounterClient.deploy(runtime, alice);   // @Init: creates an instance, alice signs and pays
counter.increment(bob, BigInteger.valueOf(5));                   // @Action: (caller, arguments...)
counter.reset(alice);                                            // @Action @OnlyOwner
BigInteger n = counter.count();                                  // @View: reads the state, no transaction
var closed = counter.close(alice);                               // @Destroy: burns the token, pays out
```

The methods follow from the contract:

| Contract | Generated |
|---|---|
| `@Init` with arguments `a, b` | `static <Name>Client deploy(StateRuntime runtime, Account callerAccount, a, b [, BigInteger payLovelace])` |
| `@Action` / `@Destroy` with arguments `a` | `CallResult<State> name(Account callerAccount, a [, BigInteger payLovelace] [, Value payAssets] [, Account... cosigners])` |
| `@View` with arguments `a` | `T name(a)`: runs on the current state, off chain |
| (always) | `static at(runtime, instanceId)`, `static contract(runtime)`, `state()`, `lovelace()`, `fullValue()`, `instanceId()`, `instance()`, and `SPEC` |

`payLovelace` appears when the method is `@Payable`, `payAssets` when it takes native assets (`Funds`),
`cosigners` with `@Quorum`, and an `Authorization` with `@AuthorizedBy`. A contract with `@Params` takes the params
record in `deploy`, `at` and `contract`:

```java title="examples/vault/.../VaultApp.java"
var vault = VaultClient.deploy(runtime, alice, BigInteger.valueOf(unlockAt), ADA.multiply(BigInteger.TEN));   // @Payable init
vault.deposit(bob, ADA.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(5)));                                                       // @Payable action
```

```java title="examples/treasury/.../TreasuryClient.java (generated signatures)"
public static TreasuryClient deploy(StateRuntime runtime, Treasury.Config params, Account callerAccount,
                                    JulcList<byte[]> council, BigInteger quorum, BigInteger payLovelace)
public CallResult<Treasury.State> pay(Account callerAccount, byte[] to, BigInteger amount, Account... cosigners)
public CallResult<Treasury.State> freeze(Account callerAccount, boolean frozen, Authorization authorization)
```

Accounts are CCL `Account`s (`new Account(Networks.testnet(), mnemonic)`). The caller pays the fee, signs when the
method needs it (`Ctx` or a signer annotation), and is `ctx.caller()`.

###### Results

Each action and destroy returns a `CallResult<S>`:

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `txHash()` | The transaction, included on chain |
| `state()` | The state after the call; `null` after a destroy |
| `payouts()` | The `Payout`s the contract made |
| `events()`, `events(Class)` | The events the method emitted ([ADR-0009](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/)) |

###### Reconnect to an instance

An instance is identified by its id, the hex name of its thread token. Keep `counter.instanceId()` and reconnect
later, from any process:

```java title="examples/counter/.../CounterDevnetTest.java"
var again = CounterClient.at(runtime, counter.instanceId());
again.reset(alice);
```

##### Read state

| Call | Reads |
|---|---|
| `client.state()` | The current state, decoded from the inline datum |
| `client.<view>(...)` | A `@View`, computed from the current state on the JVM |
| `client.lovelace()` | Lovelace the state UTxO holds, deposit included |
| `client.fullValue()` | Everything it holds: lovelace, the thread token, native assets |
| `client.instance().utxo()` | The state UTxO itself (a CCL `Utxo`) |

Each read queries the chain, so two reads can see two different states if someone calls in between. When an
instance has been destroyed (or never existed), reads throw `InstanceNotFoundException`.

##### Errors

| Exception | Means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `RequireException` (`julc-state-api`) | A rule failed on the JVM: your `Require.that`, a signer or time annotation, a payout rule. Nothing was submitted | Show `getMessage()` to the user |
| `ContentionException` | The state kept moving; gave up after `maxRetries` | Retry later, or use [batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/) for hot state |
| `SubmitException` | The builder failed or the node rejected the transaction; nothing was accepted | Inspect the message; safe to rebuild |
| `PendingTransactionException` | Submitted, but not seen on chain in time. It may still land | Check `txHash()` before trying again; for a keyed call, look up every hash in `attempts()` |
| `InstanceNotFoundException` | No UTxO holds the instance's token | The instance was destroyed, or the id is wrong |

All but `RequireException` extend `JoustException`.

> **A retried call runs against the new state:** 

When the runtime retries after contention, it re-runs your method on the state it finds. If a call must not go
through at a different state (a swap at a worse price), put the bound in the arguments and check it with `Require`:
the DEX's swaps take a `minOut`.

##### Where payouts go

A payout names a 28-byte key hash. The runtime decides the address:

- **The caller, holding keys here:** their **enterprise** address (same payment key, no stake key). QuickTx takes
  the fee from outputs at the fee payer's own address, so a payout sent there would be under-paid.
- **The caller, as a `WalletAccount`:** the address the wallet gave, which the wallet shows. Prepared transactions
  restore those payouts after balancing.
- **Anyone else:** the address registered with the builder's `address(pkh, bech32)`, else their enterprise address.

Funds at an enterprise address are spendable with the same key, but some wallets list only base addresses. The
examples move them with `DevKit.sweepEnterprise(account)`.

##### Below the client: handles and instances

The generated client is a thin wrapper. When you need more, use what it wraps:

```java
StateContractHandle<Counter.State> contract = CounterClient.contract(runtime);
contract.address();                     // the script address every instance lives at
contract.policyId();                    // = the script hash
contract.ensureReferenceScript(payer);  // publish the script once (deploy does this too)
StateInstance<Counter.State> inst = contract.at(instanceId);
inst.utxo(); inst.state(); inst.lovelace(); inst.value();
inst.view(s -> Counter.count(s));       // any function of the state
```

Before a wallet user can call a contract, its reference script must be on chain, because the prepare path cannot
publish it (the wallet's keys are not there). Publish it with `ensureReferenceScript(account)` (the dApp's server does this at start), let a first
Java `deploy` do it, or have a wallet sign the transaction `prepareReferenceScript(payerAddress)` returns (null when
the script is already there).

Owned objects and intents have their own handles (`OwnedObject`, `IntentHandle`, `Batcher`), which the generated
clients expose as typed methods, for example `BankClient.open(...)` returning an `AccountObject`, and
`PoolClient.donateIntent(...)`, `batch(...)`, `pendingIntents()`. See [Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/) and
[Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/).

Keyed objects (ADR-0016) use `KeyedList` and `KeyedObject`: the generated
client offers, for example, `RegistryClient.claim(...)` returning an `EntryObject`, `entry(key)`, `entryExists(key)`
and `entryKeys()`. Every keyed operation spends one designated wallet input in all its attempts, so a retry can never
land twice. See [Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/#calling-keyed-objects-from-java).

##### Several calls in one transaction: Compose

`Compose` runs ordinary client calls into **one atomic transaction**: they all land, or none does. Each validator
still checks only its own transition, so composing adds no trust.

```java title="examples/oracle/.../OracleDevnetTest.java"
String tx = Compose.of(runtime, buyer)
        .add(() -> shop.buy(buyer, BigInteger.ONE, BigInteger.valueOf(3_000_000)))
        .add(() -> oracle2.post(publisher2, BigInteger.valueOf(5_000_000)))
        .submit();
```

`Compose.of(runtime, payer)` takes the account that pays the fee. It runs the calls twice: once to learn each call's
validity window, then again in the intersection, so every `Ctx` matches the final transaction. It refuses, before
submitting:

- the same UTxO spent by two calls;
- two calls minting under one policy;
- calls whose validity windows do not overlap;
- a key that signs for more than one call (its signature would count for every `@SignedBy` in the transaction),
  unless you call `allowSharedSigners()`.

Composition is how [deposits](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/), [migrations](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/upgrades/) and moves of owned objects
between instances run. See [Reads and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/).

##### Browser wallets: WalletAccount and PreparedTx

A user with a CIP-30 browser wallet (Eternl, Lace, ...) keeps their keys in the wallet. To call a contract for them,
the runtime builds the transaction **unsigned**, for the wallet to sign:

1. **Name the caller by address.** `WalletAccount.of(bech32, network)` is an `Account` known only by its address
   (the wallet's `getChangeAddress()`). It fails closed: every key method throws.

2. **Prepare.** Wrap the calls in `Compose` and call `prepare()` instead of `submit()`. The payer and every caller
   must be `WalletAccount`s; a call that needs a key held by the server (a co-signer, an authorization) is refused.

3. **Sign in the wallet.** Give `prepared.cbor()` to the wallet's `signTx(cbor, true)`. It returns a witness set
   holding only its signatures.

4. **Submit.** `prepared.submit(witnessSet)` checks each signature against the transaction hash, adds them without
   re-encoding the body, submits and waits. Or `prepared.withWitnesses(witnessSet)` returns the signed CBOR for the
   wallet's own `submitTx`.

```java title="examples/wallet/.../WalletDevnetTest.java"
var ann = WalletAccount.of(annKeys.baseAddress(), Networks.testnet());
var counter = CounterClient.deploy(runtime, admin);

var prepared = Compose.of(runtime, ann).add(() -> counter.increment(ann, BigInteger.TWO)).prepare();
String witness = cip30SignTx(annKeys, prepared.cbor());     // what the wallet's signTx(cbor, true) returns
String txHash = prepared.submit(witness);
```

`PreparedTx` also exposes `txHash()`, `requiredSigners()` (hex key hashes that must sign), `validTo()` (the last
valid slot: sign and submit before it), `plan()` and a copy of the `transaction()`. A witness set that carries
anything but signatures, a signature by the wrong key or over another transaction, or a missing required signer is
refused before submission.

Pages should not trust whoever prepared the transaction: [JavaScript clients](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/) verify
every prepared transaction against the contract's description before asking the wallet. See [Wallets](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/).

##### The prepare service: julc-state-server

`julc-state-server` serves your generated clients over HTTP, so a JavaScript page can have transactions prepared for
its user's wallet. It holds no keys and never sees a signed transaction: pages verify, sign and submit through their
wallets.

```java title="examples/dapp/.../DappServer.java (abridged)"
JoustServer server = JoustServer.builder(runtime)
        .contract(CounterClient.class)
        .contract(BankClient.class)
        .allowOrigin("http://localhost:5174")
        .staticFiles(frontend.resolve("dist"))          // optional: serve the built page too
        .preparesPerMinute(30)
        .build()
        .start("127.0.0.1", 8095);
```

| Endpoint | Request | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/contracts` | | Each served contract's deployment: policy, address, network, reference script |
| `GET /api/description?contract=` | The contract's class name | Its description |
| `POST /api/prepare` | `{ contract, kind, method, instance, object, args, pay, address }` | `{ cbor, txHash, validTo, signers, plan, instance?, object? }` |
| `POST /api/view` | `{ contract, instance, view, args }` | `{ value }` (`view` null: the state) |

`kind` is `init`, `action`, `destroy`, `ownedInit`, `ownedAction` or `ownedDestroy`; `address` is the wallet's
address; `contract` is the contract's fully qualified class name, e.g. `org.julclang.state.examples.counter.Counter`.
Each prepare runs the call through the generated client exactly as Java code would, inside `Compose.prepare()`.

The service applies a per-client rate limit (`preparesPerMinute`, default 30; `viewsPerMinute`, default 120), a bound
on concurrent prepares (`concurrentPrepares`, default 4), a 64 KiB request limit and a strict CORS allow-list
(`allowOrigin`, exact match). Calls that need a co-signer (`@Quorum`, `@AuthorizedBy`) are refused. `handler(path,
handler)` adds your own endpoints (the dApp adds a chain proxy and a DevKit top-up).

> **Note:** 

A JavaScript app can also prepare transactions with no server at all: the runtime engine runs JOUST's runtime in Node
or a page worker. See [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/).

##### Debugging

- `log(...)` on the builder prints each submission and each retry.
- `onBuilt(...)` sees every transaction the runtime builds, before it is submitted or returned.
- `-Djoust.dumpTx=<dir>` writes each submitted transaction's CBOR to `<dir>/<txHash>.cbor`.
- A contract built with `-Ajoust.traces=true` traces the name of each failing validator check (larger scripts;
  debugging only).
