## Building apps: JavaScript

### JavaScript clients

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

A JavaScript app calls a JOUST contract through three parts that do not trust one another:

- a **client** (generated, or `JoustContract`) that holds the contract's description and its deployment;
- a **prepare service** that builds the unsigned transaction: the runtime engine in Node or in a page's worker, or a
  Java service over HTTP;
- a **chain view** the client reads on its own, to verify what the service built.

Every call goes the same way: encode the call from the description, have the service prepare it, **verify** it, show
it for review, have the wallet sign, submit, and wait for the chain. This page covers each part. For pages
specifically, see [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/); for wallets, [Wallets](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/).

##### Generated clients

`joust build` writes a client for each contract next to its description: `build/joust/<Contract>.js` and
`<Contract>.d.ts`. The module inlines the description, so the page **pins** it: a service can never hand the page a
different contract to verify against.

For a contract built with Gradle, generate the same client from the description the processor writes
(`META-INF/joust/<package>.<Contract>.json`) with `joust-gen`, the bin of `@julclang/state-client`:

```sh
npx joust-gen build/classes/java/main/META-INF/joust/com.example.Counter.json --out src/generated
#### joust-gen <description.json>... --out <dir> [--import <module>]
```

`--import` replaces the module the client imports `JoustContract` from (default `@julclang/state-client`). Both
`joust build` and `joust-gen` call `generate(description)` from `@julclang/state-client/codegen`.

###### What a client contains

For a contract `C`:

| Generated | From | Methods |
|---|---|---|
| `class C` | the contract | `constructor(options)`, `deploy(wallet, args, pay?)` (the `@Init`), `at(instanceId)`, `contract` (the `JoustContract`) |
| `class CInstance` | one instance | `id`, `read()`, `state()`, one method per `@Action` and `@Destroy` |
| method of a `@Batched` action | | submits an intent (see [Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/)) |
| method of a `@Quorum` or `@AuthorizedBy` action | | takes a further `opts`: `{ cosigners, governor }` |
| `@OwnedInit` methods, a lookup method, `objects()` | owned objects | on `CInstance`; each creation returns `{ ..., object }` |
| `class C<Type>Object` | one owned object | `id`, `read()`, one method per owned action and destroy |

`pay` appears only on payable methods. Since ADR-0015 M4 every call is generated, including those that need MerkleMap
proofs, foreign reads, sends, moves, deposits and batches: the engine prepares them and the page verifier covers each.

```js
import { Bank } from './build/joust/Bank.js';

const bank = new Bank({ service, chain, deployment });
const { instance } = await bank.deploy(wallet, { withdrawLimit: 50_000_000n });
const { object: account } = await instance.open(wallet, {}, { lovelace: 10_000_000n });
await account.withdraw(wallet, { amount: 2_000_000n });
console.log(await account.read());   // { ref, type: 'Account', value: { ... }, lovelace }
```

##### `JoustContract`

The generated classes are thin wrappers. You can use `JoustContract` from `@julclang/state-client` directly, with a
description you load yourself:

```js
import { JoustContract, httpService, blockfrostChain } from '@julclang/state-client';

const counter = new JoustContract({
  description,            // the contract's description, bundled with the app
  deployment,             // { contract, policy, address, networkId, referenceScripts }, bundled
  service,                // a prepare service
  chain,                  // the app's own chain view
  onReview: async ({ contract, call, report, txHash }) => { /* show it; throw to cancel */ },
});
const { instance } = await counter.deploy(wallet, {});
await counter.at(instance).call(wallet, 'increment', { by: 3n });
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `description` | the contract's description (never fetched from the service) |
| `deployment` | `{ contract, policy, address, networkId, referenceScripts }`, from `deployments.<network>.json`; also `params`, `mapVerifier`, `outputVerifier` when the contract has them, and optionally `slotConfig` (below) |
| `service` | a prepare service: `engineService`, `engineWorker` or `httpService` |
| `chain` | a chain view: `chainOf(provider)` or `blockfrostChain(url)` |
| `onReview` | `async (review) => void`, called after verification and before signing; throw to cancel |
| `limits` | overrides of the verifier's limits (`DEFAULT_LIMITS`, below) |
| `requirePlan` | `false` to accept a service that sends no plan (a JOUST service always does) |

###### Calls

| Method | What it does | Resolves to |
|---|---|---|
| `contract.deploy(wallet, args?, pay?)` | creates an instance with the `@Init` method | `{ txHash, report, instance }` (the id, hex) |
| `contract.at(id)` | an instance (`JoustInstance`) | |
| `instance.call(wallet, name, args?, pay?, opts?)` | an action or destroy; `opts`: `{ cosigners, governor }` | `{ txHash, report }` |
| `instance.create(wallet, name, args?, pay?)` | an `@OwnedInit` creation | `{ txHash, report, object }` |
| `instance.object(id)` | an owned object (`JoustObject`) | |
| `object.call(wallet, name, args?, pay?)` | an owned action or destroy | `{ txHash, report }` |
| `instance.keyed(type)` | a keyed type's list (`JoustKeyedList`): `insert`, `find`, `exists`, `keys`, `object(key).call(...)`; see [Keyed objects in JavaScript](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/keyed-objects-js/) (on `main`, next release) | |
| `instance.intent(wallet, name, args?, pay?, opts?)` | locks an intent for a `@Batched` action; `opts.deadline` in ms (default 30 minutes) | `{ txHash, report, created, intent }` |
| `instance.cancelIntent(wallet, intentId)` | withdraws the wallet's pending intent | `{ txHash, report, created }` |
| `instance.batch(wallet, opts?)` | as a batcher, applies up to `opts.max` (8) intents | `{ txHash, report, applied, skipped }` |
| `contract.registerStake(wallet)` | registers the contract's stake credential (ADR-0010) | the hash, or `null` if registered already |
| `contract.delegate(wallet, pool, opts?)` | delegates its stake through its `@Certify` handler | `{ txHash, report }` |
| `contract.collect(wallet, opts?)` | withdraws its rewards through `@Withdraw`; `opts.amount`, `opts.args` | `{ txHash, report }` |

`wallet` is always a [CIP-30](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/) API object. `pay` is `{ lovelace?, assets? }`, with assets as
`[[policyHex, [[assetNameHex, quantity]]]]`. A missing argument, a payment to a method that is not payable, or a wallet
on another network is refused before anything is prepared.

###### Reading state

| Method | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `instance.read()` | `{ ref, state, lovelace }`, or `null` once destroyed |
| `instance.state()` | the decoded state, or `null` |
| `instance.objects()` | every owned object of the instance: `[{ id, type, value, lovelace }]` |
| `object.read()` | `{ ref, type, value, lovelace }`, or `null` once closed |
| `instance.pendingIntents()` | the instance's intents on chain: `[{ intent, ref, owner, deadline, received, call, lovelace }]` |

These read the chain view, by the instance's or object's token at the deployment's address, and decode with the
description. A MerkleMap field decodes as its root (`{ root, reads, writes }`); read its values through a mirror (see
[MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/)).

> **Views:** 
The description lists the contract's `@View` methods (`x-joust.views`), but the JavaScript client generates no view
methods yet. Read the state with `state()` and compute in JavaScript, or call a Java prepare service's view endpoint
through `httpService(url).view({ contract, instance, view, args })` (`julc-state-server`'s `POST /api/view`).

##### In Node: `joustRuntime`

In Node, `@julclang/joust-runtime` gives you everything at once: the engine as a prepare service, a chain view over
one provider, and the deployments. This is the template's test:

```js title="test/counter.test.js"
import { joustRuntime, devWallet, devkitTopUp } from '@julclang/joust-runtime';
import { Counter } from '../build/joust/Counter.js';

const rt = joustRuntime({ chainUrl: deployed.chain, contracts, clock: deployed.clock, networkId: deployed.networkId,
  deployments: deployed.contracts, ttlMs: 20_000 });
const wallet = devWallet({ chain: rt.chain, mnemonic: generateMnemonic(wordlist, 256) });
await devkitTopUp(wallet.address, 100, config.networks.devkit.admin, { chain: rt.chain });

const counter = new Counter(rt.options('app.Counter'));
const { instance } = await counter.deploy(wallet, {});
await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 5n });
```

`rt.options(contract)` returns `{ service, chain, deployment }` for a generated client, finding the deployment by the
contract's full title (`app.Counter`) or its simple name. The runtime's members:

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `rt.provider` (also `rt.api`) | the chain provider: the one given, or `blockfrostProvider(chainUrl, { projectId })` |
| `rt.chain` | `chainOf(provider)`: the chain view the verifier reads |
| `rt.service` | the engine as a prepare service (each request gets its deployment's `@Params` and every pinned reference script) |
| `rt.deployments` | the deployments, by contract title |
| `rt.options(contract, extra?)` | `{ service, chain, deployment, ...extra }` for a client |
| `rt.ensureDeployment(contract, wallet, params?)` | the contract's deployment, publishing its reference script first if it is not on chain; also publishes JOUST's map and output verifiers when the contract needs them |
| `rt.ensureGovernor(name, params, wallet)` | a plain JuLC validator from `validators.json` as an `@AuthorizedBy` governor: parameters applied, stake credential registered once |
| `rt.compose(wallet, steps, extra?)` | several calls in one transaction |

Every option of `joustRuntime` is in the [`@julclang/joust-runtime` reference](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/joust-runtime/#joustruntimeoptions).
`ensureDeployment` checks the publishing transaction before the wallet signs it: it may pay only the contract's
address (holding the script) and the payer.

###### Composition

`rt.compose` puts several spending calls into one transaction ([Reads and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/)).
Each step names a `JoustContract` (a generated client's `.contract`), the method, the instance and the arguments. From
the Fees example's flow:

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js"
await rt.compose(buyer, [
  { contract: stall, method: 'sell', instance: stallId, args: { price: 10n * ADA }, pay: { lovelace: 10n * ADA } },
  { contract: pot, method: 'collect', instance: potId, args: {} },
]);
```

`verifyComposed` checks each call against its own description and deployment, then the transaction as a whole.
`extra` may carry `onReview` (called with `{ calls, report, txHash }`) and `limits`.

##### Prepare services

A prepare service is any object with `prepare(request)`. Clients do not care which one they get:

| Service | Where the engine runs | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `engineService(o)` (`@julclang/joust-runtime`; `rt.service`) | in this Node process | tests, scripts, backends |
| `engineWorker(worker, o)` (`@julclang/joust-runtime/page`) | in a page's Web Worker | pages ([Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/)) |
| `httpService(url)` (`@julclang/state-client`) | in a server: `POST <url>/prepare` | a Java prepare service ([Java runtime](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/java-runtime/)), or `joust dev`'s `/joust/service` |

The request is plain JSON, which the client builds:

```js
{
  contract: 'app.Counter',            // the description's title
  kind: 'action',                     // init, action, destroy, ownedInit, ownedAction, ownedDestroy, ...
  method: 'increment',
  instance: '9f1c...', object: null,
  args: { by: '1' },                  // JSON conventions (below)
  pay: { lovelace: '0', assets: [] },
  address: 'addr_test1...',           // the wallet's funding address
  walletUtxos: [ /* the UTxOs the wallet reports there */ ],
  // cosigners: [keyHash...], governor: { script, signers }   when the call has them
}
```

It answers `{ cbor, txHash, validTo, signers, plan }`, plus `instance` or `object` for a creation. The engine builds
only from `walletUtxos`, the UTxOs the wallet itself reports at its funding address, so it never picks an input the
wallet does not know about.

##### Verification

Before `onReview`, and before the wallet is asked, the client verifies the prepared transaction against what it knows
itself: the pinned description and deployment, the wallet's UTxOs, the chain (tip, protocol parameters, the outputs the
transaction reads) and the call it asked for. Nothing the service says is taken on trust: the transaction hash is the
client's own, computed from the body bytes, and the service's plan must match the plan the client derives.

| Call | Verifier (`@julclang/state-client`) |
|---|---|
| creations, actions, destroys, owned calls | `verifyPrepared` |
| `rt.compose` | `verifyComposed` |
| intents, cancels, batches | `verifyIntent`, `verifyCancel`, `verifyBatch` |
| `delegate`, `collect` | `verifyPurpose` |
| `registerStake`, `ensureGovernor` | `verifyRegistration` |

For a single call, `verifyPrepared` refuses:

- inputs other than the wallet's own UTxOs and the instance or object the call targets;
- a redeemer that is not exactly the call, with the page's arguments, on the target input; a `Ctx` whose caller is not
  this wallet, or whose received amount is not the page's payment;
- certificates, votes, proposals, treasury donations, metadata, and withdrawals other than zero withdrawals to the
  verifiers or governor the deployment pins;
- a mint by an action that does not mint; anything but its own token burned by a destroy; anything but its new token
  minted by a creation; any mint under another policy;
- anything but exactly one continuation of the instance or object, with an inline datum that decodes;
- a transaction that does not balance; a wallet losing more than its payment plus the fee (plus the minimum ADA of a
  new UTxO); others receiving more than the script releases;
- a fee above the protocol's for this size and budget (times 1.2, plus `feeMargin`) or above `maxFee`; execution
  budgets above the protocol's limits;
- collateral that is not the wallet's, not returned to the wallet, or above `maxCollateral`;
- a validity interval that is too long or starts too late (and, for a call that reads `Ctx`, one backdated);
- required signers other than the wallet's keys and the co-signers the page named; reference inputs the page does not
  know.

The pinned validator checks the rest on chain: that the next state is what the method computes, that payouts are paid
and that the script's value is conserved.

###### `VerificationError`

A refused transaction throws `VerificationError`. Its `problems` is a list of reasons; its `report` is what the
verifier read.

```js
import { VerificationError } from '@julclang/state-client';

try {
  await instance.increment(wallet, { by: 1n });
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof VerificationError) console.error('refused before signing:', e.problems);
  else throw e;   // a contract refusal (Require.that's message), a wallet decline, a chain error
}
```

`rt.compose` refuses with an `Error` carrying the same `problems` and `report` fields.

| `report` field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `fee` | the transaction's fee (lovelace, `bigint`) |
| `walletNet` | what the wallet loses in lovelace, fee included; negative when it gains |
| `next` | the next state (or object value), decoded; `null` for a destroy |
| `redeemer` | the decoded redeemer |
| `created` | the new instance or object id, for a creation |
| `outputs` | the transaction's outputs: `[{ address, value }]` |
| `plan` | the plan the client derived from the transaction |

###### Limits

`limits` overrides any of `DEFAULT_LIMITS`:

| Limit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `maxCollateral` | `5_000_000n` | lovelace a failing script may cost the wallet |
| `maxValiditySlots` | `900` | the transaction must expire within this many slots of now (15 minutes) |
| `maxStartSlots` | `60` | its validity may start at most this many slots after now |
| `maxBackdateSlots` | `120` | a `Ctx` call's validity may start at most this many slots before now |
| `feeMargin` | `500_000n` | lovelace allowed over 1.2 times the protocol's fee |
| `maxFee` | `3_000_000n` | an absolute fee bound, which does not rely on the chain API's parameters |

"Now" is the chain's tip. Give the deployment a `slotConfig` (`{ zeroSlot, zeroTimeMs, slotLengthMs }`) and the
verifier also checks the validity against the page's own clock, so a lying chain API cannot stretch the window.

##### JSON conventions

Arguments, payments and decoded state use one JSON form, recorded in each description's `x-joust.encoding.json`:

| Schema | JavaScript value |
|---|---|
| integer | `bigint`, a decimal string, or a safe integer; decoded as `bigint` |
| bytes | lowercase hex string |
| record (constructor) | an object by field name |
| sealed variant | an object with `"$variant"` (its constructor's title) |
| `Bool` | `true` / `false` |
| `Optional` | `null` for none, else the value |
| list | an array |
| map | an array of `[key, value]` pairs, encoded in canonical key order |
| `Data` | hex CBOR of any Plutus data |

`toJson(value)` turns `bigint`s into decimal strings, so a value can go through `JSON.stringify`. Requests to a service
use it. To encode or decode by schema yourself, use `codec(description)`:

```js
import { codec } from '@julclang/state-client';

const c = codec(description);
const data = c.encode({ dataType: 'integer' }, 5n, 'by');   // Plutus data
const state = c.decode(description['x-joust'].state, inlineDatumHex);
```

  - [Pages: worker, Vite, static builds](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/)
  - [@julclang/state-client reference](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/state-client/)

### Wallets

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

JOUST never holds a user's keys. A transaction is prepared without them, verified by the page, and signed by the
user's wallet. To the client, a wallet is a **CIP-30 API object**: what a browser wallet extension's `enable()`
returns. CIP-30 is the Cardano standard for dApp-to-wallet communication; JOUST's clients use six of its calls:

| CIP-30 call | Used for |
|---|---|
| `getNetworkId()` | refusing a wallet on another network than the deployment |
| `getChangeAddress()`, `getUsedAddresses()` | the wallet's addresses and payment keys |
| `getUtxos()` | the wallet's UTxOs: the engine builds from them, the verifier checks against them |
| `signTx(cbor, true)` | a witness set for the prepared transaction (partial signing) |
| `submitTx(cbor)` | submitting the signed transaction |

Anything that implements these works: Eternl, Lace, any CIP-30 extension, the dev wallet below, or your own test
double.

##### Browser wallets

The template's page finds the browser's wallets with the Cardano Foundation's connector,
`@cardano-foundation/cardano-connect-with-wallet-core` (0.2.12, framework-independent). It lists the extensions,
including those injected after the page loads, and enables the chosen one with a network check:

```js title="page/main.js"
import { Wallet, NetworkType } from '@cardano-foundation/cardano-connect-with-wallet-core';
import { walletView } from '@julclang/state-client';

// Extensions inject themselves after load, some late: list them as they arrive.
Wallet.addEventListener('installedWalletExtensions', walletChoices);
Wallet.startInjectWalletListener();

// Connect the one the user chose (key: its name in window.cardano, such as "eternl" or "lace").
await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  Wallet.connect(key, net.networkId === 1 ? NetworkType.MAINNET : NetworkType.TESTNET, resolve, reject).catch(reject);
});
const api = await window.cardano[key].enable();
const view = await walletView(api);
if (view.networkId !== net.networkId) throw new Error(`the wallet is on network ${view.networkId}; this app is on ${net.network}`);
```

The connector only selects and enables a wallet. The verifier and the signing flow do not depend on it: any code that
ends with a CIP-30 API object works.

> **Browser wallets cannot join a DevKit:** 
Eternl and Lace connect to public networks only. On Yaci DevKit, use the [dev wallet](#the-dev-wallet); for a real
wallet, use [preview](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/deploy-preview/).

##### What the client reads from a wallet

`walletView(api)` takes a snapshot of the wallet:

```js
const view = await walletView(api);
// { api, networkId, change, addresses, keyHashes, utxos }
//   change      the change address (bech32)
//   addresses   the change address and the used addresses (bech32)
//   keyHashes   their payment key hashes (hex)
//   utxos       Map "txHash#index" -> { address, value: Map unit -> bigint, inlineDatum, datumHash }
```

From it the client picks the **funding address**: the change address when it holds lovelace, otherwise the wallet
address holding the most. The request to the service carries that address and `walletUtxos`, the UTxOs the wallet
itself reports there. The engine builds only from those, so it never spends an input the wallet does not know about.
This matters on public networks: chain APIs behind load balancers can lag one another, and a wallet keeps its own
index.

Payouts to the caller go to the funding address too. A contract may also send to the caller's key
(`ctx.caller()`): the verifier counts the enterprise address of one of the wallet's own payment keys as the
wallet's, so such an output is allowed. A wallet key under someone else's stake key is not.

##### Signing and submitting

1. The client verifies the prepared transaction. A refusal throws `VerificationError`; the wallet is not asked.
2. It calls `onReview` (below), if the client has one.
3. It asks the wallet for a witness set: `signTx(cbor, true)`. Co-signers' wallets, if the call has any, sign the
   same transaction.
4. It adds the witnesses to the **original** transaction bytes (`assemble`), refusing any change to the body, and
   checks that the signed transaction's hash is the one it computed before signing.
5. It submits through the user's wallet (`submitTx`) and checks the hash the wallet returns.
6. It waits for the chain view to show the transaction (`awaitTx`).

Because the body bytes never change after verification, the wallet signs exactly the transaction the page checked.

##### The review step

`onReview` runs after verification and before the wallet is asked. It is your place to show the user what the
transaction does, in your app's terms. Resolve to go on; throw to cancel.

```js
const counter = new Counter({ service, chain, deployment, onReview: async ({ contract, call, report, txHash }) => {
  // call:   { kind, meta (the description's entry), args, pay, instance?, object? }
  // report: { fee, walletNet, next, redeemer, created, outputs, ... }
  if (!confirm(`${contract}.${call.meta.name}: your wallet pays ${report.walletNet} lovelace (fee ${report.fee})`)) {
    throw new Error('cancelled before signing');
  }
} });
```

The [Counter dApp tutorial](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/counter-dapp/#6-the-review-dialog) shows the template's dialog. The wallet
shows its own prompt as well; the review step adds what only the page knows: which contract, which call, the next
state.

##### Co-signers

Methods with `@Quorum` or `@AuthorizedBy` need other keys to sign ([Authorization](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/)).
Pass their wallets, as CIP-30 API objects on the same network, in `opts.cosigners`:

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js"
await t.call(a, 'pay', { to: bob.keyHash, amount: 10n * ADA }, {}, { cosigners: [watched] });
```

Each co-signer is named by the payment key of its change address. The calling wallet counts towards a quorum already,
and naming a wallet twice is refused. The verifier requires every named co-signer to be a required signer, and every
required signer to be the wallet's key or a named co-signer. Each co-signer signs the same transaction before it is
submitted.

##### The dev wallet

`devWallet` (from `@julclang/state-client/devwallet`, re-exported by `@julclang/joust-runtime`) is a CIP-30 wallet
for development networks: one key from a mnemonic, with UTxOs read and transactions submitted through a chain view.

```js
import { devWallet } from '@julclang/state-client/devwallet';

const wallet = devWallet({ chain, mnemonic, networkId: 0 });
wallet.address;   // its base address (bech32)
wallet.keyHash;   // its payment key hash (hex)
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `chain` | (required) | the chain view it reads UTxOs from and submits through |
| `mnemonic` | `DEVKIT_MNEMONIC` | a BIP39 mnemonic; the default is DevKit's, whose genesis accounts are funded |
| `index` | `0` | the payment key `m/1852'/1815'/0'/0/<index>` (stake key `m/1852'/1815'/0'/2/0`) |
| `networkId` | `0` | `0` for test networks, `1` for mainnet |
| `confirm` | yes | `async (txHex) => boolean`, asked before signing, like a real wallet's prompt |

It derives keys as cardano-client-lib does, so the same mnemonic gives the same address on the JVM. It implements
`getNetworkId`, `getUtxos`, `getBalance`, `getCollateral` (none), `getUsedAddresses`, `getUnusedAddresses`,
`getChangeAddress`, `getRewardAddresses`, `signTx` and `submitTx`. `deriveAccount(mnemonic, index, networkId)` gives
the keys and addresses without a wallet.

The template's page uses it for its in-page DevKit key, kept in `localStorage`:

```js title="page/main.js"
const { devWallet } = await import('@julclang/state-client/devwallet');
const mnemonic = localStorage.getItem('joust.devkitKey') ?? generateMnemonic(wordlist, 256);
localStorage.setItem('joust.devkitKey', mnemonic);
app.api = devWallet({ chain, mnemonic, networkId: net.networkId });
```

The page's **Top up** button posts the address to `/dev/topup` on `joust dev` or `joust serve`, which funds it from
DevKit's faucet. In Node, `devkitTopUp(address, ada, adminUrl, { chain })` does the same, and falls back to DevKit's
genesis accounts when the faucet is dry. `joust deploy` uses a dev wallet too, with `JOUST_MNEMONIC` or a DevKit key it
keeps in `.joust/`.

> **Never use the dev wallet with real funds:** 
Its key lives in your page's JavaScript (and, in the template, in `localStorage`). It is for DevKit and for tests on
test networks only.

`@julclang/state-client/devwallet` loads libsodium (cardano-js-sdk's crypto) with a top-level await when it is
imported; the template imports it only when the user chooses the DevKit key.

##### Wallets in Java

On the JVM, a dApp backend that prepares transactions for browser wallets uses `WalletAccount`: an account that has
only an address, never a key, and fails closed if asked to sign. See the
[Java off-chain runtime](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/java-runtime/).

##### Security notes

- **Keys never enter the engine.** The runtime engine (Wasm, in Node or in a worker) receives addresses, UTxOs and
  co-signers' key hashes, never a key. Signing happens only in the wallet.
- **The page verifies, the wallet signs.** Every prepared transaction is verified against the pinned description and
  deployment and the wallet's own UTxOs before `signTx` is called. The engine, the service and the chain API are not
  trusted.
- **Collateral is bounded.** A transaction that runs a script names collateral, which the network takes only if a
  script fails. The verifier requires it to be the wallet's own UTxOs, with a collateral return to the wallet and at
  most 5 ADA at risk (`limits.maxCollateral`).
- **The wallet loses at most what the call says**: its payment and the fee (and a new UTxO's minimum ADA for a
  creation). Required signers are the wallet's and the named co-signers only; the transaction expires within 15
  minutes.
- **Networks are checked twice**: the connector checks the wallet's network type, and the client compares
  `getNetworkId()` with the deployment's.

### Pages: worker, Vite, static builds

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

A JOUST page prepares its own transactions. The runtime engine, about 20 MB of Wasm, runs in a Web Worker; the page
verifies every transaction the worker returns, then asks the user's wallet to sign. No backend builds anything: a
built page is static files plus a chain API. This page explains each piece: the worker, the Vite plugin, the
`virtual:joust/network` module, static builds and their integrity checks, and MerkleMap reads.

##### The pieces

![A JOUST page from the browser to the chain](../../../assets/diagrams/browser-path.svg)

| Piece | Package | Runs in |
|---|---|---|
| `engine.worker.js` (one import) | `@julclang/joust-runtime/worker` | the worker: loads the engine, keeps MerkleMap mirrors, prepares calls |
| `engineWorker(worker, options)` | `@julclang/joust-runtime/page` | the page: a prepare service that talks to the worker |
| the client, the verifier, the chain view | `@julclang/state-client` and the generated `<Contract>.js` | the page |
| `virtual:joust/network` and the browser polyfills | `@julclang/joust/vite` | the build (or `joust dev`'s Vite) |

`@julclang/joust-runtime/page` has no dependencies, so the page's own bundle does not grow with the engine.

##### The engine in a worker

The worker is one line:

```js title="page/engine.worker.js"
import '@julclang/joust-runtime/worker';
```

The page starts it as a module worker and wraps it:

```js title="page/main.js"
import { engineWorker } from '@julclang/joust-runtime/page';
import net from 'virtual:joust/network';

const service = engineWorker(new Worker(new URL('./engine.worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' }), {
  engine: net.engine, chain: net.chain, clock: net.clock, networkId: net.networkId, ttlMs: net.ttlMs,
  deployments: net.deployments, contracts: net.contracts, validators: net.validators,
});
await service.ready;   // the engine has loaded (once per page load)
```

`new URL('./engine.worker.js', import.meta.url)` is the pattern bundlers recognise: Vite builds the worker as its own
bundle. `engineWorker` returns:

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ready` | a promise that resolves once the engine has loaded in the worker |
| `prepare(request)` | a prepare service's `prepare`, so a generated client works unchanged |
| `mapValue(root, key, units?)` | a MerkleMap value from the worker's mirror ([below](#reading-merklemap-values)) |
| `deployments(d)` | new deployments for the calls that follow (after a redeploy) |
| `terminate()` | stops the worker; pending and later calls reject |

Its options are what the worker's runtime needs:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `engine` | `{ url, integrity: { script, wasm } }`: where `joust-runtime.js` is served (its `.wasm` beside it) and the two files' SRI hashes; or just a URL, unchecked |
| `contracts`, `validators` | `contracts.json` and `validators.json` as `joust build` writes them |
| `chain` | a Blockfrost-style chain API, absolute or relative to the page |
| `projectId` | a Blockfrost project id, only for a chain API that needs one and may see it |
| `clock`, `networkId`, `ttlMs` | the network's slot clock, id and the TTL of prepared transactions |
| `deployments` | `{ [contract]: deployment }` |
| `mirrorCache` | the IndexedDB database for MerkleMap mirrors (default `"joust-mirrors"`); `false` keeps them in memory |

URLs are resolved against the page, not the worker's script, which a bundler puts elsewhere.

###### The listening handshake

A module worker takes messages before its imports' top-level awaits settle (libsodium's, through
`@julclang/state-client`), and drops them silently. So the worker posts `{ joust: 'listening' }` once its message
handler is in place, and `engineWorker` posts nothing before it hears that. Each request then carries an id; the
worker answers `{ id, ok, value }` or `{ id, ok: false, error }`. A worker that cannot start at all (a module that fails
to load, memory) fires `error`, which rejects every pending and later call with `the engine worker failed: ...`.

###### Loading the engine

The engine is a GraalVM Web Image: a classic script that fetches its Wasm from its own URL plus `.wasm`. A module
worker cannot `importScripts`, so the worker fetches the script, sets `__filename` to its URL, and evaluates it in the
worker's global scope ([`js/joust-runtime/src/browser/engine.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/joust-runtime/src/browser/engine.js)).
Node-only modules have browser twins through `package.json` `imports` with the `browser` condition: `#engine` (this
loader) and `#file-map-store` (no file system in a page). Any bundler that honours the `browser` condition picks them.

The worker starts loading the engine as soon as it is initialised, so the first call does not wait for all 20 MB.

> **The worker is not trusted either:** 
The worker holds no keys. The page verifies every transaction it returns against the pinned description and
deployment before the wallet is asked, exactly as it would one from a remote service.

##### The Vite plugin

```js title="vite.config.js"
// The page (page/) under joust dev or vite build: @julclang/joust/vite makes the runtime packages work in browsers.
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { joust } from '@julclang/joust/vite';

const here = (p) => fileURLToPath(new URL(p, import.meta.url));

export default { root: here('page'), build: { outDir: here('dist'), emptyOutDir: true }, plugins: [joust({ root: here('.') })] };
```

`joust({ root, network })` takes the project's root (where `joust.config.json` and `build/joust` are; default the
working directory) and, for builds, the network (below). It does five things
([`js/joust/src/vite.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/joust/src/vite.js)):

- **Node polyfills.** cardano-js-sdk's crypto dependencies (`pbkdf2`, `safe-buffer`, `readable-stream`) expect Node's
  `buffer`, `events`, `util` and `stream`, and the `process` global; Aiken's MPF (the MerkleMap mirrors) uses
  `assert`. The plugin aliases them to their browser versions and injects the `Buffer` and `process` globals.
  Without them a page fails at load (`Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'from')`). Every polyfill is
  resolved from the plugin's own package by absolute path, so it works with any `node_modules` layout (npm, pnpm,
  linked packages).
- **One `Buffer` class.** The injected `Buffer` global and every `buffer`/`node:buffer` import resolve to the same
  module, so a library that checks `instanceof Buffer` (Aiken's MPF) accepts Buffers made elsewhere.
- **es2022.** The packages use top-level await, so the dev server's dependency bundling and builds target es2022.
- **Workers.** Workers are built as ES modules with the same aliases and globals. In a worker's bundle the globals are
  injected after the CommonJS conversion (`enforce: 'post'`), or a CommonJS dependency that uses `Buffer`
  (`serialize-error`) would lose its exports. The dependency scan includes `*.worker.js` files, so Vite does not
  discover the worker's dependencies at run time and reload the page.
- **The build's clients.** The page may import `../build/joust/Counter.js` from outside its own directory: the
  project root is in Vite's `server.fs.allow`.

And it provides `virtual:joust/network`.

##### `virtual:joust/network`

What the page runs on, as one default export:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `network` | the network's name (`devkit`, `preview`, ...) |
| `networkId` | `0` or `1` |
| `chain` | the chain API for the page: `/chain`, or the network's `pageChain` |
| `clock` | `{ zeroSlot, zeroTimeMs, slotLengthMs }` |
| `ttlMs` | how long prepared transactions stay valid |
| `explorer` | the network's block-explorer transaction URL, `{tx}` for the hash, or `null` |
| `deployments` | `{ [contract]: deployment }` |
| `contracts` | `contracts.json` |
| `validators` | `validators.json` (in builds) |
| `engine` | `{ url, integrity: { script, wasm } }` |

It is resolved differently in development and in a build:

**joust dev:**

Under `joust dev` the module fetches `/joust/network.json` and then the contracts when the page loads, with
`cache: 'no-store'`. A save redeploys, so a reload picks up the new deployment. `network.json` names the engine at
`/joust/engine/joust-runtime.js`, with hashes the dev server computes from the files it serves: development runs the
same integrity check as a build.

**vite build:**

In `vite build` the module is **inlined**, for one network, from `build/joust`: `contracts.json`,
`validators.json` if there is one, and `deployments.<network>.json`. The clock is the one `joust deploy` recorded, so
a build reads no chain. The network is chosen in this order:

1. the plugin's `network` option;
2. the `JOUST_NETWORK` environment variable;
3. Vite's mode, when it names a network (`vite build --mode preview`);
4. `joust.config.json`'s `network`.

A build fails if `contracts.json` or the network's deployments file is missing (`run joust build first`,
`deploy first`).

##### Static builds

```sh
npm run build:page          # vite build: the config's network (devkit)
npm run build:page:preview  # vite build --mode preview
```

- dist/
  - index.html
  - assets/ the page's bundle and the worker's bundle
  - joust/
    - engine-1a2b3c4d/
      - joust-runtime.js the engine's script
      - joust-runtime.js.wasm the engine's Wasm module

The plugin copies the engine's two files into `dist/joust/engine-<id>/`, where `<id>` is 8 hex characters derived
from the files' hashes: a new engine gets a new path, so caches never serve a stale one. The engine's URL in the page
follows Vite's `base`. The engine is loaded at run time and is not bundled; the worker's bundle itself measured 702 kB
in ADR-0015 §13.11.

`dist/` is plain static files. It needs, from wherever it is hosted:

- a **chain API** at the page's `chain`: `/chain` by default, a proxy that adds the Blockfrost project id; or a
  network's `pageChain`, an API a browser may call directly ([Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/));
- on DevKit, `/dev/topup` if the page offers a faucet button.

`joust serve` gives exactly that:

```sh
npm run serve               # joust serve: dist/ at http://127.0.0.1:5178, /chain, and on DevKit /dev/topup
```

It builds, deploys and bundles nothing, and has no engine route or prepare service. See the
[CLI](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/cli-and-projects/) and [Deploy to preview](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/deploy-preview/#5-host-it) for hosting.

##### SRI: the engine is checked by its hashes

The page's own code pins the engine's sha384 hashes (`net.engine.integrity`). The worker:

1. fetches the script with `fetch(url, { integrity: script })`;
2. while the engine loads, wraps the global `fetch` so that the one request for `<url>.wasm` carries
   `integrity: wasm` (the engine fetches its Wasm itself);
3. evaluates the script only after the browser has accepted its bytes.

A browser refuses a file whose bytes differ, wherever it is served from. The engine never starts, and `service.ready`
rejects with a message that the engine `does not match its integrity hash`. `page.test.js` checks this with two
tampered builds, one character of the script and one bit of the Wasm.

So the engine can sit on a CDN you do not control. And even an engine that passed its check is not trusted with the
wallet: the page verifies what it builds.

##### MerkleMap mirrors in the page

A contract with MerkleMaps keeps only each map's root on chain. The worker keeps the maps themselves, as **mirrors**
over Aiken's MPF, answers the engine's proof requests from them, and stores them in **IndexedDB** (database
`joust-mirrors`, through `level`'s browser build), so a reload or the next visit does not rebuild them. Without
IndexedDB, the worker warns and keeps them in memory. A map the page has never seen (another device, another user's
writes) is rebuilt from the chain's history, every claim checked against its root.
[MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/) explains how.

###### Reading MerkleMap values

A page reads a map value without a transaction through `mapValue`:

```js
const state = await token.at(id).state();                 // { admin, supply, balances: { root, reads, writes } }
const unit = deployment.policy + id;                      // the instance's token: its history rebuilds the map
const hex = await service.mapValue(state.balances.root, ownerKeyHash, [unit]);
const balance = hex === null ? 0n : BigInt('0x' + (hex || '0'));
```

`mapValue(root, key, units)` answers from the worker's mirror: the value as hex, or `null` when the key is absent. Keys
and values are the raw bytes the contract used, as hex. A root the mirror has not seen is first rebuilt from the
history of `units`. How to read the value depends on how the contract stored it: `MerkleMaps.putInt` stores a
non-negative integer as minimal big-endian bytes (zero is the empty byte string), as above.

##### Explorer links

Each network may name an `explorer`: a transaction page with `{tx}` for the hash. DevKit's default is Yaci Viewer
(`http://localhost:5173/transactions/{tx}`), preview's is Cardanoscan
(`https://preview.cardanoscan.io/transaction/{tx}`). The page gets it as `net.explorer` (or `null`):

```js title="page/main.js"
const txLink = (hash) => (net.explorer
  ? el('a', { href: net.explorer.replace('{tx}', hash), target: '_blank', rel: 'noopener' }, short(hash))
  : short(hash));
```

##### Without a worker

A page can also use a prepare service over HTTP: `joust dev` serves the engine in its own process at
`/joust/service`, so `httpService('/joust/service')` works during development. The page verifies that service's
transactions the same way. A built page has no such service: use the worker.

  - [Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/)
  - [MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/)
  - [@julclang/joust reference](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/joust-cli/)

### The joust CLI and projects

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/apps/cli-and-projects/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

`@julclang/joust` is the command line of a JOUST project. It compiles contracts with the toolchain engine (JOUST's
annotation processor and JuLC's compiler, compiled to Wasm), publishes their reference scripts, and serves pages
during development and after a build. It needs Node 22 or newer and nothing else: no JDK, no Gradle.

##### A project

`npm create joust <dir>` makes one from its template. By default the contract is `.jsc` and a Node script calls it;
`-- --lang java` writes it in Java, and `-- --template web` writes a page instead of the script
([create-joust](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/joust-cli/#create-joust)):

- contracts/ your contracts: .java and .jsc files, in package folders
  - app/
    - Counter.jsc
    - Counter.abi.json the .jsc contract's ABI manifest, committed
- index.js the Node script (node template)
- page/ the page (web template): index.html, main.js, engine.worker.js
- test/ Node tests (node --test)
- build/
  - joust/ everything joust build and joust deploy write
- dist/ the built page (vite build)
- .joust/ local state: the DevKit deployer key
- joust.config.json
- vite.config.js the page's Vite config (web template)
- package.json

`joust.config.json` says where the contracts are, where the build goes, and which networks to use. The template's:

```json title="joust.config.json"
{
  "contracts": "contracts",
  "out": "build/joust",
  "network": "devkit",
  "networks": {
    "devkit": { "chain": "http://localhost:8080/api/v1", "admin": "http://localhost:10000", "networkId": 0 }
  }
}
```

Every key, with its default, is in the [`joust.config.json` reference](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/config/). The template's
`.gitignore` leaves out `node_modules/`, `build/`, `.joust/` and `dist/`.

> **Keep .joust/ out of version control:** 
`.joust/devkit-wallet.json` holds a mnemonic (written with mode `0600`). It is a DevKit key, never to be used on a
public network, but it is still a key.

##### `joust build`

```sh
joust build [--src <dir>] [--out <dir>] [--accept-abi]
```

Compiles every `.java` and `.jsc` file under `contracts/` (or `--src`) into `build/joust/` (or `--out`), with the
toolchain engine, in-process. The `.jsc` language is JOUST's contract language ([.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/)). Plain JuLC
validators (`@WithdrawValidator`, `@SpendingValidator`, ...) in the same folder are compiled too, for use as
governors. Diagnostics are printed as `<file>:<line>: error: <message>`, a `.jsc` diagnostic with its column and
code (`app/Counter.jsc:20:13: error[JSC0502]: <message>`, as Gradle prints it); on an error the command exits with status 1 and writes
no contract.

Each `.jsc` contract has an ABI manifest, `<Contract>.abi.json`, committed beside the `.jsc` file. The build fails
when it is missing (`JSC0003`) or differs from what the contract now compiles to (`JSC0002`); `--accept-abi` writes it
instead, to review and commit ([the ABI manifest](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/#the-abi-manifest)). The Java each `.jsc` file lowered
to is written to `build/joust/generated/`, with its source map, also when the build failed (not for a file whose
manifest was refused).

| File in `build/joust/` | What it is |
|---|---|
| `contracts.json` | for the runtime engine: `[{ description, script, transitions, manifest, built: { joust } }]`, one per contract |
| `<Contract>.json` | the contract's description (CIP-57 schemas plus `x-joust`, version 2) |
| `<Contract>.plutus` | the compiled validator, CBOR hex |
| `<Contract>.js`, `<Contract>.d.ts` | the typed client and its types ([JavaScript clients](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/)) |
| `validators.json` | plain JuLC validators, if any: `[{ name, package, purpose, script, scriptHash, params, built }]` |
| `<Validator>.plutus` | each plain validator's script (parameters not applied) |
| `joust.lock.json` | the toolchain version, the description version and each contract's script hash |
| `deployments.<network>.json` | written by `joust deploy` (below) |

```json title="build/joust/joust.lock.json"
{
  "joust": "<version>",
  "descriptionVersion": 2,
  "contracts": {
    "app.Counter": { "scriptHash": "572399fa2a90a0452c3b29da48af6b90905ac8cfb503e1af803c942c" }
  }
}
```

Each contract in `contracts.json` records the toolchain version that built it. The runtime refuses a description of
another version than 2, and a contract built by an incompatible toolchain: another major version, or another minor
while the major is 0. Rebuild with a matching `@julclang/joust` if you see `built by JOUST ...; this runtime is ...`.

The toolchain compiles exactly as the Gradle build does: ADR-0015's parity tests compare the outputs byte for byte. So
a contract can move between the npm path and the [Java path](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/) unchanged.

###### Program manifests

The runtime engine runs each contract method as its **transition program**: the same Java, compiled by JuLC, evaluated
by JuLC's VM. Each contract's `manifest` in `contracts.json` records what its programs were compiled from and how: the
JuLC version and compiler options, hashes of the validator script, the description (in canonical JSON, so a
description given as an object matches too), every library source and each program, and each program's argument
layout ([ADR-0020](https://joust.julc.dev/project/architecture-decisions/) D8). The engine checks it before it runs any program, and refuses
a contract whose programs do not match their script, description or manifest, or were compiled by another JuLC version
or with other options, with `the transition programs do not match their manifest` and the remedy: build the contracts
again with the `@julclang/joust` that matches the runtime. The runtime checks a bundle's manifests when it is created,
and their JuLC version once the engine has loaded, before any call. A `contracts.json` from before manifests is refused
the same way.

The manifest gives consistency, not integrity: whoever can change the programs can change the manifest too, and the
validators still decide what the chain accepts. The engine cannot read the library sources, so their hashes are
checked by JOUST's CI (a fresh compile must equal the manifest), not at run time.

> **Caution:** 
The engine accepts programs compiled by its own JuLC version only. A runtime with a newer JuLC refuses an older build
until you run `joust build` again; if the newer JuLC compiles your validator differently, its script hash (and so its
address and policy) changes, and live instances stay at the old one. How to upgrade deployed apps across JuLC versions
is an open decision (ADR-0020 §12.4).

The engine also checks each program's inputs (the state, the arguments, the `Ctx`) against the contract's declared
types before it runs it, and refuses a malformed one by name: `Counter.increment: the argument by does not fit its
declared type`. A contract's own refusal (`Require.that`) keeps its message, whatever it starts with.

##### `joust deploy`

```sh
joust deploy [--network <name>]
```

For each contract in `contracts.json`, on the config's network (or `--network`):

1. Asks the runtime engine for the contract's deployment: its policy (the script hash), address and reference
   scripts.
2. If its reference script is not on chain yet, has the engine build the publishing transaction, checks that it pays
   only the contract's address (with the script) and the deployer, signs and submits it.
3. Publishes JOUST's map verifier or output verifier once per network, when the contract needs one (MerkleMaps;
   sends, deposits).
4. Writes `build/joust/deployments.<network>.json`.

```json title="build/joust/deployments.devkit.json"
{
  "network": "devkit",
  "networkId": 0,
  "chain": "http://localhost:8080/api/v1",
  "clock": { "zeroSlot": 0, "zeroTimeMs": 1793975371000, "slotLengthMs": 1000 },
  "contracts": {
    "app.Counter": {
      "contract": "app.Counter",
      "policy": "572399fa2a90a0452c3b29da48af6b90905ac8cfb503e1af803c942c",
      "address": "addr_test1wptj8x0692g2q3fv8v5a5j90dwgfqkkge76s8cd0sq7fgtq9nldys",
      "networkId": 0,
      "referenceScripts": ["1e4834390dae0f76de76b65d83b0f15fd99b7eb7d2e1da50e0cb1e7c10bd15c0#0"]
    }
  }
}
```

This file is what apps and pages pin: a page built for a network inlines it. The deployer is:

- `JOUST_MNEMONIC`, when it is set (required on any network without a DevKit admin API);
- otherwise, on DevKit only, a key `joust deploy` makes and keeps in `.joust/<network>-wallet.json`, topped up with
  1000 ADA from the faucet whenever it holds less than 200 ADA.

A contract with `@Params` is deployed with the values in the config's `params`, under its full title or simple name;
without them it is skipped, with a message. Each params value is its own deployment
([Params, invariants and events](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/params-invariants-events/)):

```json title="joust.config.json"
{ "params": { "Shop": { "oracle": { "policy": "<oracle policy hex>", "instance": "<oracle instance id hex>" }, "maxAgeMs": "600000" } } }
```

Here `Shop` is `examples/oracle`'s, whose `@Params` record is `Config(ForeignInstance oracle, BigInteger maxAgeMs)`.
The values follow the description's schema in the [JSON conventions](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/#json-conventions).

##### `joust dev`

```sh
joust dev [--network <name>] [--port <port>] [--accept-abi]
```

The development loop, on one port (default **5178**, or the config's `dev.port`):

1. **Attach** to the network's chain: probe the chain API (`/blocks/latest`) and, on a DevKit, its admin API. If it
   does not answer and the network has a `start` command, run it and wait up to three minutes.
2. **Build and deploy**, then start a prepare service over the result.
3. **Serve**: the page, the chain proxy, the build, the engine and the faucet (routes below).
4. **Watch** `contracts/`: a saved `.java` or `.jsc` file rebuilds and redeploys (debounced; one run at a time, and a
   save during a run queues one more). A failed build waits for the next save. A `.jsc` file whose ABI manifest is
   missing or changed fails the build unless `joust dev` was started with `--accept-abi`; the server keeps serving
   the last good build meanwhile.

| Route | What it serves |
|---|---|
| `/chain/<path>` | the network's chain API, proxied (GET, and `POST /chain/tx/submit`); a project id stays in the server |
| `/joust/network.json` | `{ network, networkId, chain: "/chain", engine, contracts, service, clock, ttlMs, explorer, deployments }` |
| `/joust/<file>` | the build: `contracts.json`, `validators.json`, `deployments.<network>.json`, the clients |
| `/joust/engine/<file>` | the runtime engine, streamed with an ETag (a reload revalidates instead of downloading 20 MB) |
| `POST /joust/service/prepare` | the engine in this process as a prepare service, for `httpService('/joust/service')`; a contract's refusal answers 422 with `{ error }` |
| `POST /dev/topup` | `{ address, ada? }` (default 1000 ADA) from DevKit's faucet; DevKit only |
| anything else | the page: through Vite when the project has `vite` and `page/index.html`, else the page directory's files |

The page directory is the config's `page`, else `page/` if it exists, else the project root. With Vite, the dev server
uses the project's `vite.config.js` (beside the page, or at the root), which should use `@julclang/joust/vite`; without
one, it uses that plugin alone. Vite runs in middleware mode behind the dev server, with live reload over the same
port, so two dev servers do not collide.

The deploys, the prepare service and the page's `/chain` share **one upstream session**: Blockfrost's load-balancer
affinity cookie is kept, so the page verifies against the chain state the engine built from.

###### Logging

`joust dev` logs its own steps (attach, build, deploy, serve). Vite's messages are hidden below `warn`; set
`JOUST_VITE_LOG=info` to see dependency bundling and page reloads:

```sh
JOUST_VITE_LOG=info npx joust dev
```

##### `joust serve`

```sh
joust serve [--network <name>] [--dir <dir>] [--port <port>]
```

Serves a built page (`vite build`, default `dist/`) as a static host would, plus what a static page cannot carry
itself: the chain API at `/chain` and, on DevKit, the faucet at `/dev/topup`. Nothing is built, deployed or bundled, and
there is no engine route or prepare service: the page brings the engine, with its integrity hashes, and prepares its
own transactions. It refuses to start without `<dir>/index.html`.

##### `joust version`

```sh
joust version      # or joust --version
```

Prints the package's version, the one recorded in `contracts.json` and `joust.lock.json`.

##### The template's scripts

The template's `package.json` maps npm scripts onto these commands; the npm quick start lists them for the
[node](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/#the-project) and [web](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/#a-browser-page) templates. Use `npx joust ...` for anything the scripts do not cover, such as `npx joust deploy --network mynet`.

  - [@julclang/joust reference](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/joust-cli/)
  - [joust.config.json](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/config/)
  - [Pages: worker, Vite, static builds](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/)

### Networks and chain providers

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

Everything JOUST does off chain reads the chain: the engine fetches the UTxOs and parameters a transaction needs, the
page verifier reads the outputs a transaction spends, and `joust deploy` looks for reference scripts. A **network**
in `joust.config.json` says where that chain is and how its time works. A **chain provider** is the JavaScript object
that reads it.

##### Networks

Two networks are built in ([`js/joust/src/config.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/joust/src/config.js)):

```js title="js/joust/src/config.js"
networks: {
  // Yaci DevKit: Yaci Store's Blockfrost-compatible API, and the admin API (slot clock, faucet).
  devkit: { chain: 'http://localhost:8080/api/v1', admin: 'http://localhost:10000', networkId: 0,
    explorer: 'http://localhost:5173/transactions/{tx}' },   // DevKit's Yaci Viewer
  // Cardano preview through Blockfrost (its project id from the environment, never the config).
  preview: {
    chain: 'https://cardano-preview.blockfrost.io/api/v0', projectIdEnv: 'BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID', networkId: 0,
    clock: { zeroSlot: 0, zeroTimeMs: 1666656000000, slotLengthMs: 1000 },
    explorer: 'https://preview.cardanoscan.io/transaction/{tx}',
  },
},
```

The config's `network` (default `devkit`) is the default for every command; `--network <name>` picks another.

###### Custom networks

Add a network under `networks` in `joust.config.json`. A network with the name of a built-in one is **merged over
it**, key by key, so you only write what changes:

```json title="joust.config.json"
{
  "network": "devkit",
  "networks": {
    "devkit": { "start": "yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store" },
    "preview": { "pageChain": "https://chain.example.org/api/v0" }
  }
}
```

Here `devkit` keeps its chain, admin API and explorer and gains a `start` command, which `joust dev` and `joust serve`
run when DevKit is not answering. `preview` keeps everything and gains a `pageChain` for built pages. A network with a
new name needs at least `chain`, `networkId` and either `admin` (a DevKit) or `clock`.

> **A public network's clock must be exact:** 
A network's `clock` maps slots to time: slot `zeroSlot` began at `zeroTimeMs`, and every later slot lasts
`slotLengthMs`. It must agree with the network for every slot a transaction uses. On a network whose earlier eras had
other slot lengths, anchor the clock in the current era: take a recent block's `slot` and `time` (POSIX seconds) from
the chain API's `/blocks/latest` and use `{ "zeroSlot": slot, "zeroTimeMs": time * 1000, "slotLengthMs": 1000 }`.
JOUST checked preview's built-in clock against the tip.

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `chain` | a Blockfrost-style chain API (Blockfrost, or Yaci Store's `/api/v1`) |
| `admin` | a Yaci DevKit admin API: the slot clock and the faucet; marks the network as a DevKit |
| `networkId` | `0` for test networks, `1` for mainnet |
| `projectIdEnv` | the environment variable that holds the chain API's project id |
| `projectId` | the project id itself (avoid: prefer `projectIdEnv`) |
| `clock` | `{ zeroSlot, zeroTimeMs, slotLengthMs }`; not needed with `admin` |
| `explorer` | a transaction page, `{tx}` standing for the hash |
| `pageChain` | the chain API a built page calls, instead of `/chain` |
| `start` | a shell command that starts the network (a DevKit) |
| `provider`, `ogmios` | `"ogmios"` and its URL, for `joust deploy` ([below](#ogmios)) |

The [`joust.config.json` reference](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/config/) has every key and default.

##### Chain providers

A **chain provider** is the JavaScript counterpart of cardano-client-lib's `BackendService`: a few chain reads that
answer plain, normalised objects. The runtime turns them into the engine's snapshot and the page's chain view, so a
provider never sees either format. It is defined in
[`js/state-client/src/providers.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/state-client/src/providers.js):

| Method | Answers |
|---|---|
| `tip()` | `{ slot, hash, height, epoch, time }` (`time` in POSIX seconds, if known) |
| `protocolParams()` | Blockfrost's parameter object (snake case: `min_fee_a`, `cost_models_raw`, ...) |
| `utxos(address)` | the complete unspent set at the address: `[Utxo]` |
| `assetUtxos(address, unit)` | *(optional)* the UTxOs there holding `unit`; otherwise the runtime filters `utxos` |
| `output(ref)` | one output by `"txHash#index"`, or `null` |
| `scriptCbor(hash)` | a Plutus script's CBOR, as Blockfrost's `/scripts/{hash}/cbor` serves it, or `null` |
| `submit(cbor)` | submits a signed transaction; answers its hash |
| `awaitTx(hash, opts)` | resolves once the transaction is on chain |
| `txCbor(hash)` | *(optional)* a transaction's CBOR, or `null` |
| `account(stakeAddress)` | *(optional)* `{ registered, rewards }`; `registered` is `undefined` when the API cannot tell |
| `assetHistory(unit)` | *(optional)* the hashes of the transactions that moved a token, oldest first |
| `redeemers(txHash)` | *(optional)* a transaction's redeemers: `[{ purpose, index, data }]` |

A `Utxo` is `{ txHash, index, address, value: [{ unit, quantity }], datumHash, inlineDatum, referenceScriptHash }`,
with `unit` either `"lovelace"` or the policy id followed by the asset name (hex), `quantity` a decimal string, and
absent fields `null`. `assetHistory` and `redeemers` rebuild [MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/) from the chain.

###### Using a provider

```js
import { joustRuntime, blockfrostProvider, ogmiosProvider } from '@julclang/joust-runtime';

// a Blockfrost-style API by URL (a blockfrostProvider is made for you)
const rt = joustRuntime({ chainUrl: 'http://localhost:8080/api/v1', contracts, clock, networkId: 0, deployments });

// or any provider: Blockfrost, Yaci Store, Ogmios, your own
const rt2 = joustRuntime({ provider: ogmiosProvider('http://localhost:1337'), contracts, clock, networkId: 0, deployments });
```

The same provider backs the engine's reads and the page verifier's chain view (`rt.chain`, `chainOf(provider)`), so
the verifier reads from the source the engine built from. In a page, `blockfrostChain(url)` is shorthand for
`chainOf(blockfrostProvider(url))`.

**Blockfrost and Yaci Store:**

`blockfrostProvider(baseUrl, { projectId?, fetchImpl? })` reads Blockfrost or any Blockfrost-style API, such as Yaci
Store's `http://localhost:8080/api/v1`. It implements every method above. It also exposes `get(path)`, the raw API,
for anything the interface does not cover.

What a public Blockfrost taught it, since Blockfrost sits behind a load balancer whose backends, indexes and submit
node can each be a moment apart:

- **It is sticky.** It keeps the `__cflb` affinity cookie, so every request reaches one backend and what it reads only
  moves forward. (A browser keeps the cookie itself.)
- **`awaitTx` waits for every index the next call reads**: each output's address, each spent input's removal, and the
  by-asset index of each new token.
- **`submit` retries.** On `BadInputsUTxO` it resubmits the same signed transaction (up to 10 times, 3 s apart), for a
  submit node a block behind. Nothing is signed again; the transaction stays valid until its TTL.
- **Collateral outputs are skipped.** Blockfrost lists a transaction's collateral return among its outputs, flagged;
  `output()` ignores it.
- **Redeemer data is checked** against its hash before a mirror uses it.

Yaci Store answers registered and unknown stake credentials alike, so `account()` reports `registered: undefined`
there. Code that registers a credential (`registerStake`, `ensureGovernor`) then attempts the registration and treats
the ledger's "already registered" refusal as success.

**Ogmios:**

`ogmiosProvider(url, { fetchImpl? })` reads Ogmios v6 over HTTP JSON-RPC: the node's own ledger state.

- It serves unspent outputs only, and no transaction CBOR.
- Protocol parameters are mapped to Blockfrost's object as cardano-client-lib's Ogmios supplier maps them
  (`ogmiosParams`).
- Scripts are known by their hash from the reference-script outputs it has served.
- A transaction is on chain once its first output is.
- `account()` tells registration exactly, from `rewardAccountSummaries`.
- It has no history (`assetHistory`, `redeemers`), so it cannot rebuild a MerkleMap mirror alone.

All 14 example flows of `js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js` pass over Ogmios on DevKit (`PROVIDER=ogmios`), as
over Yaci Store.

**Your own:**

Any object with the required methods is a provider: an indexer, a cache, a test double. `providers.test.js` checks
Ogmios against Yaci Store with `conformance(candidate, reference, probes)` on the tip, protocol parameters, an
address's UTxOs, reference-script outputs and stake accounts; the same check applies to any provider.

###### Ogmios

`joust deploy` reads a network through Ogmios when the network says so:

```json title="joust.config.json"
{ "networks": { "devkit": { "provider": "ogmios", "ogmios": "http://localhost:1337" } } }
```

`ogmios` defaults to `http://localhost:1337`. `joust dev` and `joust serve` still use the network's `chain`: they probe
it, proxy it at `/chain`, and their runtimes read it.

##### The `/chain` proxy

A Blockfrost project id is a secret. It must never reach a page, where anyone can read it. So pages never call
Blockfrost directly: `joust dev` and `joust serve` proxy the network's chain API at `/chain` on their own origin, adding
the project id in the server ([`js/joust/src/routes.js`](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/blob/main/js/joust/src/routes.js)):

- `GET /chain/<path>?<query>` goes to `<chain>/<path>?<query>`, with the header `project_id`;
- `POST /chain/tx/submit` is forwarded with its body and content type;
- the status, content type and body come back unchanged.

The proxy keeps one upstream session, with Blockfrost's affinity cookie, for everything the server reads: the deploys,
the prepare service and every page's `/chain`. So a page verifies against the chain state the deployment and the
engine saw.

The project id is read only from the environment variable `projectIdEnv` names (`BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID` for
preview). A command stops with a message naming the variable if it is not set.

For a page hosted elsewhere, give it the same proxy, or a chain API a browser may call directly as the network's
`pageChain`. See [Deploy to preview](https://joust.julc.dev/tutorials/deploy-preview/#5-host-it).

##### Clocks

Cardano measures time in **slots**. A contract that uses time ([Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/)) sees it as a transaction's
validity interval, in slots, so the runtime must turn milliseconds into slots exactly as the network does. A clock is
`{ zeroSlot, zeroTimeMs, slotLengthMs }`.

| Network | Clock |
|---|---|
| DevKit | read from the admin API (`devkitClock(adminUrl)`, `/local-cluster/api/admin/devnet`): its start time and slot length |
| preview | from preview's genesis: `{ zeroSlot: 0, zeroTimeMs: 1666656000000, slotLengthMs: 1000 }` |
| custom | the network's `clock`; a network without `clock` or `admin` is refused |

`joust deploy` records the clock in `deployments.<network>.json`, and a built page inlines that one, so a build needs
no chain. A DevKit's clock changes every time it restarts: deploy and build the page again after a restart.

##### TTLs

Every prepared transaction expires: its **TTL** (time to live) is the end of its validity interval. Short TTLs keep a
prepared transaction from lingering, and the page verifier refuses one that is valid for more than 900 slots
(15 minutes, `limits.maxValiditySlots`).

| Where | Default |
|---|---|
| a page (`virtual:joust/network`'s `ttlMs`) and `joust dev`'s prepare service | 20 s on a DevKit (a network with `admin`), 180 s elsewhere; the config's `dev.ttlMs` overrides both |
| `joustRuntime` / `engineService` in Node | the `ttlMs` option; 120 s if not given |

DevKit's time horizon is only minutes ahead, so a long TTL there fails with a `PastHorizon` error; the template's test
passes `ttlMs: 20_000`. On a public network the TTL must also cover the time the user takes to read the review and sign
in the wallet.

### Keyed objects in JavaScript

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/apps/keyed-objects-js/

> **Experimental:** 
The npm path runs JOUST's toolchain and runtime as WebAssembly built with GraalVM Web Image, which is itself experimental. Java with Gradle and cardano-client-lib is the supported, first-class path: see [Quick start: Java](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

[Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/) are owned objects with a unique key, kept in a sorted on-chain list. From
JavaScript you insert, look up, update, remove and retire them as you call any other contract: the runtime engine
prepares the transaction, the page verifies it, and the wallet signs. Two things are different, and this page is about
them: what the page checks before the wallet is asked, and how a retry can never make two transactions land.

##### Calls

`instance.keyed(type)` gives a keyed type's list, by the type's simple name. From the registry's flow on DevKit (the
JavaScript twin of the Java example):

```js title="js/joust-runtime/test/examples.test.js"
const created = await reg.deploy(admin, {});
const inst = reg.at(created.instance);
const entries = inst.keyed('Entry');
const ballots = inst.keyed('Ballot');
assert.deepEqual(await entries.keys(), []);
// A ballot (signedKey) and a keyed action on it.
const cast = await ballots.insert(ann, 'cast', { voter: ann.keyHash, choice: 3n });
assert.equal(cast.key, ann.keyHash);
await ballots.object(ann.keyHash).call(ann, 'change', { choice: 7n });
assert.equal((await ballots.find(ann.keyHash)).value.choice, 7n);
// A name (payable), a payable keyed action, a withdrawal paid to the owner.
const NAME = '6e616d65';
await entries.insert(ann, 'claim', { name: NAME, tier: 1n, guardians: [ann.keyHash], needed: 1n }, { lovelace: 5n * ADA });
const name = entries.object(NAME);
await name.call(ann, 'upgrade', { tier: 2n }, { lovelace: 2n * ADA });
await name.call(ann, 'withdraw', { amount: ADA });
```

`reg` is a `JoustContract` and `ann` a CIP-30 wallet. Keys are hex strings.

| `JoustKeyedList` member | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `find(key)` | `{ ref, key, retired, value, lovelace }`, or `null` when the chain API returned nothing |
| `exists(key)` | whether the key is taken, live or retired |
| `keys()` | `[{ key, retired, value }]` in list order, walked from the head |
| `insert(wallet, method, args?, pay?, opts?)` | `{ txHash, report, key }`: an `@OwnedInit` of that type |
| `object(key)` | a `JoustKeyedObject` |
| `unit(key)` | the key's token unit (policy and name, hex) |

| `JoustKeyedObject` member | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `key` | the key (hex) |
| `read()` | `{ ref, key, retired, value, lovelace }`, or `null` |
| `call(wallet, name, args?, pay?, opts?)` | `{ txHash, report }`: a keyed action, a remove or a retire. `opts`: `{ cosigners, abandon }` |

Every node the list returns is validated against the description: its token, address, datum, instance and key. A
walk that finds a missing link or keys out of order is reported as an inconsistent answer from the chain API: such a
list cannot exist on chain.

**Generated clients.** `joust-gen` and `joust build` generate keyed members too. For the registry, the instance class
gets `cast(wallet, args, opts?)`, `claim(wallet, args, pay?, opts?)` and `grant(...)` (each resolving to
`{ txHash, report, key, object }`), `ballot(key)` and `entry(key)`, `ballotExists(key)`, `entryKeys()` and so on, and
`RegistryEntryObject` has `read()` and one method per keyed action, remove and retire.

##### Who prepares keyed calls

The **runtime engine** prepares keyed calls, in Node (`engineService`, `rt.service`) or in a page's worker
(`engineWorker`): see [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/). For an insert or a remove it lists the contract's state address to find
the neighbour; `@julclang/joust-runtime` fetches that listing up front. The Java prepare service
(`julc-state-server`) refuses keyed calls.

When the neighbour is cooling down ([Cooldown and window](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/#cooldown-and-window)) and the
call's window would start further ahead than the page allows, the engine refuses the call with the slot to prepare
again at, as a field of its answer (`retryAtSlot`; a prepare service over HTTP sends it in its error body). The
client waits for that slot and prepares again, so a call can take a minute or more. The message also says "prepare
again at slot N", but only for people: the client never reads the slot from text, which a contract could forge
(ADR-0020 §12.1). A window that starts a little
ahead is submitted when it starts.

##### What the page checks

A keyed call goes through `verifyKeyed`, beside the checks every call gets
([Verification](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/#verification)). It reads the contract's description, never the service's
word. Among its rules (ADR-0016 D11):

- **The anchor.** The node an insert or a remove relinks must be spent with `Link`, named by the mint redeemer, and
  carry the token its datum implies. Its output must be the same node with only `next` and `linkedAt` changed, at the
  same address, with no reference script.
- **The new key.** For an insert, the page reads the key from the new node's datum and checks that the minted token is
  that key's.
- **Heads** are accepted only when a keyed contract's instance is created, each funded with exactly its deposit.
- **Funds.** Every script input's value is authenticated: read from the transaction that produced it, whose body must
  hash to the input's id (or, when the chain API serves no transaction CBOR, bound through the call's `Ctx`). Top-ups
  of an anchor or a retired node are allowed only up to what a raised ledger minimum requires, at most 10 ADA each,
  and count against the wallet's net outflow. So a hostile service cannot hide a gift to a neighbour or pay a third
  party.
- **Time.** The deployment must pin the network's slot clock (`slotConfig`), and the chain API's tip must agree with
  the page's clock within 120 slots. The page then checks each relink's window, `linkedAt` and the neighbour's cooldown.
  `joust deploy` and `rt.options(...)` pin the clock for keyed contracts.
- **One keyed call per transaction.** A composition containing a keyed call is refused (`verifyComposed`,
  `runComposed`).

The page also refuses, for now, a keyed call with an `@AuthorizedBy` governor.

##### Retries that survive a reload

A keyed call can be rejected because someone else took the gap or moved the neighbour, and a wallet or a relay can
answer "rejected" for a transaction that still lands. If the page simply prepared a new transaction, both could land.
The page prevents it the way the Java runtime does: with a **designated input**.

1. Before the first attempt of an operation, the client picks one ordinary input of the wallet (the largest ADA-only
   UTxO of at least 5 ADA at its funding address) and **records** it in a retry store, before the wallet is asked to
   sign.
2. Every attempt of that operation, first and retries, must spend that input. The page refuses to ask the wallet to
   sign one that does not, so two attempts can never both land.
3. The record is kept in IndexedDB in a browser (`defaultRetryStore()`; memory in Node), one per wallet and network.
   After a reload, a keyed call of that wallet is still a retry of the recorded operation and must spend the same
   input.
4. The record ends when the call is confirmed, or once every attempt's window has passed by the page's own clock.
   If the wallet and the chain API then still show the designated input, nothing landed: the call fails and the next
   call starts a new operation. Otherwise one attempt *may have landed*: the record stays as a tombstone, and every
   further keyed call of the wallet is refused until the application has checked and calls
   `contract.acknowledgeKeyed(wallet)`.

While an attempt may still land, a failing call throws `PendingKeyedOperation`; its `record` names the designated
input and the attempts (`{ txHash, validTo }`). Retry the same call, or let the user abandon the operation explicitly
with `contract.abandonKeyed(wallet)` or `opts.abandon: true` (an earlier attempt may then still land).

A page runs **one keyed call at a time per network**, across its tabs (Web Locks). A keyed call that starts while
another is in flight is refused at once with `KeyedCallInProgress`; calls are never queued.

| Option or export | What it is |
|---|---|
| `retryStore` (a `JoustContract` option) | Where records are kept: `indexedDbRetryStore(name?)`, `memoryRetryStore()`, or your own `{ all, put, delete }` |
| `defaultRetryStore()` | IndexedDB in a browser, memory elsewhere |
| `abandonKeyed(wallet)` | Drops the wallet's record or tombstone: the user's explicit choice |
| `acknowledgeKeyed(wallet)` | Drops only a tombstone ("may have landed"), never a live operation |
| `PendingKeyedOperation` | Thrown while an attempt may still land; `record.designated`, `record.attempts` |
| `KeyedCallInProgress` | Thrown when another keyed call is in flight on the network |
| `designatedFor(walletView)` | The input the client would designate (for display) |

> **Tip:** 
Keep an ADA-only UTxO of at least 5 ADA in the wallet for keyed calls: without one, the call is refused before
anything is prepared.

  - [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/)
