### Troubleshooting

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/reference/troubleshooting/

Each entry gives a **symptom** (often the exact message), its **cause** and the **fix**. Messages in quotes are copied
from the JOUST sources; `...` stands for the part that varies. The entries are grouped by where the problem shows up:
the build, the contract's logic, transactions, JavaScript pages, and Yaci DevKit.

> **Tip:** 
Two habits catch most problems early. Run the contract's methods as plain Java (or through the harness) before you
touch a network, and read the whole message: JOUST's errors name the call, the rule and usually the fix.

##### Build and compiler

###### "Undefined variable: OutputLib" (or any julc-stdlib class)

**Cause.** JuLC compiles the generated validator from source, and finds library sources by scanning the annotation
processor path. A rebuilt **jar** of `julc-state-api` on that path, in a long-lived Gradle daemon, can make the scan
silently find nothing (a stale `JarFile` cache, an `IOException` swallowed). JuLC then misses julc-stdlib's sources
too, so the first stdlib class the validator uses is "undefined" (ADR-0001 F16).

**Fix.** Stop the daemon with `./gradlew --stop` and build again. Inside the JOUST repository, put the
`onchainSources` **directory** artifact on the processor path, not the jar:

```groovy
annotationProcessor project(path: ':julc-state-api', configuration: 'onchainSources')
```

###### Gradle cannot resolve the `julc` artifacts

**Cause.** JOUST is not on Maven Central yet: its releases are in the BloxBean release repository. JuLC's releases are
on Maven Central and in the BloxBean release repository (its release candidates only in the latter). A
development snapshot of JOUST, and an early JOUST release candidate that was built against a JuLC development snapshot,
also need the BloxBean snapshot repository. Releases since then pin JuLC releases only.

**Fix.** List `https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/releases` beside `mavenCentral()`, and in `pluginManagement` too for the
Gradle plugin `org.julclang.joust` (`joust new` writes both). Add `https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/snapshots` only for
a snapshot. Take the JuLC version from the `julc` entry of `gradle/libs.versions.toml` at your JOUST release's tag, or
let the plugin choose it. See [Quick start: Java & Gradle](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/).

###### "'...' in a @StateContract: JuLC treats it as an unbounded integer on-chain while the JVM wraps or rounds it ... Use BigInteger"

Also: "fixed-width arithmetic (...) in a @StateContract: the JVM wraps, on-chain does not. Use BigInteger", and
"'x' is int in a @StateContract (inferred or declared); fixed-width numbers diverge between the JVM and on-chain".

**Cause.** `SubsetLint` rejects `int`, `long`, `short`, `char`, `float`, `double` and the narrowing calls (`intValue()`,
`longValueExact()`, ...) in contract code. The same method runs on the JVM and on chain; on the JVM these types wrap
or round, on chain integers are unbounded, so the two runs could compute different states.

**Fix.** Use `BigInteger` everywhere in contract code, including `var` locals whose inferred type is a fixed-width
number.

###### "constructing MerkleMap in a @StateContract" or "MerkleMap.reads() in a @StateContract"

**Cause.** A `MerkleMap` is built by the runtime with the reads it proved. A hand-made one carries reads nobody proved,
and its internals (`reads()`, `writes()`, `root()`) differ between the JVM run and the on-chain run.

**Fix.** Start a map with `MerkleMaps.empty()` and use the `MerkleMaps` helpers only. Keep `MerkleMap` as a top-level
state component. See [MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/).

###### The processor rejects the contract's shape

The processor checks the contract before generating anything. The common messages:

| Message | Fix |
|---|---|
| "@StateContract must be on a top-level class" / "@StateContract class must be public" | Make the contract a public top-level class |
| "contract methods must be public static" | Every annotated method is `public static` |
| "contract method names must be unique (no overloading): ..." | Rename the overload |
| "a @StateContract needs exactly one @Init method, found ..." | Keep one `@Init` |
| "@Init must return the state record" | Return the state (or a result record holding it) |
| "@StateContract(maxDatumBytes) must be between 16 and 8192" | Pick a size in range |
| "@StateContract(maxValidityMs) must be at least 60000 (one minute)" | Raise `maxValidityMs` |
| "@Batched actions and MerkleMap state cannot be combined yet ..." | Not supported yet: choose one of the two |
| "@Owned objects and MerkleMap state cannot be combined yet: a @Shared read has no proof path" | Put the maps inside the owned objects (ADR-0012), or drop one |
| "an @Into move needs an @Admits action: the destination must consent (ADR-0012 D3)" | Add the `@Admits` action on the destination |

See [Annotations](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/annotations/) for each annotation's rules.

###### JuLC refuses code that is valid Java

**Cause.** Contract code is compiled by JuLC, which accepts a subset of Java. Outside the subset:
- `throw` (use `Require.that(cond, "msg")`);
- generic records, and classes other than records and sealed interfaces;
- reassigned locals (only loop accumulators may change);
- `Function.apply`;
- an accessor on a call's result (`f(x).field()`): give the result a typed local first;
- static calls through anything but an imported simple class name.

**Fix.** Rewrite in the subset. See [Java](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/java/) and [Require and errors](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/require-and-errors/).

###### A contract with `@Votes` or `@Propose` fails to compile its blueprint

**Cause.** JuLC's pinned CIP-57 revision has no vocabulary for the VOTE and PROPOSE purposes yet.

**Fix.** Compile without a blueprint, as `examples/staking/build.gradle` does:

```groovy
tasks.named('compileJava') { options.compilerArgs += ['-Ajulc.blueprint=false'] }
```

###### A validator fails on chain and you cannot tell which check

**Fix.** Compile with the processor option `-Ajoust.traces=true`: each failing generated check then traces its name.
The scripts grow, so use it only while debugging. `examples/staking` wires it to `-Pjoust.traces`.

###### "...: the applied script is ... bytes; a reference script must fit a 16 KB transaction (ADR-0009 r2)"

**Cause.** Contracts read their script by reference, and the transaction that publishes it is limited to 16 KB. Many
owned types, moves, MerkleMaps and native assets in one contract add up (ADR-0012 measured 16.7 KB for three owned
types with moves and maps).

**Fix.** Split the contract, or drop features it does not need. See [Fees and script size](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/)
and the sizes in [Examples](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/examples/).

##### Contract logic

###### A call passes on the JVM and fails on chain (or the reverse) when comparing keys

**Cause.** `byte[]` compared with `==` or `.equals`. On chain it compares bytes; on the JVM it compares references, so
two equal keys are "different". The lint does not catch this yet.

**Fix.** Always compare byte strings with `ByteStringLib.equals(a, b)`.

###### "...: the new ... state contains a map whose keys are not in canonical order ... Keep state maps ordered with org.julclang.state.api.SortedMaps"

**Cause.** cardano-client-lib writes inline datums as canonical CBOR, with map keys sorted. The validator recomputes
the state with JuLC's ordered maps. If the state's map is not already in canonical order, the datum written differs
from the one the validator computes, and the call would fail on chain; the runtime refuses it first.

**Fix.** Build and update state maps with `SortedMaps`. A deposit memo has the same rule ("a deposit memo contains a
map whose keys are not in canonical order").

###### A map update leaves the old entry behind

**Cause.** `JulcMap.insert` prepends: a key inserted twice is there twice. `getOrDefault` is not available on chain.

**Fix.** Update with `delete(k).insert(k, v)`, or use the `SortedMaps` helpers.

###### A deadline check fails although the deadline is still ahead

**Cause.** `Clock.before(ctx, t)` holds only if the **whole** validity window ends by `t` (`ctx.validTo() <= t`). With
a 10-minute window, a deadline 5 minutes away is not "before".

**Fix.** Leave the deadline more room than the window, or shorten the window (`StateRuntime.Builder.ttl`).
`Clock.after` uses the window's start. See [Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/).

###### A time bound reads -1

**Cause.** JuLC's `IntervalLib.finite*Bound` returns -1 for an infinite bound.

**Fix.** Check that the bound is `Finite` before comparing. In a `@StateContract`, read time through `Ctx` and `Clock`
instead: the generated validator checks that `validFrom` and `validTo` equal the transaction's finite bounds.

###### A `ClassCastException` building a datum on the JVM

**Cause.** `(PlutusData) (Object) record` works on chain (a record is Data) but throws on the JVM.

**Fix.** Build datums with `Builtins.constrData`, `bData` and `iData`.

###### A `Value` redeemer field decodes wrongly

**Cause.** Redeemer fields typed `Value` mis-decode in JuLC.

**Fix.** Type the field `PlutusData`. A native `Value` also cannot be a JuLC loop accumulator: use recursion.

###### "...: a destroy must pay out everything the instance holds (...)"

**Cause.** A `@Destroy` ends the instance, so its payouts (and sends) must account for all it holds:
`ctx.balance()` in a destroy is everything in the state UTxO, deposit included.

**Fix.** Pay out `ctx.balance()` in full, as `Counter.close` does with `Payouts.of(s.owner(), ctx.balance())`.

##### Transactions and the chain

###### A call is refused with the contract's own message ("insufficient balance")

This is the intended behaviour. The client runs the method off chain first, so a failing `Require` costs nothing and
nothing is submitted:
- in Java, the generated client throws `RequireException` with the message;
- in JavaScript, the engine's refusal carries the contract's `Require` message (read from the traces), and the page
  shows it before the wallet is asked to sign.

**Fix.** Change the call (for example, transfer no more than the balance).

###### "...: the state kept moving" (`ContentionException`)

**Cause.** Several callers spent the same instance at once. The runtime rebuilds a call the node rejected because
the state moved, up to `maxRetries` times (default 3), then gives up.

**Fix.** Retry later, or design for parallel use: per-user [owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/) or
[batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/).

###### "...: submission outcome unknown (...)" or "...: not seen on chain within ..." (`PendingTransactionException`)

**Cause.** The transaction was sent but its fate is not known (a timeout, a lost answer), or it has not appeared
within `confirmTimeout`.

**Fix.** Look the transaction hash up before you retry: it may still land. Do not sign a second transaction for the
same call blindly. "included, but the new state is not visible yet" means the indexer is behind: read again shortly.

###### "... instance ... not found at ..." (`InstanceNotFoundException`)

**Cause.** No UTxO at the contract's address holds the instance's token: a wrong instance id, another network or
deployment, or the instance was destroyed.

**Fix.** Check the instance id (32 bytes of hex) and the deployment you load.

###### "...: a send to the caller's own base address would pay the fee out of it; send to its enterprise address instead (ADR-0007 r2)"

**Cause.** QuickTx takes the fee from an output at the fee payer's address. A payout or send to that address could
pay the fee out of the recipient's funds.

**Fix.** Send to the caller's enterprise address. The runtime does this for payouts itself.

###### "composition: the calls' validity windows do not overlap"

**Cause.** A `Compose` puts several calls in one transaction, so they need one validity window.

**Fix.** Align the calls' time rules. See [Reads and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/).

###### "no MerkleMap store: add cardano-client-merkle-patricia-forestry-rocksdb, or give the runtime one (StateRuntime.Builder.mapStore), or set -Djoust.mapStore=memory for tests"

**Cause.** A contract with MerkleMaps needs a node store for its mirror. The JVM default is RocksDB (`./.joust/mpf`),
loaded by name.

**Fix.** Add the RocksDB dependency, give the builder a store, or use `-Djoust.mapStore=memory` in tests (the JOUST
build sets it for every Gradle test).

###### Blockfrost answers 403 or 400 with BadInputsUTxO

- `.../blocks/latest: 403 ...` (any path, status 403): the request reached Blockfrost without a project id. A page
  should read the chain through `/chain`, the proxy `joust dev` and `joust serve` run, which adds the id; never put the
  id in a page. For the CLI, set it in the environment (below).
- "network preview reads its chain API's project id from BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID: set it (export
  BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID=...)": export the variable before `joust deploy --network preview` or
  `joust dev --network preview`.
- `submit failed: 400 ... BadInputsUTxO`: Blockfrost's submit node can be a block behind its index. The provider
  already resubmits the same signed transaction a few times; if it still fails, the inputs really were spent.

See [Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/).

##### JavaScript and pages

###### A page fails at load: "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'from')"

**Cause.** cardano-js-sdk's crypto dependencies (`pbkdf2`, `safe-buffer`, `readable-stream`) expect Node's `buffer`,
`events`, `util`, `stream` and `process`. Without them the page fails as it loads. Node tests do not catch this.

**Fix.** Add the JOUST Vite plugin. It aliases those modules to browser versions, injects `Buffer` and `process`, and
sets `es2022` for top-level await:

```js title="vite.config.js"
import { joust } from '@julclang/joust/vite';
export default { plugins: [joust()] };
```

See [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/).

###### MerkleMap proofs fail in a page that sets up its own polyfills

**Cause.** Aiken's MPF (the mirror's trie) checks `instanceof Buffer` against the global `Buffer`.
vite-plugin-node-polyfills' shim bundles its own copy of `buffer`, so its global and an imported `node:buffer` are
different classes.

**Fix.** Use `@julclang/joust/vite`, which injects one `Buffer` class (its shim re-exports `buffer`), instead of
configuring the polyfills yourself.

###### The page reloads under `joust dev` when the engine worker starts

**Cause.** Vite found the worker's own dependencies only when the worker ran, bundled them again and reloaded the
page.

**Fix.** The plugin scans `**/*.html` and `**/*.worker.{js,mjs,ts}` up front: name your worker file `*.worker.js` (or
set `optimizeDeps.entries`). `JOUST_VITE_LOG=info` shows Vite's messages from `joust dev` (dependency bundling,
reloads).

###### A build fails with `vite-plugin-top-level-await`

**Cause.** That plugin's swc transform breaks the runtime packages.

**Fix.** Do not use it. Target `es2022`, which supports top-level await (the JOUST plugin sets it).

###### "the engine at ... did not load (or does not match its integrity hash)"

Also: "the engine's Wasm at ... did not load, or does not match its integrity hash".

**Cause.** The page pins the engine's sha384 hashes (SRI) and the browser refuses an engine whose bytes differ. The
files were changed, truncated, or come from another build.

**Fix.** Serve the build's `joust/engine-<id>/` files unchanged, from the same build as the page. Rebuild if in doubt.

###### "the prepared transaction was refused: ..." (`VerificationError`)

**Cause.** The page verifier found that the prepared transaction does something other than the call asked for: an
extra input, another redeemer, an output the wallet would pay, an unbalanced transaction, a window too long.

**Fix.** Do not sign it. If you run the service yourself, check that it serves the same build and deployment the page
pins. A service you do not control may be malicious: the verifier exists for that case.

###### "...: description version ...; this runtime reads version 2 (rebuild with joust build)"

Also: "...: built by JOUST ...; this runtime is ... (rebuild with a matching @julclang/joust)".

**Cause.** The contracts were built by another toolchain version. The runtime requires description version 2 and the
same major version (the same minor while the major is 0).

**Fix.** Install matching `@julclang/joust` and `@julclang/joust-runtime` versions and run `joust build` again. See
[Contract description](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/description-format/).

###### "the MerkleMap mirror has no node ...: this app did not build that map's history"

**Cause.** The engine asked the mirror for a map node it does not hold: the mirror's store was lost, or this app never
saw the map's history.

**Fix.** Keep the mirror's store between runs (a page keeps it in IndexedDB, the JVM in `./.joust/mpf`). A mirror can
rebuild a map from the chain's history, checking every claim against its root. See
[MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/).

###### "not enough lovelace for the outputs, the change and the fee"

**Cause.** The paying wallet cannot cover the call.

**Fix.** Fund the wallet. On DevKit, `joust dev` serves a faucet at `/dev/topup`, and the template page has a "Top up"
button for its in-page key.

###### Imports go missing in the JOUST repository's JS packages

**Cause.** Installing in one package of `js/` can prune another's linked dependencies.

**Fix.** Re-run `npm install` in `js/state-client` (or the package whose imports went missing). For the
`examples/wallet` Node demo, run `npm install` in `examples/wallet/js` first.

##### Yaci DevKit

###### "Yaci DevKit is not reachable (chain ..., admin ...). Start it with Yaci Store enabled"

**Cause.** `joust dev` and the DevKit tests need Yaci Store's API on `:8080` and the admin API on `:10000`.

**Fix.** Start it with `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`, or give the network a `start` command in
`joust.config.json`. Gradle tests tagged `devnet` are skipped while DevKit is down.

###### PastHorizon

**Cause.** The ledger converts validity bounds to time only within its stability window. That is about 36 hours on
mainnet but only minutes on a local devnet, so a 10-minute TTL (the runtime's default) is past the horizon.

**Fix.** Keep the TTL short on DevKit:
- Java: `StateRuntime.Builder.ttl(Duration.ofSeconds(20))`, as `examples/devkit`'s `DevKit` helper does;
- pages: the runtime uses 20 seconds on a DevKit network (one with an admin API) and 180 seconds elsewhere; set
  `dev.ttlMs` in `joust.config.json` to change it.

###### "DevKit: the faucet is dry and no genesis account can pay ... lovelace"

**Cause.** The DevKit faucet ran dry, and the fallback, the genesis accounts of the default mnemonic (20 base
addresses with 10,000 ADA each), cannot pay either.

**Fix.** The top-up helpers (`DevKit.topUp` in Java, `devkitTopUp` in JavaScript) already fall back to the genesis
accounts. If both are empty, start a fresh DevKit chain.

###### Registering a stake credential fails with "already registered"

**Cause.** Yaci Store cannot tell whether a stake credential is registered: it answers alike for registered and
unknown ones. So the registration is attempted, and the ledger refuses it the second time.

**Fix.** Nothing, if you use the runtime: it treats the ledger's "already registered" refusal
(`StakeKeyRegistered`, `StakeKeyAlreadyRegistered`) as success. Do the same in your own code. Blockfrost reports the
status, so there the registration is skipped.

###### Staking rewards are zero in a test

**Cause.** DevKit pays rewards only across epochs, and a test runs within one.

**Fix.** Expect a zero balance when a staking flow collects within a test. See
[Staking and governance](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/staking-and-governance/).

##### Next steps

- [Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/)
- [Security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/)
- [Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/)
- [Glossary](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/glossary/)

### Glossary

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/reference/glossary/

Short definitions of the Cardano terms JOUST builds on and the JOUST terms the docs use. Each entry links to the page
that covers it in depth.

##### A–C

###### ADA, lovelace and tADA

ADA is Cardano's currency. **Lovelace** is its smallest unit: 1 ADA = 1,000,000 lovelace. Contract code counts in
lovelace (`BigInteger`). **tADA** is test ADA on a test network (preview, Yaci DevKit), with no value.

###### Anchor

In a [keyed object](#keyed-object) list, the node an insert goes after: the greatest key below the new one (the list's
head at least). The insert spends it and relinks it to the new key. See [Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/).

###### Attack suite

`Attacks` in `julc-state-testkit`: for every transaction a test accepts, it applies every applicable mutation (a
replaced datum, a lovelace skimmed, a required signer missing, two thread tokens minted, ...) and requires the validator to reject each
one (ADR-0001 D16). See [Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/).

###### Batcher

Anyone who collects pending [intents](#intent) and applies them to an instance in one transaction (ADR-0004). The
batcher is permissionless: the validator checks each intent's effect, so the batcher cannot cheat. See
[Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/).

###### Blockfrost

A hosted Cardano chain API. JOUST reads the chain through Blockfrost-style APIs: Blockfrost itself (for preview,
with a project id from `BLOCKFROST_PREVIEW_PROJECT_ID`) or Yaci Store's compatible API on DevKit. See
[Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/).

###### ByAction

The mint redeemer a contract uses to mint or burn its own user tokens (LP tokens, NFTs) during an action. It names the
input being spent (`by`), so the mint is valid only together with that call (ADR-0007). See
[Native assets, mints and sends](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/).

###### CCL (cardano-client-lib)

The Java library for Cardano transactions JOUST's off-chain runtime builds on (QuickTx, addresses, CBOR). A JOUST
release brings the version it was built with (`gradle/libs.versions.toml` at its tag). See
[Java off-chain runtime](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/java-runtime/).

###### CIP-30

The browser-wallet standard (Eternl, Lace, ...). A page asks the wallet for its addresses and UTxOs, and to sign
(`signTx`) and submit a transaction. JOUST pages verify every transaction before the wallet is asked to sign. See
[Wallets](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/).

###### CIP-57

The Plutus blueprint standard: a JSON document typing a script's datum and redeemers. A JOUST
[description](#description) is a CIP-57 document with an extra `x-joust` key. See
[Contract description](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/description-format/).

###### Collateral

Lovelace a transaction with scripts puts up, taken only if a script fails during validation. The runtime adds it;
the page verifier checks it. See [Fees and script size](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/).

###### Compose

The runtime's way to put several contracts' calls into one transaction (ADR-0011), for example a purchase that reads
an oracle and a post to that oracle. `Compose.prepare()` builds the transaction for a wallet to sign. See
[Reads and composition](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/reads-and-composition/).

###### Ctx

The record of transaction facts a contract method may read: `caller`, `received`, `balance`, `validFrom`, `validTo`.
The client supplies it and the generated validator checks every field against the transaction. See
[Ctx, funds and payouts](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/).

##### D–I

###### Datum

The data attached to a UTxO at a script address. A JOUST instance's datum is its state record. See
[State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/).

###### Deployment

A contract published to a network: its applied script hash (policy), address and reference-script UTxOs. `joust deploy`
writes them to `deployments.<network>.json`; they are not part of the description. See
[The joust CLI and projects](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/cli-and-projects/).

###### Deposit

A payment from one contract call into another JOUST instance, taken in by a `@Receives` action in the same composed
transaction (ADR-0011 D3). See [Deposits](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/deposits/).

###### Description

The JSON document the processor writes for each contract (`META-INF/joust/<package>.<Contract>.json`): CIP-57 plus
`x-joust`, version 2. Clients encode calls, decode state and verify transactions from it. See
[Contract description](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/description-format/).

###### Designated input

One ordinary (ADA-only) UTxO of the wallet that every attempt of a keyed operation spends, first attempt and retries
alike, so at most one attempt can ever land. A page records it in IndexedDB, so a retry after a reload must spend it
too. See [Keyed objects in JavaScript](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/keyed-objects-js/#retries-that-survive-a-reload).

###### Double satisfaction

An attack where one output is counted as paying two obligations in the same transaction. JOUST tags payouts with the
instance they come from, and claims sends in a shared output registry, so no output counts twice. See
[Security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/).

###### Engine

The JOUST runtime compiled to WebAssembly (GraalVM [Web Image](#web-image)), shipped in `@julclang/joust-runtime`. It
prepares transactions in Node or in a page's worker, as a pure function of a call request and a chain snapshot: all
I/O stays in JavaScript (ADR-0015 D5). A second engine, the toolchain, compiles contracts in Node for `joust build`.
See [@julclang/joust-runtime](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/joust-runtime/).

###### Governor

A plain JuLC validator, used as a withdraw-zero script, whose approval an `@AuthorizedBy` method requires. A call it
approves withdraws zero from its stake credential with an `Approvals` redeemer naming exactly that call (ADR-0009 D3).
See [Authorization](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/authorization/).

###### Harness

`StateHarness` in `julc-state-testkit`: evaluates the compiled validator against transactions shaped like the
runtime's, without a network, and reports the budget. See [Testing](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/testing/).

###### Holding

The datum of an [owned object](#owned-object): the owning instance's id and the owned record. With several owned types
each has its own `Holding_<Type>` (ADR-0012). See [Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/).

###### Inline datum

A datum stored in the output itself rather than by hash. JOUST state is always an inline datum, written as canonical
CBOR (map keys sorted). See [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/).

###### Instance

One deployed copy of a contract's state: a UTxO at the contract's script address holding the instance's
[thread token](#thread-token) and the state as its inline datum. One contract type (one script) has many instances.
See [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/).

###### Intent

A request a user locks at the contract's address for a `@Batched` action: the call, its payment, a refund address and
a deadline. Its token is 29 bytes starting `0x49`. A [batcher](#batcher) applies it; the owner can cancel it. See
[Batched intents](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/batched-intents/).

##### J–O

###### .jsc

JOUST's compact contract language, lowered to a Java `@StateContract` at build time (ADR-0005). See
[.jsc](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/jsc/).

###### JuLC

The Java to UPLC compiler JOUST builds on (julc.dev). It compiles the generated validator, and the transition programs,
from a subset of Java. See [Java](https://joust.julc.dev/languages/java/).

###### Keyed object

An [owned object](#owned-object) with a key (`@Owned(key = "...")`): at most one per key and instance, each its own
UTxO with a 29-byte token starting `0x4B`, kept in a sorted on-chain list whose neighbours prove uniqueness (ADR-0016).
See [Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/).

###### MapVerifier

The shared withdraw-zero script (`julc-state-verifier`) that checks every [MerkleMap](#merklemap) claim in a
transaction: each read and write proven against the old root, leading to the new root (ADR-0002 D9). Published and
registered once per network. See [MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/).

###### MerkleMap

A state component holding an unbounded key-value map as a 32-byte [root](#root). Calls carry proofs of the keys they
read and write. See [MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/).

###### Min-ADA

The lovelace every output must hold, which grows with its size. Each state UTxO keeps `@StateContract(minAda)`
lovelace for it. See [Ctx, funds and payouts](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/).

###### Minting policy

A script that decides when tokens under its policy id may be minted or burned. A JOUST contract's validator is also
its minting policy: it mints the thread token when an instance is created and burns it when the instance is
destroyed. See [How JOUST works](https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/).

###### Mirror

The off-chain copy of a MerkleMap (an MPF trie) that answers the proofs a call needs. The JVM keeps it in RocksDB
(`./.joust/mpf`), a page in IndexedDB; a missing map is rebuilt from the chain's history, every claim checked
against its root. See [MerkleMap mirrors](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/map-mirrors/).

###### MPF (Merkle Patricia Forestry)

The authenticated trie behind MerkleMaps, with Aiken's on-chain format: a 32-byte root and compact membership and
non-membership proofs. See [MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/).

###### Ogmios

A JSON interface to a Cardano node. `@julclang/state-client` has an Ogmios chain provider beside the Blockfrost one.
See [Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/).

###### Output verifier

The shared withdraw-zero script that checks the output-claim registry: each `Send` claims one output, so no output
counts for two obligations (ADR-0007 D5). See [Native assets, mints and sends](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/).

###### Owned object

A per-user UTxO beside an instance (`@Owned` record), with its own 29-byte token starting `0x4F`. Users act on their
own objects in parallel, reading the shared state by reference (ADR-0003, ADR-0012). See
[Owned objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/owned-objects/).

##### P–S

###### Page

A browser app over JOUST contracts: it calls typed clients, prepares transactions in a worker (the engine) or through
a service, verifies them, and has a CIP-30 wallet sign. See [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/).

###### Page verifier

The checks a page runs on a prepared transaction before the wallet signs it (`verifyPrepared` and its relatives in
`@julclang/state-client`): exactly the call asked for, only the wallet's and the target's inputs, the right redeemers
and mint, a balanced transaction, a bounded outflow and a short validity window. A malicious service cannot get
anything else signed. See [JavaScript clients](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/javascript-clients/).

###### Payout

`Payout(to, lovelace)`: lovelace a call pays to a key, returned by an action or destroy (`Payouts.of(...)`). The
validator requires a matching output, tagged against double satisfaction. See
[Ctx, funds and payouts](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/ctx-and-funds/).

###### Prepare service

A server that builds a transaction for a wallet address without holding its keys: `julc-state-server` over HTTP
(`/api/prepare`), or the engine at `/joust/service` under `joust dev`. The page trusts it with nothing and verifies its
result. See [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/).

###### Redeemer

The argument given to a script when a transaction spends, mints or withdraws through it. In JOUST the redeemer names
the call and carries its arguments (and `Ctx`); the client builds it. See [How JOUST works](https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/).

###### Reference script

A script stored in a UTxO that transactions read instead of carrying it, which keeps them small and cheap. Every JOUST
contract reads its script by reference; the first deploy of a contract type publishes it. See
[Fees and script size](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/fees-and-size/).

###### Require

`Require.that(cond, "msg")`: the contract's way to refuse a call. On the JVM it throws `RequireException` with the
message; on chain it traces the message and fails. See [Require and errors](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/require-and-errors/).

###### Retire

A keyed object's exit that needs no neighbour (`@OwnedDestroy(retire = true)`): the owner takes everything but the
deposit, and the object stays in the list as a retired node, so its key is taken for good. See
[Keyed objects](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/keyed-objects/).

###### Root

The 32-byte hash that stands for a whole MerkleMap in the state. A call's proofs lead from the old root to the new one.
See [MerkleMaps](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/merklemaps/).

###### Script purpose

Why a script runs: spending a UTxO, minting, withdrawing rewards, certifying, voting or proposing. JOUST methods use
spend and mint; `@Withdraw`, `@Certify`, `@Votes` and `@Propose` handle the others (ADR-0010). See
[Staking and governance](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/staking-and-governance/).

###### Seed

The input a creation spends whose reference (`txId`, `index`) makes the new token name unique: the instance, object
or intent id is a hash of it. See [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/).

###### Send

`Send(to, value, datum)`: an output a call sends to any address, key or script, with any datum and native assets
(ADR-0007). See [Native assets, mints and sends](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/assets-mints-sends/).

###### SRI (Subresource Integrity)

The browser check that a fetched file matches a hash. A built page pins the engine's sha384 hashes, and the worker
fetches the engine's script and Wasm with them, so a browser refuses an engine whose bytes differ, wherever it is
served from. See [Pages](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/pages/).

###### State

The record a contract keeps, stored as the instance's inline datum. Contract methods take it and return the next
one. See [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/).

###### State IR

The processor's internal model of a contract (`ContractIR`), between reading the source and generating the validator,
client and description. It is what makes several surface languages and storage strategies possible. See
[How JOUST works](https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/).

##### T–Z

###### Thread token

The token that marks an instance's state UTxO: minted once when the instance is created (one-shot, from the
[seed](#seed)), carried by every continuing output, burned on destroy. Its name is 32 bytes. A UTxO without it is not
the instance. See [Security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/).

###### Transition program

A contract method compiled on its own to UPLC, which the engine runs (in JuLC's VM) to compute the next state where
the contract's Java classes do not exist (ADR-0015 D3). See [@julclang/joust-runtime](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/joust-runtime/).

###### TTL and validity interval

A transaction's validity interval is the time range in which it may be included; the TTL is its upper bound. `Ctx`'s
`validFrom` and `validTo` are that interval, which the contract treats as "now". On DevKit keep it short, or the node
answers PastHorizon (see [Troubleshooting](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/troubleshooting/#pasthorizon)). See [Time](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/time/).

###### UPLC

Untyped Plutus Core, the language Cardano's script interpreter runs. JuLC compiles the generated validator to UPLC
(Plutus V3).

###### UTxO

An unspent transaction output: an address, a value (ADA and native assets) and optionally a datum. Cardano has no
accounts: a transaction spends UTxOs and creates new ones. A JOUST instance is a UTxO whose datum is the state. See
[How JOUST works](https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/).

###### Validator

The script that decides whether a UTxO at its address may be spent (and, in JOUST, whether tokens may be minted). The
processor generates `<Name>Validator`, which re-runs your method on chain and checks the result. See
[How JOUST works](https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/).

###### View

A `@View` method: reads the state off chain, with no transaction. See [State and lifecycle](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/state-and-lifecycle/).

###### WalletAccount

An address-only account for the Java runtime: it has no keys, so the transaction is prepared (`Compose.prepare()`) for
a wallet to sign (ADR-0013). See [Wallets](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/wallets/).

###### Web Image

GraalVM's compilation of Java to WebAssembly plus JavaScript, which builds the two engines. Developers never need
GraalVM; only the engines' builds do. See [Status and roadmap](https://joust.julc.dev/project/status-and-roadmap/).

###### Withdraw-zero

A pattern that runs a script once per transaction: the transaction withdraws zero rewards from the script's stake
credential, which makes the script run with the whole transaction in view. JOUST's MapVerifier, output verifier and
governors use it. See [Security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/).

###### Yaci DevKit

A local Cardano network for development: `yaci-devkit up --enable-yaci-store`. It has a faucet and a time horizon of
minutes. See [Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/).

###### Yaci Store

The indexer that runs with DevKit and serves a Blockfrost-compatible API on `:8080` (the admin API is on `:10000`).
Yaci Viewer, the explorer, is on `:5173`. See [Networks and chain providers](https://joust.julc.dev/apps/networks-and-providers/).

##### Next steps

- [How JOUST works](https://joust.julc.dev/start/how-it-works/)
- [Troubleshooting](https://joust.julc.dev/reference/troubleshooting/)

## AI

### Using JOUST with AI

URL: https://joust.julc.dev/ai/

JOUST is newer than the training data of today's models, so an AI agent knows nothing about it. Left alone, it writes
code that looks like plain Java, Plutus or Solidity and does not compile. This site publishes the context an agent
needs, generated from the repository at build time, so it stays in step with the code.

##### TL;DR

Give your agent the [AI starter pack](https://joust.julc.dev/ai/starter-pack/) before it writes any JOUST code. For questions beyond it, add
the full documentation dump.

| File | What it holds | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| [`/ai/starter-pack.md`](https://joust.julc.dev/ai/starter-pack/) | The rules, idioms, canonical contracts, anti-patterns and an error-to-fix table, as raw markdown | Always. It is written for machine ingestion: dense, explicit and imperative |
| [`/llms.txt`](https://joust.julc.dev/llms.txt) | A curated index ([llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/) convention): what JOUST is, the key rules, every page with its summary | For agents that browse: it tells them which page to fetch |
| [`/llms-full.txt`](https://joust.julc.dev/llms-full.txt) | Every page of this site in sidebar order, as one markdown file | For long-lived projects and full coverage (guides, reference, tutorials) |
| [`/ai/catalog.json`](https://joust.julc.dev/ai/catalog.json) | Every annotation of `julc-state-api` (targets, elements, defaults, Javadoc), every example, the npm packages and the CLI commands | For tools and agents that want structured data instead of prose |
| `/ai/index.md` | This page as raw markdown | When you paste setup instructions into a tool |

`catalog.json` is built from the annotation sources in `julc-state-api` and from the table in `examples/README.md`, so
an annotation element the agent finds there exists in the code.

##### Per-tool setup

###### Claude Code

Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` at the start of every session. Put the starter pack in your project:

```sh
curl -o CLAUDE.md https://joust.julc.dev/ai/starter-pack.md
```

If your project already has a `CLAUDE.md`, keep it and add a short section instead, so the agent fetches the pack when
it needs it:

```md title="CLAUDE.md"
##### JOUST
This project writes Cardano contracts with JOUST (a @StateContract in Java, or .jsc).
Before writing or changing contract code, read https://joust.julc.dev/ai/starter-pack.md and follow it strictly:
- contract code is the JuLC subset of Java: BigInteger (never int/long), records, immutable locals,
  Require.that(cond, "msg"), ByteStringLib.equals for byte[] (never == or .equals);
- state maps: SortedMaps (inline) or MerkleMap (only as a direct state component, through MerkleMaps helpers);
- after every change run the build and the tests (./gradlew build, or npx joust build && npm test).
For anything the pack does not cover, look it up in https://joust.julc.dev/llms-full.txt.
```

For all your projects at once, add one line to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`:

```md
When working in a JOUST project, follow the rules at https://joust.julc.dev/ai/starter-pack.md
```

###### ChatGPT, Claude.ai and other chat assistants

For a project (a Claude project, a custom GPT), attach `starter-pack.md` and `llms-full.txt` as project files. For a
one-off conversation, paste the recommended prompt below.

###### Codex, Aider and other coding agents

Most agents have a project context file (an `AGENTS.md`, a conventions file, an "always include" list). Put
`https://joust.julc.dev/ai/starter-pack.md` there, or download it into the repository and point the tool at the file.

##### Working without an MCP server

JOUST has no MCP server. You do not need one: the feedback loop is your build, which an agent with a shell can run
itself. The annotation processor rejects a malformed contract at compile time with a message that names the rule (and
usually the ADR behind it), the tests run your methods on the JVM, and the harness runs the compiled validator. Tell
the agent to run those after each change and to read the messages: they are written to be acted on.

| Path | The agent runs | What it catches |
|---|---|---|
| Java and Gradle | `./gradlew build` | Shape errors from the processor (`@Init must return the state record`), the numeric lint (`int`/`long` in a contract), JuLC compile errors, failing tests |
| npm | `npx joust build`, then `npm test` | The same checks, through the Wasm toolchain (no JDK), then calls on Yaci DevKit |

##### A recommended prompt

Paste this at the start of a conversation, then describe your contract:

```text
I am writing a Cardano smart contract with JOUST (State Contract Simplified). A contract is a
@StateContract class: a state record plus public static @Init/@Action/@Destroy/@View methods.
The same method runs off chain (to build the transaction) and on chain (compiled by JuLC,
where the generated validator checks the output datum equals its result).

Read the JOUST AI starter pack at https://joust.julc.dev/ai/starter-pack.md and follow it
strictly. In particular:
- Contract code is the JuLC subset of Java: BigInteger only (no int, long, double), records
  and sealed interfaces, no generic records, immutable locals, no exceptions, no null.
- Rules are Require.that(condition, "message"). Compare byte[] with ByteStringLib.equals.
- An @Action returns the state, or a record with 'state' and any of payouts, sends, mint,
  accepted, events, deposits. A @Destroy returns JulcList<Payout> (or such a record without
  'state') and takes Ctx. Ctx is the last parameter (Funds after it, if any).
- Maps in the state: SortedMaps for small inline maps; MerkleMap (via MerkleMaps helpers)
  for unbounded ones, only as a direct component of the state record.
- Use only annotations and classes that exist in org.julclang.state.api; if unsure, say so
  instead of inventing one.

Contract to write: <describe the state, who may do what, and when>.
Then write JVM unit tests for each method and, if the project has julc-state-testkit,
StateHarness tests that run the compiled validator with Attacks.assertAllRejected.
```

##### Verify what the agent writes

An agent's code that compiles is not yet a correct contract. Check it the way the examples are checked, from cheapest
to most realistic.

1. **Build.** `./gradlew build` (or `npx joust build`). The processor enforces the contract's shape and the subset
   rules. A warning matters too: "this @StateContract has no @Destroy method" means every instance locks its min-ADA
   deposit forever.

2. **Run the methods on the JVM.** They are plain static methods: call them with a `Ctx` and assert on the state, and
   on the `RequireException` message for each rule. This is where you check the business logic.

3. **Run the compiled validator.** `StateHarness` (from `julc-state-testkit`) evaluates the validator the build
   produced against transactions shaped like the runtime's, and `Attacks.assertAllRejected(h, tx)` mutates each
   accepted transaction (the datum replaced, token dust added, a payout under-paid or paid to someone else, the
   required signer missing, the thread token sent to a key address, the validity range widened, and more) and requires
   every applicable mutation to fail. Ask for a harness test per action, and for a rejected case per rule.

4. **Run it on Yaci DevKit.** The generated client (Java) or typed client (JavaScript) builds, submits and confirms
   real transactions on a local network. The examples tag these tests `devnet`; they are skipped when DevKit is not
   running.

5. **Read the rules yourself.** Ask: who can call each method (`@OnlyOwner`, `@SignedBy`, a check on `ctx.caller()`)?
   What stops a payout larger than the balance? Can every instance and owned object be closed? The
   [security model](https://joust.julc.dev/contracts/security-model/) lists what the generated validator checks for you and what remains
   your contract's job.

> **Caution:** 
JOUST is experimental and pre-release: its releases are in the BloxBean release repository and on npmjs.org, and
nothing is on Maven Central. An agent that "remembers" a version or a registry is guessing: take the version from the newest release
whose tag starts with `v` on the [releases page](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/releases) (or
`npm view @julclang/joust version`), and the setup from the
[Java quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-java/) or the [npm quick start](https://joust.julc.dev/start/quick-start-npm/).

##### Why this works

The starter pack gives an agent, in one read, what it cannot infer from Java alone: the subset JuLC compiles, the shape
rules the processor enforces, the reason the JVM and on-chain runs must agree (and the traps where they would not, such
as `byte[]` equality and fixed-width numbers), and complete examples taken from the tested contracts in `examples/`.
The processor's error messages close the loop: they name the rule that was broken, so the agent can fix its own code.

If an agent keeps getting a pattern wrong, [open an issue](https://github.com/bloxbean/joust/issues): the failure
probably belongs in the starter pack.
